The Lord’s servant flees youthful passions, refuses foolish controversies, and corrects opponents with gentleness, hoping God may grant repentance and escape from the devil’s snare. Now in a large house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of clay. Some are for honor and some for dishonor. 2 Timothy 2:20 If anyone therefore purges himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, and suitable for the master’s use, prepared for every good work. 2 Timothy 2:21 Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart. 2 Timothy 2:22 But refuse foolish and ignorant questionings, knowing that they generate strife. 2 Timothy 2:23 The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient, 2 Timothy 2:24 in gentleness correcting those who oppose him. Perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth, 2 Timothy 2:25 and they may recover themselves out of the devil’s snare, having been taken captive by him to do his will. 2 Timothy 2:26

title: 2 Timothy 2:8–13
context: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the offspring of David: Paul is bound, but the word of God is not. He endures everything for the chosen ones’ sake, that they may obtain salvation, and seals the charge with a trustworthy saying about dying, enduring, denying, and the Lord’s faithfulness.
text: 2 Timothy 2:8–13 2 Timothy Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the offspring of David: Paul is bound, but the word of God is not. He endures everything for the chosen ones’ sake, that they may obtain salvation, and seals the charge with a trustworthy saying about dying, enduring, denying, and the Lord’s faithfulness. Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the offspring of David, according to my Good News, 2 Timothy 2:8 in which I suffer hardship to the point of chains as a criminal. But God’s word isn’t chained. 2 Timothy 2:9 Therefore I endure all things for the chosen ones’ sake, that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory. 2 Timothy 2:10 This saying is trustworthy: “For if we died with him, we will also live with him. 2 Timothy 2:11 If we endure, we will also reign with him. If we deny him, he also will deny us. 2 Timothy 2:12 If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself.” 2 Timothy 2:13

title: 2 Timothy 3:1–9
context: Paul warns Timothy that last-days difficulty will rise inside the church: people will love self and pleasure more than God, keeping a form of godliness while denying its power. Some will capture the unstable, always learning yet never arriving at the truth—opposing it as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses—yet their folly will not stay hidden.
text: 2 Timothy 3:1–9 2 Timothy Paul warns Timothy that last-days difficulty will rise inside the church: people will love self and pleasure more than God, keeping a form of godliness while denying its power. Some will capture the unstable, always learning yet never arriving at the truth—opposing it as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses—yet their folly will not stay hidden. But know this: that in the last days, grievous times will come. 2 Timothy 3:1 For men will be lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, 2 Timothy 3:2 without natural affection, unforgiving, slanderers, without self-control, fierce, not lovers of good, 2 Timothy 3:3 traitors, headstrong, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, 2 Timothy 3:4 holding a form of godliness but having denied its power. Turn away from these, also. 2 Timothy 3:5 For some of these are people who creep into houses and take captive gullible women loaded down with sins, led away by various lusts, 2 Timothy 3:6 always learning and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth. 2 Timothy 3:7 Even as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind, who concerning the faith are rejected. 2 Timothy 3:8 But they will proceed no further. For their folly will be evident to all men, as theirs also came to be. 2 Timothy 3:9

title: 2 Timothy 3:10–17
context: Timothy is set over against the impostors: he has followed Paul’s teaching, conduct, faith, love, and sufferings, and the Lord rescued Paul from them all. All who desire a godly life in Christ will suffer persecution. But evil men go from bad to worse. Timothy must continue in what he learned; the sacred writings are able to make him wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus, and all Scripture is God-breathed—profitable so that each person who belongs to God may be complete.
text: 2 Timothy 3:10–17 2 Timothy Timothy is set over against the impostors: he has followed Paul’s teaching, conduct, faith, love, and sufferings, and the Lord rescued Paul from them all. All who desire a godly life in Christ will suffer persecution. But evil men go from bad to worse. Timothy must continue in what he learned; the sacred writings are able to make him wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus, and all Scripture is God-breathed—profitable so that each person who belongs to God may be complete. But you followed my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love, steadfastness, 2 Timothy 3:10 persecutions, and sufferings—those things that happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. I endured those persecutions. The Lord delivered me out of them all. 2 Timothy 3:11 Yes, and all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution. 2 Timothy 3:12 But evil men and impostors will grow worse and worse, deceiving and being deceived. 2 Timothy 3:13 But you remain in the things which you have learned and have been assured of, knowing from whom you have learned them. 2 Timothy 3:14 From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. 2 Timothy 3:15 Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, 2 Timothy 3:16 that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work. 2 Timothy 3:17

title: 2 Timothy 4:1–8
context: Paul charges Timothy before God and Christ Jesus, the coming Judge: preach the word in season and out, with patience and teaching, because they will not listen to the sound doctrine. Timothy must stay sober in all things, suffer hardship, do an evangelist’s work, and fulfill his ministry. Paul is already poured out; he has fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith—and a crown of righteousness awaits him and all who have loved the Lord’s appearing.
text: 2 Timothy 4:1–8 2 Timothy Paul charges Timothy before God and Christ Jesus, the coming Judge: preach the word in season and out, with patience and teaching, because they will not listen to the sound doctrine. Timothy must stay sober in all things, suffer hardship, do an evangelist’s work, and fulfill his ministry. Paul is already poured out; he has fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith—and a crown of righteousness awaits him and all who have loved the Lord’s appearing. I command you therefore before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead at his appearing and his Kingdom: 2 Timothy 4:1 preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort with all patience and teaching. 2 Timothy 4:2 For the time will come when they will not listen to the sound doctrine, but having itching ears, will heap up for themselves teachers after their own lusts, 2 Timothy 4:3 and will turn away their ears from the truth, and turn away to fables. 2 Timothy 4:4 But you be sober in all things, suffer hardship, do the work of an evangelist, and fulfill your ministry. 2 Timothy 4:5 For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure has come. 2 Timothy 4:6 I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith. 2 Timothy 4:7 From now on, the crown of righteousness is stored up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give to me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all those who have loved his appearing. 2 Timothy 4:8

title: 2 Timothy 4:16–22
context: At Paul’s first defense no one stood by him; all deserted, and he asks that it not be held against them. The Lord stood by him and strengthened him so the message was fully proclaimed to the Gentiles, and he was delivered out of the mouth. He trusts the Lord to rescue him from every evil work and bring him safely into the heavenly kingdom. Greetings follow—Prisca, Aquila, Onesiphorus’s household—and a last plea to come before winter, with grace.
text: 2 Timothy 4:16–22 2 Timothy At Paul’s first defense no one stood by him; all deserted, and he asks that it not be held against them. The Lord stood by him and strengthened him so the message was fully proclaimed to the Gentiles, and he was delivered out of the mouth. He trusts the Lord to rescue him from every evil work and bring him safely into the heavenly kingdom. Greetings follow—Prisca, Aquila, Onesiphorus’s household—and a last plea to come before winter, with grace. At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me. May it not be held against them. 2 Timothy 4:16 But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, that through me the message might be fully proclaimed, and that all the Gentiles might hear. So I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion. 2 Timothy 4:17 And the Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will preserve me for his heavenly Kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen. 2 Timothy 4:18 Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the house of Onesiphorus. 2 Timothy 4:19 Erastus remained at Corinth, but I left Trophimus at Miletus sick. 2 Timothy 4:20 Be diligent to come before winter. Eubulus salutes you, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers. 2 Timothy 4:21 The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen. 2 Timothy 4:22

title: 2 Timothy 4:9–15
context: Paul turns to personal need: come soon. Demas left me, having loved this present world, has deserted him; Crescens and Titus are away; Luke alone remains. Mark, once a departure story himself, is now useful—bring him. Tychicus has been sent to Ephesus. Bring the cloak, the books, and especially the parchments; Alexander the coppersmith did great harm and opposed the message, the Lord will repay him, and Timothy must beware.
text: 2 Timothy 4:9–15 2 Timothy Paul turns to personal need: come soon. Demas left me, having loved this present world, has deserted him; Crescens and Titus are away; Luke alone remains. Mark, once a departure story himself, is now useful—bring him. Tychicus has been sent to Ephesus. Bring the cloak, the books, and especially the parchments; Alexander the coppersmith did great harm and opposed the message, the Lord will repay him, and Timothy must beware. Be diligent to come to me soon, 2 Timothy 4:9 for Demas left me, having loved this present world, and went to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia; and Titus to Dalmatia. 2 Timothy 4:10 Only Luke is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service. 2 Timothy 4:11 But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus. 2 Timothy 4:12 Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come—and the books, especially the parchments. 2 Timothy 4:13 Alexander the coppersmith did much evil to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. 2 Timothy 4:14 Beware of him, for he greatly opposed our words. 2 Timothy 4:15

title: 3 John 1:1–8
context: The elder writes to Gaius the beloved, whom he loves in truth: prayer that body and affairs would match a prospering soul; joy that the brothers testified to Gaius’s walking in the truth; then praise for faithful work toward traveling brothers—strangers who have gone out for the Name, taking nothing from the Gentiles—so that those who send them are fellow workers for the truth.
text: 3 John 1:1–8 3 John The elder writes to Gaius the beloved, whom he loves in truth: prayer that body and affairs would match a prospering soul; joy that the brothers testified to Gaius’s walking in the truth; then praise for faithful work toward traveling brothers—strangers who have gone out for the Name, taking nothing from the Gentiles—so that those who send them are fellow workers for the truth. The elder to Gaius the beloved, whom I love in truth. 3 John 1:1 Beloved, I pray that you may prosper in all things and be healthy, even as your soul prospers. 3 John 1:2 For I rejoiced greatly when brothers came and testified about your truth, even as you walk in truth. 3 John 1:3 I have no greater joy than this: to hear about my children walking in truth. 3 John 1:4 Beloved, you do a faithful work in whatever you accomplish for those who are brothers and strangers. 3 John 1:5 They have testified about your love before the assembly. You will do well to send them forward on their journey in a way worthy of God, 3 John 1:6 because for the sake of the Name they went out, taking nothing from the Gentiles. 3 John 1:7 We therefore ought to receive such, that we may be fellow workers for the truth. 3 John 1:8

title: 3 John 1:9–15
context: The elder had written to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not acknowledge apostolic authority: wicked nonsense, refusal to welcome the brothers, stopping those who would, putting them out. Gaius is told not to imitate evil but good. He who does good is of God. He who does evil hasn’t seen God. Demetrius has a good testimony of all, and of the truth. Then pen and ink yield to the hope of face-to-face speech, peace, and friends greeted by name.
text: 3 John 1:9–15 3 John The elder had written to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not acknowledge apostolic authority: wicked nonsense, refusal to welcome the brothers, stopping those who would, putting them out. Gaius is told not to imitate evil but good. He who does good is of God. He who does evil hasn’t seen God. Demetrius has a good testimony of all, and of the truth. Then pen and ink yield to the hope of face-to-face speech, peace, and friends greeted by name. I wrote to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, doesn’t accept what we say. 3 John 1:9 Therefore, if I come, I will call attention to his deeds which he does, unjustly accusing us with wicked words. Not content with this, he doesn’t receive the brothers himself, and those who would, he forbids and throws out of the assembly. 3 John 1:10 Beloved, don’t imitate that which is evil, but that which is good. He who does good is of God. He who does evil hasn’t seen God. 3 John 1:11 Demetrius has the testimony of all, and of the truth itself; yes, we also testify, and you know that our testimony is true. 3 John 1:12 I had many things to write to you, but I am unwilling to write to you with ink and pen; 3 John 1:13 but I hope to see you soon. Then we will speak face to face. 3 John 1:14 Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends by name. 3 John 1:15

title: Acts 1:1–11
context: Luke opens his second volume to Theophilus by recalling the first, which told what Jesus began to do and teach. For forty days the risen Jesus showed himself alive and spoke about God’s kingdom, then told the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit. When they asked about restoring the kingdom to Israel, he turned them to their mission as witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. He was taken up into a cloud, and two men in white promised that he would return in the same way.
text: Acts 1:1–11 Acts Luke opens his second volume to Theophilus by recalling the first, which told what Jesus began to do and teach. For forty days the risen Jesus showed himself alive and spoke about God’s kingdom, then told the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit. When they asked about restoring the kingdom to Israel, he turned them to their mission as witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. He was taken up into a cloud, and two men in white promised that he would return in the same way. The first book I wrote, Theophilus, concerned all that Jesus began both to do and to teach, Acts 1:1 until the day in which he was received up, after he had given commandment through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen. Acts 1:2 To these he also showed himself alive after he suffered, by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days and speaking about God’s Kingdom. Acts 1:3 Being assembled together with them, he commanded them, “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me. Acts 1:4 For John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” Acts 1:5 Therefore, when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?” Acts 1:6 He said to them, “It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority. Acts 1:7 But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” Acts 1:8 When he had said these things, as they were looking, he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight. Acts 1:9 While they were looking steadfastly into the sky as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white clothing, Acts 1:10 who also said, “You men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into the sky? This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky.” Acts 1:11

title: Acts 1:12–26
context: The apostles return to Jerusalem and devote themselves to prayer with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. Peter explains that Judas’s betrayal and death fulfilled Scripture, and that another must take his office. Two candidates who had been with Jesus from John’s baptism to the ascension are put forward; the believers pray, cast lots, and Matthias is added to the eleven.
text: Acts 1:12–26 Acts The apostles return to Jerusalem and devote themselves to prayer with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. Peter explains that Judas’s betrayal and death fulfilled Scripture, and that another must take his office. Two candidates who had been with Jesus from John’s baptism to the ascension are put forward; the believers pray, cast lots, and Matthias is added to the eleven. Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. Acts 1:12 When they had come in, they went up into the upper room where they were staying, that is Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James. Acts 1:13 All these with one accord continued steadfastly in prayer and supplication, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers. Acts 1:14 In these days, Peter stood up in the middle of the disciples (and the number of names was about one hundred twenty), and said, Acts 1:15 “Brothers, it was necessary that this Scripture should be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke before by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who was guide to those who took Jesus. Acts 1:16 For he was counted with us, and received his portion in this ministry. Acts 1:17 Now this man obtained a field with the reward for his wickedness; and falling headlong, his body burst open and all his intestines gushed out. Acts 1:18 It became known to everyone who lived in Jerusalem that in their language that field was called ‘Akeldama,’ that is, ‘The field of blood.’ Acts 1:19 For it is written in the book of Psalms, ‘Let his habitation be made desolate. Let no one dwell in it;’ and, ‘Let another take his office.’ Acts 1:20 “Of the men therefore who have accompanied us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, Acts 1:21 beginning from the baptism of John to the day that he was received up from us, of these one must become a witness with us of his resurrection.” Acts 1:22 They put forward two: Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias. Acts 1:23 They prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all men, show which one of these two you have chosen Acts 1:24 to take part in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas fell away, that he might go to his own place.” Acts 1:25 They drew lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias; and he was counted with the eleven apostles. Acts 1:26

title: Acts 10:1–23
context: Cornelius, a God-fearing Roman centurion in Caesarea who prays and gives generously, sees an angel who tells him to send for Peter in Joppa. The next day, while his messengers are on the way, Peter falls into a trance on a rooftop and sees a sheet full of unclean animals, with a voice telling him to kill and eat; when he refuses, the voice says not to call unclean what God has cleansed. As Peter ponders the vision, the Spirit tells him to go with the men without hesitation, and he hosts them and sets out the following day.
text: Acts 10:1–23 Acts Cornelius, a God-fearing Roman centurion in Caesarea who prays and gives generously, sees an angel who tells him to send for Peter in Joppa. The next day, while his messengers are on the way, Peter falls into a trance on a rooftop and sees a sheet full of unclean animals, with a voice telling him to kill and eat; when he refuses, the voice says not to call unclean what God has cleansed. As Peter ponders the vision, the Spirit tells him to go with the men without hesitation, and he hosts them and sets out the following day. Now there was a certain man in Caesarea, Cornelius by name, a centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment, Acts 10:1 a devout man, and one who feared God with all his house, who gave gifts for the needy generously to the people, and always prayed to God. Acts 10:2 At about the ninth hour of the day, he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God coming to him and saying to him, “Cornelius!” Acts 10:3 He, fastening his eyes on him and being frightened, said, “What is it, Lord?” He said to him, “Your prayers and your gifts to the needy have gone up for a memorial before God. Acts 10:4 Now send men to Joppa, and get Simon, who is also called Peter. Acts 10:5 He is staying with a tanner named Simon, whose house is by the seaside. Acts 10:6 When the angel who spoke to him had departed, Cornelius called two of his household servants and a devout soldier of those who waited on him continually. Acts 10:7 Having explained everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. Acts 10:8 Now on the next day as they were on their journey and got close to the city, Peter went up on the housetop to pray at about noon. Acts 10:9 He became hungry and desired to eat, but while they were preparing, he fell into a trance. Acts 10:10 He saw heaven opened and a certain container descending to him, like a great sheet let down by four corners on the earth, Acts 10:11 in which were all kinds of four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, reptiles, and birds of the sky. Acts 10:12 A voice came to him, “Rise, Peter, kill and eat!” Acts 10:13 But Peter said, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” Acts 10:14 A voice came to him again the second time, “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.” Acts 10:15 This was done three times, and immediately the thing was received up into heaven. Acts 10:16 Now while Peter was very perplexed in himself what the vision which he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood before the gate, Acts 10:17 and called and asked whether Simon, who was also called Peter, was lodging there. Acts 10:18 While Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men seek you. Acts 10:19 But arise, get down, and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them.” Acts 10:20 Peter went down to the men, and said, “Behold, I am he whom you seek. Why have you come?” Acts 10:21 They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, and well spoken of by all the nation of the Jews, was directed by a holy angel to invite you to his house, and to listen to what you say.” Acts 10:22 So he called them in and provided a place to stay. On the next day Peter arose and went out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. Acts 10:23

title: Acts 10:24–48
context: Cornelius has gathered relatives and friends to hear Peter. Peter explains that God has shown him not to call anyone unclean, and Cornelius recounts his vision. Peter declares that God shows no partiality and that in every nation whoever fears him is acceptable. He proclaims Jesus, anointed with the Spirit, crucified, raised, and appointed judge, through whose name everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Spirit falls on the Gentile hearers, who speak in tongues and praise God, and Peter orders them baptized.
text: Acts 10:24–48 Acts Cornelius has gathered relatives and friends to hear Peter. Peter explains that God has shown him not to call anyone unclean, and Cornelius recounts his vision. Peter declares that God shows no partiality and that in every nation whoever fears him is acceptable. He proclaims Jesus, anointed with the Spirit, crucified, raised, and appointed judge, through whose name everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Spirit falls on the Gentile hearers, who speak in tongues and praise God, and Peter orders them baptized. On the next day they entered into Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends. Acts 10:24 When Peter entered, Cornelius met him, fell down at his feet, and worshiped him. Acts 10:25 But Peter raised him up, saying, “Stand up! I myself am also a man.” Acts 10:26 As he talked with him, he went in and found many gathered together. Acts 10:27 He said to them, “You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation, but God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean. Acts 10:28 Therefore I also came without complaint when I was sent for. I ask therefore, why did you send for me?” Acts 10:29 Cornelius said, “Four days ago, I was fasting until this hour; and at the ninth hour, I prayed in my house, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing Acts 10:30 and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer is heard, and your gifts to the needy are remembered in the sight of God. Acts 10:31 Send therefore to Joppa and summon Simon, who is also called Peter. He is staying in the house of a tanner named Simon, by the seaside. When he comes, he will speak to you.’ Acts 10:32 Therefore I sent to you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God to hear all things that have been commanded you by God.” Acts 10:33 Peter opened his mouth and said, “Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism; Acts 10:34 but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him. Acts 10:35 The word which he sent to the children of Israel, preaching good news of peace by Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all— Acts 10:36 you yourselves know what happened, which was proclaimed throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached; Acts 10:37 how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. Acts 10:38 We are witnesses of everything he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem; whom they also killed, hanging him on a tree. Acts 10:39 God raised him up the third day and gave him to be revealed, Acts 10:40 not to all the people, but to witnesses who were chosen before by God, to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. Acts 10:41 He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that this is he who is appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead. Acts 10:42 All the prophets testify about him, that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins.” Acts 10:43 While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word. Acts 10:44 They of the circumcision who believed were amazed, as many as came with Peter, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles. Acts 10:45 For they heard them speaking in other languages and magnifying God. Then Peter answered, Acts 10:46 “Can anyone forbid these people from being baptized with water? They have received the Holy Spirit just like us.” Acts 10:47 He commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay some days. Acts 10:48

title: Acts 11:1–18
context: News reaches Judea that Gentiles have received God’s word, and circumcised believers criticize Peter for eating with uncircumcised men. Peter explains step by step: the vision, the Spirit’s instruction, the angel’s message to Cornelius, and the Spirit falling on the Gentiles as on the apostles at the beginning. If God gave them the same gift, who was Peter to stand in God’s way? The critics fall silent and glorify God, concluding that God has granted the Gentiles repentance to life.
text: Acts 11:1–18 Acts News reaches Judea that Gentiles have received God’s word, and circumcised believers criticize Peter for eating with uncircumcised men. Peter explains step by step: the vision, the Spirit’s instruction, the angel’s message to Cornelius, and the Spirit falling on the Gentiles as on the apostles at the beginning. If God gave them the same gift, who was Peter to stand in God’s way? The critics fall silent and glorify God, concluding that God has granted the Gentiles repentance to life. Now the apostles and the brothers who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles had also received the word of God. Acts 11:1 When Peter had come up to Jerusalem, those who were of the circumcision contended with him, Acts 11:2 saying, “You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them!” Acts 11:3 But Peter began, and explained to them in order, saying, Acts 11:4 “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: a certain container descending, like it was a great sheet let down from heaven by four corners. It came as far as me. Acts 11:5 When I had looked intently at it, I considered, and saw the four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky. Acts 11:6 I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter, kill and eat!’ Acts 11:7 But I said, ‘Not so, Lord, for nothing unholy or unclean has ever entered into my mouth.’ Acts 11:8 But a voice answered me the second time out of heaven, ‘What God has cleansed, don’t you call unclean.’ Acts 11:9 This was done three times, and all were drawn up again into heaven. Acts 11:10 Behold, immediately three men stood before the house where I was, having been sent from Caesarea to me. Acts 11:11 The Spirit told me to go with them without discriminating. These six brothers also accompanied me, and we entered into the man’s house. Acts 11:12 He told us how he had seen the angel standing in his house and saying to him, ‘Send to Joppa and get Simon, who is called Peter, Acts 11:13 who will speak to you words by which you will be saved, you and all your house.’ Acts 11:14 As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, even as on us at the beginning. Acts 11:15 I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said, ‘John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.’ Acts 11:16 If then God gave to them the same gift as us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I, that I could withstand God?” Acts 11:17 When they heard these things, they held their peace and glorified God, saying, “Then God has also granted to the Gentiles repentance to life!” Acts 11:18

title: Acts 11:19–30
context: Believers scattered after Stephen’s death preach as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, at first only to Jews, but some from Cyprus and Cyrene speak to Greeks, and a great number believe. The Jerusalem church sends Barnabas, who rejoices at God’s grace and encourages them, and many more are added. Barnabas brings Saul from Tarsus, and they teach in Antioch for a year, where the disciples are first called Christians. When Agabus predicts a famine, the disciples send relief to Judea through Barnabas and Saul.
text: Acts 11:19–30 Acts Believers scattered after Stephen’s death preach as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, at first only to Jews, but some from Cyprus and Cyrene speak to Greeks, and a great number believe. The Jerusalem church sends Barnabas, who rejoices at God’s grace and encourages them, and many more are added. Barnabas brings Saul from Tarsus, and they teach in Antioch for a year, where the disciples are first called Christians. When Agabus predicts a famine, the disciples send relief to Judea through Barnabas and Saul. They therefore who were scattered abroad by the oppression that arose about Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except to Jews only. Acts 11:19 But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who, when they had come to Antioch, spoke to the Hellenists, preaching the Lord Jesus. Acts 11:20 The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord. Acts 11:21 The report concerning them came to the ears of the assembly which was in Jerusalem. They sent out Barnabas to go as far as Antioch, Acts 11:22 who, when he had come, and had seen the grace of God, was glad. He exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord. Acts 11:23 For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, and many people were added to the Lord. Acts 11:24 Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul. Acts 11:25 When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch. Acts 11:26 Now in these days, prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. Acts 11:27 One of them named Agabus stood up and indicated by the Spirit that there should be a great famine all over the world, which also happened in the days of Claudius. Acts 11:28 As any of the disciples had plenty, each determined to send relief to the brothers who lived in Judea; Acts 11:29 which they also did, sending it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul. Acts 11:30

title: Acts 12:1–25
context: King Herod kills James the brother of John and, seeing that this pleases the Jewish leaders, arrests Peter during the feast, while the church prays earnestly for him. On the night before his trial an angel wakes Peter, his chains fall off, and he walks out past the guards into the city. He goes to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where the servant girl Rhoda is so overjoyed that she leaves him knocking at the gate. Herod executes the guards; later, accepting praise as a god in Caesarea, he is struck by an angel and dies. The word of God continues to grow, and Barnabas and Saul return with John Mark.
text: Acts 12:1–25 Acts King Herod kills James the brother of John and, seeing that this pleases the Jewish leaders, arrests Peter during the feast, while the church prays earnestly for him. On the night before his trial an angel wakes Peter, his chains fall off, and he walks out past the guards into the city. He goes to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where the servant girl Rhoda is so overjoyed that she leaves him knocking at the gate. Herod executes the guards; later, accepting praise as a god in Caesarea, he is struck by an angel and dies. The word of God continues to grow, and Barnabas and Saul return with John Mark. Now about that time, King Herod stretched out his hands to oppress some of the assembly. Acts 12:1 He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword. Acts 12:2 When he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also. This was during the days of unleavened bread. Acts 12:3 When he had arrested him, he put him in prison and delivered him to four squads of four soldiers each to guard him, intending to bring him out to the people after the Passover. Acts 12:4 Peter therefore was kept in the prison, but constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him. Acts 12:5 The same night when Herod was about to bring him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains. Guards in front of the door kept the prison. Acts 12:6 And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him up, saying, “Stand up quickly!” His chains fell off his hands. Acts 12:7 The angel said to him, “Get dressed and put on your sandals.” He did so. He said to him, “Put on your cloak and follow me.” Acts 12:8 And he went out and followed him. He didn’t know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he saw a vision. Acts 12:9 When they were past the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened to them by itself. They went out and went down one street, and immediately the angel departed from him. Acts 12:10 When Peter had come to himself, he said, “Now I truly know that the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from everything the Jewish people were expecting.” Acts 12:11 Thinking about that, he came to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying. Acts 12:12 When Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer. Acts 12:13 When she recognized Peter’s voice, she didn’t open the gate for joy, but ran in and reported that Peter was standing in front of the gate. Acts 12:14 They said to her, “You are crazy!” But she insisted that it was so. They said, “It is his angel.” Acts 12:15 But Peter continued knocking. When they had opened, they saw him and were amazed. Acts 12:16 But he, beckoning to them with his hand to be silent, declared to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. He said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place. Acts 12:17 Now as soon as it was day, there was no small stir among the soldiers about what had become of Peter. Acts 12:18 When Herod had sought for him and didn’t find him, he examined the guards, then commanded that they should be put to death. He went down from Judea to Caesarea, and stayed there. Acts 12:19 Now Herod was very angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came with one accord to him and, having made Blastus, the king’s personal aide, their friend, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food. Acts 12:20 On an appointed day, Herod dressed himself in royal clothing, sat on the throne, and gave a speech to them. Acts 12:21 The people shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” Acts 12:22 Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died. Acts 12:23 But the word of God grew and multiplied. Acts 12:24 Barnabas and Saul returned to Jerusalem when they had fulfilled their service, also taking with them John who was called Mark. Acts 12:25

title: Acts 13:1–12
context: In the church at Antioch, while prophets and teachers worship and fast, the Holy Spirit tells them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which he has called them. After fasting, prayer, and the laying on of hands, they sail to Cyprus with John Mark and preach in the synagogues. At Paphos the proconsul Sergius Paulus wants to hear the word, but the sorcerer Elymas opposes them. Saul, also called Paul, filled with the Spirit, rebukes him and pronounces temporary blindness, and the proconsul believes, astonished at the teaching about the Lord.
text: Acts 13:1–12 Acts In the church at Antioch, while prophets and teachers worship and fast, the Holy Spirit tells them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which he has called them. After fasting, prayer, and the laying on of hands, they sail to Cyprus with John Mark and preach in the synagogues. At Paphos the proconsul Sergius Paulus wants to hear the word, but the sorcerer Elymas opposes them. Saul, also called Paul, filled with the Spirit, rebukes him and pronounces temporary blindness, and the proconsul believes, astonished at the teaching about the Lord. Now in the assembly that was at Antioch there were some prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. Acts 13:1 As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.” Acts 13:2 Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away. Acts 13:3 So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia. From there they sailed to Cyprus. Acts 13:4 When they were at Salamis, they proclaimed God’s word in the Jewish synagogues. They also had John as their attendant. Acts 13:5 When they had gone through the island to Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew whose name was Bar Jesus, Acts 13:6 who was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of understanding. This man summoned Barnabas and Saul, and sought to hear the word of God. Acts 13:7 But Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. Acts 13:8 But Saul, who is also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, fastened his eyes on him Acts 13:9 and said, “You son of the devil, full of all deceit and all cunning, you enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord? Acts 13:10 Now, behold, the hand of the Lord is on you, and you will be blind, not seeing the sun for a season!” Immediately a mist and darkness fell on him. He went around seeking someone to lead him by the hand. Acts 13:11 Then the proconsul, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord. Acts 13:12

title: Acts 13:13–41
context: Paul’s company sails to Perga, where John Mark leaves them, and goes on to Pisidian Antioch. Invited to speak in the synagogue, Paul recounts God’s choosing of Israel, the exodus, the judges, and the kings up to David, from whose offspring God has brought Israel a Savior, Jesus. Though Jerusalem’s rulers condemned him, fulfilling the prophets, God raised him from the dead, as the psalms foretold. Through him forgiveness of sins is proclaimed, and everyone who believes is justified from everything the law of Moses could not justify. Paul ends by warning his hearers not to be the scoffers the prophets described.
text: Acts 13:13–41 Acts Paul’s company sails to Perga, where John Mark leaves them, and goes on to Pisidian Antioch. Invited to speak in the synagogue, Paul recounts God’s choosing of Israel, the exodus, the judges, and the kings up to David, from whose offspring God has brought Israel a Savior, Jesus. Though Jerusalem’s rulers condemned him, fulfilling the prophets, God raised him from the dead, as the psalms foretold. Through him forgiveness of sins is proclaimed, and everyone who believes is justified from everything the law of Moses could not justify. Paul ends by warning his hearers not to be the scoffers the prophets described. Now Paul and his company set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. John departed from them and returned to Jerusalem. Acts 13:13 But they, passing on from Perga, came to Antioch of Pisidia. They went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day and sat down. Acts 13:14 After the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent to them, saying, “Brothers, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, speak.” Acts 13:15 Paul stood up, and gesturing with his hand said, “Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen. Acts 13:16 The God of this people chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they stayed as aliens in the land of Egypt, and with an uplifted arm, he led them out of it. Acts 13:17 For a period of about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. Acts 13:18 When he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land for an inheritance for about four hundred fifty years. Acts 13:19 After these things, he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet. Acts 13:20 Afterward they asked for a king, and God gave to them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. Acts 13:21 When he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, to whom he also testified, ‘I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my heart, who will do all my will.’ Acts 13:22 From this man’s offspring, God has brought salvation to Israel according to his promise, Acts 13:23 before his coming, when John had first preached the baptism of repentance to Israel. Acts 13:24 As John was fulfilling his course, he said, ‘What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. But behold, one comes after me, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.’ Acts 13:25 “Brothers, children of the stock of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, the word of this salvation is sent out to you. Acts 13:26 For those who dwell in Jerusalem, and their rulers, because they didn’t know him, nor the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. Acts 13:27 Though they found no cause for death, they still asked Pilate to have him killed. Acts 13:28 When they had fulfilled all things that were written about him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. Acts 13:29 But God raised him from the dead, Acts 13:30 and he was seen for many days by those who came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses to the people. Acts 13:31 We bring you good news of the promise made to the fathers, Acts 13:32 that God has fulfilled this to us, their children, in that he raised up Jesus. As it is also written in the second psalm, ‘You are my Son. Today I have become your father.’ Acts 13:33 “Concerning that he raised him up from the dead, now no more to return to corruption, he has spoken thus: ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’ Acts 13:34 Therefore he says also in another psalm, ‘You will not allow your Holy One to see decay.’ Acts 13:35 For David, after he had in his own generation served the counsel of God, fell asleep, was laid with his fathers, and saw decay. Acts 13:36 But he whom God raised up saw no decay. Acts 13:37 Be it known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man is proclaimed to you remission of sins; Acts 13:38 and by him everyone who believes is justified from all things, from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses. Acts 13:39 Beware therefore, lest that come on you which is spoken in the prophets: Acts 13:40 ‘Behold, you scoffers! Wonder and perish, for I work a work in your days, a work which you will in no way believe, if one declares it to you.’” Acts 13:41

title: Acts 13:42–52
context: The people beg Paul and Barnabas to speak again the next Sabbath, and many follow them. When almost the whole city gathers, jealous Jewish leaders contradict and slander Paul. Paul and Barnabas declare that since the word was rejected and the hearers judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, they will turn to the Gentiles, as the Lord commanded them to be a light to the nations. The Gentiles rejoice, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believe. The word spreads, but persecution drives the missionaries out, and they shake the dust off their feet and move on to Iconium, while the disciples are filled with joy and the Spirit.
text: Acts 13:42–52 Acts The people beg Paul and Barnabas to speak again the next Sabbath, and many follow them. When almost the whole city gathers, jealous Jewish leaders contradict and slander Paul. Paul and Barnabas declare that since the word was rejected and the hearers judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, they will turn to the Gentiles, as the Lord commanded them to be a light to the nations. The Gentiles rejoice, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believe. The word spreads, but persecution drives the missionaries out, and they shake the dust off their feet and move on to Iconium, while the disciples are filled with joy and the Spirit. So when the Jews went out of the synagogue, the Gentiles begged that these words might be preached to them the next Sabbath. Acts 13:42 Now when the synagogue broke up, many of the Jews and of the devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas; who, speaking to them, urged them to continue in the grace of God. Acts 13:43 The next Sabbath, almost the whole city was gathered together to hear the word of God. Acts 13:44 But when the Jews saw the multitudes, they were filled with jealousy, and contradicted the things which were spoken by Paul, and blasphemed. Acts 13:45 Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, and said, “It was necessary that God’s word should be spoken to you first. Since indeed you thrust it from yourselves, and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. Acts 13:46 For so has the Lord commanded us, saying, ‘I have set you as a light for the Gentiles, that you should bring salvation to the uttermost parts of the earth.’” Acts 13:47 As the Gentiles heard this, they were glad and glorified the word of God. As many as were appointed to eternal life believed. Acts 13:48 The Lord’s word was spread abroad throughout all the region. Acts 13:49 But the Jews stirred up the devout and prominent women and the chief men of the city, and stirred up a persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and threw them out of their borders. Acts 13:50 But they shook off the dust of their feet against them, and came to Iconium. Acts 13:51 The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit. Acts 13:52

title: Acts 14:1–18
context: In Iconium many Jews and Greeks believe, but opponents poison minds against the brothers. Paul and Barnabas stay a long time, speaking boldly while the Lord confirms his word with signs, until a plot to stone them drives them to Lystra and Derbe. In Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth who had faith to be made well, and the crowd hails Barnabas as Zeus and Paul as Hermes and prepares to sacrifice to them. Tearing their clothes, the apostles insist they are only men and urge the people to turn from idols to the living God, who made all things and has never left himself without witness.
text: Acts 14:1–18 Acts In Iconium many Jews and Greeks believe, but opponents poison minds against the brothers. Paul and Barnabas stay a long time, speaking boldly while the Lord confirms his word with signs, until a plot to stone them drives them to Lystra and Derbe. In Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth who had faith to be made well, and the crowd hails Barnabas as Zeus and Paul as Hermes and prepares to sacrifice to them. Tearing their clothes, the apostles insist they are only men and urge the people to turn from idols to the living God, who made all things and has never left himself without witness. In Iconium, they entered together into the synagogue of the Jews, and so spoke that a great multitude both of Jews and of Greeks believed. Acts 14:1 But the disbelieving Jews stirred up and embittered the souls of the Gentiles against the brothers. Acts 14:2 Therefore they stayed there a long time, speaking boldly in the Lord, who testified to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. Acts 14:3 But the multitude of the city was divided. Part sided with the Jews and part with the apostles. Acts 14:4 When some of both the Gentiles and the Jews, with their rulers, made a violent attempt to mistreat and stone them, Acts 14:5 they became aware of it and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra, Derbe, and the surrounding region. Acts 14:6 There they preached the Good News. Acts 14:7 At Lystra a certain man sat, impotent in his feet, a cripple from his mother’s womb, who never had walked. Acts 14:8 He was listening to Paul speaking, who, fastening eyes on him and seeing that he had faith to be made whole, Acts 14:9 said with a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet!” He leaped up and walked. Acts 14:10 When the multitude saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voice, saying in the language of Lycaonia, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” Acts 14:11 They called Barnabas “Jupiter”, and Paul “Mercury”, because he was the chief speaker. Acts 14:12 The priest of Jupiter, whose temple was in front of their city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates, and would have made a sacrifice along with the multitudes. Acts 14:13 But when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of it, they tore their clothes and sprang into the multitude, crying out, Acts 14:14 “Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of the same nature as you, and bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them; Acts 14:15 who in the generations gone by allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. Acts 14:16 Yet he didn’t leave himself without witness, in that he did good and gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.” Acts 14:17 Even saying these things, they hardly stopped the multitudes from making a sacrifice to them. Acts 14:18

title: Acts 14:19–28
context: Opponents from Antioch and Iconium win over the crowd, who stone Paul and drag him out of the city, thinking he is dead. As the disciples gather around him, he gets up and goes back into the city, then leaves for Derbe, where many become disciples. Paul and Barnabas return through Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, strengthening the disciples, urging them to continue in the faith, and telling them that through many hardships we must enter God’s kingdom. They appoint elders with prayer and fasting, then return to Antioch and report how God had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.
text: Acts 14:19–28 Acts Opponents from Antioch and Iconium win over the crowd, who stone Paul and drag him out of the city, thinking he is dead. As the disciples gather around him, he gets up and goes back into the city, then leaves for Derbe, where many become disciples. Paul and Barnabas return through Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, strengthening the disciples, urging them to continue in the faith, and telling them that through many hardships we must enter God’s kingdom. They appoint elders with prayer and fasting, then return to Antioch and report how God had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. But some Jews from Antioch and Iconium came there, and having persuaded the multitudes, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. Acts 14:19 But as the disciples stood around him, he rose up, and entered into the city. On the next day he went out with Barnabas to Derbe. Acts 14:20 When they had preached the Good News to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, Acts 14:21 strengthening the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom. Acts 14:22 When they had appointed elders for them in every assembly, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord on whom they had believed. Acts 14:23 They passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. Acts 14:24 When they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia. Acts 14:25 From there they sailed to Antioch, from where they had been committed to the grace of God for the work which they had fulfilled. Acts 14:26 When they had arrived and had gathered the assembly together, they reported all the things that God had done with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the nations. Acts 14:27 They stayed there with the disciples for a long time. Acts 14:28

title: Acts 15:1–21
context: Men from Judea teach in Antioch that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. Paul and Barnabas dispute this and go to Jerusalem, where some believing Pharisees insist on circumcision and the law. At the council Peter recalls that God gave the Gentiles the Spirit and cleansed their hearts by faith, and declares that Jews and Gentiles alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus. Barnabas and Paul recount God’s signs among the Gentiles. James cites Amos on the rebuilt tent of David and proposes not to burden the Gentiles but to ask them to abstain from idol pollution, sexual immorality, strangled meat, and blood.
text: Acts 15:1–21 Acts Men from Judea teach in Antioch that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. Paul and Barnabas dispute this and go to Jerusalem, where some believing Pharisees insist on circumcision and the law. At the council Peter recalls that God gave the Gentiles the Spirit and cleansed their hearts by faith, and declares that Jews and Gentiles alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus. Barnabas and Paul recount God’s signs among the Gentiles. James cites Amos on the rebuilt tent of David and proposes not to burden the Gentiles but to ask them to abstain from idol pollution, sexual immorality, strangled meat, and blood. Some men came down from Judea and taught the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved.” Acts 15:1 Therefore when Paul and Barnabas had no small discord and discussion with them, they appointed Paul, Barnabas, and some others of them to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question. Acts 15:2 They, being sent on their way by the assembly, passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles. They caused great joy to all the brothers. Acts 15:3 When they had come to Jerusalem, they were received by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and they reported everything that God had done with them. Acts 15:4 But some of the sect of the Pharisees who believed rose up, saying, “It is necessary to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.” Acts 15:5 The apostles and the elders were gathered together to see about this matter. Acts 15:6 When there had been much discussion, Peter rose up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that a good while ago God made a choice among you that by my mouth the nations should hear the word of the Good News and believe. Acts 15:7 God, who knows the heart, testified about them, giving them the Holy Spirit, just like he did to us. Acts 15:8 He made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith. Acts 15:9 Now therefore why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? Acts 15:10 But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.” Acts 15:11 All the multitude kept silence, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul reporting what signs and wonders God had done among the nations through them. Acts 15:12 After they were silent, James answered, “Brothers, listen to me. Acts 15:13 Simeon has reported how God first visited the nations to take out of them a people for his name. Acts 15:14 This agrees with the words of the prophets. As it is written, Acts 15:15 ‘After these things I will return. I will again build the tabernacle of David, which has fallen. I will again build its ruins. I will set it up Acts 15:16 that the rest of men may seek after the Lord: all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who does all these things.’ Acts 15:17 “All of God’s works are known to him from eternity. Acts 15:18 Therefore my judgment is that we don’t trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God, Acts 15:19 but that we write to them that they abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood. Acts 15:20 For Moses from generations of old has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath.” Acts 15:21

title: Acts 15:22–41
context: The apostles, elders, and whole church choose Judas Barsabbas and Silas to go with Paul and Barnabas to Antioch, carrying a letter that disowns those who troubled the Gentiles and states that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them to lay on them no burden beyond a few necessary things. The Antioch believers rejoice at the encouragement. Later Paul proposes revisiting the churches, but he and Barnabas disagree sharply over taking John Mark and part ways; Barnabas sails to Cyprus with Mark, while Paul takes Silas through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
text: Acts 15:22–41 Acts The apostles, elders, and whole church choose Judas Barsabbas and Silas to go with Paul and Barnabas to Antioch, carrying a letter that disowns those who troubled the Gentiles and states that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them to lay on them no burden beyond a few necessary things. The Antioch believers rejoice at the encouragement. Later Paul proposes revisiting the churches, but he and Barnabas disagree sharply over taking John Mark and part ways; Barnabas sails to Cyprus with Mark, while Paul takes Silas through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole assembly, to choose men out of their company, and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, chief men among the brothers. Acts 15:22 They wrote these things by their hand: “The apostles, the elders, and the brothers, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: greetings. Acts 15:23 Because we have heard that some who went out from us have troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, saying, ‘You must be circumcised and keep the law,’ to whom we gave no commandment; Acts 15:24 it seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose out men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, Acts 15:25 men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Acts 15:26 We have sent therefore Judas and Silas, who themselves will also tell you the same things by word of mouth. Acts 15:27 For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things: Acts 15:28 that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality, from which if you keep yourselves, it will be well with you. Farewell.” Acts 15:29 So, when they were sent off, they came to Antioch. Having gathered the multitude together, they delivered the letter. Acts 15:30 When they had read it, they rejoiced over the encouragement. Acts 15:31 Judas and Silas, also being prophets themselves, encouraged the brothers with many words and strengthened them. Acts 15:32 After they had spent some time there, they were dismissed in peace from the brothers to the apostles. Acts 15:33 But Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also. Acts 15:35 After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.” Acts 15:36 Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also. Acts 15:37 But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work. Acts 15:38 Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, Acts 15:39 but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God. Acts 15:40 He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies. Acts 15:41

title: Acts 16:1–15
context: At Lystra Paul takes Timothy, whose mother is Jewish and father Greek, and circumcises him because of the Jews in the area. They deliver the council’s decisions, and the churches grow. The Spirit prevents them from preaching in Asia and Bithynia, and at Troas Paul sees a vision of a Macedonian man pleading for help. They sail to Philippi, and on the Sabbath at the riverside they speak to women gathered for prayer. Lydia, a seller of purple cloth who worships God, listens, and the Lord opens her heart to respond to Paul’s message. She and her household are baptized, and she urges them to stay at her house.
text: Acts 16:1–15 Acts At Lystra Paul takes Timothy, whose mother is Jewish and father Greek, and circumcises him because of the Jews in the area. They deliver the council’s decisions, and the churches grow. The Spirit prevents them from preaching in Asia and Bithynia, and at Troas Paul sees a vision of a Macedonian man pleading for help. They sail to Philippi, and on the Sabbath at the riverside they speak to women gathered for prayer. Lydia, a seller of purple cloth who worships God, listens, and the Lord opens her heart to respond to Paul’s message. She and her household are baptized, and she urges them to stay at her house. He came to Derbe and Lystra; and behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewess who believed, but his father was a Greek. Acts 16:1 The brothers who were at Lystra and Iconium gave a good testimony about him. Acts 16:2 Paul wanted to have him go out with him, and he took and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those parts, for they all knew that his father was a Greek. Acts 16:3 As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered the decrees to them to keep which had been ordained by the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem. Acts 16:4 So the assemblies were strengthened in the faith, and increased in number daily. Acts 16:5 When they had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. Acts 16:6 When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow them. Acts 16:7 Passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas. Acts 16:8 A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him and saying, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.” Acts 16:9 When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had called us to preach the Good News to them. Acts 16:10 Setting sail therefore from Troas, we made a straight course to Samothrace, and the day following to Neapolis; Acts 16:11 and from there to Philippi, which is a city of Macedonia, the foremost of the district, a Roman colony. We were staying some days in this city. Acts 16:12 On the Sabbath day we went outside of the city by a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together. Acts 16:13 A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard us. The Lord opened her heart to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul. Acts 16:14 When she and her household were baptized, she begged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” So she persuaded us. Acts 16:15

title: Acts 16:16–40
context: In Philippi a slave girl with a spirit of divination follows Paul for days, crying that these men proclaim the way of salvation, until Paul commands the spirit to leave her. Her owners, losing their profit, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed. At midnight, as they pray and sing, an earthquake opens the doors. The jailer is about to kill himself when Paul stops him; trembling, he asks what he must do to be saved, and they answer, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.” He and his household hear the word, are baptized, and rejoice. The next day Paul, a Roman citizen, insists that the magistrates release them personally.
text: Acts 16:16–40 Acts In Philippi a slave girl with a spirit of divination follows Paul for days, crying that these men proclaim the way of salvation, until Paul commands the spirit to leave her. Her owners, losing their profit, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed. At midnight, as they pray and sing, an earthquake opens the doors. The jailer is about to kill himself when Paul stops him; trembling, he asks what he must do to be saved, and they answer, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.” He and his household hear the word, are baptized, and rejoice. The next day Paul, a Roman citizen, insists that the magistrates release them personally. As we were going to prayer, a certain girl having a spirit of divination met us, who brought her masters much gain by fortune telling. Acts 16:16 Following Paul and us, she cried out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us a way of salvation!” Acts 16:17 She was doing this for many days. But Paul, becoming greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” It came out that very hour. Acts 16:18 But when her masters saw that the hope of their gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. Acts 16:19 When they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men, being Jews, are agitating our city Acts 16:20 and advocate customs which it is not lawful for us to accept or to observe, being Romans.” Acts 16:21 The multitude rose up together against them and the magistrates tore their clothes from them, then commanded them to be beaten with rods. Acts 16:22 When they had laid many stripes on them, they threw them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them safely. Acts 16:23 Having received such a command, he threw them into the inner prison and secured their feet in the stocks. Acts 16:24 But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them. Acts 16:25 Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened. Acts 16:26 The jailer, being roused out of sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. Acts 16:27 But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, “Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!” Acts 16:28 He called for lights, sprang in, fell down trembling before Paul and Silas, Acts 16:29 brought them out, and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” Acts 16:30 They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.” Acts 16:31 They spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house. Acts 16:32 He took them the same hour of the night and washed their stripes, and was immediately baptized, he and all his household. Acts 16:33 He brought them up into his house and set food before them, and rejoiced greatly with all his household, having believed in God. Acts 16:34 But when it was day, the magistrates sent the sergeants, saying, “Let those men go.” Acts 16:35 The jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go; now therefore come out and go in peace.” Acts 16:36 But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly without a trial, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison! Do they now release us secretly? No, most certainly, but let them come themselves and bring us out!” Acts 16:37 The sergeants reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans, Acts 16:38 and they came and begged them. When they had brought them out, they asked them to depart from the city. Acts 16:39 They went out of the prison and entered into Lydia’s house. When they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them, then departed. Acts 16:40

title: Acts 17:1–15
context: In Thessalonica Paul reasons from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths that the Christ had to suffer and rise, and some Jews and many God-fearing Greeks and leading women are persuaded. Jealous opponents form a mob, attack Jason’s house, and accuse the believers of turning the world upside down and proclaiming another king, Jesus. Sent to Berea, Paul finds Jews more noble-minded, who receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily, and many believe. When agitators arrive from Thessalonica, Paul is sent on to Athens.
text: Acts 17:1–15 Acts In Thessalonica Paul reasons from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths that the Christ had to suffer and rise, and some Jews and many God-fearing Greeks and leading women are persuaded. Jealous opponents form a mob, attack Jason’s house, and accuse the believers of turning the world upside down and proclaiming another king, Jesus. Sent to Berea, Paul finds Jews more noble-minded, who receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily, and many believe. When agitators arrive from Thessalonica, Paul is sent on to Athens. Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue. Acts 17:1 Paul, as was his custom, went in to them; and for three Sabbath days reasoned with them from the Scriptures, Acts 17:2 explaining and demonstrating that the Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.” Acts 17:3 Some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas: of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and not a few of the chief women. Acts 17:4 But the unpersuaded Jews took along some wicked men from the marketplace and gathering a crowd, set the city in an uproar. Assaulting the house of Jason, they sought to bring them out to the people. Acts 17:5 When they didn’t find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the rulers of the city, crying, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also, Acts 17:6 whom Jason has received. These all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus!” Acts 17:7 The multitude and the rulers of the city were troubled when they heard these things. Acts 17:8 When they had taken security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. Acts 17:9 The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. When they arrived, they went into the Jewish synagogue. Acts 17:10 Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so. Acts 17:11 Many of them therefore believed; also of the prominent Greek women, and not a few men. Acts 17:12 But when the Jews of Thessalonica had knowledge that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Beroea also, they came there likewise, agitating the multitudes. Acts 17:13 Then the brothers immediately sent out Paul to go as far as to the sea, and Silas and Timothy still stayed there. Acts 17:14 But those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens. Receiving a commandment to Silas and Timothy that they should come to him very quickly, they departed. Acts 17:15

title: Acts 17:16–34
context: Waiting in Athens, Paul is distressed by the city full of idols and reasons in the synagogue and the marketplace. Epicurean and Stoic philosophers bring him to the Areopagus to explain his new teaching. Paul begins from their altar to an unknown god and proclaims the Creator who does not live in temples, gives life to all, made every nation from one man, and set their times and boundaries so that they would seek him. God overlooked the times of ignorance but now commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day to judge the world by the man he raised from the dead. Some mock, some want to hear more, and a few believe.
text: Acts 17:16–34 Acts Waiting in Athens, Paul is distressed by the city full of idols and reasons in the synagogue and the marketplace. Epicurean and Stoic philosophers bring him to the Areopagus to explain his new teaching. Paul begins from their altar to an unknown god and proclaims the Creator who does not live in temples, gives life to all, made every nation from one man, and set their times and boundaries so that they would seek him. God overlooked the times of ignorance but now commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day to judge the world by the man he raised from the dead. Some mock, some want to hear more, and a few believe. Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols. Acts 17:16 So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who met him. Acts 17:17 Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also were conversing with him. Some said, “What does this babbler want to say?” Others said, “He seems to be advocating foreign deities,” because he preached Jesus and the resurrection. Acts 17:18 They took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is, which you are speaking about? Acts 17:19 For you bring certain strange things to our ears. We want to know therefore what these things mean.” Acts 17:20 Now all the Athenians and the strangers living there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing. Acts 17:21 Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said, “You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things. Acts 17:22 For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I also found an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What therefore you worship in ignorance, I announce to you. Acts 17:23 The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands. Acts 17:24 He isn’t served by men’s hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath and all things. Acts 17:25 He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings, Acts 17:26 that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. Acts 17:27 ‘For in him we live, move, and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’ Acts 17:28 Being then the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art and design of man. Acts 17:29 The times of ignorance therefore God overlooked. But now he commands that all people everywhere should repent, Acts 17:30 because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained; of which he has given assurance to all men, in that he has raised him from the dead.” Acts 17:31 Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said, “We want to hear you again concerning this.” Acts 17:32 Thus Paul went out from among them.
