Acts 17:33 But certain men joined with him and believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them. Acts 17:34

title: Acts 18:1–17
context: In Corinth Paul stays with Aquila and Priscilla, fellow tentmakers expelled from Rome, and reasons in the synagogue each Sabbath. When opposition grows, he turns to the Gentiles and teaches next door in the house of Titius Justus; the synagogue ruler Crispus and many Corinthians believe. The Lord tells Paul in a vision not to be afraid, for no one will harm him and he has many people in this city, so Paul stays eighteen months. When opponents bring him before the proconsul Gallio, Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about Jewish law.
text: Acts 18:1–17 Acts In Corinth Paul stays with Aquila and Priscilla, fellow tentmakers expelled from Rome, and reasons in the synagogue each Sabbath. When opposition grows, he turns to the Gentiles and teaches next door in the house of Titius Justus; the synagogue ruler Crispus and many Corinthians believe. The Lord tells Paul in a vision not to be afraid, for no one will harm him and he has many people in this city, so Paul stays eighteen months. When opponents bring him before the proconsul Gallio, Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about Jewish law. After these things Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth. Acts 18:1 He found a certain Jew named Aquila, a man of Pontus by race, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to depart from Rome. He came to them, Acts 18:2 and because he practiced the same trade, he lived with them and worked, for by trade they were tent makers. Acts 18:3 He reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath and persuaded Jews and Greeks. Acts 18:4 When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was compelled by the Spirit, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ. Acts 18:5 When they opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his clothing and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean. From now on, I will go to the Gentiles!” Acts 18:6 He departed there and went into the house of a certain man named Justus, one who worshiped God, whose house was next door to the synagogue. Acts 18:7 Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his house. Many of the Corinthians, when they heard, believed and were baptized. Acts 18:8 The Lord said to Paul in the night by a vision, “Don’t be afraid, but speak and don’t be silent; Acts 18:9 for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.” Acts 18:10 He lived there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. Acts 18:11 But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat, Acts 18:12 saying, “This man persuades men to worship God contrary to the law.” Acts 18:13 But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If indeed it were a matter of wrong or of wicked crime, you Jews, it would be reasonable that I should bear with you; Acts 18:14 but if they are questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves. For I don’t want to be a judge of these matters.” Acts 18:15 So he drove them from the judgment seat. Acts 18:16 Then all the Greeks seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the judgment seat. Gallio didn’t care about any of these things. Acts 18:17

title: Acts 18:18–28
context: Paul stays in Corinth for a while, cuts his hair at Cenchreae because of a vow, and sails with Priscilla and Aquila to Ephesus, where he reasons briefly in the synagogue and promises to return if God wills. He travels to Caesarea, Jerusalem, and Antioch, then strengthens the disciples in Galatia and Phrygia. Meanwhile Apollos, an eloquent Alexandrian who knows only John’s baptism, teaches accurately about Jesus in Ephesus; Priscilla and Aquila explain the way of God more accurately to him, and he goes to Achaia, where he greatly helps believers and refutes opponents from the Scriptures.
text: Acts 18:18–28 Acts Paul stays in Corinth for a while, cuts his hair at Cenchreae because of a vow, and sails with Priscilla and Aquila to Ephesus, where he reasons briefly in the synagogue and promises to return if God wills. He travels to Caesarea, Jerusalem, and Antioch, then strengthens the disciples in Galatia and Phrygia. Meanwhile Apollos, an eloquent Alexandrian who knows only John’s baptism, teaches accurately about Jesus in Ephesus; Priscilla and Aquila explain the way of God more accurately to him, and he goes to Achaia, where he greatly helps believers and refutes opponents from the Scriptures. Paul, having stayed after this many more days, took his leave of the brothers, and sailed from there for Syria, together with Priscilla and Aquila. He shaved his head in Cenchreae, for he had a vow. Acts 18:18 He came to Ephesus, and he left them there; but he himself entered into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. Acts 18:19 When they asked him to stay with them a longer time, he declined; Acts 18:20 but taking his leave of them, he said, “I must by all means keep this coming feast in Jerusalem, but I will return again to you if God wills.” Then he set sail from Ephesus. Acts 18:21 When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the assembly, and went down to Antioch. Acts 18:22 Having spent some time there, he departed and went through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, in order, establishing all the disciples. Acts 18:23 Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures. Acts 18:24 This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John. Acts 18:25 He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately. Acts 18:26 When he had determined to pass over into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him; and wrote to the disciples to receive him. When he had come, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace; Acts 18:27 for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ. Acts 18:28

title: Acts 19:1–20
context: In Ephesus Paul finds about twelve disciples who know only John’s baptism and have not heard of the Holy Spirit. He explains that John pointed to Jesus; they are baptized in Jesus’ name, and when Paul lays hands on them, the Spirit comes and they speak in tongues and prophesy. Paul preaches in the synagogue for three months, then teaches daily in the hall of Tyrannus for two years, so that all Asia hears the word. God does extraordinary miracles through him. When the seven sons of Sceva try to use Jesus’ name as a formula, an evil spirit overpowers them, and many believers confess their practices and burn their magic books. The word of the Lord grows mightily.
text: Acts 19:1–20 Acts In Ephesus Paul finds about twelve disciples who know only John’s baptism and have not heard of the Holy Spirit. He explains that John pointed to Jesus; they are baptized in Jesus’ name, and when Paul lays hands on them, the Spirit comes and they speak in tongues and prophesy. Paul preaches in the synagogue for three months, then teaches daily in the hall of Tyrannus for two years, so that all Asia hears the word. God does extraordinary miracles through him. When the seven sons of Sceva try to use Jesus’ name as a formula, an evil spirit overpowers them, and many believers confess their practices and burn their magic books. The word of the Lord grows mightily. While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, having passed through the upper country, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples. Acts 19:1 He said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They said to him, “No, we haven’t even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” Acts 19:2 He said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” Acts 19:3 Paul said, “John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, saying to the people that they should believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Christ Jesus.” Acts 19:4 When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Acts 19:5 When Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them and they spoke with other languages and prophesied. Acts 19:6 They were about twelve men in all. Acts 19:7 He entered into the synagogue and spoke boldly for a period of three months, reasoning and persuading about the things concerning God’s Kingdom. Acts 19:8 But when some were hardened and disobedient, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude, he departed from them and separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the school of Tyrannus. Acts 19:9 This continued for two years, so that all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks. Acts 19:10 God worked special miracles by the hands of Paul, Acts 19:11 so that even handkerchiefs or aprons were carried away from his body to the sick, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out. Acts 19:12 But some of the itinerant Jews, exorcists, took on themselves to invoke over those who had the evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, “We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.” Acts 19:13 There were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who did this. Acts 19:14 The evil spirit answered, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?” Acts 19:15 The man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, overpowered them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. Acts 19:16 This became known to all, both Jews and Greeks, who lived at Ephesus. Fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified. Acts 19:17 Many also of those who had believed came, confessing and declaring their deeds. Acts 19:18 Many of those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. They counted their price, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver. Acts 19:19 So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty. Acts 19:20

title: Acts 19:21–41
context: Paul resolves in the Spirit to go through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem and then to Rome. In Ephesus a silversmith named Demetrius, who makes shrines of Artemis, rouses the craftsmen by warning that Paul’s teaching threatens their trade and the goddess’s honor. The city fills with confusion, and the crowd rushes into the theater, shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” for two hours. The town clerk finally quiets them, points out that the Christians have not robbed temples or blasphemed the goddess, directs any complaint to the courts, and dismisses the assembly.
text: Acts 19:21–41 Acts Paul resolves in the Spirit to go through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem and then to Rome. In Ephesus a silversmith named Demetrius, who makes shrines of Artemis, rouses the craftsmen by warning that Paul’s teaching threatens their trade and the goddess’s honor. The city fills with confusion, and the crowd rushes into the theater, shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” for two hours. The town clerk finally quiets them, points out that the Christians have not robbed temples or blasphemed the goddess, directs any complaint to the courts, and dismisses the assembly. Now after these things had ended, Paul determined in the Spirit, when he had passed through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” Acts 19:21 Having sent into Macedonia two of those who served him, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while. Acts 19:22 About that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the Way. Acts 19:23 For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen, Acts 19:24 whom he gathered together with the workmen of like occupation, and said, “Sirs, you know that by this business we have our wealth. Acts 19:25 You see and hear that not at Ephesus alone, but almost throughout all Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away many people, saying that they are no gods that are made with hands. Acts 19:26 Not only is there danger that this our trade come into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be counted as nothing and her majesty destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worships.” Acts 19:27 When they heard this they were filled with anger, and cried out, saying, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” Acts 19:28 The whole city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul’s companions in travel. Acts 19:29 When Paul wanted to enter in to the people, the disciples didn’t allow him. Acts 19:30 Certain also of the Asiarchs, being his friends, sent to him and begged him not to venture into the theater. Acts 19:31 Some therefore cried one thing, and some another, for the assembly was in confusion. Most of them didn’t know why they had come together. Acts 19:32 They brought Alexander out of the multitude, the Jews putting him forward. Alexander beckoned with his hand, and would have made a defense to the people. Acts 19:33 But when they perceived that he was a Jew, all with one voice for a time of about two hours cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” Acts 19:34 When the town clerk had quieted the multitude, he said, “You men of Ephesus, what man is there who doesn’t know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great goddess Artemis, and of the image which fell down from Zeus? Acts 19:35 Seeing then that these things can’t be denied, you ought to be quiet and to do nothing rash. Acts 19:36 For you have brought these men here, who are neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers of your goddess. Acts 19:37 If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen who are with him have a matter against anyone, the courts are open and there are proconsuls. Let them press charges against one another. Acts 19:38 But if you seek anything about other matters, it will be settled in the regular assembly. Acts 19:39 For indeed we are in danger of being accused concerning today’s riot, there being no cause. Concerning it, we wouldn’t be able to give an account of this commotion.” Acts 19:40 When he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly. Acts 19:41

title: Acts 2:1–13
context: On the day of Pentecost the believers are gathered when a sound like a rushing wind fills the house and tongues like fire rest on each of them. Filled with the Holy Spirit, they speak in other languages, and Jews from every nation living in Jerusalem hear the mighty works of God in their own languages. Some are amazed and ask what it means, while others mock and say the disciples are drunk.
text: Acts 2:1–13 Acts On the day of Pentecost the believers are gathered when a sound like a rushing wind fills the house and tongues like fire rest on each of them. Filled with the Holy Spirit, they speak in other languages, and Jews from every nation living in Jerusalem hear the mighty works of God in their own languages. Some are amazed and ask what it means, while others mock and say the disciples are drunk. Now when the day of Pentecost had come, they were all with one accord in one place. Acts 2:1 Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. Acts 2:2 Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them. Acts 2:3 They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak. Acts 2:4 Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under the sky. Acts 2:5 When this sound was heard, the multitude came together and were bewildered, because everyone heard them speaking in his own language. Acts 2:6 They were all amazed and marveled, saying to one another, “Behold, aren’t all these who speak Galileans? Acts 2:7 How do we hear, everyone in our own native language? Acts 2:8 Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Acts 2:9 Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, the parts of Libya around Cyrene, visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes, Acts 2:10 Cretans and Arabians—we hear them speaking in our languages the mighty works of God!” Acts 2:11 They were all amazed and were perplexed, saying to one another, “What does this mean?” Acts 2:12 Others, mocking, said, “They are filled with new wine.” Acts 2:13

title: Acts 2:14–36
context: Peter stands with the eleven and explains that the believers are not drunk; this is the outpouring of the Spirit promised through Joel, and whoever calls on the Lord’s name will be saved. He proclaims Jesus of Nazareth, approved by God through miracles, delivered up by God’s set purpose and foreknowledge and crucified by lawless men, but raised by God because death could not hold him. Citing Psalms 16 and 110, Peter argues that David foresaw the resurrection and exaltation of the Christ, and he concludes that God has made the crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ.
text: Acts 2:14–36 Acts Peter stands with the eleven and explains that the believers are not drunk; this is the outpouring of the Spirit promised through Joel, and whoever calls on the Lord’s name will be saved. He proclaims Jesus of Nazareth, approved by God through miracles, delivered up by God’s set purpose and foreknowledge and crucified by lawless men, but raised by God because death could not hold him. Citing Psalms 16 and 110, Peter argues that David foresaw the resurrection and exaltation of the Christ, and he concludes that God has made the crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ. But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice and spoke out to them, “You men of Judea and all you who dwell at Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words. Acts 2:14 For these aren’t drunken, as you suppose, seeing it is only the third hour of the day. Acts 2:15 But this is what has been spoken through the prophet Joel: Acts 2:16 ‘It will be in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your young men will see visions. Your old men will dream dreams. Acts 2:17 Yes, and on my servants and on my handmaidens in those days, I will pour out my Spirit, and they will prophesy. Acts 2:18 I will show wonders in the sky above, and signs on the earth beneath: blood, and fire, and billows of smoke. Acts 2:19 The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes. Acts 2:20 It will be that whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.’ Acts 2:21 “Men of Israel, hear these words! Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God to you by mighty works and wonders and signs which God did by him among you, even as you yourselves know, Acts 2:22 him, being delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you have taken by the hand of lawless men, crucified and killed; Acts 2:23 whom God raised up, having freed him from the agony of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it. Acts 2:24 For David says concerning him, ‘I saw the Lord always before my face, for he is on my right hand, that I should not be moved. Acts 2:25 Therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced. Moreover my flesh also will dwell in hope, Acts 2:26 because you will not leave my soul in Hades, neither will you allow your Holy One to see decay. Acts 2:27 You made known to me the ways of life. You will make me full of gladness with your presence.’ Acts 2:28 “Brothers, I may tell you freely of the patriarch David, that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Acts 2:29 Therefore, being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that of the fruit of his body, according to the flesh, he would raise up the Christ to sit on his throne, Acts 2:30 he foreseeing this, spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that his soul wasn’t left in Hades, and his flesh didn’t see decay. Acts 2:31 This Jesus God raised up, to which we all are witnesses. Acts 2:32 Being therefore exalted by the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this which you now see and hear. Acts 2:33 For David didn’t ascend into the heavens, but he says himself, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit by my right hand Acts 2:34 until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’ Acts 2:35 “Let all the house of Israel therefore know certainly that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.” Acts 2:36

title: Acts 2:37–47
context: Cut to the heart, the crowd asks what they should do. Peter calls them to repent and be baptized in Jesus’ name for the forgiveness of sins, promising the gift of the Spirit to them, their children, and all who are far off, as many as the Lord calls. About three thousand receive his word and are baptized. The new community devotes itself to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer; they share their goods, worship with gladness, and the Lord adds daily those who are being saved.
text: Acts 2:37–47 Acts Cut to the heart, the crowd asks what they should do. Peter calls them to repent and be baptized in Jesus’ name for the forgiveness of sins, promising the gift of the Spirit to them, their children, and all who are far off, as many as the Lord calls. About three thousand receive his word and are baptized. The new community devotes itself to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer; they share their goods, worship with gladness, and the Lord adds daily those who are being saved. Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” Acts 2:37 Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. Acts 2:38 For the promise is to you and to your children, and to all who are far off, even as many as the Lord our God will call to himself.” Acts 2:39 With many other words he testified and exhorted them, saying, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation!” Acts 2:40 Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls. Acts 2:41 They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer. Acts 2:42 Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles. Acts 2:43 All who believed were together, and had all things in common. Acts 2:44 They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need. Acts 2:45 Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, Acts 2:46 praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved. Acts 2:47

title: Acts 20:1–16
context: After the uproar Paul encourages the disciples and travels through Macedonia to Greece, where he spends three months before a plot changes his route. Companions from several churches travel with him. At Troas, on the first day of the week, the believers gather to break bread, and Paul talks until midnight; a young man named Eutychus falls asleep, drops from a third-story window, and is taken up dead, but Paul embraces him and he is restored to life. Paul then hurries along the coast, sailing past Ephesus to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost.
text: Acts 20:1–16 Acts After the uproar Paul encourages the disciples and travels through Macedonia to Greece, where he spends three months before a plot changes his route. Companions from several churches travel with him. At Troas, on the first day of the week, the believers gather to break bread, and Paul talks until midnight; a young man named Eutychus falls asleep, drops from a third-story window, and is taken up dead, but Paul embraces him and he is restored to life. Paul then hurries along the coast, sailing past Ephesus to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost. After the uproar had ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, took leave of them, and departed to go into Macedonia. Acts 20:1 When he had gone through those parts and had encouraged them with many words, he came into Greece. Acts 20:2 When he had spent three months there, and a plot was made against him by Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he determined to return through Macedonia. Acts 20:3 These accompanied him as far as Asia: Sopater of Beroea, Aristarchus and Secundus of the Thessalonians, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia. Acts 20:4 But these had gone ahead, and were waiting for us at Troas. Acts 20:5 We sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and came to them at Troas in five days, where we stayed seven days. Acts 20:6 On the first day of the week, when the disciples were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day; and continued his speech until midnight. Acts 20:7 There were many lights in the upper room where we were gathered together. Acts 20:8 A certain young man named Eutychus sat in the window, weighed down with deep sleep. As Paul spoke still longer, being weighed down by his sleep, he fell down from the third floor and was taken up dead. Acts 20:9 Paul went down and fell upon him, and embracing him said, “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.” Acts 20:10 When he had gone up, had broken bread and eaten, and had talked with them a long while, even until break of day, he departed. Acts 20:11 They brought the boy in alive, and were greatly comforted. Acts 20:12 But we, going ahead to the ship, set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there; for he had so arranged, intending himself to go by land. Acts 20:13 When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene. Acts 20:14 Sailing from there, we came the following day opposite Chios. The next day we touched at Samos and stayed at Trogyllium, and the day after we came to Miletus. Acts 20:15 For Paul had determined to sail past Ephesus, that he might not have to spend time in Asia; for he was hastening, if it were possible for him, to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost. Acts 20:16

title: Acts 20:17–38
context: At Miletus Paul summons the Ephesian elders and recalls how he served among them with humility, tears, and trials, declaring everything profitable and testifying to Jews and Greeks about repentance toward God and faith in Jesus. Bound by the Spirit, he goes to Jerusalem expecting imprisonment and does not count his life dear. He is innocent of everyone’s blood because he did not shrink from declaring the whole counsel of God. He charges the elders to guard themselves and the flock, over which the Spirit made them overseers, to shepherd the church of God which he bought with his own blood, and warns that wolves will come. He commends them to God and the word of his grace, reminds them of his labor and Jesus’ words that it is more blessed to give than to receive, prays with them, and departs amid tears.
text: Acts 20:17–38 Acts At Miletus Paul summons the Ephesian elders and recalls how he served among them with humility, tears, and trials, declaring everything profitable and testifying to Jews and Greeks about repentance toward God and faith in Jesus. Bound by the Spirit, he goes to Jerusalem expecting imprisonment and does not count his life dear. He is innocent of everyone’s blood because he did not shrink from declaring the whole counsel of God. He charges the elders to guard themselves and the flock, over which the Spirit made them overseers, to shepherd the church of God which he bought with his own blood, and warns that wolves will come. He commends them to God and the word of his grace, reminds them of his labor and Jesus’ words that it is more blessed to give than to receive, prays with them, and departs amid tears. From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called to himself the elders of the assembly. Acts 20:17 When they had come to him, he said to them, “You yourselves know, from the first day that I set foot in Asia, how I was with you all the time, Acts 20:18 serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears, and with trials which happened to me by the plots of the Jews; Acts 20:19 how I didn’t shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, teaching you publicly and from house to house, Acts 20:20 testifying both to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God and faith toward our Lord Jesus. Acts 20:21 Now, behold, I go bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there; Acts 20:22 except that the Holy Spirit testifies in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions wait for me. Acts 20:23 But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God. Acts 20:24 “Now, behold, I know that you all, among whom I went about preaching God’s Kingdom, will see my face no more. Acts 20:25 Therefore I testify to you today that I am clean from the blood of all men, Acts 20:26 for I didn’t shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. Acts 20:27 Take heed, therefore, to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood. Acts 20:28 For I know that after my departure, vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock. Acts 20:29 Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them. Acts 20:30 Therefore watch, remembering that for a period of three years I didn’t cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears. Acts 20:31 Now, brothers, I entrust you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. Acts 20:32 I coveted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing. Acts 20:33 You yourselves know that these hands served my necessities, and those who were with me. Acts 20:34 In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ ” Acts 20:35 When he had spoken these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. Acts 20:36 They all wept freely, and fell on Paul’s neck and kissed him, Acts 20:37 sorrowing most of all because of the word which he had spoken, that they should see his face no more. Then they accompanied him to the ship. Acts 20:38

title: Acts 21:1–16
context: Paul’s company sails from Miletus to Tyre, where disciples, speaking through the Spirit, urge him not to go to Jerusalem; after a week they kneel and pray on the beach and part. At Caesarea they stay with Philip the evangelist, whose four daughters prophesy. The prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and foretells that the Jews will bind Paul and hand him over to the Gentiles. Everyone begs Paul not to go, but he declares he is ready to be bound and even to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and they fall silent, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.”
text: Acts 21:1–16 Acts Paul’s company sails from Miletus to Tyre, where disciples, speaking through the Spirit, urge him not to go to Jerusalem; after a week they kneel and pray on the beach and part. At Caesarea they stay with Philip the evangelist, whose four daughters prophesy. The prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and foretells that the Jews will bind Paul and hand him over to the Gentiles. Everyone begs Paul not to go, but he declares he is ready to be bound and even to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and they fall silent, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.” When we had departed from them and had set sail, we came with a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. Acts 21:1 Having found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail. Acts 21:2 When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left hand, we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for the ship was there to unload her cargo. Acts 21:3 Having found disciples, we stayed there seven days. These said to Paul through the Spirit that he should not go up to Jerusalem. Acts 21:4 When those days were over, we departed and went on our journey. They all, with wives and children, brought us on our way until we were out of the city. Kneeling down on the beach, we prayed. Acts 21:5 After saying goodbye to each other, we went on board the ship, and they returned home again. Acts 21:6 When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais. We greeted the brothers and stayed with them one day. Acts 21:7 On the next day, we who were Paul’s companions departed and came to Caesarea. We entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. Acts 21:8 Now this man had four virgin daughters who prophesied. Acts 21:9 As we stayed there some days, a certain prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. Acts 21:10 Coming to us and taking Paul’s belt, he bound his own feet and hands, and said, “The Holy Spirit says: ‘So the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt, and will deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’” Acts 21:11 When we heard these things, both we and the people of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem. Acts 21:12 Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” Acts 21:13 When he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.” Acts 21:14 After these days we took up our baggage and went up to Jerusalem. Acts 21:15 Some of the disciples from Caesarea also went with us, bringing one Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we would stay. Acts 21:16

title: Acts 21:17–40
context: The Jerusalem believers welcome Paul, and James and the elders glorify God for his report about the Gentiles. They warn him that thousands of law-observant Jewish believers have heard he teaches Jews to abandon Moses, and they advise him to join four men completing a vow to show he keeps the law. Near the end of the seven days, Jews from Asia see him in the temple, stir up the crowd, and falsely claim he brought Greeks inside. The mob drags Paul out and tries to kill him until the Roman commander intervenes, arrests him, and, after learning he is a citizen of Tarsus, permits him to address the people from the barracks steps.
text: Acts 21:17–40 Acts The Jerusalem believers welcome Paul, and James and the elders glorify God for his report about the Gentiles. They warn him that thousands of law-observant Jewish believers have heard he teaches Jews to abandon Moses, and they advise him to join four men completing a vow to show he keeps the law. Near the end of the seven days, Jews from Asia see him in the temple, stir up the crowd, and falsely claim he brought Greeks inside. The mob drags Paul out and tries to kill him until the Roman commander intervenes, arrests him, and, after learning he is a citizen of Tarsus, permits him to address the people from the barracks steps. When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. Acts 21:17 The day following, Paul went in with us to James; and all the elders were present. Acts 21:18 When he had greeted them, he reported one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles through his ministry. Acts 21:19 They, when they heard it, glorified God. They said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law. Acts 21:20 They have been informed about you, that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children and not to walk after the customs. Acts 21:21 What then? The assembly must certainly meet, for they will hear that you have come. Acts 21:22 Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow. Acts 21:23 Take them and purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses for them, that they may shave their heads. Then all will know that there is no truth in the things that they have been informed about you, but that you yourself also walk keeping the law. Acts 21:24 But concerning the Gentiles who believe, we have written our decision that they should observe no such thing, except that they should keep themselves from food offered to idols, from blood, from strangled things, and from sexual immorality.” Acts 21:25 Then Paul took the men, and the next day purified himself and went with them into the temple, declaring the fulfillment of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for every one of them. Acts 21:26 When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, when they saw him in the temple, stirred up all the multitude and laid hands on him, Acts 21:27 crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches all men everywhere against the people, and the law, and this place. Moreover, he also brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place!” Acts 21:28 For they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Acts 21:29 All the city was moved and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple. Immediately the doors were shut. Acts 21:30 As they were trying to kill him, news came up to the commanding officer of the regiment that all Jerusalem was in an uproar. Acts 21:31 Immediately he took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. They, when they saw the chief captain and the soldiers, stopped beating Paul. Acts 21:32 Then the commanding officer came near, arrested him, commanded him to be bound with two chains, and inquired who he was and what he had done. Acts 21:33 Some shouted one thing and some another, among the crowd. When he couldn’t find out the truth because of the noise, he commanded him to be brought into the barracks. Acts 21:34 When he came to the stairs, he was carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd; Acts 21:35 for the multitude of the people followed after, crying out, “Away with him!” Acts 21:36 As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he asked the commanding officer, “May I speak to you?” He said, “Do you know Greek? Acts 21:37 Aren’t you then the Egyptian who before these days stirred up to sedition and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the Assassins?” Acts 21:38 But Paul said, “I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.” Acts 21:39 When he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the stairs, beckoned with his hand to the people. When there was a great silence, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, saying, Acts 21:40

title: Acts 22:1–21
context: Speaking in Hebrew from the barracks steps, Paul describes his upbringing under Gamaliel and his zeal in persecuting the Way. He recounts his encounter with the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus, his blindness, and Ananias’s message that the God of their fathers had appointed him to know his will, see the Righteous One, and be his witness to all people. Ananias urged him to be baptized and wash away his sins, calling on the Lord’s name. Later, while praying in the temple, Paul saw the Lord telling him to leave Jerusalem because he would send him far away to the Gentiles.
text: Acts 22:1–21 Acts Speaking in Hebrew from the barracks steps, Paul describes his upbringing under Gamaliel and his zeal in persecuting the Way. He recounts his encounter with the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus, his blindness, and Ananias’s message that the God of their fathers had appointed him to know his will, see the Righteous One, and be his witness to all people. Ananias urged him to be baptized and wash away his sins, calling on the Lord’s name. Later, while praying in the temple, Paul saw the Lord telling him to leave Jerusalem because he would send him far away to the Gentiles. “Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense which I now make to you.” Acts 22:1 When they heard that he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, they were even more quiet. He said, Acts 22:2 “I am indeed a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, instructed according to the strict tradition of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God, even as you all are today. Acts 22:3 I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women, Acts 22:4 as also the high priest and all the council of the elders testify, from whom also I received letters to the brothers, and traveled to Damascus to bring them also who were there to Jerusalem in bonds to be punished. Acts 22:5 “As I made my journey and came close to Damascus, about noon suddenly a great light shone around me from the sky. Acts 22:6 I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ Acts 22:7 I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ He said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you persecute.’ Acts 22:8 “Those who were with me indeed saw the light and were afraid, but they didn’t understand the voice of him who spoke to me. Acts 22:9 I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ The Lord said to me, ‘Arise, and go into Damascus. There you will be told about all things which are appointed for you to do.’ Acts 22:10 When I couldn’t see for the glory of that light, being led by the hand of those who were with me, I came into Damascus. Acts 22:11 “One Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well reported of by all the Jews who lived in Damascus, Acts 22:12 came to me, and standing by me said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight!’ In that very hour I looked up at him. Acts 22:13 He said, ‘The God of our fathers has appointed you to know his will, and to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his mouth. Acts 22:14 For you will be a witness for him to all men of what you have seen and heard. Acts 22:15 Now why do you wait? Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord.’ Acts 22:16 “When I had returned to Jerusalem and while I prayed in the temple, I fell into a trance Acts 22:17 and saw him saying to me, ‘Hurry and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not receive testimony concerning me from you.’ Acts 22:18 I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that I imprisoned and beat in every synagogue those who believed in you. Acts 22:19 When the blood of Stephen, your witness, was shed, I also was standing by, consenting to his death, and guarding the cloaks of those who killed him.’ Acts 22:20 “He said to me, ‘Depart, for I will send you out far from here to the Gentiles.’ ” Acts 22:21

title: Acts 22:22–30
context: At the word “Gentiles,” the crowd erupts, demanding Paul’s death, throwing off cloaks and flinging dust into the air. The commander orders Paul brought into the barracks and examined by flogging, but as they stretch him out, Paul asks the centurion whether it is lawful to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen. Alarmed, the commander, who had bought his own citizenship at great price, learns that Paul was born a citizen, and the interrogators withdraw. The next day the commander releases Paul’s bonds and brings him before the chief priests and the council to learn the charges.
text: Acts 22:22–30 Acts At the word “Gentiles,” the crowd erupts, demanding Paul’s death, throwing off cloaks and flinging dust into the air. The commander orders Paul brought into the barracks and examined by flogging, but as they stretch him out, Paul asks the centurion whether it is lawful to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen. Alarmed, the commander, who had bought his own citizenship at great price, learns that Paul was born a citizen, and the interrogators withdraw. The next day the commander releases Paul’s bonds and brings him before the chief priests and the council to learn the charges. They listened to him until he said that; then they lifted up their voice and said, “Rid the earth of this fellow, for he isn’t fit to live!” Acts 22:22 As they cried out, threw off their cloaks, and threw dust into the air, Acts 22:23 the commanding officer commanded him to be brought into the barracks, ordering him to be examined by scourging, that he might know for what crime they shouted against him like that. Acts 22:24 When they had tied him up with straps, Paul asked the centurion who stood by, “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man who is a Roman, and not found guilty?” Acts 22:25 When the centurion heard it, he went to the commanding officer and told him, “Watch what you are about to do, for this man is a Roman!” Acts 22:26 The commanding officer came and asked him, “Tell me, are you a Roman?” He said, “Yes.” Acts 22:27 The commanding officer answered, “I bought my citizenship for a great price.” Paul said, “But I was born a Roman.” Acts 22:28 Immediately those who were about to examine him departed from him, and the commanding officer also was afraid when he realized that he was a Roman, because he had bound him. Acts 22:29 But on the next day, desiring to know the truth about why he was accused by the Jews, he freed him from the bonds and commanded the chief priests and all the council to come together, and brought Paul down and set him before them. Acts 22:30

title: Acts 23:1–11
context: Before the council Paul declares that he has lived in all good conscience before God, and the high priest Ananias orders him struck. Paul rebukes him as a whitewashed wall, then apologizes when told he is the high priest. Seeing the council divided between Sadducees and Pharisees, Paul declares he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and the dispute grows so violent that the commander removes him. That night the Lord stands by Paul and tells him to take courage, for as he has testified in Jerusalem, he must also testify in Rome.
text: Acts 23:1–11 Acts Before the council Paul declares that he has lived in all good conscience before God, and the high priest Ananias orders him struck. Paul rebukes him as a whitewashed wall, then apologizes when told he is the high priest. Seeing the council divided between Sadducees and Pharisees, Paul declares he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and the dispute grows so violent that the commander removes him. That night the Lord stands by Paul and tells him to take courage, for as he has testified in Jerusalem, he must also testify in Rome. Paul, looking steadfastly at the council, said, “Brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience until today.” Acts 23:1 The high priest, Ananias, commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth. Acts 23:2 Then Paul said to him, “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit to judge me according to the law, and command me to be struck contrary to the law?” Acts 23:3 Those who stood by said, “Do you malign God’s high priest?” Acts 23:4 Paul said, “I didn’t know, brothers, that he was high priest. For it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’” Acts 23:5 But when Paul perceived that the one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Men and brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged!” Acts 23:6 When he had said this, an argument arose between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the crowd was divided. Acts 23:7 For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit; but the Pharisees confess all of these. Acts 23:8 A great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ part stood up, and contended, saying, “We find no evil in this man. But if a spirit or angel has spoken to him, let’s not fight against God!” Acts 23:9 When a great argument arose, the commanding officer, fearing that Paul would be torn in pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him by force from among them and bring him into the barracks. Acts 23:10 The following night, the Lord stood by him and said, “Cheer up, Paul, for as you have testified about me at Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.” Acts 23:11

title: Acts 23:12–35
context: More than forty men vow not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul, planning an ambush with the chief priests’ help. Paul’s nephew hears of the plot and reports it to Paul and then to the commander. The commander sends Paul by night under heavy guard to Governor Felix in Caesarea, with a letter explaining that Paul is accused only over questions of Jewish law and has done nothing deserving death or chains. Felix agrees to hear the case when the accusers arrive and keeps Paul in Herod’s palace.
text: Acts 23:12–35 Acts More than forty men vow not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul, planning an ambush with the chief priests’ help. Paul’s nephew hears of the plot and reports it to Paul and then to the commander. The commander sends Paul by night under heavy guard to Governor Felix in Caesarea, with a letter explaining that Paul is accused only over questions of Jewish law and has done nothing deserving death or chains. Felix agrees to hear the case when the accusers arrive and keeps Paul in Herod’s palace. When it was day, some of the Jews banded together and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul. Acts 23:12 There were more than forty people who had made this conspiracy. Acts 23:13 They came to the chief priests and the elders, and said, “We have bound ourselves under a great curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul. Acts 23:14 Now therefore, you with the council inform the commanding officer that he should bring him down to you tomorrow, as though you were going to judge his case more exactly. We are ready to kill him before he comes near.” Acts 23:15 But Paul’s sister’s son heard they were lying in wait, and he came and entered into the barracks and told Paul. Acts 23:16 Paul summoned one of the centurions and said, “Bring this young man to the commanding officer, for he has something to tell him.” Acts 23:17 So he took him and brought him to the commanding officer and said, “Paul, the prisoner, summoned me and asked me to bring this young man to you. He has something to tell you.” Acts 23:18 The commanding officer took him by the hand, and going aside, asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?” Acts 23:19 He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though intending to inquire somewhat more accurately concerning him. Acts 23:20 Therefore don’t yield to them, for more than forty men lie in wait for him, who have bound themselves under a curse to neither eat nor drink until they have killed him. Now they are ready, looking for the promise from you.” Acts 23:21 So the commanding officer let the young man go, charging him, “Tell no one that you have revealed these things to me.” Acts 23:22 He called to himself two of the centurions, and said, “Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred men armed with spears, at the third hour of the night.” Acts 23:23 He asked them to provide mounts, that they might set Paul on one, and bring him safely to Felix the governor. Acts 23:24 He wrote a letter like this: Acts 23:25 “Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix: Greetings. Acts 23:26 “This man was seized by the Jews, and was about to be killed by them when I came with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman. Acts 23:27 Desiring to know the cause why they accused him, I brought him down to their council. Acts 23:28 I found him to be accused about questions of their law, but not to be charged with anything worthy of death or of imprisonment. Acts 23:29 When I was told that the Jews lay in wait for the man, I sent him to you immediately, charging his accusers also to bring their accusations against him before you. Farewell.” Acts 23:30 So the soldiers, carrying out their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. Acts 23:31 But on the next day they left the horsemen to go with him, and returned to the barracks. Acts 23:32 When they came to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul to him. Acts 23:33 When the governor had read it, he asked what province he was from. When he understood that he was from Cilicia, he said, Acts 23:34 “I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive.” He commanded that he be kept in Herod’s palace. Acts 23:35

title: Acts 24:1–27
context: Five days later the high priest and the orator Tertullus accuse Paul before Felix of being a troublemaker, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, and a temple profaner. Paul answers that he came to worship, caused no disturbance, and serves the God of his fathers according to the Way, believing the Law and Prophets and hoping in the resurrection of the just and unjust, striving always for a clear conscience. Felix, well informed about the Way, postpones the case. Later he and Drusilla hear Paul speak about faith in Christ, and when Paul reasons about righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix becomes afraid and sends him away. Hoping for a bribe, Felix keeps Paul in custody for two years.
text: Acts 24:1–27 Acts Five days later the high priest and the orator Tertullus accuse Paul before Felix of being a troublemaker, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, and a temple profaner. Paul answers that he came to worship, caused no disturbance, and serves the God of his fathers according to the Way, believing the Law and Prophets and hoping in the resurrection of the just and unjust, striving always for a clear conscience. Felix, well informed about the Way, postpones the case. Later he and Drusilla hear Paul speak about faith in Christ, and when Paul reasons about righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix becomes afraid and sends him away. Hoping for a bribe, Felix keeps Paul in custody for two years. After five days, the high priest, Ananias, came down with certain elders and an orator, one Tertullus. They informed the governor against Paul. Acts 24:1 When he was called, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying, “Seeing that by you we enjoy much peace, and that prosperity is coming to this nation by your foresight, Acts 24:2 we accept it in all ways and in all places, most excellent Felix, with all thankfulness. Acts 24:3 But that I don’t delay you, I entreat you to bear with us and hear a few words. Acts 24:4 For we have found this man to be a plague, an instigator of insurrections among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. Acts 24:5 He even tried to profane the temple, and we arrested him. Acts 24:6 By examining him yourself you may ascertain all these things of which we accuse him.” Acts 24:8 The Jews also joined in the attack, affirming that these things were so. Acts 24:9 When the governor had beckoned to him to speak, Paul answered, “Because I know that you have been a judge of this nation for many years, I cheerfully make my defense, Acts 24:10 seeing that you can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship at Jerusalem. Acts 24:11 In the temple they didn’t find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the synagogues or in the city. Acts 24:12 Nor can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me. Acts 24:13 But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, so I serve the God of our fathers, believing all things which are according to the law, and which are written in the prophets; Acts 24:14 having hope toward God, which these also themselves look for, that there will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust. Acts 24:15 In this I also practice always having a conscience void of offense toward God and men. Acts 24:16 Now after some years, I came to bring gifts for the needy to my nation, and offerings; Acts 24:17 amid which certain Jews from Asia found me purified in the temple, not with a mob, nor with turmoil. Acts 24:18 They ought to have been here before you and to make accusation if they had anything against me. Acts 24:19 Or else let these men themselves say what injustice they found in me when I stood before the council, Acts 24:20 unless it is for this one thing that I cried standing among them, ‘Concerning the resurrection of the dead I am being judged before you today!’” Acts 24:21 But Felix, having more exact knowledge concerning the Way, deferred them, saying, “When Lysias, the commanding officer, comes down, I will decide your case.” Acts 24:22 He ordered the centurion that Paul should be kept in custody and should have some privileges, and not to forbid any of his friends to serve him or to visit him. Acts 24:23 After some days, Felix came with Drusilla his wife, who was a Jewess, and sent for Paul and heard him concerning the faith in Christ Jesus. Acts 24:24 As he reasoned about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, Felix was terrified, and answered, “Go your way for this time, and when it is convenient for me, I will summon you.” Acts 24:25 Meanwhile, he also hoped that money would be given to him by Paul, that he might release him. Therefore also he sent for him more often and talked with him. Acts 24:26 But when two years were fulfilled, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus, and desiring to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul in bonds. Acts 24:27

title: Acts 25:1–27
context: The new governor Festus visits Jerusalem, where the chief priests ask him to bring Paul there, planning to ambush him. Festus hears the case in Caesarea, where the accusers bring serious but unproven charges. When Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asks whether Paul will stand trial in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, and Festus grants the appeal. King Agrippa and Bernice arrive, and Festus explains that the dispute concerns their religion and a dead man named Jesus whom Paul claims is alive. Agrippa asks to hear Paul, and the next day Festus presents him to the assembled dignitaries, admitting he has nothing definite to write to the emperor.
text: Acts 25:1–27 Acts The new governor Festus visits Jerusalem, where the chief priests ask him to bring Paul there, planning to ambush him. Festus hears the case in Caesarea, where the accusers bring serious but unproven charges. When Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asks whether Paul will stand trial in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, and Festus grants the appeal. King Agrippa and Bernice arrive, and Festus explains that the dispute concerns their religion and a dead man named Jesus whom Paul claims is alive. Agrippa asks to hear Paul, and the next day Festus presents him to the assembled dignitaries, admitting he has nothing definite to write to the emperor. Festus therefore, having come into the province, after three days went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. Acts 25:1 Then the high priest and the principal men of the Jews informed him against Paul, and they begged him, Acts 25:2 asking a favor against him, that he would summon him to Jerusalem, plotting to kill him on the way. Acts 25:3 However Festus answered that Paul should be kept in custody at Caesarea, and that he himself was about to depart shortly. Acts 25:4 “Let them therefore”, he said, “that are in power among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong in the man, let them accuse him.” Acts 25:5 When he had stayed among them more than ten days, he went down to Caesarea, and on the next day he sat on the judgment seat, and commanded Paul to be brought. Acts 25:6 When he had come, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing against him many and grievous charges which they could not prove, Acts 25:7 while he said in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar, have I sinned at all.” Acts 25:8 But Festus, desiring to gain favor with the Jews, answered Paul and said, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be judged by me there concerning these things?” Acts 25:9 But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be tried. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you also know very well. Acts 25:10 For if I have done wrong and have committed anything worthy of death, I don’t refuse to die; but if none of those things is true that they accuse me of, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar!” Acts 25:11 Then Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answered, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go.” Acts 25:12 Now when some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. Acts 25:13 As he stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a certain man left a prisoner by Felix; Acts 25:14 about whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, asking for a sentence against him. Acts 25:15 I answered them that it is not the custom of the Romans to give up any man to destruction before the accused has met the accusers face to face and has had opportunity to make his defense concerning the matter laid against him. Acts 25:16 When therefore they had come together here, I didn’t delay, but on the next day sat on the judgment seat and commanded the man to be brought. Acts 25:17 When the accusers stood up, they brought no charges against him of such things as I supposed; Acts 25:18 but had certain questions against him about their own religion and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive. Acts 25:19 Being perplexed how to inquire concerning these things, I asked whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and there be judged concerning these matters. Acts 25:20 But when Paul had appealed to be kept for the decision of the emperor, I commanded him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar.” Acts 25:21 Agrippa said to Festus, “I also would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” he said, “you shall hear him.” Acts 25:22 So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had come with great pomp, and they had entered into the place of hearing with the commanding officers and the principal men of the city, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. Acts 25:23 Festus said, “King Agrippa, and all men who are here present with us, you see this man about whom all the multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both at Jerusalem and here, crying that he ought not to live any longer. Acts 25:24 But when I found that he had committed nothing worthy of death, and as he himself appealed to the emperor, I determined to send him, Acts 25:25 of whom I have no certain thing to write to my lord. Therefore I have brought him out before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, that, after examination I may have something to write. Acts 25:26 For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to also specify the charges against him.” Acts 25:27

title: Acts 26:1–18
context: Given permission to speak, Paul tells King Agrippa that he has lived as a strict Pharisee and now stands on trial for the hope promised to the fathers, asking why it should seem incredible that God raises the dead. He describes how he once fiercely persecuted the saints, then recounts the light from heaven on the Damascus road and Jesus’ commission: to be a servant and witness, sent to the Gentiles to open their eyes, turn them from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, so that they receive forgiveness and a place among those sanctified by faith in Jesus.
text: Acts 26:1–18 Acts Given permission to speak, Paul tells King Agrippa that he has lived as a strict Pharisee and now stands on trial for the hope promised to the fathers, asking why it should seem incredible that God raises the dead. He describes how he once fiercely persecuted the saints, then recounts the light from heaven on the Damascus road and Jesus’ commission: to be a servant and witness, sent to the Gentiles to open their eyes, turn them from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, so that they receive forgiveness and a place among those sanctified by faith in Jesus. Agrippa said to Paul, “You may speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand, and made his defense. Acts 26:1 “I think myself happy, King Agrippa, that I am to make my defense before you today concerning all the things the Jews accuse me of, Acts 26:2 especially because you are expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews. Therefore I beg you to hear me patiently. Acts 26:3 “Indeed, all the Jews know my way of life from my youth up, which was from the beginning among my own nation and at Jerusalem; Acts 26:4 having known me from the first, if they are willing to testify, that after the strictest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee. Acts 26:5 Now I stand here to be judged for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers, Acts 26:6 which our twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hope to attain. Concerning this hope I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa! Acts 26:7 Why is it judged incredible with you if God does raise the dead? Acts 26:8 “I myself most certainly thought that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth. Acts 26:9 I also did this in Jerusalem. I both shut up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests; and when they were put to death I gave my vote against them. Acts 26:10 Punishing them often in all the synagogues, I tried to make them blaspheme. Being exceedingly enraged against them, I persecuted them even to foreign cities. Acts 26:11 “Whereupon as I traveled to Damascus with the authority and commission from the chief priests, Acts 26:12 at noon, O king, I saw on the way a light from the sky, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those who traveled with me. Acts 26:13 When we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ Acts 26:14 “I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ “He said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Acts 26:15 But arise, and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you a servant and a witness both of the things which you have seen and of the things which I will reveal to you; Acts 26:16 delivering you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you, Acts 26:17 to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive remission of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’ Acts 26:18

title: Acts 26:19–32
context: Paul says he was not disobedient to the heavenly vision but preached in Damascus, Jerusalem, Judea, and to the Gentiles that they should repent, turn to God, and do works worthy of repentance. For this he was seized, but with God’s help he stands testifying only what the prophets and Moses said: that the Christ would suffer, rise first from the dead, and proclaim light to Jews and Gentiles. Festus shouts that Paul is out of his mind, but Paul appeals to Agrippa, who asks whether Paul hopes to make him a Christian so quickly. Paul answers that he prays all his hearers would become as he is, except for the chains. The officials agree Paul could have been released had he not appealed to Caesar.
text: Acts 26:19–32 Acts Paul says he was not disobedient to the heavenly vision but preached in Damascus, Jerusalem, Judea, and to the Gentiles that they should repent, turn to God, and do works worthy of repentance. For this he was seized, but with God’s help he stands testifying only what the prophets and Moses said: that the Christ would suffer, rise first from the dead, and proclaim light to Jews and Gentiles. Festus shouts that Paul is out of his mind, but Paul appeals to Agrippa, who asks whether Paul hopes to make him a Christian so quickly. Paul answers that he prays all his hearers would become as he is, except for the chains. The officials agree Paul could have been released had he not appealed to Caesar. “Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, Acts 26:19 but declared first to them of Damascus, at Jerusalem, and throughout all the country of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance. Acts 26:20 For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. Acts 26:21 Having therefore obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen, Acts 26:22 how the Christ must suffer, and how, by the resurrection of the dead, he would be first to proclaim light both to these people and to the Gentiles.” Acts 26:23 As he thus made his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are crazy! Your great learning is driving you insane!” Acts 26:24 But he said, “I am not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reasonableness. Acts 26:25 For the king knows of these things, to whom also I speak freely. For I am persuaded that none of these things is hidden from him, for this has not been done in a corner. Acts 26:26 King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.” Acts 26:27 Agrippa said to Paul, “With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?” Acts 26:28 Paul said, “I pray to God, that whether with little or with much, not only you, but also all that hear me today, might become such as I am, except for these bonds.” Acts 26:29 The king rose up with the governor and Bernice, and those who sat with them. Acts 26:30 When they had withdrawn, they spoke to one another, saying, “This man does nothing worthy of death or of bonds.” Acts 26:31 Agrippa said to Festus, “This man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.” Acts 26:32

title: Acts 27:1–26
context: Paul sails for Italy as a prisoner under a centurion named Julius, who treats him kindly. Contrary winds slow the voyage, and at Fair Havens Paul warns that continuing will bring loss, but the centurion follows the pilot and owner. A violent northeaster drives the ship for days until all hope of rescue is abandoned. Paul then stands up and tells them to take heart: an angel of God has assured him that he must stand before Caesar and that God has granted him the lives of all who sail with him, though they will run aground on an island.
text: Acts 27:1–26 Acts Paul sails for Italy as a prisoner under a centurion named Julius, who treats him kindly. Contrary winds slow the voyage, and at Fair Havens Paul warns that continuing will bring loss, but the centurion follows the pilot and owner. A violent northeaster drives the ship for days until all hope of rescue is abandoned. Paul then stands up and tells them to take heart: an angel of God has assured him that he must stand before Caesar and that God has granted him the lives of all who sail with him, though they will run aground on an island. When it was determined that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan band. Acts 27:1 Embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to places on the coast of Asia, we put to sea, Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica being with us. Acts 27:2 The next day, we touched at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him permission to go to his friends and refresh himself. Acts 27:3 Putting to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary. Acts 27:4 When we had sailed across the sea which is off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia. Acts 27:5 There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy, and he put us on board. Acts 27:6 When we had sailed slowly many days, and had come with difficulty opposite Cnidus, the wind not allowing us further, we sailed under the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone. Acts 27:7 With difficulty sailing along it we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea. Acts 27:8 When much time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous because the Fast had now already gone by, Paul admonished them Acts 27:9 and said to them, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.” Acts 27:10 But the centurion gave more heed to the master and to the owner of the ship than to those things which were spoken by Paul. Acts 27:11 Because the haven was not suitable to winter in, the majority advised going to sea from there, if by any means they could reach Phoenix and winter there, which is a port of Crete, looking southwest and northwest. Acts 27:12 When the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to shore. Acts 27:13 But before long, a stormy wind beat down from shore, which is called Euroclydon. Acts 27:14 When the ship was caught and couldn’t face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along. Acts 27:15 Running under the lee of a small island called Clauda, we were able, with difficulty, to secure the boat. Acts 27:16 After they had hoisted it up, they used cables to help reinforce the ship. Fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis sand bars, they lowered the sea anchor, and so were driven along. Acts 27:17 As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard. Acts 27:18 On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands. Acts 27:19 When neither sun nor stars shone on us for many days, and no small storm pressed on us, all hope that we would be saved was now taken away. Acts 27:20 When they had been long without food, Paul stood up in the middle of them and said, “Sirs, you should have listened to me, and not have set sail from Crete and have gotten this injury and loss. Acts 27:21 Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. Acts 27:22 For there stood by me this night an angel, belonging to the God whose I am and whom I serve, Acts 27:23 saying, ‘Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. Behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’ Acts 27:24 Therefore, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me. Acts 27:25 But we must run aground on a certain island.” Acts 27:26

title: Acts 27:27–44
context: On the fourteenth night the sailors sense land and try to escape in the lifeboat, but Paul tells the centurion that unless they stay in the ship, the others cannot be saved, and the soldiers cut the boat loose. At dawn Paul urges everyone to eat, gives thanks to God before them all, and they are encouraged. The ship runs aground and breaks apart; the soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. Some swim and others float on planks, and all 276 reach land safely.
text: Acts 27:27–44 Acts On the fourteenth night the sailors sense land and try to escape in the lifeboat, but Paul tells the centurion that unless they stay in the ship, the others cannot be saved, and the soldiers cut the boat loose. At dawn Paul urges everyone to eat, gives thanks to God before them all, and they are encouraged. The ship runs aground and breaks apart; the soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. Some swim and others float on planks, and all 276 reach land safely. But when the fourteenth night had come, as we were driven back and forth in the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors surmised that they were drawing near to some land. Acts 27:27 They took soundings and found twenty fathoms. After a little while, they took soundings again, and found fifteen fathoms. Acts 27:28 Fearing that we would run aground on rocky ground, they let go four anchors from the stern, and wished for daylight. Acts 27:29 As the sailors were trying to flee out of the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they would lay out anchors from the bow, Acts 27:30 Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, “Unless these stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.” Acts 27:31 Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let it fall off. Acts 27:32 While the day was coming on, Paul begged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you wait and continue fasting, having taken nothing. Acts 27:33 Therefore I beg you to take some food, for this is for your safety; for not a hair will perish from any of your heads.” Acts 27:34 When he had said this and had taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all; then he broke it and began to eat. Acts 27:35 Then they all cheered up, and they also took food. Acts 27:36 In all, we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship. Acts 27:37 When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea. Acts 27:38 When it was day, they didn’t recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, and they decided to try to drive the ship onto it. Acts 27:39 Casting off the anchors, they left them in the sea, at the same time untying the rudder ropes. Hoisting up the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach. Acts 27:40 But coming to a place where two seas met, they ran the vessel aground. The bow struck and remained immovable, but the stern began to break up by the violence of the waves. Acts 27:41 The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim out and escape. Acts 27:42 But the centurion, desiring to save Paul, stopped them from their purpose, and commanded that those who could swim should throw themselves overboard first to go toward the land; Acts 27:43 and the rest should follow, some on planks and some on other things from the ship. So they all escaped safely to the land. Acts 27:44

title: Acts 28:1–16
context: The survivors find themselves on Malta, where the islanders show unusual kindness and build a fire. A viper fastens on Paul’s hand, and the islanders think he is a murderer pursued by justice, but when he shakes it off unharmed, they decide he is a god. Paul heals the father of Publius, the chief official, and many other sick islanders, and they honor the travelers and supply their needs. After three months they sail on to Italy, believers from Rome come out to meet them, and Paul thanks God and takes courage. In Rome he is allowed to live by himself with a soldier guarding him.
text: Acts 28:1–16 Acts The survivors find themselves on Malta, where the islanders show unusual kindness and build a fire. A viper fastens on Paul’s hand, and the islanders think he is a murderer pursued by justice, but when he shakes it off unharmed, they decide he is a god.
