Paul heals the father of Publius, the chief official, and many other sick islanders, and they honor the travelers and supply their needs. After three months they sail on to Italy, believers from Rome come out to meet them, and Paul thanks God and takes courage. In Rome he is allowed to live by himself with a soldier guarding him. When we had escaped, then they learned that the island was called Malta. Acts 28:1 The natives showed us uncommon kindness; for they kindled a fire and received us all, because of the present rain and because of the cold. Acts 28:2 But when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. Acts 28:3 When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has escaped from the sea, yet Justice has not allowed to live.” Acts 28:4 However he shook off the creature into the fire, and wasn’t harmed. Acts 28:5 But they expected that he would have swollen or fallen down dead suddenly, but when they watched for a long time and saw nothing bad happen to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god. Acts 28:6 Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and courteously entertained us for three days. Acts 28:7 The father of Publius lay sick of fever and dysentery. Paul entered in to him, prayed, and laying his hands on him, healed him. Acts 28:8 Then when this was done, the rest also who had diseases in the island came and were cured. Acts 28:9 They also honored us with many honors; and when we sailed, they put on board the things that we needed. Acts 28:10 After three months, we set sail in a ship of Alexandria which had wintered in the island, whose figurehead was “The Twin Brothers.” Acts 28:11 Touching at Syracuse, we stayed there three days. Acts 28:12 From there we circled around and arrived at Rhegium. After one day, a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli, Acts 28:13 where we found brothers, and were entreated to stay with them for seven days. So we came to Rome. Acts 28:14 From there the brothers, when they heard of us, came to meet us as far as The Market of Appius and The Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage. Acts 28:15 When we entered into Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard, but Paul was allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guarded him. Acts 28:16

title: Acts 28:17–31
context: Paul calls the Jewish leaders in Rome and explains that he is in chains for the hope of Israel, though he has done nothing against his people. They have heard nothing against him but want to hear about this sect that is spoken against everywhere. On an appointed day he explains from morning to evening about the kingdom of God, persuading them about Jesus from the Law and the Prophets. Some are persuaded and others disbelieve. As they leave, Paul quotes Isaiah’s words about a people who hear but do not understand and declares that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, who will listen. For two years Paul lives in his own rented house, welcoming all and proclaiming the kingdom and the Lord Jesus with boldness, without hindrance.
text: Acts 28:17–31 Acts Paul calls the Jewish leaders in Rome and explains that he is in chains for the hope of Israel, though he has done nothing against his people. They have heard nothing against him but want to hear about this sect that is spoken against everywhere. On an appointed day he explains from morning to evening about the kingdom of God, persuading them about Jesus from the Law and the Prophets. Some are persuaded and others disbelieve. As they leave, Paul quotes Isaiah’s words about a people who hear but do not understand and declares that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, who will listen. For two years Paul lives in his own rented house, welcoming all and proclaiming the kingdom and the Lord Jesus with boldness, without hindrance. After three days Paul called together those who were the leaders of the Jews. When they had come together, he said to them, “I, brothers, though I had done nothing against the people or the customs of our fathers, still was delivered prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans, Acts 28:17 who, when they had examined me, desired to set me free, because there was no cause of death in me. Acts 28:18 But when the Jews spoke against it, I was constrained to appeal to Caesar, not that I had anything about which to accuse my nation. Acts 28:19 For this cause therefore I asked to see you and to speak with you. For because of the hope of Israel I am bound with this chain.” Acts 28:20 They said to him, “We neither received letters from Judea concerning you, nor did any of the brothers come here and report or speak any evil of you. Acts 28:21 But we desire to hear from you what you think. For, as concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against.” Acts 28:22 When they had appointed him a day, many people came to him at his lodging. He explained to them, testifying about God’s Kingdom, and persuading them concerning Jesus, both from the law of Moses and from the prophets, from morning until evening. Acts 28:23 Some believed the things which were spoken, and some disbelieved. Acts 28:24 When they didn’t agree among themselves, they departed after Paul had spoken one message: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, Acts 28:25 saying, ‘Go to this people and say, in hearing, you will hear, but will in no way understand. In seeing, you will see, but will in no way perceive. Acts 28:26 For this people’s heart has grown callous. Their ears are dull of hearing. Their eyes they have closed. Lest they should see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again, then I would heal them.’ Acts 28:27 “Be it known therefore to you that the salvation of God is sent to the nations, and they will listen.” Acts 28:28 When he had said these words, the Jews departed, having a great dispute among themselves. Acts 28:29 Paul stayed two whole years in his own rented house and received all who were coming to him, Acts 28:30 preaching God’s Kingdom and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance. Acts 28:31

title: Acts 3:1–10
context: At the hour of prayer Peter and John meet a man lame from birth who begs at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. Peter has no money to give, but in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth he tells the man to walk and lifts him up. The man’s feet are made strong at once, and he enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God, while the people who knew him are filled with wonder.
text: Acts 3:1–10 Acts At the hour of prayer Peter and John meet a man lame from birth who begs at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. Peter has no money to give, but in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth he tells the man to walk and lifts him up. The man’s feet are made strong at once, and he enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God, while the people who knew him are filled with wonder. Peter and John were going up into the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. Acts 3:1 A certain man who was lame from his mother’s womb was being carried, whom they laid daily at the door of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask gifts for the needy of those who entered into the temple. Acts 3:2 Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive gifts for the needy. Acts 3:3 Peter, fastening his eyes on him, with John, said, “Look at us.” Acts 3:4 He listened to them, expecting to receive something from them. Acts 3:5 But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!” Acts 3:6 He took him by the right hand and raised him up. Immediately his feet and his ankle bones received strength. Acts 3:7 Leaping up, he stood and began to walk. He entered with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God. Acts 3:8 All the people saw him walking and praising God. Acts 3:9 They recognized him, that it was he who used to sit begging for gifts for the needy at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. They were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. Acts 3:10

title: Acts 3:11–26
context: As a crowd gathers in Solomon’s Porch, Peter denies that the healing came from his own power or piety. The God of Abraham has glorified his servant Jesus, whom the people denied and killed, but whom God raised. Faith in Jesus’ name has made the man whole. Peter grants that they acted in ignorance and that God fulfilled the prophets’ word that the Christ would suffer, then calls them to repent and turn so their sins may be blotted out. Jesus is the prophet Moses promised, and God sent him first to Israel to bless them by turning each one from wickedness.
text: Acts 3:11–26 Acts As a crowd gathers in Solomon’s Porch, Peter denies that the healing came from his own power or piety. The God of Abraham has glorified his servant Jesus, whom the people denied and killed, but whom God raised. Faith in Jesus’ name has made the man whole. Peter grants that they acted in ignorance and that God fulfilled the prophets’ word that the Christ would suffer, then calls them to repent and turn so their sins may be blotted out. Jesus is the prophet Moses promised, and God sent him first to Israel to bless them by turning each one from wickedness. As the lame man who was healed held on to Peter and John, all the people ran together to them in the porch that is called Solomon’s, greatly wondering. Acts 3:11 When Peter saw it, he responded to the people, “You men of Israel, why do you marvel at this man? Why do you fasten your eyes on us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk? Acts 3:12 The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Servant Jesus, whom you delivered up and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had determined to release him. Acts 3:13 But you denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, Acts 3:14 and killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead, to which we are witnesses. Acts 3:15 By faith in his name, his name has made this man strong, whom you see and know. Yes, the faith which is through him has given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all. Acts 3:16 “Now, brothers, I know that you did this in ignorance, as did also your rulers. Acts 3:17 But the things which God announced by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he thus fulfilled. Acts 3:18 “Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out, so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord, Acts 3:19 and that he may send Christ Jesus, who was ordained for you before, Acts 3:20 whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things, which God spoke long ago by the mouth of his holy prophets. Acts 3:21 For Moses indeed said to the fathers, ‘The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him in all things whatever he says to you. Acts 3:22 It will be that every soul that will not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed from among the people.’ Acts 3:23 Yes, and all the prophets from Samuel and those who followed after, as many as have spoken, also told of these days. Acts 3:24 You are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘All the families of the earth will be blessed through your offspring.’ Acts 3:25 God, having raised up his servant Jesus, sent him to you first to bless you, in turning away every one of you from your wickedness.” Acts 3:26

title: Acts 4:1–22
context: The priests, the temple captain, and the Sadducees arrest Peter and John for proclaiming the resurrection in Jesus, yet about five thousand men believe. The next day, before the council, Peter, filled with the Spirit, declares that the lame man was healed in the name of Jesus Christ, whom they crucified and God raised, the rejected stone now made the cornerstone, and that salvation is found in no other name. The rulers are astonished at the boldness of these unschooled men. Unable to deny the miracle, they order them to stop speaking in Jesus’ name, but Peter and John answer that they must obey God and cannot stop telling what they have seen and heard.
text: Acts 4:1–22 Acts The priests, the temple captain, and the Sadducees arrest Peter and John for proclaiming the resurrection in Jesus, yet about five thousand men believe. The next day, before the council, Peter, filled with the Spirit, declares that the lame man was healed in the name of Jesus Christ, whom they crucified and God raised, the rejected stone now made the cornerstone, and that salvation is found in no other name. The rulers are astonished at the boldness of these unschooled men. Unable to deny the miracle, they order them to stop speaking in Jesus’ name, but Peter and John answer that they must obey God and cannot stop telling what they have seen and heard. As they spoke to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came to them, Acts 4:1 being upset because they taught the people and proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. Acts 4:2 They laid hands on them, and put them in custody until the next day, for it was now evening. Acts 4:3 But many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to be about five thousand. Acts 4:4 In the morning, their rulers, elders, and scribes were gathered together in Jerusalem. Acts 4:5 Annas the high priest was there, with Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and as many as were relatives of the high priest. Acts 4:6 When they had stood Peter and John in the middle of them, they inquired, “By what power, or in what name, have you done this?” Acts 4:7 Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “You rulers of the people and elders of Israel, Acts 4:8 if we are examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed, Acts 4:9 may it be known to you all, and to all the people of Israel, that in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, this man stands here before you whole in him. Acts 4:10 He is ‘the stone which was regarded as worthless by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner.’ Acts 4:11 There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that is given among men, by which we must be saved!” Acts 4:12 Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus. Acts 4:13 Seeing the man who was healed standing with them, they could say nothing against it. Acts 4:14 But when they had commanded them to go aside out of the council, they conferred among themselves, Acts 4:15 saying, “What shall we do to these men? Because indeed a notable miracle has been done through them, as can be plainly seen by all who dwell in Jerusalem, and we can’t deny it. Acts 4:16 But so that this spreads no further among the people, let’s threaten them, that from now on they don’t speak to anyone in this name.” Acts 4:17 They called them, and commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus. Acts 4:18 But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves, Acts 4:19 for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.” Acts 4:20 When they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people; for everyone glorified God for that which was done. Acts 4:21 For the man on whom this miracle of healing was performed was more than forty years old. Acts 4:22

title: Acts 4:23–37
context: Released, Peter and John report to the believers, who pray together to the sovereign Lord, Creator of all. Quoting Psalm 2, they acknowledge that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and Israel gathered against Jesus to do what God’s hand and counsel had foreordained. They ask not for safety but for boldness to speak and for God to stretch out his hand to heal. The place shakes, they are filled with the Spirit and speak boldly. The believers are of one heart and soul, sharing everything so that no one is in need, and Barnabas sells a field and brings the money to the apostles.
text: Acts 4:23–37 Acts Released, Peter and John report to the believers, who pray together to the sovereign Lord, Creator of all. Quoting Psalm 2, they acknowledge that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and Israel gathered against Jesus to do what God’s hand and counsel had foreordained. They ask not for safety but for boldness to speak and for God to stretch out his hand to heal. The place shakes, they are filled with the Spirit and speak boldly. The believers are of one heart and soul, sharing everything so that no one is in need, and Barnabas sells a field and brings the money to the apostles. Being let go, they came to their own company and reported all that the chief priests and the elders had said to them. Acts 4:23 When they heard it, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord and said, “O Lord, you are God, who made the sky, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them; Acts 4:24 who by the mouth of your servant David, said, ‘Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing? Acts 4:25 The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers plot together, against the Lord, and against his Christ.’ Acts 4:26 “For truly, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, Acts 4:27 to do whatever your hand and your counsel foreordained to happen. Acts 4:28 Now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness, Acts 4:29 while you stretch out your hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus.” Acts 4:30 When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness. Acts 4:31 The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul. Not one of them claimed that anything of the things which he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common. Acts 4:32 With great power, the apostles gave their testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. Great grace was on them all. Acts 4:33 For neither was there among them any who lacked, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them, and brought the proceeds of the things that were sold, Acts 4:34 and laid them at the apostles’ feet; and distribution was made to each, according as anyone had need. Acts 4:35 Joses, who by the apostles was also called Barnabas (which is, being interpreted, Son of Encouragement), a Levite, a man of Cyprus by race, Acts 4:36 having a field, sold it and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet. Acts 4:37

title: Acts 5:1–16
context: Ananias and Sapphira sell property, keep back part of the price, and present the rest as if it were the whole. Peter tells Ananias he has lied not to men but to the Holy Spirit, and he falls dead; three hours later Sapphira repeats the lie and dies as well, and great fear comes on the church. The apostles perform many signs, the people hold them in high regard, and multitudes of men and women believe. The sick are carried into the streets in the hope that Peter’s shadow might fall on them, and crowds from nearby towns bring the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits, and all are healed.
text: Acts 5:1–16 Acts Ananias and Sapphira sell property, keep back part of the price, and present the rest as if it were the whole. Peter tells Ananias he has lied not to men but to the Holy Spirit, and he falls dead; three hours later Sapphira repeats the lie and dies as well, and great fear comes on the church. The apostles perform many signs, the people hold them in high regard, and multitudes of men and women believe. The sick are carried into the streets in the hope that Peter’s shadow might fall on them, and crowds from nearby towns bring the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits, and all are healed. But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession, Acts 5:1 and kept back part of the price, his wife also being aware of it, then brought a certain part and laid it at the apostles’ feet. Acts 5:2 But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back part of the price of the land? Acts 5:3 While you kept it, didn’t it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power? How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven’t lied to men, but to God.” Acts 5:4 Ananias, hearing these words, fell down and died. Great fear came on all who heard these things. Acts 5:5 The young men arose and wrapped him up, and they carried him out and buried him. Acts 5:6 About three hours later, his wife, not knowing what had happened, came in. Acts 5:7 Peter answered her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” She said, “Yes, for so much.” Acts 5:8 But Peter asked her, “How is it that you have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.” Acts 5:9 She fell down immediately at his feet and died. The young men came in and found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her by her husband. Acts 5:10 Great fear came on the whole assembly, and on all who heard these things. Acts 5:11 By the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were done among the people. They were all with one accord in Solomon’s porch. Acts 5:12 None of the rest dared to join them; however, the people honored them. Acts 5:13 More believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women. Acts 5:14 They even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mattresses, so that as Peter came by, at least his shadow might overshadow some of them. Acts 5:15 The multitude also came together from the cities around Jerusalem, bringing sick people and those who were tormented by unclean spirits; and they were all healed. Acts 5:16

title: Acts 5:17–42
context: Jealous, the high priest and Sadducees jail the apostles, but an angel opens the prison at night and sends them to preach in the temple. Brought before the council and charged with defying its order, Peter answers that they must obey God rather than men: God raised and exalted Jesus as Prince and Savior to give Israel repentance and forgiveness, and the apostles and the Holy Spirit are witnesses. The council wants to kill them, but Gamaliel advises caution: if this movement is of men it will fail, but if it is of God, they cannot overthrow it. The apostles are beaten and released, rejoicing to suffer for the Name, and keep teaching daily.
text: Acts 5:17–42 Acts Jealous, the high priest and Sadducees jail the apostles, but an angel opens the prison at night and sends them to preach in the temple. Brought before the council and charged with defying its order, Peter answers that they must obey God rather than men: God raised and exalted Jesus as Prince and Savior to give Israel repentance and forgiveness, and the apostles and the Holy Spirit are witnesses. The council wants to kill them, but Gamaliel advises caution: if this movement is of men it will fail, but if it is of God, they cannot overthrow it. The apostles are beaten and released, rejoicing to suffer for the Name, and keep teaching daily. But the high priest rose up, and all those who were with him (which is the sect of the Sadducees), and they were filled with jealousy Acts 5:17 and laid hands on the apostles, then put them in public custody. Acts 5:18 But an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night, and brought them out and said, Acts 5:19 “Go stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.” Acts 5:20 When they heard this, they entered into the temple about daybreak and taught. But the high priest and those who were with him came and called the council together, with all the senate of the children of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought. Acts 5:21 But the officers who came didn’t find them in the prison. They returned and reported, Acts 5:22 “We found the prison shut and locked, and the guards standing before the doors, but when we opened them, we found no one inside!” Acts 5:23 Now when the high priest, the captain of the temple, and the chief priests heard these words, they were very perplexed about them and what might become of this. Acts 5:24 One came and told them, “Behold, the men whom you put in prison are in the temple, standing and teaching the people.” Acts 5:25 Then the captain went with the officers, and brought them without violence, for they were afraid that the people might stone them. Acts 5:26 When they had brought them, they set them before the council. The high priest questioned them, Acts 5:27 saying, “Didn’t we strictly command you not to teach in this name? Behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and intend to bring this man’s blood on us.” Acts 5:28 But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men. Acts 5:29 The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree. Acts 5:30 God exalted him with his right hand to be a Prince and a Savior, to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins. Acts 5:31 We are his witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.” Acts 5:32 But they, when they heard this, were cut to the heart, and were determined to kill them. Acts 5:33 But one stood up in the council, a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, honored by all the people, and commanded to put the apostles out for a little while. Acts 5:34 He said to them, “You men of Israel, be careful concerning these men, what you are about to do. Acts 5:35 For before these days Theudas rose up, making himself out to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves. He was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were dispersed and came to nothing. Acts 5:36 After this man, Judas of Galilee rose up in the days of the enrollment, and drew away some people after him. He also perished, and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered abroad. Acts 5:37 Now I tell you, withdraw from these men and leave them alone. For if this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown. Acts 5:38 But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, and you would be found even to be fighting against God!” Acts 5:39 They agreed with him. Summoning the apostles, they beat them and commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. Acts 5:40 They therefore departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name. Acts 5:41 Every day, in the temple and at home, they never stopped teaching and preaching Jesus, the Christ. Acts 5:42

title: Acts 6:1–15
context: As the church grows, Greek-speaking Jewish believers complain that their widows are overlooked in the daily distribution. The twelve ask the believers to choose seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom to oversee the work, so the apostles can devote themselves to prayer and the word. The seven, including Stephen and Philip, are set before the apostles, who pray and lay hands on them, and the word spreads, with many priests coming to faith. Stephen, full of grace and power, does great signs, and when opponents cannot withstand his wisdom, they bring false witnesses who accuse him of speaking against the temple and the law. The council sees his face like the face of an angel.
text: Acts 6:1–15 Acts As the church grows, Greek-speaking Jewish believers complain that their widows are overlooked in the daily distribution. The twelve ask the believers to choose seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom to oversee the work, so the apostles can devote themselves to prayer and the word. The seven, including Stephen and Philip, are set before the apostles, who pray and lay hands on them, and the word spreads, with many priests coming to faith. Stephen, full of grace and power, does great signs, and when opponents cannot withstand his wisdom, they bring false witnesses who accuse him of speaking against the temple and the law. The council sees his face like the face of an angel. Now in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplying, a complaint arose from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily service. Acts 6:1 The twelve summoned the multitude of the disciples and said, “It is not appropriate for us to forsake the word of God and serve tables. Acts 6:2 Therefore, select from among you, brothers, seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business. Acts 6:3 But we will continue steadfastly in prayer and in the ministry of the word.” Acts 6:4 These words pleased the whole multitude. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch, Acts 6:5 whom they set before the apostles. When they had prayed, they laid their hands on them. Acts 6:6 The word of God increased and the number of the disciples greatly multiplied in Jerusalem. A great company of the priests were obedient to the faith. Acts 6:7 Stephen, full of faith and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. Acts 6:8 But some of those who were of the synagogue called “The Libertines”, and of the Cyrenians, of the Alexandrians, and of those of Cilicia and Asia arose, disputing with Stephen. Acts 6:9 They weren’t able to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke. Acts 6:10 Then they secretly induced men to say, “We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God.” Acts 6:11 They stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes, and came against him and seized him, then brought him in to the council, Acts 6:12 and set up false witnesses who said, “This man never stops speaking blasphemous words against this holy place and the law. Acts 6:13 For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place, and will change the customs which Moses delivered to us.” Acts 6:14 All who sat in the council, fastening their eyes on him, saw his face like it was the face of an angel. Acts 6:15

title: Acts 7:1–29
context: Asked by the high priest whether the charges are true, Stephen retells Israel’s story. The God of glory appeared to Abraham outside the land, promised it to his offspring, and foretold their slavery and rescue. The patriarchs sold Joseph out of jealousy, yet God was with him and used him to save the family in famine. When Israel multiplied in Egypt and was oppressed, Moses was born, raised in Pharaoh’s house, and later tried to defend his people, but they did not understand that God meant to deliver them through him, and he fled to Midian.
text: Acts 7:1–29 Acts Asked by the high priest whether the charges are true, Stephen retells Israel’s story. The God of glory appeared to Abraham outside the land, promised it to his offspring, and foretold their slavery and rescue. The patriarchs sold Joseph out of jealousy, yet God was with him and used him to save the family in famine. When Israel multiplied in Egypt and was oppressed, Moses was born, raised in Pharaoh’s house, and later tried to defend his people, but they did not understand that God meant to deliver them through him, and he fled to Midian. The high priest said, “Are these things so?” Acts 7:1 He said, “Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran, Acts 7:2 and said to him, ‘Get out of your land and away from your relatives, and come into a land which I will show you.’ Acts 7:3 Then he came out of the land of the Chaldaeans and lived in Haran. From there, when his father was dead, God moved him into this land where you are now living. Acts 7:4 He gave him no inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on. He promised that he would give it to him for a possession, and to his offspring after him, when he still had no child. Acts 7:5 God spoke in this way: that his offspring would live as aliens in a strange land, and that they would be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years. Acts 7:6 ‘I will judge the nation to which they will be in bondage,’ said God, ‘and after that they will come out and serve me in this place.’ Acts 7:7 He gave him the covenant of circumcision. So Abraham became the father of Isaac, and circumcised him the eighth day. Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob became the father of the twelve patriarchs. Acts 7:8 “The patriarchs, moved with jealousy against Joseph, sold him into Egypt. God was with him Acts 7:9 and delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He made him governor over Egypt and all his house. Acts 7:10 Now a famine came over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction. Our fathers found no food. Acts 7:11 But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent out our fathers the first time. Acts 7:12 On the second time Joseph was made known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family was revealed to Pharaoh. Acts 7:13 Joseph sent and summoned Jacob his father and all his relatives, seventy-five souls. Acts 7:14 Jacob went down into Egypt and he died, himself and our fathers; Acts 7:15 and they were brought back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham bought for a price in silver from the children of Hamor of Shechem. Acts 7:16 “But as the time of the promise came close which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt, Acts 7:17 until there arose a different king who didn’t know Joseph. Acts 7:18 The same took advantage of our race and mistreated our fathers, and forced them to abandon their babies, so that they wouldn’t stay alive. Acts 7:19 At that time Moses was born, and was exceedingly handsome to God. He was nourished three months in his father’s house. Acts 7:20 When he was abandoned, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up and reared him as her own son. Acts 7:21 Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. He was mighty in his words and works. Acts 7:22 But when he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. Acts 7:23 Seeing one of them suffer wrong, he defended him and avenged him who was oppressed, striking the Egyptian. Acts 7:24 He supposed that his brothers understood that God, by his hand, was giving them deliverance; but they didn’t understand. Acts 7:25 “The day following, he appeared to them as they fought, and urged them to be at peace again, saying, ‘Sirs, you are brothers. Why do you wrong one another?’ Acts 7:26 But he who did his neighbor wrong pushed him away, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Acts 7:27 Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’ Acts 7:28 Moses fled at this saying, and became a stranger in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons. Acts 7:29

title: Acts 7:30–53
context: Forty years later God speaks to Moses from a burning bush in the wilderness, calls the ground holy, and sends him to deliver Israel. The same Moses whom the people rejected became their ruler and deliverer, led them out with signs, received living words at Sinai, and foretold a prophet like himself. Yet the fathers refused him, turned to the golden calf, and later worshiped the host of heaven. Israel had the tabernacle and later Solomon’s temple, but the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. Stephen ends by charging his hearers with resisting the Holy Spirit as their fathers did, betraying and murdering the Righteous One, and failing to keep the law they received.
text: Acts 7:30–53 Acts Forty years later God speaks to Moses from a burning bush in the wilderness, calls the ground holy, and sends him to deliver Israel. The same Moses whom the people rejected became their ruler and deliverer, led them out with signs, received living words at Sinai, and foretold a prophet like himself. Yet the fathers refused him, turned to the golden calf, and later worshiped the host of heaven. Israel had the tabernacle and later Solomon’s temple, but the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. Stephen ends by charging his hearers with resisting the Holy Spirit as their fathers did, betraying and murdering the Righteous One, and failing to keep the law they received. “When forty years were fulfilled, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a flame of fire in a bush. Acts 7:30 When Moses saw it, he wondered at the sight. As he came close to see, the voice of the Lord came to him, Acts 7:31 ‘I am the God of your fathers: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’ Moses trembled and dared not look. Acts 7:32 The Lord said to him, ‘Take off your sandals, for the place where you stand is holy ground. Acts 7:33 I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and have heard their groaning. I have come down to deliver them. Now come, I will send you into Egypt.’ Acts 7:34 “This Moses whom they refused, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and a judge?’—God has sent him as both a ruler and a deliverer by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. Acts 7:35 This man led them out, having worked wonders and signs in Egypt, in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years. Acts 7:36 This is that Moses who said to the children of Israel, ‘The Lord our God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me.’ Acts 7:37 This is he who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel that spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, who received living revelations to give to us, Acts 7:38 to whom our fathers wouldn’t be obedient, but rejected him and turned back in their hearts to Egypt, Acts 7:39 saying to Aaron, ‘Make us gods that will go before us, for as for this Moses who led us out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.’ Acts 7:40 They made a calf in those days, and brought a sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their hands. Acts 7:41 But God turned away and gave them up to serve the army of the sky, as it is written in the book of the prophets, ‘Did you offer to me slain animals and sacrifices forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? Acts 7:42 You took up the tabernacle of Moloch, the star of your god Rephan, the figures which you made to worship, so I will carry you away beyond Babylon.’ Acts 7:43 “Our fathers had the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness, even as he who spoke to Moses commanded him to make it according to the pattern that he had seen; Acts 7:44 which also our fathers, in their turn, brought in with Joshua when they entered into the possession of the nations whom God drove out before the face of our fathers to the days of David, Acts 7:45 who found favor in the sight of God, and asked to find a habitation for the God of Jacob. Acts 7:46 But Solomon built him a house. Acts 7:47 However, the Most High doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands, as the prophet says, Acts 7:48 ‘heaven is my throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build me?’ says the Lord. ‘Or what is the place of my rest? Acts 7:49 Didn’t my hand make all these things?’ Acts 7:50 “You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit! As your fathers did, so you do. Acts 7:51 Which of the prophets didn’t your fathers persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, of whom you have now become betrayers and murderers. Acts 7:52 You received the law as it was ordained by angels, and didn’t keep it!” Acts 7:53

title: Acts 7:54–60
context: Enraged, the council grinds their teeth at Stephen. Full of the Holy Spirit, he sees the glory of God and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. They cover their ears, drive him out of the city, and stone him, laying their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. Stephen commits his spirit to the Lord Jesus and prays that this sin not be held against them, then falls asleep.
text: Acts 7:54–60 Acts Enraged, the council grinds their teeth at Stephen. Full of the Holy Spirit, he sees the glory of God and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. They cover their ears, drive him out of the city, and stone him, laying their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. Stephen commits his spirit to the Lord Jesus and prays that this sin not be held against them, then falls asleep. Now when they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed at him with their teeth. Acts 7:54 But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God, Acts 7:55 and said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!” Acts 7:56 But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears, then rushed at him with one accord. Acts 7:57 They threw him out of the city and stoned him. The witnesses placed their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. Acts 7:58 They stoned Stephen as he called out, saying, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!” Acts 7:59 He kneeled down and cried with a loud voice, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” When he had said this, he fell asleep. Acts 7:60

title: Acts 8:1–25
context: Saul approves of Stephen’s death, and a severe persecution scatters the believers through Judea and Samaria, while Saul ravages the church. The scattered believers preach the word, and Philip proclaims Christ in Samaria, where signs and healings bring great joy. Simon, a sorcerer the Samaritans revered, also believes and is baptized. When Peter and John come and pray, the Samaritans receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. Simon offers money for this power, and Peter rebukes him sharply and calls him to repent.
text: Acts 8:1–25 Acts Saul approves of Stephen’s death, and a severe persecution scatters the believers through Judea and Samaria, while Saul ravages the church. The scattered believers preach the word, and Philip proclaims Christ in Samaria, where signs and healings bring great joy. Simon, a sorcerer the Samaritans revered, also believes and is baptized. When Peter and John come and pray, the Samaritans receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. Simon offers money for this power, and Peter rebukes him sharply and calls him to repent. Saul was consenting to his death. A great persecution arose against the assembly which was in Jerusalem in that day. They were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles. Acts 8:1 Devout men buried Stephen and lamented greatly over him. Acts 8:2 But Saul ravaged the assembly, entering into every house and dragged both men and women off to prison. Acts 8:3 Therefore those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word. Acts 8:4 Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ. Acts 8:5 The multitudes listened with one accord to the things that were spoken by Philip when they heard and saw the signs which he did. Acts 8:6 For unclean spirits came out of many of those who had them. They came out, crying with a loud voice. Many who had been paralyzed and lame were healed. Acts 8:7 There was great joy in that city. Acts 8:8 But there was a certain man, Simon by name, who used to practice sorcery in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, making himself out to be some great one, Acts 8:9 to whom they all listened, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is that great power of God.” Acts 8:10 They listened to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his sorceries. Acts 8:11 But when they believed Philip preaching good news concerning God’s Kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Acts 8:12 Simon himself also believed. Being baptized, he continued with Philip. Seeing signs and great miracles occurring, he was amazed. Acts 8:13 Now when the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them, Acts 8:14 who, when they had come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit; Acts 8:15 for as yet he had fallen on none of them. They had only been baptized in the name of Christ Jesus. Acts 8:16 Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit. Acts 8:17 Now when Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, Acts 8:18 saying, “Give me also this power, that whomever I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.” Acts 8:19 But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! Acts 8:20 You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart isn’t right before God. Acts 8:21 Repent therefore of this, your wickedness, and ask God if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. Acts 8:22 For I see that you are in the poison of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity.” Acts 8:23 Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that none of the things which you have spoken happen to me.” Acts 8:24 They therefore, when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, and preached the Good News to many villages of the Samaritans. Acts 8:25

title: Acts 8:26–40
context: An angel sends Philip to the desert road toward Gaza, where an Ethiopian official, treasurer to the queen, is returning from worship in Jerusalem and reading Isaiah. Prompted by the Spirit, Philip asks whether he understands, and the man invites him to explain the passage about the sheep led to slaughter. Philip tells him the good news about Jesus. When they come to water, the eunuch is baptized, and the Spirit carries Philip away. The official goes on his way rejoicing, and Philip preaches in the towns up to Caesarea.
text: Acts 8:26–40 Acts An angel sends Philip to the desert road toward Gaza, where an Ethiopian official, treasurer to the queen, is returning from worship in Jerusalem and reading Isaiah. Prompted by the Spirit, Philip asks whether he understands, and the man invites him to explain the passage about the sheep led to slaughter. Philip tells him the good news about Jesus. When they come to water, the eunuch is baptized, and the Spirit carries Philip away. The official goes on his way rejoicing, and Philip preaches in the towns up to Caesarea. Then an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Arise, and go toward the south to the way that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. This is a desert.” Acts 8:26 He arose and went; and behold, there was a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship. Acts 8:27 He was returning and sitting in his chariot, and was reading the prophet Isaiah. Acts 8:28 The Spirit said to Philip, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.” Acts 8:29 Philip ran to him, and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, “Do you understand what you are reading?” Acts 8:30 He said, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” He begged Philip to come up and sit with him. Acts 8:31 Now the passage of the Scripture which he was reading was this, “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter. As a lamb before his shearer is silent, so he doesn’t open his mouth. Acts 8:32 In his humiliation, his judgment was taken away. Who will declare His generation? For his life is taken from the earth.” Acts 8:33 The eunuch answered Philip, “Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?” Acts 8:34 Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus. Acts 8:35 As they went on the way, they came to some water; and the eunuch said, “Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?” Acts 8:36 He commanded the chariot to stand still, and they both went down into the water, both Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. Acts 8:38 When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch didn’t see him any more, for he went on his way rejoicing. Acts 8:39 But Philip was found at Azotus. Passing through, he preached the Good News to all the cities until he came to Caesarea. Acts 8:40

title: Acts 9:1–19
context: Saul, still breathing threats against the disciples, obtains letters to arrest followers of the Way in Damascus. Near the city a light from heaven flashes around him, and he hears Jesus ask why Saul is persecuting him. Blinded, Saul is led into Damascus and fasts for three days. The Lord sends a reluctant Ananias to him, calling Saul a chosen vessel to carry his name to Gentiles, kings, and Israel. Ananias lays hands on him, Saul regains his sight, is filled with the Spirit, and is baptized.
text: Acts 9:1–19 Acts Saul, still breathing threats against the disciples, obtains letters to arrest followers of the Way in Damascus. Near the city a light from heaven flashes around him, and he hears Jesus ask why Saul is persecuting him. Blinded, Saul is led into Damascus and fasts for three days. The Lord sends a reluctant Ananias to him, calling Saul a chosen vessel to carry his name to Gentiles, kings, and Israel. Ananias lays hands on him, Saul regains his sight, is filled with the Spirit, and is baptized. But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest Acts 9:1 and asked for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. Acts 9:2 As he traveled, he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him. Acts 9:3 He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” Acts 9:4 He said, “Who are you, Lord?” The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Acts 9:5 But rise up and enter into the city, then you will be told what you must do.” Acts 9:6 The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one. Acts 9:7 Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one. They led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. Acts 9:8 He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank. Acts 9:9 Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!” He said, “Behold, it’s me, Lord.” Acts 9:10 The Lord said to him, “Arise and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judah for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying, Acts 9:11 and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.” Acts 9:12 But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem. Acts 9:13 Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” Acts 9:14 But the Lord said to him, “Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel. Acts 9:15 For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.” Acts 9:16 Ananias departed and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me that you may receive your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Acts 9:17 Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized. Acts 9:18 He took food and was strengthened. Saul stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus. Acts 9:19

title: Acts 9:20–31
context: Saul immediately proclaims in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God, astonishing those who knew why he came. He grows stronger and confounds the Jews of Damascus, who plot to kill him, but the disciples lower him over the wall in a basket. In Jerusalem the disciples fear him until Barnabas vouches for him. He speaks boldly and debates the Hellenists, who also try to kill him, so the believers send him to Tarsus. The church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria has peace and multiplies.
text: Acts 9:20–31 Acts Saul immediately proclaims in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God, astonishing those who knew why he came. He grows stronger and confounds the Jews of Damascus, who plot to kill him, but the disciples lower him over the wall in a basket. In Jerusalem the disciples fear him until Barnabas vouches for him. He speaks boldly and debates the Hellenists, who also try to kill him, so the believers send him to Tarsus. The church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria has peace and multiplies. Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God. Acts 9:20 All who heard him were amazed, and said, “Isn’t this he who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who called on this name? And he had come here intending to bring them bound before the chief priests!” Acts 9:21 But Saul increased more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived at Damascus, proving that this is the Christ. Acts 9:22 When many days were fulfilled, the Jews conspired together to kill him, Acts 9:23 but their plot became known to Saul. They watched the gates both day and night that they might kill him, Acts 9:24 but his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket. Acts 9:25 When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. Acts 9:26 But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. Acts 9:27 He was with them entering into Jerusalem, Acts 9:28 preaching boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus. He spoke and disputed against the Hellenists, but they were seeking to kill him. Acts 9:29 When the brothers knew it, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. Acts 9:30 So the assemblies throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace and were built up. They were multiplied, walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit. Acts 9:31

title: Acts 9:32–43
context: Peter travels among the believers and comes to Lydda, where he heals Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, in the name of Jesus Christ, and the residents of Lydda and Sharon turn to the Lord. In nearby Joppa the disciple Tabitha, known for good works and charity, dies. The believers send for Peter, who prays and tells her to rise, and she comes back to life. Many in Joppa believe, and Peter stays there with Simon the tanner.
text: Acts 9:32–43 Acts Peter travels among the believers and comes to Lydda, where he heals Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, in the name of Jesus Christ, and the residents of Lydda and Sharon turn to the Lord. In nearby Joppa the disciple Tabitha, known for good works and charity, dies. The believers send for Peter, who prays and tells her to rise, and she comes back to life. Many in Joppa believe, and Peter stays there with Simon the tanner. As Peter went throughout all those parts, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. Acts 9:32 There he found a certain man named Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years because he was paralyzed. Acts 9:33 Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed!” Immediately he arose. Acts 9:34 All who lived at Lydda and in Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord. Acts 9:35 Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which when translated means Dorcas. This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did. Acts 9:36 In those days, she became sick and died. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. Acts 9:37 As Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, imploring him not to delay in coming to them. Acts 9:38 Peter got up and went with them. When he had come, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the tunics and other garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them. Acts 9:39 Peter sent them all out, and knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up. Acts 9:40 He gave her his hand and raised her up. Calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. Acts 9:41 This became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. Acts 9:42 He stayed many days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon. Acts 9:43

title: Colossians 1:1–14
context: Paul greets the Colossian saints with Timothy, then thanks God for their faith, love, and hope rooted in the gospel that is bearing fruit worldwide. He keeps praying that they would be filled with knowledge of God’s will, walk worthy of the Lord, and remember the Father’s rescue: delivered from darkness, transferred into the Son’s kingdom, and given redemption, the forgiveness of our sins.
text: Colossians 1:1–14 Colossians Paul greets the Colossian saints with Timothy, then thanks God for their faith, love, and hope rooted in the gospel that is bearing fruit worldwide. He keeps praying that they would be filled with knowledge of God’s will, walk worthy of the Lord, and remember the Father’s rescue: delivered from darkness, transferred into the Son’s kingdom, and given redemption, the forgiveness of our sins. Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, Colossians 1:1 to the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Colossians 1:2 We give thanks to God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying always for you, Colossians 1:3 having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love which you have toward all the saints, Colossians 1:4 because of the hope which is laid up for you in the heavens, of which you heard before in the word of the truth of the Good News Colossians 1:5 which has come to you, even as it is in all the world and is bearing fruit and growing, as it does in you also, since the day you heard and knew the grace of God in truth, Colossians 1:6 even as you learned from Epaphras our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful servant of Christ on your behalf, Colossians 1:7 who also declared to us your love in the Spirit. Colossians 1:8 For this cause, we also, since the day we heard this, don’t cease praying and making requests for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, Colossians 1:9 that you may walk worthily of the Lord, to please him in all respects, bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God, Colossians 1:10 strengthened with all power, according to the might of his glory, for all endurance and perseverance with joy, Colossians 1:11 giving thanks to the Father, who made us fit to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light, Colossians 1:12 who delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love, Colossians 1:13 in whom we have our redemption, the forgiveness of our sins. Colossians 1:14

title: Colossians 1:15–23
context: Paul lifts the Colossians’ eyes to the cosmic Christ hymn: the Son as image of the invisible God, firstborn over creation and from the dead, Creator and Sustainer, Head of the church, in whom all fullness dwells. Through His cross God reconciles all things, making peace; then the hymn turns personal—once alienated, now reconciled in the body of his flesh, to be presented holy if they continue in the faith and hope of the gospel Paul serves.
text: Colossians 1:15–23 Colossians Paul lifts the Colossians’ eyes to the cosmic Christ hymn: the Son as image of the invisible God, firstborn over creation and from the dead, Creator and Sustainer, Head of the church, in whom all fullness dwells. Through His cross God reconciles all things, making peace; then the hymn turns personal—once alienated, now reconciled in the body of his flesh, to be presented holy if they continue in the faith and hope of the gospel Paul serves. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation. Colossians 1:15 For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him. Colossians 1:16 He is before all things, and in him all things are held together. Colossians 1:17 He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence. Colossians 1:18 For all the fullness was pleased to dwell in him, Colossians 1:19 and through him to reconcile all things to himself by him, whether things on the earth or things in the heavens, having made peace through the blood of his cross. Colossians 1:20 You, being in past times alienated and enemies in your mind in your evil deeds, Colossians 1:21 yet now he has reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and without defect and blameless before him, Colossians 1:22 if it is so that you continue in the faith, grounded and steadfast, and not moved away from the hope of the Good News which you heard, which was proclaimed in all creation under heaven, of which I, Paul, was made a servant. Colossians 1:23

title: Colossians 1:24–29
context: Paul turns from cosmic Christ to his own ministry: he rejoices in sufferings for the church, fills up what remains of Christ’s afflictions in his flesh (never an atoning lack), stewards the once-hidden mystery now revealed—Christ in you, the hope of glory—and toils to proclaim, warn, and teach everyone mature in Christ by God’s own energy.
text: Colossians 1:24–29 Colossians Paul turns from cosmic Christ to his own ministry: he rejoices in sufferings for the church, fills up what remains of Christ’s afflictions in his flesh (never an atoning lack), stewards the once-hidden mystery now revealed—Christ in you, the hope of glory—and toils to proclaim, warn, and teach everyone mature in Christ by God’s own energy. Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and fill up on my part that which is lacking of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh for his body’s sake, which is the assembly, Colossians 1:24 of which I was made a servant according to the stewardship of God which was given me toward you to fulfill the word of God, Colossians 1:25 the mystery which has been hidden for ages and generations. But now it has been revealed to his saints, Colossians 1:26 to whom God was pleased to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. Colossians 1:27 We proclaim him, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus; Colossians 1:28 for which I also labor, striving according to his working, which works in me mightily. Colossians 1:29

title: Colossians 2:1–7
context: Paul opens the heart of his struggle for Colossae and Laodicea: he wants believers he has never met face to face to be encouraged, knit together in love, and brought into the full assurance that God’s mystery is Christ. He warns against plausible delusion and calls them to walk in the Lord they have already received—rooted, built up, established, and thankful.
text: Colossians 2:1–7 Colossians Paul opens the heart of his struggle for Colossae and Laodicea: he wants believers he has never met face to face to be encouraged, knit together in love, and brought into the full assurance that God’s mystery is Christ. He warns against plausible delusion and calls them to walk in the Lord they have already received—rooted, built up, established, and thankful. For I desire to have you know how greatly I struggle for you and for those at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh; Colossians 2:1 that their hearts may be comforted, they being knit together in love, and gaining all riches of the full assurance of understanding, that they may know the mystery of God, both of the Father and of Christ, Colossians 2:2 in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. Colossians 2:3 Now I say this that no one may delude you with persuasiveness of speech. Colossians 2:4 For though I am absent in the flesh, yet I am with you in the spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order, and the steadfastness of your faith in Christ. Colossians 2:5 As therefore you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him, Colossians 2:6 rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, even as you were taught, abounding in it in thanksgiving. Colossians 2:7

title: Colossians 2:16–23
context: Because the debt is canceled and the powers disarmed in Christ, Paul frees the church from judgmental pressure over food, drink, festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths—shadows whose substance belongs to Christ. He warns against disqualification through ascetic show, angel worship, and vision-boasting that fails to hold the Head, and against elemental regulations that look wise but cannot restrain the flesh.
text: Colossians 2:16–23 Colossians Because the debt is canceled and the powers disarmed in Christ, Paul frees the church from judgmental pressure over food, drink, festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths—shadows whose substance belongs to Christ. He warns against disqualification through ascetic show, angel worship, and vision-boasting that fails to hold the Head, and against elemental regulations that look wise but cannot restrain the flesh. Let no one therefore judge you in eating or drinking, or with respect to a feast day or a new moon or a Sabbath day, Colossians 2:16 which are a shadow of the things to come; but the body is Christ’s. Colossians 2:17 Let no one rob you of your prize by self-abasement and worshiping of the angels, dwelling in the things which he has not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind, Colossians 2:18 and not holding firmly to the Head, from whom all the body, being supplied and knit together through the joints and ligaments, grows with God’s growth. Colossians 2:19 If you died with Christ from the elemental spirits of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you subject yourselves to ordinances, Colossians 2:20 “Don’t handle, nor taste, nor touch” Colossians 2:21 (all of which perish with use), according to the precepts and doctrines of men? Colossians 2:22 These things indeed appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body, but aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh. Colossians 2:23

title: Colossians 2:8–15
context: Paul warns the church not to be taken captive by philosophy and empty deceit that follows human tradition and elemental powers rather than Christ. In Christ the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily; believers are filled in Him, circumcised without hands, buried and raised with Him in baptism, made alive from death in trespasses, forgiven as the debt-record is nailed to the cross, and shown a public triumph over disarmed rulers and authorities.
text: Colossians 2:8–15 Colossians Paul warns the church not to be taken captive by philosophy and empty deceit that follows human tradition and elemental powers rather than Christ. In Christ the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily; believers are filled in Him, circumcised without hands, buried and raised with Him in baptism, made alive from death in trespasses, forgiven as the debt-record is nailed to the cross, and shown a public triumph over disarmed rulers and authorities. Be careful that you don’t let anyone rob you through his philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the elemental spirits of the world, and not after Christ. Colossians 2:8 For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, Colossians 2:9 and in him you are made full, who is the head of all principality and power. Colossians 2:10 In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ, Colossians 2:11 having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead. Colossians 2:12 You were dead through your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh. He made you alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, Colossians 2:13 wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross. Colossians 2:14 Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it. Colossians 2:15

title: Colossians 3:1–11
context: After Colossians 2’s warning against hollow philosophy, Paul grounds holy living in union with the risen Christ—seek the things above, put to death earthly vices, and put on the new man where ethnic and social barriers fall before Christ who is all and in all.
text: Colossians 3:1–11 Colossians After Colossians 2’s warning against hollow philosophy, Paul grounds holy living in union with the risen Christ—seek the things above, put to death earthly vices, and put on the new man where ethnic and social barriers fall before Christ who is all and in all. If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Colossians 3:1 Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth. Colossians 3:2 For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. Colossians 3:3 When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory. Colossians 3:4 Put to death therefore your members which are on the earth: sexual immorality, uncleanness, depraved passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry. Colossians 3:5 For these things’ sake the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience. Colossians 3:6 You also once walked in those, when you lived in them, Colossians 3:7 but now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and shameful speaking out of your mouth. Colossians 3:8 Don’t lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old man with his doings, Colossians 3:9 and have put on the new man, who is being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator, Colossians 3:10 where there can’t be Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, bondservant, or free person; but Christ is all, and in all. Colossians 3:11

title: Colossians 3:12–17
context: The new self’s wardrobe: as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, believers clothe themselves in Christlike virtues, forgive as the Lord has forgiven, bind everything with love, let Christ’s peace rule the one body, let His word dwell richly, and do all in Jesus’ name with thanksgiving.
text: Colossians 3:12–17 Colossians The new self’s wardrobe: as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, believers clothe themselves in Christlike virtues, forgive as the Lord has forgiven, bind everything with love, let Christ’s peace rule the one body, let His word dwell richly, and do all in Jesus’ name with thanksgiving. Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance; Colossians 3:12 bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do. Colossians 3:13 Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection. Colossians 3:14 And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful. Colossians 3:15 Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord. Colossians 3:16 Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him. Colossians 3:17

title: Colossians 3:18–25
context: Paul’s household code under the Lordship of Christ—mutual duties shaped by “in the Lord,” with special weight on husbands’ love, fathers’ gentleness, and workers’ sincere service to Christ, who grants the inheritance as reward and judges without partiality. Read pastorally: acknowledge the first-century slavery setting carefully without baptizing injustice, and keep Christ as true Master and impartial Judge.
text: Colossians 3:18–25 Colossians Paul’s household code under the Lordship of Christ—mutual duties shaped by “in the Lord,” with special weight on husbands’ love, fathers’ gentleness, and workers’ sincere service to Christ, who grants the inheritance as reward and judges without partiality. Read pastorally: acknowledge the first-century slavery setting carefully without baptizing injustice, and keep Christ as true Master and impartial Judge. Wives, be in subjection to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Colossians 3:18 Husbands, love your wives, and don’t be bitter against them. Colossians 3:19 Children, obey your parents in all things, for this pleases the Lord. Colossians 3:20 Fathers, don’t provoke your children, so that they won’t be discouraged. Colossians 3:21 Servants, obey in all things those who are your masters according to the flesh, not just when they are looking, as men pleasers, but in singleness of heart, fearing God. Colossians 3:22 And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, Colossians 3:23 knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ. Colossians 3:24 But he who does wrong will receive again for the wrong that he has done, and there is no partiality. Colossians 3:25

title: Colossians 4:1–6
context: Paul closes the household code and turns to prayer and wise witness. Masters answer to the heavenly Master; the church perseveres in thankful prayer for open doors; speech and conduct toward outsiders are to be gracious and wise.
text: Colossians 4:1–6 Colossians Paul closes the household code and turns to prayer and wise witness. Masters answer to the heavenly Master; the church perseveres in thankful prayer for open doors; speech and conduct toward outsiders are to be gracious and wise. Masters, give to your servants that which is just and equal, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven. Colossians 4:1 Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving, Colossians 4:2 praying together for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds, Colossians 4:3 that I may reveal it as I ought to speak. Colossians 4:4 Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time. Colossians 4:5 Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one. Colossians 4:6

title: Colossians 4:7–18
context: Paul’s final greetings: trusted coworkers (Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark, Justus, Epaphras, Luke, Demas), sister churches in the Lycus Valley, a charge to Archippus, and a handwritten close from prison—grace as the last word.
text: Colossians 4:7–18 Colossians Paul’s final greetings: trusted coworkers (Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark, Justus, Epaphras, Luke, Demas), sister churches in the Lycus Valley, a charge to Archippus, and a handwritten close from prison—grace as the last word. All my affairs will be made known to you by Tychicus, the beloved brother, faithful servant, and fellow bondservant in the Lord. Colossians 4:7 I am sending him to you for this very purpose, that he may know your circumstances and comfort your hearts, Colossians 4:8 together with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you everything that is going on here. Colossians 4:9 Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you received instructions, “if he comes to you, receive him”), Colossians 4:10 and Jesus who is called Justus. These are my only fellow workers for God’s Kingdom who are of the circumcision, men who have been a comfort to me. Colossians 4:11 Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, salutes you, always striving for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. Colossians 4:12 For I testify about him that he has great zeal for you, and for those in Laodicea, and for those in Hierapolis. Colossians 4:13 Luke the beloved physician and Demas greet you. Colossians 4:14 Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, with Nymphas and the assembly that is in his house. Colossians 4:15 When this letter has been read among you, cause it to be read also in the assembly of the Laodiceans, and that you also read the letter from Laodicea. Colossians 4:16 Tell Archippus, “Take heed to the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you fulfill it.” Colossians 4:17 I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you. Amen. Colossians 4:18

title: Daniel 1:1–7
context: In Jehoiakim’s third year Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem. The Lord gives the king of Judah into his hand, with vessels of the house of God carried to Shinar. Chosen youths of Israel are taken for the palace, trained in Chaldean learning, assigned the king’s food, and renamed. Among them are Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah of Judah.
text: Daniel 1:1–7 Daniel In Jehoiakim’s third year Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem. The Lord gives the king of Judah into his hand, with vessels of the house of God carried to Shinar. Chosen youths of Israel are taken for the palace, trained in Chaldean learning, assigned the king’s food, and renamed. Among them are Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah of Judah. In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it. Daniel 1:1 The Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with some of the vessels of the house of God; and he carried them into the land of Shinar to the house of his god. He brought the vessels into the treasure house of his god. Daniel 1:2 The king spoke to Ashpenaz, the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring in some of the children of Israel, even of the royal offspring and of the nobles: Daniel 1:3 youths in whom was no defect, but well-favored, skillful in all wisdom, endowed with knowledge, understanding science, and who had the ability to stand in the king’s palace; and that he should teach them the learning and the language of the Chaldeans.
