He struck the ram, broke both horns, trampled him. The goat became exceedingly great; the great horn was broken; four notable horns toward the four winds. Out of one, a little horn, grew toward the south, the east, and the glorious land. It grew to the host of heaven; some of the army and of the stars thrown down. It became great as the prince of the army; the regular burnt offering taken away; the sanctuary overthrown. A host given over with the continual burnt offering because of transgression; truth thrown to the ground; it acted and prospered. A holy one: how long? Two thousand three hundred evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary will be restored to its rightful state. In the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar, a vision appeared to me, even to me, Daniel, after that which appeared to me at the first. Daniel 8:1 I saw the vision. Now it was so, that when I saw, I was in the citadel of Susa, which is in the province of Elam. I saw in the vision, and I was by the river Ulai. Daniel 8:2 Then I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, a ram which had two horns stood before the river. The two horns were high, but one was higher than the other, and the higher came up last. Daniel 8:3 I saw the ram pushing westward, northward, and southward. No animals could stand before him. There wasn’t any who could deliver out of his hand, but he did according to his will, and magnified himself. Daniel 8:4 As I was considering, behold, a male goat came from the west over the surface of the whole earth, and didn’t touch the ground. The goat had a notable horn between his eyes. Daniel 8:5 He came to the ram that had the two horns, which I saw standing before the river, and ran on him in the fury of his power. Daniel 8:6 I saw him come close to the ram, and he was moved with anger against him, and struck the ram, and broke his two horns. There was no power in the ram to stand before him; but he cast him down to the ground and trampled on him. There was no one who could deliver the ram out of his hand. Daniel 8:7 The male goat magnified himself exceedingly. When he was strong, the great horn was broken; and instead of it there came up four notable horns toward the four winds of the sky. Daniel 8:8 Out of one of them came out a little horn which grew exceedingly great—toward the south, and toward the east, and toward the glorious land. Daniel 8:9 It grew great, even to the army of the sky; and it cast down some of the army and of the stars to the ground and trampled on them. Daniel 8:10 Yes, it magnified itself, even to the prince of the army; and it took away from him the continual burnt offering, and the place of his sanctuary was cast down. Daniel 8:11 The army was given over to it together with the continual burnt offering through disobedience. It cast down truth to the ground, and it did its pleasure and prospered. Daniel 8:12 Then I heard a holy one speaking; and another holy one said to that certain one who spoke, “How long will the vision about the continual burnt offering, and the disobedience that makes desolate, to give both the sanctuary and the army to be trodden under foot be?” Daniel 8:13 He said to me, “To two thousand and three hundred evenings and mornings. Then the sanctuary will be cleansed.” Daniel 8:14

title: Daniel 8:15–27
context: Daniel seeks to understand the vision; someone with the appearance of a man stands before him. A man's voice between the banks of the Ulai: Gabriel, make this man understand. Gabriel comes near; Daniel is frightened and falls on his face. Understand, son of man, the vision belongs to the time of the end. Deep sleep, face to the ground; touched and made to stand. Latter time of the indignation; appointed time of the end. Ram with two horns: kings of Media and Persia. Goat: king of Greece. Great horn: the first king. Broken horn, four in its place: four kingdoms from his nation, not with his power. Latter end, when transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, who understands riddles. Power mighty, but not by his own power; fearful destruction; destroy the mighty ones and the holy people who are the saints. Cunning, deceit prospers; in his mind he becomes great; without warning destroys many. Rises against the Prince of princes; broken, but not by human hands; the vision of the evenings and mornings is true; seal it, for it belongs to many days from now. Daniel overcome, sick some days; rose up and did the king’s business; appalled, did not understand it.
text: Daniel 8:15–27 Daniel Daniel seeks to understand the vision; someone with the appearance of a man stands before him. A man's voice between the banks of the Ulai: Gabriel, make this man understand. Gabriel comes near; Daniel is frightened and falls on his face. Understand, son of man, the vision belongs to the time of the end. Deep sleep, face to the ground; touched and made to stand. Latter time of the indignation; appointed time of the end. Ram with two horns: kings of Media and Persia. Goat: king of Greece. Great horn: the first king. Broken horn, four in its place: four kingdoms from his nation, not with his power. Latter end, when transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, who understands riddles. Power mighty, but not by his own power; fearful destruction; destroy the mighty ones and the holy people who are the saints. Cunning, deceit prospers; in his mind he becomes great; without warning destroys many. Rises against the Prince of princes; broken, but not by human hands; the vision of the evenings and mornings is true; seal it, for it belongs to many days from now. Daniel overcome, sick some days; rose up and did the king’s business; appalled, did not understand it. When I, even I Daniel, had seen the vision, I sought to understand it. Then behold, there stood before me someone with the appearance of a man. Daniel 8:15 I heard a man’s voice between the banks of the Ulai, which called and said, “Gabriel, make this man understand the vision.” Daniel 8:16 So he came near where I stood; and when he came, I was frightened, and fell on my face; but he said to me, “Understand, son of man, for the vision belongs to the time of the end.” Daniel 8:17 Now as he was speaking with me, I fell into a deep sleep with my face toward the ground; but he touched me and set me upright. Daniel 8:18 He said, “Behold, I will make you know what will be in the latter time of the indignation, for it belongs to the appointed time of the end. Daniel 8:19 The ram which you saw, that had the two horns, they are the kings of Media and Persia. Daniel 8:20 The rough male goat is the king of Greece. The great horn that is between his eyes is the first king. Daniel 8:21 As for that which was broken, in the place where four stood up, four kingdoms will stand up out of the nation, but not with his power. Daniel 8:22 “In the latter time of their kingdom, when the transgressors have come to the full, a king of fierce face, and understanding riddles, will stand up. Daniel 8:23 His power will be mighty, but not by his own power. He will destroy awesomely, and will prosper in what he does. He will destroy the mighty ones and the holy people. Daniel 8:24 Through his policy he will cause deceit to prosper in his hand. He will magnify himself in his heart, and he will destroy many in their security. He will also stand up against the prince of princes, but he will be broken without human hands. Daniel 8:25 “The vision of the evenings and mornings which has been told is true; but seal up the vision, for it belongs to many days to come.” Daniel 8:26 I, Daniel, fainted, and was sick for some days. Then I rose up and did the king’s business. I wondered at the vision, but no one understood it. Daniel 8:27

title: Daniel 9:1–19
context: In the first year of Darius the Mede, Daniel reads Jeremiah’s seventy years and turns his face to the Lord. The first movement of the chapter is confession: shame belongs to a people, mercy belongs to God, and the plea is for a city and a sanctuary called by his name.
text: Daniel 9:1–19 Daniel In the first year of Darius the Mede, Daniel reads Jeremiah’s seventy years and turns his face to the Lord. The first movement of the chapter is confession: shame belongs to a people, mercy belongs to God, and the plea is for a city and a sanctuary called by his name. In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the offspring of the Medes, who was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans— Daniel 9:1 in the first year of his reign I, Daniel, understood by the books the number of the years about which the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah the prophet for the accomplishing of the desolations of Jerusalem, even seventy years. Daniel 9:2 I set my face to the Lord God, to seek by prayer and petitions, with fasting and sackcloth and ashes. Daniel 9:3 I prayed to the LORD my God, and made confession, and said, “Oh, Lord, the great and dreadful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments, Daniel 9:4 we have sinned, and have dealt perversely, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even turning aside from your precepts and from your ordinances. Daniel 9:5 We haven’t listened to your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, and to all the people of the land. Daniel 9:6 “Lord, righteousness belongs to you, but to us confusion of face, as it is today; to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, who are near and who are far off, through all the countries where you have driven them, because of their trespass that they have trespassed against you. Daniel 9:7 Lord, to us belongs confusion of face, to our kings, to our princes, and to our fathers, because we have sinned against you. Daniel 9:8 To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against him. Daniel 9:9 We haven’t obeyed the LORD our God’s voice, to walk in his laws, which he set before us by his servants the prophets. Daniel 9:10 Yes, all Israel have transgressed your law, turning aside, and not obeying your voice. “Therefore the curse and the oath written in the law of Moses the servant of God has been poured out on us, for we have sinned against him. Daniel 9:11 He has confirmed his words, which he spoke against us and against our judges who judged us, by bringing on us a great evil; for under the whole sky, such has not been done as has been done to Jerusalem. Daniel 9:12 As it is written in the law of Moses, all this evil has come on us. Yet we have not entreated the favor of the LORD our God, that we should turn from our iniquities and have discernment in your truth. Daniel 9:13 Therefore the LORD has watched over the evil, and brought it on us; for the LORD our God is righteous in all his works which he does, and we have not obeyed his voice. Daniel 9:14 “Now, Lord our God, who has brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and have gotten yourself renown, as it is today, we have sinned. We have done wickedly. Daniel 9:15 Lord, according to all your righteousness, please let your anger and your wrath be turned away from your city Jerusalem, your holy mountain; because for our sins and for the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people have become a reproach to all who are around us. Daniel 9:16 “Now therefore, our God, listen to the prayer of your servant and to his petitions, and cause your face to shine on your sanctuary that is desolate, for the Lord’s sake. Daniel 9:17 My God, turn your ear and hear. Open your eyes and see our desolations, and the city which is called by your name; for we do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake. Daniel 9:18 Lord, hear. Lord, forgive. Lord, listen and do. Don’t defer, for your own sake, my God, because your city and your people are called by your name.” Daniel 9:19

title: Daniel 9:20–27
context: While Daniel is still confessing, Gabriel arrives at the hour of the evening sacrifice with insight and a decreed span of seventy weeks. The weeks are history with a terminus: transgression finished, iniquity atoned, an anointed one cut off, and a city left desolate—read here as both restoration’s timetable and Messiah’s work.
text: Daniel 9:20–27 Daniel While Daniel is still confessing, Gabriel arrives at the hour of the evening sacrifice with insight and a decreed span of seventy weeks. The weeks are history with a terminus: transgression finished, iniquity atoned, an anointed one cut off, and a city left desolate—read here as both restoration’s timetable and Messiah’s work. While I was speaking, praying, and confessing my sin and the sin of my people Israel, and presenting my supplication before the LORD my God for the holy mountain of my God— Daniel 9:20 yes, while I was speaking in prayer—the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, being caused to fly swiftly, touched me about the time of the evening offering. Daniel 9:21 He instructed me and talked with me, and said, “Daniel, I have now come to give you wisdom and understanding. Daniel 9:22 At the beginning of your petitions the commandment went out, and I have come to tell you, for you are greatly beloved. Therefore consider the matter and understand the vision. Daniel 9:23 “Seventy weeks are decreed on your people and on your holy city, to finish disobedience, to make an end of sins, to make reconciliation for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy. Daniel 9:24 “Know therefore and discern that from the going out of the commandment to restore and build Jerusalem to the Anointed One, the prince, will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. It will be built again, with street and moat, even in troubled times. Daniel 9:25 After the sixty-two weeks the Anointed One will be cut off, and will have nothing. The people of the prince who come will destroy the city and the sanctuary. Its end will be with a flood, and war will be even to the end. Desolations are determined. Daniel 9:26 He will make a firm covenant with many for one week. In the middle of the week he will cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease. On the wing of abominations will come one who makes desolate; and even to the decreed full end, wrath will be poured out on the desolate.” Daniel 9:27

title: Ephesians 1:1–2
context: Paul opens the letter by greeting the saints in Ephesus as an apostle by the will of God, calling them faithful in Christ and wishing them grace and peace. The greeting is brief, but it already raises themes the letter develops: God’s will, the identity of the saints, and life “in Christ.” Arminian and Reformed readers largely agree here, with small differences in how they hear words like “saints” and “faithful.”
text: Ephesians 1:1–2 Ephesians Paul opens the letter by greeting the saints in Ephesus as an apostle by the will of God, calling them faithful in Christ and wishing them grace and peace. The greeting is brief, but it already raises themes the letter develops: God’s will, the identity of the saints, and life “in Christ.” Arminian and Reformed readers largely agree here, with small differences in how they hear words like “saints” and “faithful.” Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the saints who are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus: Ephesians 1:1 Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Ephesians 1:2

title: Ephesians 1:15–23
context: Paul thanks God for the Ephesians’ faith and love and prays that they will know the hope of their calling, the riches of their inheritance, and the power that raised Christ and seated him above every authority as head over all things for the church. The prayer is common ground for both traditions. Their differences surface in how they read “calling” and how they connect God’s power with the believer’s perseverance.
text: Ephesians 1:15–23 Ephesians Paul thanks God for the Ephesians’ faith and love and prays that they will know the hope of their calling, the riches of their inheritance, and the power that raised Christ and seated him above every authority as head over all things for the church. The prayer is common ground for both traditions. Their differences surface in how they read “calling” and how they connect God’s power with the believer’s perseverance. For this cause I also, having heard of the faith in the Lord Jesus which is among you and the love which you have toward all the saints, Ephesians 1:15 don’t cease to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers, Ephesians 1:16 that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, Ephesians 1:17 having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, Ephesians 1:18 and what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to that working of the strength of his might Ephesians 1:19 which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, Ephesians 1:20 far above all rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in that which is to come. Ephesians 1:21 He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly, Ephesians 1:22 which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all. Ephesians 1:23

title: Ephesians 1:3–6
context: Ephesians opens with one long sentence of praise, and its first movement (vv. 3–6) speaks of God choosing and predestining his people in Christ. Few passages are more central to the debate over election. Arminian readers often hear a corporate election of the people found in Christ, or a choice based on foreknown faith. Reformed readers hear a personal and unconditional choice that produces faith. Both read the passage first as worship.
text: Ephesians 1:3–6 Ephesians Ephesians opens with one long sentence of praise, and its first movement (vv. 3–6) speaks of God choosing and predestining his people in Christ. Few passages are more central to the debate over election. Arminian readers often hear a corporate election of the people found in Christ, or a choice based on foreknown faith. Reformed readers hear a personal and unconditional choice that produces faith. Both read the passage first as worship. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, Ephesians 1:3 even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we would be holy and without defect before him in love, Ephesians 1:4 having predestined us for adoption as children through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his desire, Ephesians 1:5 to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he freely gave us favor in the Beloved. Ephesians 1:6

title: Ephesians 1:7–14
context: Having praised God for choosing and adopting his people (vv. 3–6), Paul names redemption through Christ’s blood, the mystery of God’s plan to sum up all things in Christ, the inheritance assigned by God’s counsel, and the seal of the Spirit. Verse 11, “him who does all things after the counsel of his will,” is a key text on God’s sovereignty. Arminian and Reformed readers differ on how far that counsel determines human choices, and agree on the comfort of the Spirit’s seal.
text: Ephesians 1:7–14 Ephesians Having praised God for choosing and adopting his people (vv. 3–6), Paul names redemption through Christ’s blood, the mystery of God’s plan to sum up all things in Christ, the inheritance assigned by God’s counsel, and the seal of the Spirit. Verse 11, “him who does all things after the counsel of his will,” is a key text on God’s sovereignty. Arminian and Reformed readers differ on how far that counsel determines human choices, and agree on the comfort of the Spirit’s seal. In him we have our redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace Ephesians 1:7 which he made to abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence, Ephesians 1:8 making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him Ephesians 1:9 to an administration of the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth, in him. Ephesians 1:10 We were also assigned an inheritance in him, having been foreordained according to the purpose of him who does all things after the counsel of his will, Ephesians 1:11 to the end that we should be to the praise of his glory, we who had before hoped in Christ. Ephesians 1:12 In him you also, having heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation—in whom, having also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, Ephesians 1:13 who is a pledge of our inheritance, to the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory. Ephesians 1:14

title: Ephesians 2:1–10
context: Paul reminds Gentile believers that they were dead in sins, following the world and the prince of the power of the air, until God, rich in mercy, made them alive with Christ. They are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and created in Christ for good works God prepared beforehand. Both traditions treasure verses 8–9. They differ on what “dead” implies about human ability and on whether faith itself is the gift named in verse 8.
text: Ephesians 2:1–10 Ephesians Paul reminds Gentile believers that they were dead in sins, following the world and the prince of the power of the air, until God, rich in mercy, made them alive with Christ. They are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and created in Christ for good works God prepared beforehand. Both traditions treasure verses 8–9. They differ on what “dead” implies about human ability and on whether faith itself is the gift named in verse 8. You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins, Ephesians 2:1 in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience. Ephesians 2:2 We also all once lived among them in the lusts of our flesh, doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest. Ephesians 2:3 But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, Ephesians 2:4 even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved— Ephesians 2:5 and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, Ephesians 2:6 that in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus; Ephesians 2:7 for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, Ephesians 2:8 not of works, that no one would boast. Ephesians 2:9 For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them. Ephesians 2:10

title: Ephesians 2:11–22
context: Paul asks Gentile believers to remember when they were far off, without Christ and without hope, and announces that they have been brought near by his blood. Christ is our peace, making Jew and Gentile one new humanity, reconciling both to God through the cross, and building them into God’s household. The passage is mostly shared ground; Arminian and Reformed readers differ chiefly on the scope of reconciliation.
text: Ephesians 2:11–22 Ephesians Paul asks Gentile believers to remember when they were far off, without Christ and without hope, and announces that they have been brought near by his blood. Christ is our peace, making Jew and Gentile one new humanity, reconciling both to God through the cross, and building them into God’s household. The passage is mostly shared ground; Arminian and Reformed readers differ chiefly on the scope of reconciliation. Therefore remember that once you, the Gentiles in the flesh, who are called “uncircumcision” by that which is called “circumcision” (in the flesh, made by hands), Ephesians 2:11 that you were at that time separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of the promise, having no hope and without God in the world. Ephesians 2:12 But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ. Ephesians 2:13 For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation, Ephesians 2:14 having abolished in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments contained in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace, Ephesians 2:15 and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it. Ephesians 2:16 He came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near. Ephesians 2:17 For through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father. Ephesians 2:18 So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God, Ephesians 2:19 being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone; Ephesians 2:20 in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; Ephesians 2:21 in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit. Ephesians 2:22

title: Ephesians 3:1–13
context: Paul, a prisoner for the Gentiles, unfolds the mystery now revealed: Gentiles are fellow heirs, one body, and fellow partakers of his promise in Christ through the gospel. Grace made him a minister of unsearchable riches so that through the church God’s manifold wisdom would be displayed, according to the eternal purpose realized in Christ, in whom we have bold access by faith.
text: Ephesians 3:1–13 Ephesians Paul, a prisoner for the Gentiles, unfolds the mystery now revealed: Gentiles are fellow heirs, one body, and fellow partakers of his promise in Christ through the gospel. Grace made him a minister of unsearchable riches so that through the church God’s manifold wisdom would be displayed, according to the eternal purpose realized in Christ, in whom we have bold access by faith. For this cause I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles, Ephesians 3:1 if it is so that you have heard of the administration of that grace of God which was given me toward you, Ephesians 3:2 how that by revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote before in few words, Ephesians 3:3 by which, when you read, you can perceive my understanding in the mystery of Christ, Ephesians 3:4 which in other generations was not made known to the children of men, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit, Ephesians 3:5 that the Gentiles are fellow heirs and fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of his promise in Christ Jesus through the Good News, Ephesians 3:6 of which I was made a servant according to the gift of that grace of God which was given me according to the working of his power. Ephesians 3:7 To me, the very least of all saints, was this grace given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, Ephesians 3:8 and to make all men see what is the administration of the mystery which for ages has been hidden in God, who created all things through Jesus Christ, Ephesians 3:9 to the intent that now through the assembly the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places, Ephesians 3:10 according to the eternal purpose which he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord. Ephesians 3:11 In him we have boldness and access in confidence through our faith in him. Ephesians 3:12 Therefore I ask that you may not lose heart at my troubles for you, which are your glory. Ephesians 3:13

title: Ephesians 3:14–21
context: Paul kneels before the Father and asks that he would grant you, according to the riches of glory, the Spirit would strengthen the inner being, that Christ would dwell in their hearts through faith, and that, rooted in love, they would comprehend with all the saints the vastness of Christ’s love and be filled with God’s fullness. Doxology answers the prayer: God is able to do far more than we ask or think.
text: Ephesians 3:14–21 Ephesians Paul kneels before the Father and asks that he would grant you, according to the riches of glory, the Spirit would strengthen the inner being, that Christ would dwell in their hearts through faith, and that, rooted in love, they would comprehend with all the saints the vastness of Christ’s love and be filled with God’s fullness. Doxology answers the prayer: God is able to do far more than we ask or think. For this cause, I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Ephesians 3:14 from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, Ephesians 3:15 that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, Ephesians 3:16 that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love, Ephesians 3:17 may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth, Ephesians 3:18 and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. Ephesians 3:19 Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us, Ephesians 3:20 to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever. Amen. Ephesians 3:21

title: Ephesians 4:1–16
context: The prisoner of the Lord urges a walk worthy of the calling: humility, gentleness, patience, and eagerness to keep the Spirit’s unity in peace. One body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, and Father ground that unity, while Christ’s measured gifts—apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers—equip the saints until the body grows up into the Head in love.
text: Ephesians 4:1–16 Ephesians The prisoner of the Lord urges a walk worthy of the calling: humility, gentleness, patience, and eagerness to keep the Spirit’s unity in peace. One body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, and Father ground that unity, while Christ’s measured gifts—apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers—equip the saints until the body grows up into the Head in love. I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, Ephesians 4:1 with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love, Ephesians 4:2 being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Ephesians 4:3 There is one body and one Spirit, even as you also were called in one hope of your calling, Ephesians 4:4 one Lord, one faith, one baptism, Ephesians 4:5 one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all. Ephesians 4:6 But to each one of us, the grace was given according to the measure of the gift of Christ. Ephesians 4:7 Therefore he says, “When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to people.” Ephesians 4:8 Now this, “He ascended”, what is it but that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth? Ephesians 4:9 He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things. Ephesians 4:10 He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; Ephesians 4:11 for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ, Ephesians 4:12 until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, Ephesians 4:13 that we may no longer be children, tossed back and forth and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, in craftiness, after the wiles of error; Ephesians 4:14 but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ, Ephesians 4:15 from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love. Ephesians 4:16

title: Ephesians 4:17–24
context: Paul testifies in the Lord that the church must no longer walk in Gentile futility: darkened understanding, alienation from God’s life, ignorance, hardness, callous sensuality. That is not how they learned Christ. As truth is in Jesus, they are to put off the old self, be renewed in the spirit of their minds, and put on the new man, who in God’s likeness in righteousness and holiness.
text: Ephesians 4:17–24 Ephesians Paul testifies in the Lord that the church must no longer walk in Gentile futility: darkened understanding, alienation from God’s life, ignorance, hardness, callous sensuality. That is not how they learned Christ. As truth is in Jesus, they are to put off the old self, be renewed in the spirit of their minds, and put on the new man, who in God’s likeness in righteousness and holiness. This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles also walk, in the futility of their mind, Ephesians 4:17 being darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their hearts. Ephesians 4:18 They, having become callous, gave themselves up to lust, to work all uncleanness with greediness. Ephesians 4:19 But you didn’t learn Christ that way, Ephesians 4:20 if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, even as truth is in Jesus: Ephesians 4:21 that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, Ephesians 4:22 and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, Ephesians 4:23 and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth. Ephesians 4:24

title: Ephesians 4:25–32
context: Therefore the new self shows in speech and community: put away falsehood, be angry without sin, give the devil no room, replace stealing with honest work and generosity, and let talk build up and give grace. Do not grieve the Spirit who sealed you for redemption. Put away bitterness and malice; be kind, tenderhearted, and forgiving, as God also in Christ forgave you.
text: Ephesians 4:25–32 Ephesians Therefore the new self shows in speech and community: put away falsehood, be angry without sin, give the devil no room, replace stealing with honest work and generosity, and let talk build up and give grace. Do not grieve the Spirit who sealed you for redemption. Put away bitterness and malice; be kind, tenderhearted, and forgiving, as God also in Christ forgave you. Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbor, for we are members of one another. Ephesians 4:25 “Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, Ephesians 4:26 and don’t give place to the devil. Ephesians 4:27 Let him who stole steal no more; but rather let him labor, producing with his hands something that is good, that he may have something to give to him who has need. Ephesians 4:28 Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear. Ephesians 4:29 Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Ephesians 4:30 Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice. Ephesians 4:31 And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you. Ephesians 4:32

title: Ephesians 5:1–14
context: A pastoral paragraph on imitating God, walking in love, holiness, and children of light.
text: Ephesians 5:1–14 Ephesians A pastoral paragraph on imitating God, walking in love, holiness, and children of light. Be therefore imitators of God, as beloved children. Ephesians 5:1 Walk in love, even as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance. Ephesians 5:2 But sexual immorality, and all uncleanness or covetousness, let it not even be mentioned among you, as becomes saints; Ephesians 5:3 nor filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not appropriate, but rather giving of thanks. Ephesians 5:4 Know this for sure, that no sexually immoral person, nor unclean person, nor covetous man (who is an idolater), has any inheritance in the Kingdom of Christ and God. Ephesians 5:5 Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience. Ephesians 5:6 Therefore don’t be partakers with them. Ephesians 5:7 For you were once darkness, but are now light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, Ephesians 5:8 for the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth, Ephesians 5:9 proving what is well pleasing to the Lord. Ephesians 5:10 Have no fellowship with the unfruitful deeds of darkness, but rather even reprove them. Ephesians 5:11 For it is a shame even to speak of the things which are done by them in secret. Ephesians 5:12 But all things, when they are reproved, are revealed by the light, for everything that reveals is light. Ephesians 5:13 Therefore he says, “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” Ephesians 5:14

title: Ephesians 5:15–21
context: Paul urges believers to walk carefully as wise people, making the most of the time because the days are evil, understanding the Lord’s will, and being filled with the Spirit rather than with wine. That filling shows itself in songs, thanksgiving, and mutual submission. Both traditions read this as practical holiness; they differ in how they describe the believer’s cooperation with the Spirit.
text: Ephesians 5:15–21 Ephesians Paul urges believers to walk carefully as wise people, making the most of the time because the days are evil, understanding the Lord’s will, and being filled with the Spirit rather than with wine. That filling shows itself in songs, thanksgiving, and mutual submission. Both traditions read this as practical holiness; they differ in how they describe the believer’s cooperation with the Spirit. Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, Ephesians 5:15 redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Ephesians 5:16 Therefore, don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. Ephesians 5:17 Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit, Ephesians 5:18 speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; Ephesians 5:19 giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father; Ephesians 5:20 subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ. Ephesians 5:21

title: Ephesians 5:22–33
context: Paul speaks to wives and husbands: wives are to submit as the church to Christ, and husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. The passage ends with the “great mystery” of Christ and the church. Christians debate its application to marriage today, but that debate does not divide neatly along Arminian and Reformed lines. Their main difference here concerns whom Christ gave himself for.
text: Ephesians 5:22–33 Ephesians Paul speaks to wives and husbands: wives are to submit as the church to Christ, and husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. The passage ends with the “great mystery” of Christ and the church. Christians debate its application to marriage today, but that debate does not divide neatly along Arminian and Reformed lines. Their main difference here concerns whom Christ gave himself for. Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord. Ephesians 5:22 For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the assembly, being himself the savior of the body. Ephesians 5:23 But as the assembly is subject to Christ, so let the wives also be to their own husbands in everything. Ephesians 5:24 Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her, Ephesians 5:25 that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, Ephesians 5:26 that he might present the assembly to himself gloriously, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she should be holy and without defect. Ephesians 5:27 Even so husbands also ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. He who loves his own wife loves himself. Ephesians 5:28 For no man ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, even as the Lord also does the assembly, Ephesians 5:29 because we are members of his body, of his flesh and bones. Ephesians 5:30 “For this cause a man will leave his father and mother and will be joined to his wife. Then the two will become one flesh.” Ephesians 5:31 This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the assembly. Ephesians 5:32 Nevertheless each of you must also love his own wife even as himself; and let the wife see that she respects her husband. Ephesians 5:33

title: Ephesians 6:1–9
context: Paul addresses children and parents, then slaves and masters. Children are to obey in the Lord, fathers are not to provoke their children, slaves are to serve as to Christ, and masters are to stop threatening, because their Master in heaven shows no partiality. Both traditions read these instructions as discipleship within households and agree that they do not endorse slavery as an institution.
text: Ephesians 6:1–9 Ephesians Paul addresses children and parents, then slaves and masters. Children are to obey in the Lord, fathers are not to provoke their children, slaves are to serve as to Christ, and masters are to stop threatening, because their Master in heaven shows no partiality. Both traditions read these instructions as discipleship within households and agree that they do not endorse slavery as an institution. Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. Ephesians 6:1 “Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise: Ephesians 6:2 “that it may be well with you, and you may live long on the earth.” Ephesians 6:3 You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. Ephesians 6:4 Servants, be obedient to those who according to the flesh are your masters, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as to Christ, Ephesians 6:5 not in the way of service only when eyes are on you, as men pleasers, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, Ephesians 6:6 with good will doing service as to the Lord and not to men, Ephesians 6:7 knowing that whatever good thing each one does, he will receive the same good again from the Lord, whether he is bound or free. Ephesians 6:8 You masters, do the same things to them, and give up threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no partiality with him. Ephesians 6:9

title: Ephesians 6:10–20
context: Paul closes his teaching with a call to be strong in the Lord and to put on the full armor of God against the schemes of the devil. Truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God make up the armor, and prayer runs through it all. Arminian and Reformed readers agree the armor is God’s gift; they differ on what it means that believers must take it up and stand.
text: Ephesians 6:10–20 Ephesians Paul closes his teaching with a call to be strong in the Lord and to put on the full armor of God against the schemes of the devil. Truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God make up the armor, and prayer runs through it all. Arminian and Reformed readers agree the armor is God’s gift; they differ on what it means that believers must take it up and stand. Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. Ephesians 6:10 Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. Ephesians 6:11 For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world’s rulers of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Ephesians 6:12 Therefore put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. Ephesians 6:13 Stand therefore, having the utility belt of truth buckled around your waist, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, Ephesians 6:14 and having fitted your feet with the preparation of the Good News of peace, Ephesians 6:15 above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the fiery darts of the evil one. Ephesians 6:16 And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; Ephesians 6:17 with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints. Ephesians 6:18 Pray for me, that utterance may be given to me in opening my mouth, to make known with boldness the mystery of the Good News, Ephesians 6:19 for which I am an ambassador in chains; that in it I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak. Ephesians 6:20

title: Ephesians 6:21–24
context: Paul’s closing to the Ephesian church—Tychicus sent to tell how he is, then a benediction of peace, love with faith, and grace for those who love Christ with love incorruptible.
text: Ephesians 6:21–24 Ephesians Paul’s closing to the Ephesian church—Tychicus sent to tell how he is, then a benediction of peace, love with faith, and grace for those who love Christ with love incorruptible. But that you also may know my affairs, how I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will make known to you all things. Ephesians 6:21 I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know our state and that he may comfort your hearts. Ephesians 6:22 Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Ephesians 6:23 Grace be with all those who love our Lord Jesus Christ with incorruptible love. Amen. Ephesians 6:24

title: Genesis 1:1–5
context: The Bible opens not with Israel or the law but with God speaking a world into being. Genesis 1:1–5 is day one of the creation week: heavens and earth, the formless deep, the Spirit hovering, then light summoned, named, and judged good. Evening and morning mark the first day. The pericope establishes that everything begins with God’s word, not with rival gods or eternal matter.
text: Genesis 1:1–5 Genesis The Bible opens not with Israel or the law but with God speaking a world into being. Genesis 1:1–5 is day one of the creation week: heavens and earth, the formless deep, the Spirit hovering, then light summoned, named, and judged good. Evening and morning mark the first day. The pericope establishes that everything begins with God’s word, not with rival gods or eternal matter. In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. Genesis 1:1 The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters. Genesis 1:2 God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. Genesis 1:3 God saw the light, and saw that it was good. God divided the light from the darkness. Genesis 1:4 God called the light “day”, and the darkness he called “night”. There was evening and there was morning, the first day. Genesis 1:5

title: Genesis 1:14–19
context: Day four places lights in the expanse already made: for signs and seasons, days and years, and to give light on the earth. Verses 14–19 refuse to treat sun and moon as deities; they are creatures assigned to rule the day and night as servants. The week’s rhythm now has visible markers in the sky.
text: Genesis 1:14–19 Genesis Day four places lights in the expanse already made: for signs and seasons, days and years, and to give light on the earth. Verses 14–19 refuse to treat sun and moon as deities; they are creatures assigned to rule the day and night as servants. The week’s rhythm now has visible markers in the sky. God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the sky to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs to mark seasons, days, and years; Genesis 1:14 and let them be for lights in the expanse of the sky to give light on the earth;” and it was so. Genesis 1:15 God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night. He also made the stars. Genesis 1:16 God set them in the expanse of the sky to give light to the earth, Genesis 1:17 and to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. God saw that it was good. Genesis 1:18 There was evening and there was morning, a fourth day. Genesis 1:19

title: Genesis 1:20–23
context: Day five fills the waters and skies with living swarms. Verses 20–23 introduce blessing for the first time—“Be fruitful and multiply”—spoken to sea creatures and birds according to their kinds. Life is not an accident of the elements; God creates it, names it good, and sends it forth with His benediction.
text: Genesis 1:20–23 Genesis Day five fills the waters and skies with living swarms. Verses 20–23 introduce blessing for the first time—“Be fruitful and multiply”—spoken to sea creatures and birds according to their kinds. Life is not an accident of the elements; God creates it, names it good, and sends it forth with His benediction. God said, “Let the waters abound with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth in the open expanse of the sky.” Genesis 1:20 God created the large sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarmed, after their kind, and every winged bird after its kind. God saw that it was good. Genesis 1:21 God blessed them, saying, “Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.” Genesis 1:22 There was evening and there was morning, a fifth day. Genesis 1:23

title: Genesis 1:24–31
context: The sixth day completes the land’s living creatures according to kinds, then turns to the week’s climax: humanity in God’s image, male and female, blessed with fruitfulness, dominion, and daily bread. Verses 24–31 end with God surveying everything He has made—very good. Image, blessing, and vocation sit at the heart of later disagreements, even as both camps confess the Creator’s goodness.
text: Genesis 1:24–31 Genesis The sixth day completes the land’s living creatures according to kinds, then turns to the week’s climax: humanity in God’s image, male and female, blessed with fruitfulness, dominion, and daily bread. Verses 24–31 end with God surveying everything He has made—very good. Image, blessing, and vocation sit at the heart of later disagreements, even as both camps confess the Creator’s goodness. God said, “Let the earth produce living creatures after their kind, livestock, creeping things, and animals of the earth after their kind;” and it was so. Genesis 1:24 God made the animals of the earth after their kind, and the livestock after their kind, and everything that creeps on the ground after its kind. God saw that it was good. Genesis 1:25 God said, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” Genesis 1:26 God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them. Genesis 1:27 God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.” Genesis 1:28 God said, “Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food. Genesis 1:29 To every animal of the earth, and to every bird of the sky, and to everything that creeps on the earth, in which there is life, I have given every green herb for food;” and it was so. Genesis 1:30 God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day. Genesis 1:31

title: Genesis 1:6–8
context: After light, God continues the week by making an expanse in the middle of the waters. Verses 6–8 are day two: sky-space named Heaven, waters above and below distinguished, evening and morning. The Creator is not only originator but arranger—making room in which later life will live and move.
text: Genesis 1:6–8 Genesis After light, God continues the week by making an expanse in the middle of the waters. Verses 6–8 are day two: sky-space named Heaven, waters above and below distinguished, evening and morning. The Creator is not only originator but arranger—making room in which later life will live and move. God said, “Let there be an expanse in the middle of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.” Genesis 1:6 God made the expanse, and divided the waters which were under the expanse from the waters which were above the expanse; and it was so. Genesis 1:7 God called the expanse “sky”. There was evening and there was morning, a second day. Genesis 1:8

title: Genesis 1:9–13
context: Day three gathers the waters so dry land appears, then fills that land with vegetation according to kinds. Verses 9–13 give Earth and Seas their names, pronounce the land good, and let the earth sprout seed-bearing plants and fruit trees—still before the sun is mentioned. Habitable earth and fruitfulness come by the same creating word.
text: Genesis 1:9–13 Genesis Day three gathers the waters so dry land appears, then fills that land with vegetation according to kinds. Verses 9–13 give Earth and Seas their names, pronounce the land good, and let the earth sprout seed-bearing plants and fruit trees—still before the sun is mentioned. Habitable earth and fruitfulness come by the same creating word. God said, “Let the waters under the sky be gathered together to one place, and let the dry land appear;” and it was so. Genesis 1:9 God called the dry land “earth”, and the gathering together of the waters he called “seas”. God saw that it was good. Genesis 1:10 God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth;” and it was so. Genesis 1:11 The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good. Genesis 1:12 There was evening and there was morning, a third day. Genesis 1:13

title: Genesis 10:1–20
context: After the flood, Genesis lists Noah’s sons and traces Japheth and Ham—coastlands, Nimrod’s kingdom, Canaan’s territory—as nations take shape under God’s care.
text: Genesis 10:1–20 Genesis After the flood, Genesis lists Noah’s sons and traces Japheth and Ham—coastlands, Nimrod’s kingdom, Canaan’s territory—as nations take shape under God’s care. Now this is the history of the generations of the sons of Noah and of Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood. Genesis 10:1 The sons of Japheth were: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. Genesis 10:2 The sons of Gomer were: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. Genesis 10:3 The sons of Javan were: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. Genesis 10:4 Of these were the islands of the nations divided in their lands, everyone after his language, after their families, in their nations. Genesis 10:5 The sons of Ham were: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. Genesis 10:6 The sons of Cush were: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah were: Sheba and Dedan. Genesis 10:7 Cush became the father of Nimrod. He began to be a mighty one on the earth. Genesis 10:8 He was a mighty hunter before the LORD. Therefore it is said, “like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD”. Genesis 10:9 The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. Genesis 10:10 Out of that land he went into Assyria, and built Nineveh, Rehoboth Ir, Calah, Genesis 10:11 and Resen between Nineveh and the great city Calah. Genesis 10:12 Mizraim became the father of Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Genesis 10:13 Pathrusim, Casluhim (which the Philistines descended from), and Caphtorim. Genesis 10:14 Canaan became the father of Sidon (his firstborn), Heth, Genesis 10:15 the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, Genesis 10:16 the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, Genesis 10:17 the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Afterward the families of the Canaanites were spread abroad. Genesis 10:18 The border of the Canaanites was from Sidon—as you go toward Gerar—to Gaza—as you go toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim—to Lasha. Genesis 10:19 These are the sons of Ham, after their families, according to their languages, in their lands and their nations. Genesis 10:20

title: Genesis 10:21–32
context: The table turns to Shem, father of Eber, then Peleg and Joktan, and closes: from these clans the nations spread abroad after the flood.
text: Genesis 10:21–32 Genesis The table turns to Shem, father of Eber, then Peleg and Joktan, and closes: from these clans the nations spread abroad after the flood. Children were also born to Shem (the elder brother of Japheth), the father of all the children of Eber. Genesis 10:21 The sons of Shem were: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram. Genesis 10:22 The sons of Aram were: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash. Genesis 10:23 Arpachshad became the father of Shelah. Shelah became the father of Eber. Genesis 10:24 To Eber were born two sons. The name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided. His brother’s name was Joktan. Genesis 10:25 Joktan became the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Genesis 10:26 Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Genesis 10:27 Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Genesis 10:28 Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan. Genesis 10:29 Their dwelling extended from Mesha, as you go toward Sephar, the mountain of the east. Genesis 10:30 These are the sons of Shem, by their families, according to their languages, lands, and nations. Genesis 10:31 These are the families of the sons of Noah, by their generations, according to their nations. The nations divided from these on the earth after the flood. Genesis 10:32

title: Genesis 11:1–9
context: After the flood, the whole earth still shares one language. People settle in Shinar, brick a city and a tower, and reach for a name lest they be dispersed. The LORD comes down, confuses their speech, and scatters them abroad on the surface of all the earth—judgment on pride that also fills the world. The place is called Babel.
text: Genesis 11:1–9 Genesis After the flood, the whole earth still shares one language. People settle in Shinar, brick a city and a tower, and reach for a name lest they be dispersed. The LORD comes down, confuses their speech, and scatters them abroad on the surface of all the earth—judgment on pride that also fills the world. The place is called Babel. The whole earth was of one language and of one speech. Genesis 11:1 As they traveled east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there. Genesis 11:2 They said to one another, “Come, let’s make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.” They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar. Genesis 11:3 They said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.” Genesis 11:4 The LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men built. Genesis 11:5 The LORD said, “Behold, they are one people, and they all have one language, and this is what they begin to do. Now nothing will be withheld from them, which they intend to do. Genesis 11:6 Come, let’s go down, and there confuse their language, that they may not understand one another’s speech.” Genesis 11:7 So the LORD scattered them abroad from there on the surface of all the earth. They stopped building the city. Genesis 11:8 Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. From there, the LORD scattered them abroad on the surface of all the earth. Genesis 11:9

title: Genesis 11:10–32
context: After Babel, the camera quiets on Shem. Ordinary years carry the promise-line through Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, and Nahor to Terah. Abram, Nahor, and Haran are named; Haran dies in Ur; Sarai is barren. Terah takes Abram, Lot, and Sarai toward Canaan, settles in Haran, and dies there—the setup for chapter 12.
text: Genesis 11:10–32 Genesis After Babel, the camera quiets on Shem. Ordinary years carry the promise-line through Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, and Nahor to Terah. Abram, Nahor, and Haran are named; Haran dies in Ur; Sarai is barren. Terah takes Abram, Lot, and Sarai toward Canaan, settles in Haran, and dies there—the setup for chapter 12. This is the history of the generations of Shem: Shem was one hundred years old when he became the father of Arpachshad two years after the flood. Genesis 11:10 Shem lived five hundred years after he became the father of Arpachshad, and became the father of more sons and daughters. Genesis 11:11 Arpachshad lived thirty-five years and became the father of Shelah. Genesis 11:12 Arpachshad lived four hundred three years after he became the father of Shelah, and became the father of more sons and daughters. Genesis 11:13 Shelah lived thirty years, and became the father of Eber. Genesis 11:14 Shelah lived four hundred three years after he became the father of Eber, and became the father of more sons and daughters. Genesis 11:15 Eber lived thirty-four years, and became the father of Peleg. Genesis 11:16 Eber lived four hundred thirty years after he became the father of Peleg, and became the father of more sons and daughters. Genesis 11:17 Peleg lived thirty years, and became the father of Reu. Genesis 11:18 Peleg lived two hundred nine years after he became the father of Reu, and became the father of more sons and daughters. Genesis 11:19 Reu lived thirty-two years, and became the father of Serug. Genesis 11:20 Reu lived two hundred seven years after he became the father of Serug, and became the father of more sons and daughters. Genesis 11:21 Serug lived thirty years, and became the father of Nahor. Genesis 11:22 Serug lived two hundred years after he became the father of Nahor, and became the father of more sons and daughters. Genesis 11:23 Nahor lived twenty-nine years, and became the father of Terah. Genesis 11:24 Nahor lived one hundred nineteen years after he became the father of Terah, and became the father of more sons and daughters. Genesis 11:25 Terah lived seventy years, and became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Genesis 11:26 Now this is the history of the generations of Terah. Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran became the father of Lot. Genesis 11:27 Haran died in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldees, while his father Terah was still alive. Genesis 11:28 Abram and Nahor married wives. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, who was also the father of Iscah. Genesis 11:29 Sarai was barren. She had no child. Genesis 11:30 Terah took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran, his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram’s wife. They went from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan. They came to Haran and lived there. Genesis 11:31 The days of Terah were two hundred five years. Terah died in Haran. Genesis 11:32

title: Genesis 12:1–9
context: After Babel’s scattering, the Lord calls Abram out of country, kindred, and father’s house toward a land He will show. Promise piles on promise: a great nation, a great name, blessing that will reach all the families of the earth. Abram goes; altars rise at Shechem and Bethel as the Canaanites still occupy the land.
text: Genesis 12:1–9 Genesis After Babel’s scattering, the Lord calls Abram out of country, kindred, and father’s house toward a land He will show. Promise piles on promise: a great nation, a great name, blessing that will reach all the families of the earth. Abram goes; altars rise at Shechem and Bethel as the Canaanites still occupy the land. Now the LORD said to Abram, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you. Genesis 12:1 I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing. Genesis 12:2 I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who treats you with contempt. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” Genesis 12:3 So Abram went, as the LORD had told him. Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. Genesis 12:4 Abram took Sarai his wife, Lot his brother’s son, all their possessions that they had gathered, and the people whom they had acquired in Haran, and they went to go into the land of Canaan. They entered into the land of Canaan. Genesis 12:5 Abram passed through the land to the place of Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. At that time, Canaanites were in the land. Genesis 12:6 The LORD appeared to Abram and said, “I will give this land to your offspring.” He built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him. Genesis 12:7 He left from there to go to the mountain on the east of Bethel and pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west, and Ai on the east. There he built an altar to the LORD and called on the LORD’s name. Genesis 12:8 Abram traveled, still going on toward the South. Genesis 12:9

title: Genesis 12:10–20
context: Famine drives Abram down to Egypt. Fear for his life leads him to pass Sarai off as his sister; she is taken into Pharaoh’s house, Abram is enriched, and the LORD strikes Pharaoh’s household. The pagan king rebukes the patriarch and sends them away—promise threatened, then preserved by God, not by Abram’s scheme.
text: Genesis 12:10–20 Genesis Famine drives Abram down to Egypt. Fear for his life leads him to pass Sarai off as his sister; she is taken into Pharaoh’s house, Abram is enriched, and the LORD strikes Pharaoh’s household. The pagan king rebukes the patriarch and sends them away—promise threatened, then preserved by God, not by Abram’s scheme. There was a famine in the land. Abram went down into Egypt to live as a foreigner there, for the famine was severe in the land. Genesis 12:10 When he had come near to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, “See now, I know that you are a beautiful woman to look at. Genesis 12:11 It will happen that when the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife.’ They will kill me, but they will save you alive. Genesis 12:12 Please say that you are my sister, that it may be well with me for your sake, and that my soul may live because of you.” Genesis 12:13 When Abram had come into Egypt, some Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful. Genesis 12:14 The princes of Pharaoh saw her, and praised her to Pharaoh; and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house. Genesis 12:15 He dealt well with Abram for her sake. He had sheep, cattle, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys, and camels. Genesis 12:16 The LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife. Genesis 12:17 Pharaoh called Abram and said, “What is this that you have done to me? Why didn’t you tell me that she was your wife? Genesis 12:18 Why did you say, ‘She is my sister,’ so that I took her to be my wife? Now therefore, see your wife, take her, and go your way.” Genesis 12:19 Pharaoh commanded men concerning him, and they escorted him away with his wife and all that he had. Genesis 12:20

title: Genesis 13:1–13
context: After Egypt, Abram goes up into the Negeb with Sarai, Lot, and great wealth. Herds crowd the land, strife breaks out, and Abram yields first choice. Lot takes the Jordan valley toward Sodom; Abram remains in Canaan.
text: Genesis 13:1–13 Genesis After Egypt, Abram goes up into the Negeb with Sarai, Lot, and great wealth. Herds crowd the land, strife breaks out, and Abram yields first choice. Lot takes the Jordan valley toward Sodom; Abram remains in Canaan. Abram went up out of Egypt—he, his wife, all that he had, and Lot with him—into the South. Genesis 13:1 Abram was very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold. Genesis 13:2 He went on his journeys from the South as far as Bethel, to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai, Genesis 13:3 to the place of the altar, which he had made there at the first. There Abram called on the LORD’s name. Genesis 13:4 Lot also, who went with Abram, had flocks, herds, and tents. Genesis 13:5 The land was not able to bear them, that they might live together; for their possessions were so great that they couldn’t live together. Genesis 13:6 There was strife between the herdsmen of Abram’s livestock and the herdsmen of Lot’s livestock. The Canaanites and the Perizzites lived in the land at that time. Genesis 13:7 Abram said to Lot, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives. Genesis 13:8 Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left.” Genesis 13:9 Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, as you go to Zoar. Genesis 13:10 So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one another. Genesis 13:11 Abram lived in the land of Canaan, and Lot lived in the cities of the plain, and moved his tent as far as Sodom. Genesis 13:12 Now the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners against the LORD. Genesis 13:13

title: Genesis 13:14–18
context: After Lot separates, the Lord tells Abram to lift his eyes: all the land in every direction, offspring like the dust, walk the length and breadth. Abram settles by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar there to the LORD.
text: Genesis 13:14–18 Genesis After Lot separates, the Lord tells Abram to lift his eyes: all the land in every direction, offspring like the dust, walk the length and breadth. Abram settles by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar there to the LORD. The LORD said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, “Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, Genesis 13:14 for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever. Genesis 13:15 I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if a man can count the dust of the earth, then your offspring may also be counted. Genesis 13:16 Arise, walk through the land in its length and in its width; for I will give it to you.” Genesis 13:17 Abram moved his tent, and came and lived by the oaks of Mamre, which are in Hebron, and built an altar there to the LORD. Genesis 13:18

title: Genesis 14:1–12
context: After Lot settled toward Sodom, a coalition of eastern kings raids Canaan. Five cities of the plain revolt, lose in the Valley of Siddim, and Lot is carried off with Sodom’s goods—kinship and location catching him in a war he did not start.
text: Genesis 14:1–12 Genesis After Lot settled toward Sodom, a coalition of eastern kings raids Canaan. Five cities of the plain revolt, lose in the Valley of Siddim, and Lot is carried off with Sodom’s goods—kinship and location catching him in a war he did not start. In the days of Amraphel, king of Shinar; Arioch, king of Ellasar; Chedorlaomer, king of Elam; and Tidal, king of Goiim, Genesis 14:1 they made war with Bera, king of Sodom; Birsha, king of Gomorrah; Shinab, king of Admah; Shemeber, king of Zeboiim; and the king of Bela (also called Zoar). Genesis 14:2 All these joined together in the valley of Siddim (also called the Salt Sea). Genesis 14:3 They served Chedorlaomer for twelve years, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled. Genesis 14:4 In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him came and struck the Rephaim in Ashteroth Karnaim, the Zuzim in Ham, the Emim in Shaveh Kiriathaim, Genesis 14:5 and the Horites in their Mount Seir, to El Paran, which is by the wilderness. Genesis 14:6 They returned, and came to En Mishpat (also called Kadesh), and struck all the country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites, that lived in Hazazon Tamar. Genesis 14:7 The king of Sodom, and the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (also called Zoar) went out; and they set the battle in array against them in the valley of Siddim Genesis 14:8 against Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar; four kings against the five. Genesis 14:9 Now the valley of Siddim was full of tar pits; and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and some fell there. Those who remained fled to the hills. Genesis 14:10 They took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their food, and went their way. Genesis 14:11 They took Lot, Abram’s brother’s son, who lived in Sodom, and his goods, and departed. Genesis 14:12

title: Genesis 14:13–16
context: News reaches Abram the Hebrew at Mamre. He musters 318 trained men born in his house, allies with Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre, pursues as far as Dan and Hobah, and brings Lot back with the people and the goods.
text: Genesis 14:13–16 Genesis News reaches Abram the Hebrew at Mamre. He musters 318 trained men born in his house, allies with Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre, pursues as far as Dan and Hobah, and brings Lot back with the people and the goods. One who had escaped came and told Abram, the Hebrew. At that time, he lived by the oaks of Mamre, the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner. They were allies of Abram. Genesis 14:13 When Abram heard that his relative was taken captive, he led out his three hundred eighteen trained men, born in his house, and pursued as far as Dan. Genesis 14:14 He divided himself against them by night, he and his servants, and struck them, and pursued them to Hobah, which is on the left hand of Damascus. Genesis 14:15 He brought back all the goods, and also brought back his relative Lot and his goods, and the women also, and the other people. Genesis 14:16

title: Genesis 14:17–24
context: Returning from victory, Abram meets two kings: Sodom’s ruler offering spoils, and Melchizedek of Salem, priest of God Most High, who brings bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives a tenth. Abram swears he will take nothing of Sodom’s, lest a wicked city claim to have made him rich.
text: Genesis 14:17–24 Genesis Returning from victory, Abram meets two kings: Sodom’s ruler offering spoils, and Melchizedek of Salem, priest of God Most High, who brings bread and wine, blesses Abram, and receives a tenth. Abram swears he will take nothing of Sodom’s, lest a wicked city claim to have made him rich. The king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, at the valley of Shaveh (that is, the King’s Valley). Genesis 14:17 Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High. Genesis 14:18 He blessed him, and said, “Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth. Genesis 14:19 Blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.” Abram gave him a tenth of all. Genesis 14:20 The king of Sodom said to Abram, “Give me the people, and take the goods for yourself.” Genesis 14:21 Abram said to the king of Sodom, “I have lifted up my hand to the LORD, God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, Genesis 14:22 that I will not take a thread nor a sandal strap nor anything that is yours, lest you should say, ‘I have made Abram rich.’ Genesis 14:23 I will accept nothing from you except that which the young men have eaten, and the portion of the men who went with me: Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. Let them take their portion.” Genesis 14:24

title: Genesis 15:1–6
context: After Abram’s rescue of Lot and his refusal of Sodom’s spoils, the word of the LORD comes in a vision: fear not, I am your shield. Childless Abram names Eliezer; God promises a son from his own body and offspring like the stars. Abram believes the LORD, and it is counted to him as righteousness—the verse Paul will make the Bible’s great proof of justification by faith.
text: Genesis 15:1–6 Genesis After Abram’s rescue of Lot and his refusal of Sodom’s spoils, the word of the LORD comes in a vision: fear not, I am your shield. Childless Abram names Eliezer; God promises a son from his own body and offspring like the stars. Abram believes the LORD, and it is counted to him as righteousness—the verse Paul will make the Bible’s great proof of justification by faith. After these things the LORD’s word came to Abram in a vision, saying, “Don’t be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward.” Genesis 15:1 Abram said, “Lord GOD, what will you give me, since I go childless, and he who will inherit my estate is Eliezer of Damascus?” Genesis 15:2 Abram said, “Behold, you have given no children to me: and, behold, one born in my house is my heir.” Genesis 15:3 Behold, the LORD’s word came to him, saying, “This man will not be your heir, but he who will come out of your own body will be your heir.” Genesis 15:4 The LORD brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So your offspring will be.” Genesis 15:5 He believed in the LORD, who credited it to him for righteousness. Genesis 15:6

title: Genesis 15:7–21
context: The same night continues: God identifies Himself as the One who brought Abram from Ur to give him the land. Abram asks how he will know; the LORD answers with a covenant rite. Animals are divided; Abram drives off birds; a deep sleep and dreadful darkness fall; then a smoking furnace and flaming torch pass between the pieces while the promise of sojourn, affliction, exodus, and land is sworn.
text: Genesis 15:7–21 Genesis The same night continues: God identifies Himself as the One who brought Abram from Ur to give him the land. Abram asks how he will know; the LORD answers with a covenant rite.
