Genesis 28:5 Now Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him away to Paddan Aram, to take him a wife from there, and that as he blessed him he gave him a command, saying, “You shall not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan;” Genesis 28:6 and that Jacob obeyed his father and his mother, and was gone to Paddan Aram. Genesis 28:7 Esau saw that the daughters of Canaan didn’t please Isaac, his father. Genesis 28:8 So Esau went to Ishmael, and took, in addition to the wives that he had, Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, the sister of Nebaioth, to be his wife. Genesis 28:9

title: Genesis 28:10–22
context: Jacob leaves Beersheba toward Haran, sleeps with a stone for a pillow, and dreams of a ladder between earth and heaven. The LORD restates Abraham’s promise, pledges His presence, and Jacob wakes to name the place Bethel—then vows oil, house, and a tenth.
text: Genesis 28:10–22 Genesis Jacob leaves Beersheba toward Haran, sleeps with a stone for a pillow, and dreams of a ladder between earth and heaven. The LORD restates Abraham’s promise, pledges His presence, and Jacob wakes to name the place Bethel—then vows oil, house, and a tenth. Jacob went out from Beersheba, and went toward Haran. Genesis 28:10 He came to a certain place, and stayed there all night, because the sun had set. He took one of the stones of the place, and put it under his head, and lay down in that place to sleep. Genesis 28:11 He dreamed and saw a stairway set upon the earth, and its top reached to heaven. Behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it. Genesis 28:12 Behold, the LORD stood above it, and said, “I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac. I will give the land you lie on to you and to your offspring. Genesis 28:13 Your offspring will be as the dust of the earth, and you will spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south. In you and in your offspring, all the families of the earth will be blessed. Genesis 28:14 Behold, I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go, and will bring you again into this land. For I will not leave you until I have done that which I have spoken of to you.” Genesis 28:15 Jacob awakened out of his sleep, and he said, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I didn’t know it.” Genesis 28:16 He was afraid, and said, “How awesome this place is! This is none other than God’s house, and this is the gate of heaven.” Genesis 28:17 Jacob rose up early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put under his head, and set it up for a pillar, and poured oil on its top. Genesis 28:18 He called the name of that place Bethel, but the name of the city was Luz at the first. Genesis 28:19 Jacob vowed a vow, saying, “If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat, and clothing to put on, Genesis 28:20 so that I come again to my father’s house in peace, and the LORD will be my God, Genesis 28:21 then this stone, which I have set up for a pillar, will be God’s house. Of all that you will give me I will surely give a tenth to you.” Genesis 28:22

title: Genesis 29:1–14
context: After Bethel’s vow, Jacob journeys east and arrives at a well in Haran country. He meets Rachel, waters Laban’s flock, weeps, and is received into Laban’s house as bone and flesh—providence bringing the promised heir to the family from which Isaac’s wife had come.
text: Genesis 29:1–14 Genesis After Bethel’s vow, Jacob journeys east and arrives at a well in Haran country. He meets Rachel, waters Laban’s flock, weeps, and is received into Laban’s house as bone and flesh—providence bringing the promised heir to the family from which Isaac’s wife had come. Then Jacob went on his journey, and came to the land of the children of the east. Genesis 29:1 He looked, and saw a well in the field, and saw three flocks of sheep lying there by it. For out of that well they watered the flocks. The stone on the well’s mouth was large. Genesis 29:2 There all the flocks were gathered. They rolled the stone from the well’s mouth, and watered the sheep, and put the stone back on the well’s mouth in its place. Genesis 29:3 Jacob said to them, “My relatives, where are you from?” They said, “We are from Haran.” Genesis 29:4 He said to them, “Do you know Laban, the son of Nahor?” They said, “We know him.” Genesis 29:5 He said to them, “Is it well with him?” They said, “It is well. See, Rachel, his daughter, is coming with the sheep.” Genesis 29:6 He said, “Behold, it is still the middle of the day, not time to gather the livestock together. Water the sheep, and go and feed them.” Genesis 29:7 They said, “We can’t, until all the flocks are gathered together, and they roll the stone from the well’s mouth. Then we will water the sheep.” Genesis 29:8 While he was yet speaking with them, Rachel came with her father’s sheep, for she kept them. Genesis 29:9 When Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban, his mother’s brother, and the sheep of Laban, his mother’s brother, Jacob went near, and rolled the stone from the well’s mouth, and watered the flock of Laban his mother’s brother. Genesis 29:10 Jacob kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice, and wept. Genesis 29:11 Jacob told Rachel that he was her father’s relative, and that he was Rebekah’s son. She ran and told her father. Genesis 29:12 When Laban heard the news of Jacob, his sister’s son, he ran to meet Jacob, and embraced him, and kissed him, and brought him to his house. Jacob told Laban all these things. Genesis 29:13 Laban said to him, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh.” Jacob stayed with him for a month. Genesis 29:14

title: Genesis 29:15–30
context: After a month, Laban opens wage-talk. Jacob loves Rachel and serves seven years that feel like days; Laban substitutes Leah at the feast, appeals to local custom, and binds Jacob to another seven years. The deceiver is deceived, and the household that will bear Israel’s tribes is formed in pain.
text: Genesis 29:15–30 Genesis After a month, Laban opens wage-talk. Jacob loves Rachel and serves seven years that feel like days; Laban substitutes Leah at the feast, appeals to local custom, and binds Jacob to another seven years. The deceiver is deceived, and the household that will bear Israel’s tribes is formed in pain. Laban said to Jacob, “Because you are my relative, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what will your wages be?” Genesis 29:15 Laban had two daughters. The name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel. Genesis 29:16 Leah’s eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and attractive. Genesis 29:17 Jacob loved Rachel. He said, “I will serve you seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter.” Genesis 29:18 Laban said, “It is better that I give her to you, than that I should give her to another man. Stay with me.” Genesis 29:19 Jacob served seven years for Rachel. They seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her. Genesis 29:20 Jacob said to Laban, “Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in to her.” Genesis 29:21 Laban gathered together all the men of the place, and made a feast. Genesis 29:22 In the evening, he took Leah his daughter, and brought her to Jacob. He went in to her. Genesis 29:23 Laban gave Zilpah his servant to his daughter Leah for a servant. Genesis 29:24 In the morning, behold, it was Leah! He said to Laban, “What is this you have done to me? Didn’t I serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?” Genesis 29:25 Laban said, “It is not done so in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn. Genesis 29:26 Fulfill the week of this one, and we will give you the other also for the service which you will serve with me for seven more years.” Genesis 29:27 Jacob did so, and fulfilled her week. He gave him Rachel his daughter as wife. Genesis 29:28 Laban gave Bilhah, his servant, to his daughter Rachel to be her servant. Genesis 29:29 He went in also to Rachel, and he loved also Rachel more than Leah, and served with him seven more years. Genesis 29:30

title: Genesis 29:31–35
context: The LORD sees that Leah is hated, opens her womb, and leaves Rachel barren for a time. Leah bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah—naming each from affliction toward praise. The unloved wife becomes mother of priesthood and of the royal, messianic line.
text: Genesis 29:31–35 Genesis The LORD sees that Leah is hated, opens her womb, and leaves Rachel barren for a time. Leah bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah—naming each from affliction toward praise. The unloved wife becomes mother of priesthood and of the royal, messianic line. The LORD saw that Leah was hated, and he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren. Genesis 29:31 Leah conceived, and bore a son, and she named him Reuben. For she said, “Because the LORD has looked at my affliction; for now my husband will love me.” Genesis 29:32 She conceived again, and bore a son, and said, “Because the LORD has heard that I am hated, he has therefore given me this son also.” She named him Simeon. Genesis 29:33 She conceived again, and bore a son. She said, “Now this time my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore his name was called Levi. Genesis 29:34 She conceived again, and bore a son. She said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” Therefore she named him Judah. Then she stopped bearing. Genesis 29:35

title: Genesis 3:1–7
context: The serpent questions God’s word, the woman answers, and a lie that they will not die opens a path of desire. She takes and eats, gives to her husband who is with her, and he eats; their eyes open to shame, and fig leaves become the first cover. Genesis 3:1–7 is the turn from innocence to transgression: a serious command, a free choice, and a world now knowing good and evil from the inside.
text: Genesis 3:1–7 Genesis The serpent questions God’s word, the woman answers, and a lie that they will not die opens a path of desire. She takes and eats, gives to her husband who is with her, and he eats; their eyes open to shame, and fig leaves become the first cover. Genesis 3:1–7 is the turn from innocence to transgression: a serious command, a free choice, and a world now knowing good and evil from the inside. Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” Genesis 3:1 The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, Genesis 3:2 but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.’” Genesis 3:3 The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t really die, Genesis 3:4 for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” Genesis 3:5 When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too. Genesis 3:6 Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves. Genesis 3:7

title: Genesis 3:16–24
context: Pain in childbearing, a disordered desire and rule between wife and husband, a cursed ground, sweat, and dust-to-dust mortality: the LORD names what sin has done. Yet He clothes them with skins, and Eve is named mother of all living, before cherubim and a flaming sword bar the way to the tree of life. Genesis 3:16–24 is judgment with mercy in it—exile that both punishes and protects, while the promise of 3:15 still stands.
text: Genesis 3:16–24 Genesis Pain in childbearing, a disordered desire and rule between wife and husband, a cursed ground, sweat, and dust-to-dust mortality: the LORD names what sin has done. Yet He clothes them with skins, and Eve is named mother of all living, before cherubim and a flaming sword bar the way to the tree of life. Genesis 3:16–24 is judgment with mercy in it—exile that both punishes and protects, while the promise of 3:15 still stands. To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. You will bear children in pain. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.” Genesis 3:16 To Adam he said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and have eaten from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life. Genesis 3:17 It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field. Genesis 3:18 You will eat bread by the sweat of your face until you return to the ground, for you were taken out of it. For you are dust, and you shall return to dust.” Genesis 3:19 The man called his wife Eve because she would be the mother of all the living. Genesis 3:20 The LORD God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them. Genesis 3:21 The LORD God said, “Behold, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand, and also take of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever—” Genesis 3:22 Therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he was taken. Genesis 3:23 So he drove out the man; and he placed cherubim at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life. Genesis 3:24

title: Genesis 3:8–15
context: The LORD God comes walking in the garden; the hiding pair are called, questioned, and exposed as they shift blame. Judgment falls first on the serpent, then a promise cuts through the curse: enmity between the serpent and the woman, between their offspring, and a head-bruising victory that will cost a wounded heel. Genesis 3:8–15 is confrontation that does not end in silence—the first gospel word after the fall.
text: Genesis 3:8–15 Genesis The LORD God comes walking in the garden; the hiding pair are called, questioned, and exposed as they shift blame. Judgment falls first on the serpent, then a promise cuts through the curse: enmity between the serpent and the woman, between their offspring, and a head-bruising victory that will cost a wounded heel. Genesis 3:8–15 is confrontation that does not end in silence—the first gospel word after the fall. They heard the LORD God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. Genesis 3:8 The LORD God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?” Genesis 3:9 The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.” Genesis 3:10 God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?” Genesis 3:11 The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” Genesis 3:12 The LORD God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” Genesis 3:13 The LORD God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, you are cursed above all livestock, and above every animal of the field. You shall go on your belly and you shall eat dust all the days of your life. Genesis 3:14 I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.” Genesis 3:15

title: Genesis 30:1–24
context: Rachel, still childless after Leah's sons, envies her sister and demands children of Jacob. Servants, names, and a mandrake bargain become the household's scorekeeping; yet God listens, remembers, and opens wombs. Dan through Joseph arrive in a rival house, and Joseph marks the turn: children are gift, not trophy, and God is kind amid the mess.
text: Genesis 30:1–24 Genesis Rachel, still childless after Leah's sons, envies her sister and demands children of Jacob. Servants, names, and a mandrake bargain become the household's scorekeeping; yet God listens, remembers, and opens wombs. Dan through Joseph arrive in a rival house, and Joseph marks the turn: children are gift, not trophy, and God is kind amid the mess. When Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister. She said to Jacob, “Give me children, or else I will die.” Genesis 30:1 Jacob’s anger burned against Rachel, and he said, “Am I in God’s place, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?” Genesis 30:2 She said, “Behold, my maid Bilhah. Go in to her, that she may bear on my knees, and I also may obtain children by her.” Genesis 30:3 She gave him Bilhah her servant as wife, and Jacob went in to her. Genesis 30:4 Bilhah conceived, and bore Jacob a son. Genesis 30:5 Rachel said, “God has judged me, and has also heard my voice, and has given me a son.” Therefore she called his name Dan. Genesis 30:6 Bilhah, Rachel’s servant, conceived again, and bore Jacob a second son. Genesis 30:7 Rachel said, “I have wrestled with my sister with mighty wrestlings, and have prevailed.” She named him Naphtali. Genesis 30:8 When Leah saw that she had finished bearing, she took Zilpah, her servant, and gave her to Jacob as a wife. Genesis 30:9 Zilpah, Leah’s servant, bore Jacob a son. Genesis 30:10 Leah said, “How fortunate!” She named him Gad. Genesis 30:11 Zilpah, Leah’s servant, bore Jacob a second son. Genesis 30:12 Leah said, “Happy am I, for the daughters will call me happy.” She named him Asher. Genesis 30:13 Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them to his mother, Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.” Genesis 30:14 Leah said to her, “Is it a small matter that you have taken away my husband? Would you take away my son’s mandrakes, also?” Rachel said, “Therefore he will lie with you tonight for your son’s mandrakes.” Genesis 30:15 Jacob came from the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him, and said, “You must come in to me; for I have surely hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” He lay with her that night. Genesis 30:16 God listened to Leah, and she conceived, and bore Jacob a fifth son. Genesis 30:17 Leah said, “God has given me my hire, because I gave my servant to my husband.” She named him Issachar. Genesis 30:18 Leah conceived again, and bore a sixth son to Jacob. Genesis 30:19 Leah said, “God has endowed me with a good dowry. Now my husband will live with me, because I have borne him six sons.” She named him Zebulun. Genesis 30:20 Afterwards, she bore a daughter, and named her Dinah. Genesis 30:21 God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her, and opened her womb. Genesis 30:22 She conceived, bore a son, and said, “God has taken away my reproach.” Genesis 30:23 She named him Joseph, saying, “May the LORD add another son to me.” Genesis 30:24

title: Genesis 30:25–43
context: After Joseph's birth, Jacob asks Laban for leave to go home. Laban, having discovered by divination that the LORD has blessed him for Jacob’s sake, bargains over wages; Jacob proposes the speckled and spotted. Laban cheats by removing those animals; Jacob pastured the rest and uses peeled sticks. The man increases greatly—labor and cunning on the page, with chapter 31 soon crediting the increase to God.
text: Genesis 30:25–43 Genesis After Joseph's birth, Jacob asks Laban for leave to go home. Laban, having discovered by divination that the LORD has blessed him for Jacob’s sake, bargains over wages; Jacob proposes the speckled and spotted. Laban cheats by removing those animals; Jacob pastured the rest and uses peeled sticks. The man increases greatly—labor and cunning on the page, with chapter 31 soon crediting the increase to God. When Rachel had borne Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, “Send me away, that I may go to my own place, and to my country. Genesis 30:25 Give me my wives and my children for whom I have served you, and let me go; for you know my service with which I have served you.” Genesis 30:26 Laban said to him, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, stay here, for I have divined that the LORD has blessed me for your sake.” Genesis 30:27 He said, “Appoint me your wages, and I will give it.” Genesis 30:28 Jacob said to him, “You know how I have served you, and how your livestock have fared with me. Genesis 30:29 For it was little which you had before I came, and it has increased to a multitude. The LORD has blessed you wherever I turned. Now when will I provide for my own house also?” Genesis 30:30 Laban said, “What shall I give you?” Jacob said, “You shall not give me anything. If you will do this thing for me, I will again feed your flock and keep it. Genesis 30:31 I will pass through all your flock today, removing from there every speckled and spotted one, and every black one among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats. This will be my hire. Genesis 30:32 So my righteousness will answer for me hereafter, when you come concerning my hire that is before you. Every one that is not speckled and spotted among the goats, and black among the sheep, that might be with me, will be considered stolen.” Genesis 30:33 Laban said, “Behold, let it be according to your word.” Genesis 30:34 That day, he removed the male goats that were streaked and spotted, and all the female goats that were speckled and spotted, every one that had white in it, and all the black ones among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons. Genesis 30:35 He set three days’ journey between himself and Jacob, and Jacob fed the rest of Laban’s flocks. Genesis 30:36 Jacob took to himself rods of fresh poplar, almond, and plane tree, peeled white streaks in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods. Genesis 30:37 He set the rods which he had peeled opposite the flocks in the watering troughs where the flocks came to drink. They conceived when they came to drink. Genesis 30:38 The flocks conceived before the rods, and the flocks produced streaked, speckled, and spotted. Genesis 30:39 Jacob separated the lambs, and set the faces of the flocks toward the streaked and all the black in Laban’s flock. He put his own droves apart, and didn’t put them into Laban’s flock. Genesis 30:40 Whenever the stronger of the flock conceived, Jacob laid the rods in front of the eyes of the flock in the watering troughs, that they might conceive among the rods; Genesis 30:41 but when the flock were feeble, he didn’t put them in. So the feebler were Laban’s, and the stronger Jacob’s. Genesis 30:42 The man increased exceedingly, and had large flocks, female servants and male servants, and camels and donkeys. Genesis 30:43

title: Genesis 31:1–21
context: Jacob hears Laban's sons charge that he has taken their father's wealth, and he sees Laban's face has turned. The LORD tells him to return to his fathers' land with the promise, "I will be with you." In the field he tells Rachel and Leah of wages changed ten times, of a dream of striped and spotted goats, and of the God of Bethel who calls him home. The sisters agree, Jacob sets out for Canaan, Rachel steals the household gods, and he crosses the Euphrates toward Gilead without telling Laban.
text: Genesis 31:1–21 Genesis Jacob hears Laban's sons charge that he has taken their father's wealth, and he sees Laban's face has turned. The LORD tells him to return to his fathers' land with the promise, "I will be with you." In the field he tells Rachel and Leah of wages changed ten times, of a dream of striped and spotted goats, and of the God of Bethel who calls him home. The sisters agree, Jacob sets out for Canaan, Rachel steals the household gods, and he crosses the Euphrates toward Gilead without telling Laban. Jacob heard Laban’s sons’ words, saying, “Jacob has taken away all that was our father’s. He has obtained all this wealth from that which was our father’s.” Genesis 31:1 Jacob saw the expression on Laban’s face, and, behold, it was not toward him as before. Genesis 31:2 The LORD said to Jacob, “Return to the land of your fathers, and to your relatives, and I will be with you.” Genesis 31:3 Jacob sent and called Rachel and Leah to the field to his flock, Genesis 31:4 and said to them, “I see the expression on your father’s face, that it is not toward me as before; but the God of my father has been with me. Genesis 31:5 You know that I have served your father with all of my strength. Genesis 31:6 Your father has deceived me, and changed my wages ten times, but God didn’t allow him to hurt me. Genesis 31:7 If he said, ‘The speckled will be your wages,’ then all the flock bore speckled. If he said, ‘The streaked will be your wages,’ then all the flock bore streaked. Genesis 31:8 Thus God has taken away your father’s livestock, and given them to me. Genesis 31:9 During mating season, I lifted up my eyes, and saw in a dream, and behold, the male goats which leaped on the flock were streaked, speckled, and grizzled. Genesis 31:10 The angel of God said to me in the dream, ‘Jacob,’ and I said, ‘Here I am.’ Genesis 31:11 He said, ‘Now lift up your eyes, and behold, all the male goats which leap on the flock are streaked, speckled, and grizzled, for I have seen all that Laban does to you. Genesis 31:12 I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar, where you vowed a vow to me. Now arise, get out from this land, and return to the land of your birth.’” Genesis 31:13 Rachel and Leah answered him, “Is there yet any portion or inheritance for us in our father’s house? Genesis 31:14 Aren’t we considered as foreigners by him? For he has sold us, and has also used up our money. Genesis 31:15 For all the riches which God has taken away from our father are ours and our children’s. Now then, whatever God has said to you, do.” Genesis 31:16 Then Jacob rose up, and set his sons and his wives on the camels, Genesis 31:17 and he took away all his livestock, and all his possessions which he had gathered, including the livestock which he had gained in Paddan Aram, to go to Isaac his father, to the land of Canaan. Genesis 31:18 Now Laban had gone to shear his sheep; and Rachel stole the teraphim that were her father’s. Genesis 31:19 Jacob deceived Laban the Syrian, in that he didn’t tell him that he was running away. Genesis 31:20 So he fled with all that he had. He rose up, passed over the River, and set his face toward the mountain of Gilead. Genesis 31:21

title: Genesis 31:22–55
context: On the third day Laban hears that Jacob has fled and pursues him seven days into Gilead, but God warns Laban in a dream to say nothing to Jacob, good or bad. The camps meet; Laban charges trickery and stolen gods; Jacob pleads fear that the daughters would be taken by force. Rachel hides the teraphim in a camel's saddle while Laban searches the tents. Jacob's anger then recounts twenty years of labor, and he names the God who saw his affliction. They raise a heap—Galeed and Mizpah—calling God to watch between them; Jacob swears by the Fear of Isaac, they sacrifice and eat, and in the morning Laban blesses his grandchildren and daughters and turns home.
text: Genesis 31:22–55 Genesis On the third day Laban hears that Jacob has fled and pursues him seven days into Gilead, but God warns Laban in a dream to say nothing to Jacob, good or bad. The camps meet; Laban charges trickery and stolen gods; Jacob pleads fear that the daughters would be taken by force. Rachel hides the teraphim in a camel's saddle while Laban searches the tents. Jacob's anger then recounts twenty years of labor, and he names the God who saw his affliction. They raise a heap—Galeed and Mizpah—calling God to watch between them; Jacob swears by the Fear of Isaac, they sacrifice and eat, and in the morning Laban blesses his grandchildren and daughters and turns home. Laban was told on the third day that Jacob had fled. Genesis 31:22 He took his relatives with him, and pursued him seven days’ journey. He overtook him in the mountain of Gilead. Genesis 31:23 God came to Laban the Syrian in a dream of the night, and said to him, “Be careful that you don’t speak to Jacob either good or bad.” Genesis 31:24 Laban caught up with Jacob. Now Jacob had pitched his tent in the mountain, and Laban with his relatives encamped in the mountain of Gilead. Genesis 31:25 Laban said to Jacob, “What have you done, that you have deceived me, and carried away my daughters like captives of the sword? Genesis 31:26 Why did you flee secretly, and deceive me, and didn’t tell me, that I might have sent you away with mirth and with songs, with tambourine and with harp; Genesis 31:27 and didn’t allow me to kiss my sons and my daughters? Now you have done foolishly. Genesis 31:28 It is in the power of my hand to hurt you, but the God of your father spoke to me last night, saying, ‘Be careful that you don’t speak to Jacob either good or bad.’ Genesis 31:29 Now, you want to be gone, because you greatly longed for your father’s house, but why have you stolen my gods?” Genesis 31:30 Jacob answered Laban, “Because I was afraid, for I said, ‘Lest you should take your daughters from me by force.’ Genesis 31:31 Anyone you find your gods with shall not live. Before our relatives, discern what is yours with me, and take it.” For Jacob didn’t know that Rachel had stolen them. Genesis 31:32 Laban went into Jacob’s tent, into Leah’s tent, and into the tent of the two female servants; but he didn’t find them. He went out of Leah’s tent, and entered into Rachel’s tent. Genesis 31:33 Now Rachel had taken the teraphim, put them in the camel’s saddle, and sat on them. Laban felt around all the tent, but didn’t find them. Genesis 31:34 She said to her father, “Don’t let my lord be angry that I can’t rise up before you; for I’m having my period.” He searched, but didn’t find the teraphim. Genesis 31:35 Jacob was angry, and argued with Laban. Jacob answered Laban, “What is my trespass? What is my sin, that you have hotly pursued me? Genesis 31:36 Now that you have felt around in all my stuff, what have you found of all your household stuff? Set it here before my relatives and your relatives, that they may judge between us two. Genesis 31:37 “These twenty years I have been with you. Your ewes and your female goats have not cast their young, and I haven’t eaten the rams of your flocks. Genesis 31:38 That which was torn of animals, I didn’t bring to you. I bore its loss. Of my hand you required it, whether stolen by day or stolen by night. Genesis 31:39 This was my situation: in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep fled from my eyes. Genesis 31:40 These twenty years I have been in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock, and you have changed my wages ten times. Genesis 31:41 Unless the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely now you would have sent me away empty. God has seen my affliction and the labor of my hands, and rebuked you last night.” Genesis 31:42 Laban answered Jacob, “The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, the flocks are my flocks, and all that you see is mine! What can I do today to these my daughters, or to their children whom they have borne? Genesis 31:43 Now come, let’s make a covenant, you and I. Let it be for a witness between me and you.” Genesis 31:44 Jacob took a stone, and set it up for a pillar. Genesis 31:45 Jacob said to his relatives, “Gather stones.” They took stones, and made a heap. They ate there by the heap. Genesis 31:46 Laban called it Jegar Sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed. Genesis 31:47 Laban said, “This heap is witness between me and you today.” Therefore it was named Galeed Genesis 31:48 and Mizpah, for he said, “The LORD watch between me and you, when we are absent one from another. Genesis 31:49 If you afflict my daughters, or if you take wives in addition to my daughters, no man is with us; behold, God is witness between me and you.” Genesis 31:50 Laban said to Jacob, “See this heap, and see the pillar, which I have set between me and you. Genesis 31:51 May this heap be a witness, and the pillar be a witness, that I will not pass over this heap to you, and that you will not pass over this heap and this pillar to me, for harm. Genesis 31:52 The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us.” Then Jacob swore by the fear of his father, Isaac. Genesis 31:53 Jacob offered a sacrifice in the mountain, and called his relatives to eat bread. They ate bread, and stayed all night in the mountain. Genesis 31:54 Early in the morning, Laban rose up, and kissed his sons and his daughters, and blessed them. Laban departed and returned to his place. Genesis 31:55

title: Genesis 32:1–21
context: Leaving Laban, Jacob meets God’s camp at Mahanaim, then sends word to Esau in Seir. Four hundred men coming with his brother leave him greatly afraid. He divides the company, prays the God of Abraham and Isaac to keep the promised good, and sends a spaced present ahead—prudence under a word he did not invent.
text: Genesis 32:1–21 Genesis Leaving Laban, Jacob meets God’s camp at Mahanaim, then sends word to Esau in Seir. Four hundred men coming with his brother leave him greatly afraid. He divides the company, prays the God of Abraham and Isaac to keep the promised good, and sends a spaced present ahead—prudence under a word he did not invent. Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him. Genesis 32:1 When he saw them, Jacob said, “This is God’s army.” He called the name of that place Mahanaim. Genesis 32:2 Jacob sent messengers in front of him to Esau, his brother, to the land of Seir, the field of Edom. Genesis 32:3 He commanded them, saying, “This is what you shall tell my lord, Esau: ‘This is what your servant, Jacob, says. I have lived as a foreigner with Laban, and stayed until now. Genesis 32:4 I have cattle, donkeys, flocks, male servants, and female servants. I have sent to tell my lord, that I may find favor in your sight.’” Genesis 32:5 The messengers returned to Jacob, saying, “We came to your brother Esau. He is coming to meet you, and four hundred men are with him.” Genesis 32:6 Then Jacob was greatly afraid and was distressed. He divided the people who were with him, along with the flocks, the herds, and the camels, into two companies. Genesis 32:7 He said, “If Esau comes to the one company, and strikes it, then the company which is left will escape.” Genesis 32:8 Jacob said, “God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, the LORD, who said to me, ‘Return to your country, and to your relatives, and I will do you good,’ Genesis 32:9 I am not worthy of the least of all the loving kindnesses, and of all the truth, which you have shown to your servant; for with just my staff I crossed over this Jordan; and now I have become two companies. Genesis 32:10 Please deliver me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau; for I fear him, lest he come and strike me and the mothers with the children. Genesis 32:11 You said, ‘I will surely do you good, and make your offspring as the sand of the sea, which can’t be counted because there are so many.’” Genesis 32:12 He stayed there that night, and took from that which he had with him a present for Esau, his brother: Genesis 32:13 two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams, Genesis 32:14 thirty milk camels and their colts, forty cows, ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten foals. Genesis 32:15 He delivered them into the hands of his servants, every herd by itself, and said to his servants, “Pass over before me, and put a space between herd and herd.” Genesis 32:16 He commanded the foremost, saying, “When Esau, my brother, meets you, and asks you, saying, ‘Whose are you? Where are you going? Whose are these before you?’ Genesis 32:17 Then you shall say, ‘They are your servant, Jacob’s. It is a present sent to my lord, Esau. Behold, he also is behind us.’” Genesis 32:18 He commanded also the second, and the third, and all that followed the herds, saying, “This is how you shall speak to Esau, when you find him. Genesis 32:19 You shall say, ‘Not only that, but behold, your servant, Jacob, is behind us.’” For, he said, “I will appease him with the present that goes before me, and afterward I will see his face. Perhaps he will accept me.” Genesis 32:20 So the present passed over before him, and he himself stayed that night in the camp. Genesis 32:21

title: Genesis 32:22–32
context: The same night Jacob sends wives, servants, and the eleven across the Jabbok and is left alone. A man wrestles him till dawn, puts the hip out, and is held for a blessing. Jacob becomes Israel at Peniel—face of God—and limps into sunrise while Israel remembers the sinew.
text: Genesis 32:22–32 Genesis The same night Jacob sends wives, servants, and the eleven across the Jabbok and is left alone. A man wrestles him till dawn, puts the hip out, and is held for a blessing. Jacob becomes Israel at Peniel—face of God—and limps into sunrise while Israel remembers the sinew. He rose up that night, and took his two wives, and his two servants, and his eleven sons, and crossed over the ford of the Jabbok. Genesis 32:22 He took them, and sent them over the stream, and sent over that which he had. Genesis 32:23 Jacob was left alone, and wrestled with a man there until the breaking of the day. Genesis 32:24 When he saw that he didn’t prevail against him, the man touched the hollow of his thigh, and the hollow of Jacob’s thigh was strained as he wrestled. Genesis 32:25 The man said, “Let me go, for the day breaks.” Jacob said, “I won’t let you go unless you bless me.” Genesis 32:26 He said to him, “What is your name?” He said, “Jacob”. Genesis 32:27 He said, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.” Genesis 32:28 Jacob asked him, “Please tell me your name.” He said, “Why is it that you ask what my name is?” So he blessed him there. Genesis 32:29 Jacob called the name of the place Peniel; for he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.” Genesis 32:30 The sun rose on him as he passed over Peniel, and he limped because of his thigh. Genesis 32:31 Therefore the children of Israel don’t eat the sinew of the hip, which is on the hollow of the thigh, to this day, because he touched the hollow of Jacob’s thigh in the sinew of the hip. Genesis 32:32

title: Genesis 33:1–20
context: After Peniel, Jacob lifts his eyes and Esau comes with four hundred men. Jacob arranges his household, bows seven times, and finds not a sword but an embrace. Gifts are pressed and received; travel plans part them—Esau to Seir, Jacob to Succoth, then safely to Shechem in Canaan, where he buys land and raises an altar: El-Elohe-Israel.
text: Genesis 33:1–20 Genesis After Peniel, Jacob lifts his eyes and Esau comes with four hundred men. Jacob arranges his household, bows seven times, and finds not a sword but an embrace. Gifts are pressed and received; travel plans part them—Esau to Seir, Jacob to Succoth, then safely to Shechem in Canaan, where he buys land and raises an altar: El-Elohe-Israel. Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, Esau was coming, and with him four hundred men. He divided the children between Leah, Rachel, and the two servants. Genesis 33:1 He put the servants and their children in front, Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear. Genesis 33:2 He himself passed over in front of them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother. Genesis 33:3 Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept. Genesis 33:4 He lifted up his eyes, and saw the women and the children; and said, “Who are these with you?” He said, “The children whom God has graciously given your servant.” Genesis 33:5 Then the servants came near with their children, and they bowed themselves. Genesis 33:6 Leah also and her children came near, and bowed themselves. After them, Joseph came near with Rachel, and they bowed themselves. Genesis 33:7 Esau said, “What do you mean by all this company which I met?” Jacob said, “To find favor in the sight of my lord.” Genesis 33:8 Esau said, “I have enough, my brother; let that which you have be yours.” Genesis 33:9 Jacob said, “Please, no, if I have now found favor in your sight, then receive my present at my hand, because I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me. Genesis 33:10 Please take the gift that I brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.” He urged him, and he took it. Genesis 33:11 Esau said, “Let’s take our journey, and let’s go, and I will go before you.” Genesis 33:12 Jacob said to him, “My lord knows that the children are tender, and that the flocks and herds with me have their young, and if they overdrive them one day, all the flocks will die. Genesis 33:13 Please let my lord pass over before his servant, and I will lead on gently, according to the pace of the livestock that are before me and according to the pace of the children, until I come to my lord to Seir.” Genesis 33:14 Esau said, “Let me now leave with you some of the people who are with me.” He said, “Why? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord.” Genesis 33:15 So Esau returned that day on his way to Seir. Genesis 33:16 Jacob traveled to Succoth, built himself a house, and made shelters for his livestock. Therefore the name of the place is called Succoth. Genesis 33:17 Jacob came in peace to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Paddan Aram; and encamped before the city. Genesis 33:18 He bought the parcel of ground where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for one hundred pieces of money. Genesis 33:19 He erected an altar there, and called it El Elohe Israel. Genesis 33:20

title: Genesis 34:1–31
context: After Jacob’s return to the land (ch. 33), Dinah goes out among the daughters of the land. Shechem the Hivite seizes and humiliates her, then seeks marriage; Jacob’s sons answer with deceitful circumcision, and Simeon and Levi slaughter the city’s males. The chapter names outrage without baptizing either the assault or the massacre.
text: Genesis 34:1–31 Genesis After Jacob’s return to the land (ch. 33), Dinah goes out among the daughters of the land. Shechem the Hivite seizes and humiliates her, then seeks marriage; Jacob’s sons answer with deceitful circumcision, and Simeon and Levi slaughter the city’s males. The chapter names outrage without baptizing either the assault or the massacre. Dinah, the daughter of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the land. Genesis 34:1 Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the land, saw her. He took her, lay with her, and humbled her. Genesis 34:2 His soul joined to Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, and he loved the young lady, and spoke kindly to the young lady. Genesis 34:3 Shechem spoke to his father, Hamor, saying, “Get me this young lady as a wife.” Genesis 34:4 Now Jacob heard that he had defiled Dinah, his daughter; and his sons were with his livestock in the field. Jacob held his peace until they came. Genesis 34:5 Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to talk with him. Genesis 34:6 The sons of Jacob came in from the field when they heard it. The men were grieved, and they were very angry, because he had done folly in Israel in lying with Jacob’s daughter, a thing that ought not to be done. Genesis 34:7 Hamor talked with them, saying, “The soul of my son, Shechem, longs for your daughter. Please give her to him as a wife. Genesis 34:8 Make marriages with us. Give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for yourselves. Genesis 34:9 You shall dwell with us, and the land will be before you. Live and trade in it, and get possessions in it.” Genesis 34:10 Shechem said to her father and to her brothers, “Let me find favor in your eyes, and whatever you will tell me I will give. Genesis 34:11 Ask me a great amount for a dowry, and I will give whatever you ask of me, but give me the young lady as a wife.” Genesis 34:12 The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and Hamor his father with deceit when they spoke, because he had defiled Dinah their sister, Genesis 34:13 and said to them, “We can’t do this thing, to give our sister to one who is uncircumcised; for that is a reproach to us. Genesis 34:14 Only on this condition will we consent to you. If you will be as we are, that every male of you be circumcised, Genesis 34:15 then will we give our daughters to you; and we will take your daughters to us, and we will dwell with you, and we will become one people. Genesis 34:16 But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, then we will take our sister, and we will be gone.” Genesis 34:17 Their words pleased Hamor and Shechem, Hamor’s son. Genesis 34:18 The young man didn’t wait to do this thing, because he had delight in Jacob’s daughter, and he was honored above all the house of his father. Genesis 34:19 Hamor and Shechem, his son, came to the gate of their city, and talked with the men of their city, saying, Genesis 34:20 “These men are peaceful with us. Therefore let them live in the land and trade in it. For behold, the land is large enough for them. Let’s take their daughters to us for wives, and let’s give them our daughters. Genesis 34:21 Only on this condition will the men consent to us to live with us, to become one people, if every male among us is circumcised, as they are circumcised. Genesis 34:22 Won’t their livestock and their possessions and all their animals be ours? Only let’s give our consent to them, and they will dwell with us.” Genesis 34:23 All who went out of the gate of his city listened to Hamor, and to Shechem his son; and every male was circumcised, all who went out of the gate of his city. Genesis 34:24 On the third day, when they were sore, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, each took his sword, came upon the unsuspecting city, and killed all the males. Genesis 34:25 They killed Hamor and Shechem, his son, with the edge of the sword, and took Dinah out of Shechem’s house, and went away. Genesis 34:26 Jacob’s sons came on the dead, and plundered the city, because they had defiled their sister. Genesis 34:27 They took their flocks, their herds, their donkeys, that which was in the city, that which was in the field, Genesis 34:28 and all their wealth. They took captive all their little ones and their wives, and took as plunder everything that was in the house. Genesis 34:29 Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, “You have troubled me, to make me odious to the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites. I am few in number. They will gather themselves together against me and strike me, and I will be destroyed, I and my house.” Genesis 34:30 They said, “Should he deal with our sister as with a prostitute?” Genesis 34:31

title: Genesis 35:1–15
context: After Shechem’s violence, God sends Jacob back to Bethel: arise, dwell, make an altar to God, who appeared when he fled Esau. Jacob puts away foreign gods; a terror from God keeps the cities from pursuit. He builds an altar at El-bethel, buries Deborah at Allon-bacuth, and God appears again—renaming him Israel, promising fruitfulness, kings, and land—then raises a pillar, pours a drink offering, and names the place Bethel.
text: Genesis 35:1–15 Genesis After Shechem’s violence, God sends Jacob back to Bethel: arise, dwell, make an altar to God, who appeared when he fled Esau. Jacob puts away foreign gods; a terror from God keeps the cities from pursuit. He builds an altar at El-bethel, buries Deborah at Allon-bacuth, and God appears again—renaming him Israel, promising fruitfulness, kings, and land—then raises a pillar, pours a drink offering, and names the place Bethel. God said to Jacob, “Arise, go up to Bethel, and live there. Make there an altar to God, who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother.” Genesis 35:1 Then Jacob said to his household, and to all who were with him, “Put away the foreign gods that are among you, purify yourselves, and change your garments. Genesis 35:2 Let’s arise, and go up to Bethel. I will make there an altar to God, who answered me in the day of my distress, and was with me on the way which I went.” Genesis 35:3 They gave to Jacob all the foreign gods which were in their hands, and the rings which were in their ears; and Jacob hid them under the oak which was by Shechem. Genesis 35:4 They traveled, and a terror of God was on the cities that were around them, and they didn’t pursue the sons of Jacob. Genesis 35:5 So Jacob came to Luz (that is, Bethel), which is in the land of Canaan, he and all the people who were with him. Genesis 35:6 He built an altar there, and called the place El Beth El; because there God was revealed to him, when he fled from the face of his brother. Genesis 35:7 Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died, and she was buried below Bethel under the oak; and its name was called Allon Bacuth. Genesis 35:8 God appeared to Jacob again, when he came from Paddan Aram, and blessed him. Genesis 35:9 God said to him, “Your name is Jacob. Your name shall not be Jacob any more, but your name will be Israel.” He named him Israel. Genesis 35:10 God said to him, “I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation and a company of nations will be from you, and kings will come out of your body. Genesis 35:11 The land which I gave to Abraham and Isaac, I will give it to you, and to your offspring after you I will give the land.” Genesis 35:12 God went up from him in the place where he spoke with him. Genesis 35:13 Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he spoke with him, a pillar of stone. He poured out a drink offering on it, and poured oil on it. Genesis 35:14 Jacob called the name of the place where God spoke with him “Bethel”. Genesis 35:15

title: Genesis 35:16–29
context: From Bethel the family travels toward Ephrath; Rachel dies in hard labor after naming Ben-oni, whom Jacob calls Benjamin, and she is buried on the way to Bethlehem. Israel camps beyond the tower of Eder; Reuben lies with Bilhah; the twelve sons are listed. Jacob reaches Isaac at Hebron, and Isaac dies at 180, gathered to his people—buried by Esau and Jacob.
text: Genesis 35:16–29 Genesis From Bethel the family travels toward Ephrath; Rachel dies in hard labor after naming Ben-oni, whom Jacob calls Benjamin, and she is buried on the way to Bethlehem. Israel camps beyond the tower of Eder; Reuben lies with Bilhah; the twelve sons are listed. Jacob reaches Isaac at Hebron, and Isaac dies at 180, gathered to his people—buried by Esau and Jacob. They traveled from Bethel. There was still some distance to come to Ephrath, and Rachel travailed. She had hard labor. Genesis 35:16 When she was in hard labor, the midwife said to her, “Don’t be afraid, for now you will have another son.” Genesis 35:17 As her soul was departing (for she died), she named him Benoni, but his father named him Benjamin. Genesis 35:18 Rachel died, and was buried on the way to Ephrath (also called Bethlehem). Genesis 35:19 Jacob set up a pillar on her grave. The same is the Pillar of Rachel’s grave to this day. Genesis 35:20 Israel traveled, and spread his tent beyond the tower of Eder. Genesis 35:21 While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and Israel heard of it. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve. Genesis 35:22 The sons of Leah: Reuben (Jacob’s firstborn), Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. Genesis 35:23 The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. Genesis 35:24 The sons of Bilhah (Rachel’s servant): Dan and Naphtali. Genesis 35:25 The sons of Zilpah (Leah’s servant): Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob, who were born to him in Paddan Aram. Genesis 35:26 Jacob came to Isaac his father, to Mamre, to Kiriath Arba (which is Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac lived as foreigners. Genesis 35:27 The days of Isaac were one hundred eighty years. Genesis 35:28 Isaac gave up the spirit and died, and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. Esau and Jacob, his sons, buried him. Genesis 35:29

title: Genesis 36:1–19
context: Genesis pauses Jacob’s story to record Esau’s generations: he is Edom. Canaanite wives, sons born in Canaan, then a move to Seir because the brothers’ possessions were too great to dwell together. Chiefs rise from Esau’s sons. God keeps the book of a nation outside the chosen line.
text: Genesis 36:1–19 Genesis Genesis pauses Jacob’s story to record Esau’s generations: he is Edom. Canaanite wives, sons born in Canaan, then a move to Seir because the brothers’ possessions were too great to dwell together. Chiefs rise from Esau’s sons. God keeps the book of a nation outside the chosen line. Now this is the history of the generations of Esau (that is, Edom). Genesis 36:1 Esau took his wives from the daughters of Canaan: Adah the daughter of Elon, the Hittite; and Oholibamah the daughter of Anah, the daughter of Zibeon, the Hivite; Genesis 36:2 and Basemath, Ishmael’s daughter, sister of Nebaioth. Genesis 36:3 Adah bore to Esau Eliphaz. Basemath bore Reuel. Genesis 36:4 Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau, who were born to him in the land of Canaan. Genesis 36:5 Esau took his wives, his sons, his daughters, and all the members of his household, with his livestock, all his animals, and all his possessions, which he had gathered in the land of Canaan, and went into a land away from his brother Jacob. Genesis 36:6 For their substance was too great for them to dwell together, and the land of their travels couldn’t bear them because of their livestock. Genesis 36:7 Esau lived in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom. Genesis 36:8 This is the history of the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in the hill country of Seir: Genesis 36:9 these are the names of Esau’s sons: Eliphaz, the son of Adah, the wife of Esau; and Reuel, the son of Basemath, the wife of Esau. Genesis 36:10 The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam, and Kenaz. Genesis 36:11 Timna was concubine to Eliphaz, Esau’s son; and she bore to Eliphaz Amalek. These are the descendants of Adah, Esau’s wife. Genesis 36:12 These are the sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These were the descendants of Basemath, Esau’s wife. Genesis 36:13 These were the sons of Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah, the daughter of Zibeon, Esau’s wife: she bore to Esau Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. Genesis 36:14 These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau: the sons of Eliphaz the firstborn of Esau: chief Teman, chief Omar, chief Zepho, chief Kenaz, Genesis 36:15 chief Korah, chief Gatam, chief Amalek. These are the chiefs who came of Eliphaz in the land of Edom. These are the sons of Adah. Genesis 36:16 These are the sons of Reuel, Esau’s son: chief Nahath, chief Zerah, chief Shammah, chief Mizzah. These are the chiefs who came of Reuel in the land of Edom. These are the sons of Basemath, Esau’s wife. Genesis 36:17 These are the sons of Oholibamah, Esau’s wife: chief Jeush, chief Jalam, chief Korah. These are the chiefs who came of Oholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau’s wife. Genesis 36:18 These are the sons of Esau (that is, Edom), and these are their chiefs. Genesis 36:19

title: Genesis 36:20–43
context: The chapter turns to Seir’s Horite inhabitants, then to Anah who found hot springs, Horite chiefs, and the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel. It closes with Esau’s chiefs listed by clans and dwelling places—Edom’s geography under God’s care.
text: Genesis 36:20–43 Genesis The chapter turns to Seir’s Horite inhabitants, then to Anah who found hot springs, Horite chiefs, and the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel. It closes with Esau’s chiefs listed by clans and dwelling places—Edom’s geography under God’s care. These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Genesis 36:20 Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These are the chiefs who came of the Horites, the children of Seir in the land of Edom. Genesis 36:21 The children of Lotan were Hori and Heman. Lotan’s sister was Timna. Genesis 36:22 These are the children of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. Genesis 36:23 These are the children of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. This is Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness, as he fed the donkeys of Zibeon his father. Genesis 36:24 These are the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah. Genesis 36:25 These are the children of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. Genesis 36:26 These are the children of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. Genesis 36:27 These are the children of Dishan: Uz and Aran. Genesis 36:28 These are the chiefs who came of the Horites: chief Lotan, chief Shobal, chief Zibeon, chief Anah, Genesis 36:29 chief Dishon, chief Ezer, and chief Dishan. These are the chiefs who came of the Horites, according to their chiefs in the land of Seir. Genesis 36:30 These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel. Genesis 36:31 Bela, the son of Beor, reigned in Edom. The name of his city was Dinhabah. Genesis 36:32 Bela died, and Jobab, the son of Zerah of Bozrah, reigned in his place. Genesis 36:33 Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place. Genesis 36:34 Husham died, and Hadad, the son of Bedad, who struck Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his place. The name of his city was Avith. Genesis 36:35 Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place. Genesis 36:36 Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth by the river, reigned in his place. Genesis 36:37 Shaul died, and Baal Hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place. Genesis 36:38 Baal Hanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his place. The name of his city was Pau. His wife’s name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab. Genesis 36:39 These are the names of the chiefs who came from Esau, according to their families, after their places, and by their names: chief Timna, chief Alvah, chief Jetheth, Genesis 36:40 chief Oholibamah, chief Elah, chief Pinon, Genesis 36:41 chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mibzar, Genesis 36:42 chief Magdiel, and chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom, according to their habitations in the land of their possession. This is Esau, the father of the Edomites. Genesis 36:43

title: Genesis 37:1–11
context: Jacob dwells in Canaan. The Joseph story opens: a seventeen-year-old bringing a bad report, a father’s favoritism and a many-colored robe, brothers who cannot speak peace, and two dreams of sheaves and stars that deepen hatred while Israel keeps the saying in mind.
text: Genesis 37:1–11 Genesis Jacob dwells in Canaan. The Joseph story opens: a seventeen-year-old bringing a bad report, a father’s favoritism and a many-colored robe, brothers who cannot speak peace, and two dreams of sheaves and stars that deepen hatred while Israel keeps the saying in mind. Jacob lived in the land of his father’s travels, in the land of Canaan. Genesis 37:1 This is the history of the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was feeding the flock with his brothers. He was a boy with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives. Joseph brought an evil report of them to their father. Genesis 37:2 Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age, and he made him a tunic of many colors. Genesis 37:3 His brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, and they hated him, and couldn’t speak peaceably to him. Genesis 37:4 Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it to his brothers, and they hated him all the more. Genesis 37:5 He said to them, “Please hear this dream which I have dreamed: Genesis 37:6 for behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and also stood upright; and behold, your sheaves came around, and bowed down to my sheaf.” Genesis 37:7 His brothers asked him, “Will you indeed reign over us? Will you indeed have dominion over us?” They hated him all the more for his dreams and for his words. Genesis 37:8 He dreamed yet another dream, and told it to his brothers, and said, “Behold, I have dreamed yet another dream: and behold, the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowed down to me.” Genesis 37:9 He told it to his father and to his brothers. His father rebuked him, and said to him, “What is this dream that you have dreamed? Will I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves down to the earth before you?” Genesis 37:10 His brothers envied him, but his father kept this saying in mind. Genesis 37:11

title: Genesis 37:12–36
context: Joseph is sent from Hebron to Shechem, then Dothan. The brothers conspire, strip the robe, throw him in a pit, sell him for twenty shekels, and fake a wild-animal death. Jacob mourns toward Sheol while Joseph is sold in Egypt to Potiphar.
text: Genesis 37:12–36 Genesis Joseph is sent from Hebron to Shechem, then Dothan. The brothers conspire, strip the robe, throw him in a pit, sell him for twenty shekels, and fake a wild-animal death. Jacob mourns toward Sheol while Joseph is sold in Egypt to Potiphar. His brothers went to feed their father’s flock in Shechem. Genesis 37:12 Israel said to Joseph, “Aren’t your brothers feeding the flock in Shechem? Come, and I will send you to them.” He said to him, “Here I am.” Genesis 37:13 He said to him, “Go now, see whether it is well with your brothers, and well with the flock; and bring me word again.” So he sent him out of the valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem. Genesis 37:14 A certain man found him, and behold, he was wandering in the field. The man asked him, “What are you looking for?” Genesis 37:15 He said, “I am looking for my brothers. Tell me, please, where they are feeding the flock.” Genesis 37:16 The man said, “They have left here, for I heard them say, ‘Let’s go to Dothan.’” Joseph went after his brothers, and found them in Dothan. Genesis 37:17 They saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to kill him. Genesis 37:18 They said to one another, “Behold, this dreamer comes. Genesis 37:19 Come now therefore, and let’s kill him, and cast him into one of the pits, and we will say, ‘An evil animal has devoured him.’ We will see what will become of his dreams.” Genesis 37:20 Reuben heard it, and delivered him out of their hand, and said, “Let’s not take his life.” Genesis 37:21 Reuben said to them, “Shed no blood. Throw him into this pit that is in the wilderness, but lay no hand on him”—that he might deliver him out of their hand, to restore him to his father. Genesis 37:22 When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped Joseph of his tunic, the tunic of many colors that was on him; Genesis 37:23 and they took him, and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty. There was no water in it. Genesis 37:24 They sat down to eat bread, and they lifted up their eyes and looked, and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing spices and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt. Genesis 37:25 Judah said to his brothers, “What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? Genesis 37:26 Come, and let’s sell him to the Ishmaelites, and not let our hand be on him; for he is our brother, our flesh.” His brothers listened to him. Genesis 37:27 Midianites who were merchants passed by, and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. The merchants brought Joseph into Egypt. Genesis 37:28 Reuben returned to the pit, and saw that Joseph wasn’t in the pit; and he tore his clothes. Genesis 37:29 He returned to his brothers, and said, “The child is no more; and I, where will I go?” Genesis 37:30 They took Joseph’s tunic, and killed a male goat, and dipped the tunic in the blood. Genesis 37:31 They took the tunic of many colors, and they brought it to their father, and said, “We have found this. Examine it, now, and see if it is your son’s tunic or not.” Genesis 37:32 He recognized it, and said, “It is my son’s tunic. An evil animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn in pieces.” Genesis 37:33 Jacob tore his clothes, and put sackcloth on his waist, and mourned for his son many days. Genesis 37:34 All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. He said, “For I will go down to Sheol to my son, mourning.” His father wept for him. Genesis 37:35 The Midianites sold him into Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, the captain of the guard. Genesis 37:36

title: Genesis 38:1–11
context: While Joseph’s story pauses, Judah goes down from his brothers, marries a Canaanite, and fathers Er, Onan, and Shelah. Er and Onan die under the LORD’s judgment; Judah withholds Shelah from Tamar and sends her home as a widow.
text: Genesis 38:1–11 Genesis While Joseph’s story pauses, Judah goes down from his brothers, marries a Canaanite, and fathers Er, Onan, and Shelah. Er and Onan die under the LORD’s judgment; Judah withholds Shelah from Tamar and sends her home as a widow. At that time, Judah went down from his brothers, and visited a certain Adullamite, whose name was Hirah. Genesis 38:1 There, Judah saw the daughter of a certain Canaanite man named Shua. He took her, and went in to her. Genesis 38:2 She conceived, and bore a son; and he named him Er. Genesis 38:3 She conceived again, and bore a son; and she named him Onan. Genesis 38:4 She yet again bore a son, and named him Shelah. He was at Chezib when she bore him. Genesis 38:5 Judah took a wife for Er, his firstborn, and her name was Tamar. Genesis 38:6 Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the LORD’s sight. So the LORD killed him. Genesis 38:7 Judah said to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife, and perform the duty of a husband’s brother to her, and raise up offspring for your brother.” Genesis 38:8 Onan knew that the offspring wouldn’t be his; and when he went in to his brother’s wife, he spilled his semen on the ground, lest he should give offspring to his brother. Genesis 38:9 The thing which he did was evil in the LORD’s sight, and he killed him also. Genesis 38:10 Then Judah said to Tamar, his daughter-in-law, “Remain a widow in your father’s house, until Shelah, my son, is grown up;” for he said, “Lest he also die, like his brothers.” Tamar went and lived in her father’s house. Genesis 38:11

title: Genesis 38:12–30
context: After Shua’s daughter dies, Tamar, still denied Shelah, veils herself at Enaim. Judah lies with her unknowingly, leaves his seal, cord, and staff, then tries to burn her for pregnancy—until she produces the pledge. He confesses she is more righteous than he; twins Perez and Zerah are born, and Perez will carry Judah’s line.
text: Genesis 38:12–30 Genesis After Shua’s daughter dies, Tamar, still denied Shelah, veils herself at Enaim. Judah lies with her unknowingly, leaves his seal, cord, and staff, then tries to burn her for pregnancy—until she produces the pledge. He confesses she is more righteous than he; twins Perez and Zerah are born, and Perez will carry Judah’s line. After many days, Shua’s daughter, the wife of Judah, died. Judah was comforted, and went up to his sheep shearers to Timnah, he and his friend Hirah, the Adullamite. Genesis 38:12 Tamar was told, “Behold, your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.” Genesis 38:13 She took off the garments of her widowhood, and covered herself with her veil, and wrapped herself, and sat in the gate of Enaim, which is on the way to Timnah; for she saw that Shelah was grown up, and she wasn’t given to him as a wife. Genesis 38:14 When Judah saw her, he thought that she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face. Genesis 38:15 He turned to her by the way, and said, “Please come, let me come in to you,” for he didn’t know that she was his daughter-in-law. She said, “What will you give me, that you may come in to me?” Genesis 38:16 He said, “I will send you a young goat from the flock.” She said, “Will you give me a pledge, until you send it?” Genesis 38:17 He said, “What pledge will I give you?” She said, “Your signet and your cord, and your staff that is in your hand.” He gave them to her, and came in to her, and she conceived by him. Genesis 38:18 She arose, and went away, and put off her veil from her, and put on the garments of her widowhood. Genesis 38:19 Judah sent the young goat by the hand of his friend, the Adullamite, to receive the pledge from the woman’s hand, but he didn’t find her. Genesis 38:20 Then he asked the men of her place, saying, “Where is the prostitute, that was at Enaim by the road?” They said, “There has been no prostitute here.” Genesis 38:21 He returned to Judah, and said, “I haven’t found her; and also the men of the place said, ‘There has been no prostitute here.’” Genesis 38:22 Judah said, “Let her keep it, lest we be shamed. Behold, I sent this young goat, and you haven’t found her.” Genesis 38:23 About three months later, Judah was told, “Tamar, your daughter-in-law, has played the prostitute. Moreover, behold, she is with child by prostitution.” Judah said, “Bring her out, and let her be burned.” Genesis 38:24 When she was brought out, she sent to her father-in-law, saying, “I am with child by the man who owns these.” She also said, “Please discern whose these are—the signet, and the cords, and the staff.” Genesis 38:25 Judah acknowledged them, and said, “She is more righteous than I, because I didn’t give her to Shelah, my son.” He knew her again no more. Genesis 38:26 In the time of her travail, behold, twins were in her womb. Genesis 38:27 When she travailed, one put out a hand, and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, “This came out first.” Genesis 38:28 As he drew back his hand, behold, his brother came out, and she said, “Why have you made a breach for yourself?” Therefore his name was called Perez. Genesis 38:29 Afterward his brother came out, who had the scarlet thread on his hand, and his name was called Zerah. Genesis 38:30

title: Genesis 39:1–18
context: Joseph is sold into Potiphar’s house. The LORD is with him; blessing spills onto an Egyptian household. Potiphar’s wife presses him day after day; he refuses as sin against God, flees, and is framed by the garment he left behind.
text: Genesis 39:1–18 Genesis Joseph is sold into Potiphar’s house. The LORD is with him; blessing spills onto an Egyptian household. Potiphar’s wife presses him day after day; he refuses as sin against God, flees, and is framed by the garment he left behind. Joseph was brought down to Egypt. Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites that had brought him down there. Genesis 39:1 The LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. He was in the house of his master the Egyptian. Genesis 39:2 His master saw that the LORD was with him, and that the LORD made all that he did prosper in his hand. Genesis 39:3 Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and Potiphar made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand. Genesis 39:4 From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. The LORD’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field. Genesis 39:5 He left all that he had in Joseph’s hand. He didn’t concern himself with anything, except for the food which he ate. Joseph was well-built and handsome. Genesis 39:6 After these things, his master’s wife set her eyes on Joseph; and she said, “Lie with me.” Genesis 39:7 But he refused, and said to his master’s wife, “Behold, my master doesn’t know what is with me in the house, and he has put all that he has into my hand. Genesis 39:8 No one is greater in this house than I am, and he has not kept back anything from me but you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” Genesis 39:9 As she spoke to Joseph day by day, he didn’t listen to her, to lie by her, or to be with her. Genesis 39:10 About this time, he went into the house to do his work, and there were none of the men of the house inside. Genesis 39:11 She caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me!” He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside. Genesis 39:12 When she saw that he had left his garment in her hand, and had run outside, Genesis 39:13 she called to the men of her house, and spoke to them, saying, “Behold, he has brought a Hebrew in to us to mock us. He came in to me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice. Genesis 39:14 When he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment by me, and ran outside.” Genesis 39:15 She laid up his garment by her, until his master came home. Genesis 39:16 She spoke to him according to these words, saying, “The Hebrew servant, whom you have brought to us, came in to me to mock me, Genesis 39:17 and as I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment by me, and ran outside.” Genesis 39:18

title: Genesis 39:19–23
context: Potiphar’s anger sends Joseph to the king’s prison. The LORD is with him there too: steadfast love, favor with the keeper, charge of the prisoners, and success the LORD makes.
text: Genesis 39:19–23 Genesis Potiphar’s anger sends Joseph to the king’s prison. The LORD is with him there too: steadfast love, favor with the keeper, charge of the prisoners, and success the LORD makes. When his master heard the words of his wife, which she spoke to him, saying, “This is what your servant did to me,” his wrath was kindled. Genesis 39:19 Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, the place where the king’s prisoners were bound, and he was there in custody. Genesis 39:20 But the LORD was with Joseph, and showed kindness to him, and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison. Genesis 39:21 The keeper of the prison committed to Joseph’s hand all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever they did there, he was responsible for it. Genesis 39:22 The keeper of the prison didn’t look after anything that was under his hand, because the LORD was with him; and that which he did, the LORD made it prosper. Genesis 39:23

title: Genesis 4:1–16
context: After Eden, life continues east of the garden: Eve bears Cain and Abel, the brothers bring offerings, the Lord regards Abel’s gift and not Cain’s, and Cain’s anger ripens into the first murder. God still speaks, warns, judges, and even marks the guilty with a severe mercy before Cain walks away from His presence.
text: Genesis 4:1–16 Genesis After Eden, life continues east of the garden: Eve bears Cain and Abel, the brothers bring offerings, the Lord regards Abel’s gift and not Cain’s, and Cain’s anger ripens into the first murder. God still speaks, warns, judges, and even marks the guilty with a severe mercy before Cain walks away from His presence. The man knew Eve his wife. She conceived, and gave birth to Cain, and said, “I have gotten a man with the LORD’s help.” Genesis 4:1 Again she gave birth, to Cain’s brother Abel. Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground. Genesis 4:2 As time passed, Cain brought an offering to the LORD from the fruit of the ground. Genesis 4:3 Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock and of its fat. The LORD respected Abel and his offering, Genesis 4:4 but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell. Genesis 4:5 The LORD said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen? Genesis 4:6 If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.” Genesis 4:7 Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him. Genesis 4:8 The LORD said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?” He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” Genesis 4:9 The LORD said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground. Genesis 4:10 Now you are cursed because of the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. Genesis 4:11 From now on, when you till the ground, it won’t yield its strength to you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.” Genesis 4:12 Cain said to the LORD, “My punishment is greater than I can bear. Genesis 4:13 Behold, you have driven me out today from the surface of the ground. I will be hidden from your face, and I will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth. Whoever finds me will kill me.” Genesis 4:14 The LORD said to him, “Therefore whoever slays Cain, vengeance will be taken on him sevenfold.” The LORD appointed a sign for Cain, so that anyone finding him would not strike him. Genesis 4:15 Cain left the LORD’s presence, and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden. Genesis 4:16

title: Genesis 4:17–26
context: Cain’s line multiplies: a city named for Enoch, generations down to Lamech, polygamy, tents, music, metalwork, and a boast of multiplied vengeance. The chapter then turns back to Adam and Eve: Seth is appointed in Abel’s place, Enosh is born, and people begin to call on the LORD’s name of the Lord.
text: Genesis 4:17–26 Genesis Cain’s line multiplies: a city named for Enoch, generations down to Lamech, polygamy, tents, music, metalwork, and a boast of multiplied vengeance. The chapter then turns back to Adam and Eve: Seth is appointed in Abel’s place, Enosh is born, and people begin to call on the LORD’s name of the Lord. Cain knew his wife. She conceived, and gave birth to Enoch. He built a city, and named the city after the name of his son, Enoch. Genesis 4:17 Irad was born to Enoch. Irad became the father of Mehujael. Mehujael became the father of Methushael. Methushael became the father of Lamech. Genesis 4:18 Lamech took two wives: the name of the first one was Adah, and the name of the second one was Zillah. Genesis 4:19 Adah gave birth to Jabal, who was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock. Genesis 4:20 His brother’s name was Jubal, who was the father of all who handle the harp and pipe. Genesis 4:21 Zillah also gave birth to Tubal Cain, the forger of every cutting instrument of bronze and iron. Tubal Cain’s sister was Naamah. Genesis 4:22 Lamech said to his wives, “Adah and Zillah, hear my voice. You wives of Lamech, listen to my speech, for I have slain a man for wounding me, a young man for bruising me. Genesis 4:23 If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.” Genesis 4:24 Adam knew his wife again. She gave birth to a son, and named him Seth, saying, “for God has given me another child instead of Abel, for Cain killed him.” Genesis 4:25 A son was also born to Seth, and he named him Enosh. At that time men began to call on the LORD’s name. Genesis 4:26

title: Genesis 40:1–23
context: In prison Joseph is assigned to Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker. Each dreams; Joseph says interpretations belong to God. The cupbearer will be restored in three days, the baker hanged. Joseph asks to be remembered. On Pharaoh’s birthday both words come true—and the cupbearer forgets him.
