text: Genesis 40:1–23 Genesis In prison Joseph is assigned to Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker. Each dreams; Joseph says interpretations belong to God. The cupbearer will be restored in three days, the baker hanged. Joseph asks to be remembered. On Pharaoh’s birthday both words come true—and the cupbearer forgets him. After these things, the butler of the king of Egypt and his baker offended their lord, the king of Egypt. Genesis 40:1 Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cup bearer and the chief baker. Genesis 40:2 He put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, into the prison, the place where Joseph was bound. Genesis 40:3 The captain of the guard assigned them to Joseph, and he took care of them. They stayed in prison many days. Genesis 40:4 They both dreamed a dream, each man his dream, in one night, each man according to the interpretation of his dream, the cup bearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were bound in the prison. Genesis 40:5 Joseph came in to them in the morning, and saw them, and saw that they were sad. Genesis 40:6 He asked Pharaoh’s officers who were with him in custody in his master’s house, saying, “Why do you look so sad today?” Genesis 40:7 They said to him, “We have dreamed a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it.” Joseph said to them, “Don’t interpretations belong to God? Please tell it to me.” Genesis 40:8 The chief cup bearer told his dream to Joseph, and said to him, “In my dream, behold, a vine was in front of me, Genesis 40:9 and in the vine were three branches. It was as though it budded, it blossomed, and its clusters produced ripe grapes. Genesis 40:10 Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand; and I took the grapes, and pressed them into Pharaoh’s cup, and I gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand.” Genesis 40:11 Joseph said to him, “This is its interpretation: the three branches are three days. Genesis 40:12 Within three more days, Pharaoh will lift up your head, and restore you to your office. You will give Pharaoh’s cup into his hand, the way you did when you were his cup bearer. Genesis 40:13 But remember me when it is well with you. Please show kindness to me, and make mention of me to Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house. Genesis 40:14 For indeed, I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon.” Genesis 40:15 When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was good, he said to Joseph, “I also was in my dream, and behold, three baskets of white bread were on my head. Genesis 40:16 In the uppermost basket there were all kinds of baked food for Pharaoh, and the birds ate them out of the basket on my head.” Genesis 40:17 Joseph answered, “This is its interpretation. The three baskets are three days. Genesis 40:18 Within three more days, Pharaoh will lift up your head from off you, and will hang you on a tree; and the birds will eat your flesh from off you.” Genesis 40:19 On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he made a feast for all his servants, and he lifted up the head of the chief cup bearer and the head of the chief baker among his servants. Genesis 40:20 He restored the chief cup bearer to his position again, and he gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand; Genesis 40:21 but he hanged the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted to them. Genesis 40:22 Yet the chief cup bearer didn’t remember Joseph, but forgot him. Genesis 40:23

title: Genesis 41:1–36
context: Two years after the cupbearer’s release, Pharaoh dreams of seven plump cows swallowed by seven thin ones, then seven good ears swallowed by seven blighted ones. Egypt’s magicians fail. The cupbearer remembers Joseph in the pit. Shaved and summoned, Joseph credits God, interprets the doubled dream as seven years of plenty then seven of famine, and urges Pharaoh to appoint a wise man and store one-fifth of the harvest so the land will not perish.
text: Genesis 41:1–36 Genesis Two years after the cupbearer’s release, Pharaoh dreams of seven plump cows swallowed by seven thin ones, then seven good ears swallowed by seven blighted ones. Egypt’s magicians fail. The cupbearer remembers Joseph in the pit. Shaved and summoned, Joseph credits God, interprets the doubled dream as seven years of plenty then seven of famine, and urges Pharaoh to appoint a wise man and store one-fifth of the harvest so the land will not perish. At the end of two full years, Pharaoh dreamed, and behold, he stood by the river. Genesis 41:1 Behold, seven cattle came up out of the river. They were sleek and fat, and they fed in the marsh grass. Genesis 41:2 Behold, seven other cattle came up after them out of the river, ugly and thin, and stood by the other cattle on the brink of the river. Genesis 41:3 The ugly and thin cattle ate up the seven sleek and fat cattle. So Pharaoh awoke. Genesis 41:4 He slept and dreamed a second time; and behold, seven heads of grain came up on one stalk, healthy and good. Genesis 41:5 Behold, seven heads of grain, thin and blasted with the east wind, sprung up after them. Genesis 41:6 The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven healthy and full ears. Pharaoh awoke, and behold, it was a dream. Genesis 41:7 In the morning, his spirit was troubled, and he sent and called for all of Egypt’s magicians and wise men. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but there was no one who could interpret them to Pharaoh. Genesis 41:8 Then the chief cup bearer spoke to Pharaoh, saying, “I remember my faults today. Genesis 41:9 Pharaoh was angry with his servants, and put me in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, with the chief baker. Genesis 41:10 We dreamed a dream in one night, he and I. Each man dreamed according to the interpretation of his dream. Genesis 41:11 There was with us there a young man, a Hebrew, servant to the captain of the guard, and we told him, and he interpreted to us our dreams. He interpreted to each man according to his dream. Genesis 41:12 As he interpreted to us, so it was. He restored me to my office, and he hanged him.” Genesis 41:13 Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon. He shaved himself, changed his clothing, and came in to Pharaoh. Genesis 41:14 Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I have dreamed a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it. I have heard it said of you, that when you hear a dream you can interpret it.” Genesis 41:15 Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, “It isn’t in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.” Genesis 41:16 Pharaoh spoke to Joseph, “In my dream, behold, I stood on the brink of the river; Genesis 41:17 and behold, seven fat and sleek cattle came up out of the river. They fed in the marsh grass; Genesis 41:18 and behold, seven other cattle came up after them, poor and very ugly and thin, such as I never saw in all the land of Egypt for ugliness. Genesis 41:19 The thin and ugly cattle ate up the first seven fat cattle; Genesis 41:20 and when they had eaten them up, it couldn’t be known that they had eaten them, but they were still ugly, as at the beginning. So I awoke. Genesis 41:21 I saw in my dream, and behold, seven heads of grain came up on one stalk, full and good; Genesis 41:22 and behold, seven heads of grain, withered, thin, and blasted with the east wind, sprung up after them. Genesis 41:23 The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven good heads of grain. I told it to the magicians, but there was no one who could explain it to me.” Genesis 41:24 Joseph said to Pharaoh, “The dream of Pharaoh is one. What God is about to do he has declared to Pharaoh. Genesis 41:25 The seven good cattle are seven years; and the seven good heads of grain are seven years. The dream is one. Genesis 41:26 The seven thin and ugly cattle that came up after them are seven years, and also the seven empty heads of grain blasted with the east wind; they will be seven years of famine. Genesis 41:27 That is the thing which I have spoken to Pharaoh. God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do. Genesis 41:28 Behold, seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt are coming. Genesis 41:29 Seven years of famine will arise after them, and all the plenty will be forgotten in the land of Egypt. The famine will consume the land, Genesis 41:30 and the plenty will not be known in the land by reason of that famine which follows; for it will be very grievous. Genesis 41:31 The dream was doubled to Pharaoh, because the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass. Genesis 41:32 “Now therefore let Pharaoh look for a discreet and wise man, and set him over the land of Egypt. Genesis 41:33 Let Pharaoh do this, and let him appoint overseers over the land, and take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt’s produce in the seven plenteous years. Genesis 41:34 Let them gather all the food of these good years that come, and store grain under the hand of Pharaoh for food in the cities, and let them keep it. Genesis 41:35 The food will be to supply the land against the seven years of famine, which will be in the land of Egypt; so that the land will not perish through the famine.” Genesis 41:36

title: Genesis 41:37–57
context: Pharaoh and his servants accept Joseph’s plan. Seeing the Spirit of God in him, Pharaoh sets Joseph over Egypt, giving ring, linen, gold, chariot, and a new name, and marrying him to Asenath. At thirty Joseph stores the seven plentiful years until grain cannot be measured, names Manasseh and Ephraim, then opens the storehouses when famine hits all lands—so the earth comes to Egypt to buy grain.
text: Genesis 41:37–57 Genesis Pharaoh and his servants accept Joseph’s plan. Seeing the Spirit of God in him, Pharaoh sets Joseph over Egypt, giving ring, linen, gold, chariot, and a new name, and marrying him to Asenath. At thirty Joseph stores the seven plentiful years until grain cannot be measured, names Manasseh and Ephraim, then opens the storehouses when famine hits all lands—so the earth comes to Egypt to buy grain. The thing was good in the eyes of Pharaoh, and in the eyes of all his servants. Genesis 41:37 Pharaoh said to his servants, “Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God?” Genesis 41:38 Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Because God has shown you all of this, there is no one so discreet and wise as you. Genesis 41:39 You shall be over my house. All my people will be ruled according to your word. Only in the throne I will be greater than you.” Genesis 41:40 Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Behold, I have set you over all the land of Egypt.” Genesis 41:41 Pharaoh took off his signet ring from his hand, and put it on Joseph’s hand, and arrayed him in robes of fine linen, and put a gold chain about his neck. Genesis 41:42 He made him ride in the second chariot which he had. They cried before him, “Bow the knee!” He set him over all the land of Egypt. Genesis 41:43 Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I am Pharaoh. Without you, no man shall lift up his hand or his foot in all the land of Egypt.” Genesis 41:44 Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Zaphenath-Paneah. He gave him Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On as a wife. Joseph went out over the land of Egypt. Genesis 41:45 Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt. Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh, and went throughout all the land of Egypt. Genesis 41:46 In the seven plenteous years the earth produced abundantly. Genesis 41:47 He gathered up all the food of the seven years which were in the land of Egypt, and laid up the food in the cities. He stored food in each city from the fields around that city. Genesis 41:48 Joseph laid up grain as the sand of the sea, very much, until he stopped counting, for it was without number. Genesis 41:49 To Joseph were born two sons before the year of famine came, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On, bore to him. Genesis 41:50 Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh, “For”, he said, “God has made me forget all my toil, and all my father’s house.” Genesis 41:51 The name of the second, he called Ephraim: “For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.” Genesis 41:52 The seven years of plenty, that were in the land of Egypt, came to an end. Genesis 41:53 The seven years of famine began to come, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread. Genesis 41:54 When all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread, and Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do.” Genesis 41:55 The famine was over all the surface of the earth. Joseph opened all the store houses, and sold to the Egyptians. The famine was severe in the land of Egypt. Genesis 41:56 All countries came into Egypt, to Joseph, to buy grain, because the famine was severe in all the earth. Genesis 41:57

title: Genesis 42:1–17
context: Famine in Canaan sends ten of Joseph’s brothers to Egypt for grain. They bow before the governor they sold, who recognizes them, remembers his dreams, speaks roughly, and holds them as alleged spies until Benjamin is named.
text: Genesis 42:1–17 Genesis Famine in Canaan sends ten of Joseph’s brothers to Egypt for grain. They bow before the governor they sold, who recognizes them, remembers his dreams, speaks roughly, and holds them as alleged spies until Benjamin is named. Now Jacob saw that there was grain in Egypt, and Jacob said to his sons, “Why do you look at one another?” Genesis 42:1 He said, “Behold, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there, and buy for us from there, so that we may live, and not die.” Genesis 42:2 Joseph’s ten brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt. Genesis 42:3 But Jacob didn’t send Benjamin, Joseph’s brother, with his brothers; for he said, “Lest perhaps harm happen to him.” Genesis 42:4 The sons of Israel came to buy among those who came, for the famine was in the land of Canaan. Genesis 42:5 Joseph was the governor over the land. It was he who sold to all the people of the land. Joseph’s brothers came, and bowed themselves down to him with their faces to the earth. Genesis 42:6 Joseph saw his brothers, and he recognized them, but acted like a stranger to them, and spoke roughly with them. He said to them, “Where did you come from?” They said, “From the land of Canaan, to buy food.” Genesis 42:7 Joseph recognized his brothers, but they didn’t recognize him. Genesis 42:8 Joseph remembered the dreams which he dreamed about them, and said to them, “You are spies! You have come to see the nakedness of the land.” Genesis 42:9 They said to him, “No, my lord, but your servants have come to buy food. Genesis 42:10 We are all one man’s sons; we are honest men. Your servants are not spies.” Genesis 42:11 He said to them, “No, but you have come to see the nakedness of the land!” Genesis 42:12 They said, “We, your servants, are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan; and behold, the youngest is today with our father, and one is no more.” Genesis 42:13 Joseph said to them, “It is like I told you, saying, ‘You are spies!’ Genesis 42:14 By this you shall be tested. By the life of Pharaoh, you shall not go out from here, unless your youngest brother comes here. Genesis 42:15 Send one of you, and let him get your brother, and you shall be bound, that your words may be tested, whether there is truth in you, or else by the life of Pharaoh surely you are spies.” Genesis 42:16 He put them all together into custody for three days. Genesis 42:17

title: Genesis 42:18–38
context: On the third day Joseph, confessing fear of God, keeps Simeon and sends the rest with grain—and their money. Conscience breaks open on the road and at home; Jacob refuses to send Benjamin, seeing only bereavement, not yet the God who is gathering his sons.
text: Genesis 42:18–38 Genesis On the third day Joseph, confessing fear of God, keeps Simeon and sends the rest with grain—and their money. Conscience breaks open on the road and at home; Jacob refuses to send Benjamin, seeing only bereavement, not yet the God who is gathering his sons. Joseph said to them the third day, “Do this, and live, for I fear God. Genesis 42:18 If you are honest men, then let one of your brothers be bound in your prison; but you go, carry grain for the famine of your houses. Genesis 42:19 Bring your youngest brother to me; so will your words be verified, and you won’t die.” They did so. Genesis 42:20 They said to one another, “We are certainly guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us, and we wouldn’t listen. Therefore this distress has come upon us.” Genesis 42:21 Reuben answered them, saying, “Didn’t I tell you, saying, ‘Don’t sin against the child,’ and you wouldn’t listen? Therefore also, behold, his blood is required.” Genesis 42:22 They didn’t know that Joseph understood them; for there was an interpreter between them. Genesis 42:23 He turned himself away from them, and wept. Then he returned to them, and spoke to them, and took Simeon from among them, and bound him before their eyes. Genesis 42:24 Then Joseph gave a command to fill their bags with grain, and to restore each man’s money into his sack, and to give them food for the way. So it was done to them. Genesis 42:25 They loaded their donkeys with their grain, and departed from there. Genesis 42:26 As one of them opened his sack to give his donkey food in the lodging place, he saw his money. Behold, it was in the mouth of his sack. Genesis 42:27 He said to his brothers, “My money is restored! Behold, it is in my sack!” Their hearts failed them, and they turned trembling to one another, saying, “What is this that God has done to us?” Genesis 42:28 They came to Jacob their father, to the land of Canaan, and told him all that had happened to them, saying, Genesis 42:29 “The man, the lord of the land, spoke roughly with us, and took us for spies of the country. Genesis 42:30 We said to him, ‘We are honest men. We are no spies. Genesis 42:31 We are twelve brothers, sons of our father; one is no more, and the youngest is today with our father in the land of Canaan.’ Genesis 42:32 The man, the lord of the land, said to us, ‘By this I will know that you are honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, and take grain for the famine of your houses, and go your way. Genesis 42:33 Bring your youngest brother to me. Then I will know that you are not spies, but that you are honest men. So I will deliver your brother to you, and you shall trade in the land.’” Genesis 42:34 As they emptied their sacks, behold, each man’s bundle of money was in his sack. When they and their father saw their bundles of money, they were afraid. Genesis 42:35 Jacob, their father, said to them, “You have bereaved me of my children! Joseph is no more, Simeon is no more, and you want to take Benjamin away. All these things are against me.” Genesis 42:36 Reuben spoke to his father, saying, “Kill my two sons, if I don’t bring him to you. Entrust him to my care, and I will bring him to you again.” Genesis 42:37 He said, “My son shall not go down with you; for his brother is dead, and he only is left. If harm happens to him along the way in which you go, then you will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to Sheol.” Genesis 42:38

title: Genesis 43:1–14
context: The famine bites again. Judah refuses a second trip without Benjamin, pledges himself as surety, and Israel yields: gifts, double money, the boy, and a prayer to God Almighty for mercy before the man—plus a bereaved father’s surrender.
text: Genesis 43:1–14 Genesis The famine bites again. Judah refuses a second trip without Benjamin, pledges himself as surety, and Israel yields: gifts, double money, the boy, and a prayer to God Almighty for mercy before the man—plus a bereaved father’s surrender. The famine was severe in the land. Genesis 43:1 When they had eaten up the grain which they had brought out of Egypt, their father said to them, “Go again, buy us a little more food.” Genesis 43:2 Judah spoke to him, saying, “The man solemnly warned us, saying, ‘You shall not see my face, unless your brother is with you.’ Genesis 43:3 If you’ll send our brother with us, we’ll go down and buy you food; Genesis 43:4 but if you don’t send him, we won’t go down, for the man said to us, ‘You shall not see my face, unless your brother is with you.’” Genesis 43:5 Israel said, “Why did you treat me so badly, telling the man that you had another brother?” Genesis 43:6 They said, “The man asked directly concerning ourselves, and concerning our relatives, saying, ‘Is your father still alive? Have you another brother?’ We just answered his questions. Is there any way we could know that he would say, ‘Bring your brother down’?” Genesis 43:7 Judah said to Israel, his father, “Send the boy with me, and we’ll get up and go, so that we may live, and not die, both we, and you, and also our little ones. Genesis 43:8 I’ll be collateral for him. From my hand will you require him. If I don’t bring him to you, and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever; Genesis 43:9 for if we hadn’t delayed, surely we would have returned a second time by now.” Genesis 43:10 Their father, Israel, said to them, “If it must be so, then do this: Take from the choice fruits of the land in your bags, and carry down a present for the man, a little balm, a little honey, spices and myrrh, nuts, and almonds; Genesis 43:11 and take double money in your hand, and take back the money that was returned in the mouth of your sacks. Perhaps it was an oversight. Genesis 43:12 Take your brother also, get up, and return to the man. Genesis 43:13 May God Almighty give you mercy before the man, that he may release to you your other brother and Benjamin. If I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved.” Genesis 43:14

title: Genesis 43:15–34
context: The brothers stand before Joseph with Benjamin, gifts, and double money. Fear at the house meets the steward’s “Peace,” Simeon’s return, and a noon meal: bows that fulfill the old dreams, hidden weeping for Rachel’s son, seats by birth order, and Benjamin’s fivefold portion.
text: Genesis 43:15–34 Genesis The brothers stand before Joseph with Benjamin, gifts, and double money. Fear at the house meets the steward’s “Peace,” Simeon’s return, and a noon meal: bows that fulfill the old dreams, hidden weeping for Rachel’s son, seats by birth order, and Benjamin’s fivefold portion. The men took that present, and they took double money in their hand, and Benjamin; and got up, went down to Egypt, and stood before Joseph. Genesis 43:15 When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the steward of his house, “Bring the men into the house, and butcher an animal, and prepare; for the men will dine with me at noon.” Genesis 43:16 The man did as Joseph commanded, and the man brought the men to Joseph’s house. Genesis 43:17 The men were afraid, because they were brought to Joseph’s house; and they said, “Because of the money that was returned in our sacks the first time, we’re brought in; that he may seek occasion against us, attack us, and seize us as slaves, along with our donkeys.” Genesis 43:18 They came near to the steward of Joseph’s house, and they spoke to him at the door of the house, Genesis 43:19 and said, “Oh, my lord, we indeed came down the first time to buy food. Genesis 43:20 When we came to the lodging place, we opened our sacks, and behold, each man’s money was in the mouth of his sack, our money in full weight. We have brought it back in our hand. Genesis 43:21 We have brought down other money in our hand to buy food. We don’t know who put our money in our sacks.” Genesis 43:22 He said, “Peace be to you. Don’t be afraid. Your God, and the God of your father, has given you treasure in your sacks. I received your money.” He brought Simeon out to them. Genesis 43:23 The man brought the men into Joseph’s house, and gave them water, and they washed their feet. He gave their donkeys fodder. Genesis 43:24 They prepared the present for Joseph’s coming at noon, for they heard that they should eat bread there. Genesis 43:25 When Joseph came home, they brought him the present which was in their hand into the house, and bowed themselves down to the earth before him. Genesis 43:26 He asked them of their welfare, and said, “Is your father well, the old man of whom you spoke? Is he yet alive?” Genesis 43:27 They said, “Your servant, our father, is well. He is still alive.” They bowed down humbly. Genesis 43:28 He lifted up his eyes, and saw Benjamin, his brother, his mother’s son, and said, “Is this your youngest brother, of whom you spoke to me?” He said, “God be gracious to you, my son.” Genesis 43:29 Joseph hurried, for his heart yearned over his brother; and he sought a place to weep. He entered into his room, and wept there. Genesis 43:30 He washed his face, and came out. He controlled himself, and said, “Serve the meal.” Genesis 43:31 They served him by himself, and them by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves, because the Egyptians don’t eat with the Hebrews, for that is an abomination to the Egyptians. Genesis 43:32 They sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth, and the men marveled with one another. Genesis 43:33 He sent portions to them from before him, but Benjamin’s portion was five times as much as any of theirs. They drank, and were merry with him. Genesis 43:34

title: Genesis 44:1–17
context: After the feast, Joseph orders sacks filled and money returned—and his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s grain. The brothers are overtaken, searched from eldest to youngest, and the cup is found. They tear their clothes, fall before Joseph, and Judah confesses a guilt God has found out. Joseph will keep only the man with the cup and send the rest home in peace—the test of whether they will abandon Rachel’s other son as they once sold Joseph.
text: Genesis 44:1–17 Genesis After the feast, Joseph orders sacks filled and money returned—and his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s grain. The brothers are overtaken, searched from eldest to youngest, and the cup is found. They tear their clothes, fall before Joseph, and Judah confesses a guilt God has found out. Joseph will keep only the man with the cup and send the rest home in peace—the test of whether they will abandon Rachel’s other son as they once sold Joseph. He commanded the steward of his house, saying, “Fill the men’s sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man’s money in his sack’s mouth. Genesis 44:1 Put my cup, the silver cup, in the sack’s mouth of the youngest, with his grain money.” He did according to the word that Joseph had spoken. Genesis 44:2 As soon as the morning was light, the men were sent away, they and their donkeys. Genesis 44:3 When they had gone out of the city, and were not yet far off, Joseph said to his steward, “Up, follow after the men. When you overtake them, ask them, ‘Why have you rewarded evil for good? Genesis 44:4 Isn’t this that from which my lord drinks, and by which he indeed divines? You have done evil in so doing.’” Genesis 44:5 He overtook them, and he spoke these words to them. Genesis 44:6 They said to him, “Why does my lord speak such words as these? Far be it from your servants that they should do such a thing! Genesis 44:7 Behold, the money, which we found in our sacks’ mouths, we brought again to you out of the land of Canaan. How then should we steal silver or gold out of your lord’s house? Genesis 44:8 With whomever of your servants it is found, let him die, and we also will be my lord’s slaves.” Genesis 44:9 He said, “Now also let it be according to your words. He with whom it is found will be my slave; and you will be blameless.” Genesis 44:10 Then they hurried, and each man took his sack down to the ground, and each man opened his sack. Genesis 44:11 He searched, beginning with the oldest, and ending at the youngest. The cup was found in Benjamin’s sack. Genesis 44:12 Then they tore their clothes, and each man loaded his donkey, and returned to the city. Genesis 44:13 Judah and his brothers came to Joseph’s house, and he was still there. They fell on the ground before him. Genesis 44:14 Joseph said to them, “What deed is this that you have done? Don’t you know that such a man as I can indeed do divination?” Genesis 44:15 Judah said, “What will we tell my lord? What will we speak? How will we clear ourselves? God has found out the iniquity of your servants. Behold, we are my lord’s slaves, both we and he also in whose hand the cup is found.” Genesis 44:16 He said, “Far be it from me that I should do so. The man in whose hand the cup is found, he will be my slave; but as for you, go up in peace to your father.” Genesis 44:17

title: Genesis 44:18–34
context: Judah draws near and pleads: the old father, the dead brother, the boy whose life is bound up with Jacob’s. He recites Joseph’s own demand, Jacob’s fear of Sheol, and his pledge to bear the blame. Then he offers himself as servant in Benjamin’s place—the sale’s leader now standing in as substitute so the beloved son can go home.
text: Genesis 44:18–34 Genesis Judah draws near and pleads: the old father, the dead brother, the boy whose life is bound up with Jacob’s. He recites Joseph’s own demand, Jacob’s fear of Sheol, and his pledge to bear the blame. Then he offers himself as servant in Benjamin’s place—the sale’s leader now standing in as substitute so the beloved son can go home. Then Judah came near to him, and said, “Oh, my lord, please let your servant speak a word in my lord’s ears, and don’t let your anger burn against your servant; for you are even as Pharaoh. Genesis 44:18 My lord asked his servants, saying, ‘Have you a father, or a brother?’ Genesis 44:19 We said to my lord, ‘We have a father, an old man, and a child of his old age, a little one; and his brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother; and his father loves him.’ Genesis 44:20 You said to your servants, ‘Bring him down to me, that I may set my eyes on him.’ Genesis 44:21 We said to my lord, ‘The boy can’t leave his father, for if he should leave his father, his father would die.’ Genesis 44:22 You said to your servants, ‘Unless your youngest brother comes down with you, you will see my face no more.’ Genesis 44:23 When we came up to your servant my father, we told him the words of my lord. Genesis 44:24 Our father said, ‘Go again and buy us a little food.’ Genesis 44:25 We said, ‘We can’t go down. If our youngest brother is with us, then we will go down: for we may not see the man’s face, unless our youngest brother is with us.’ Genesis 44:26 Your servant, my father, said to us, ‘You know that my wife bore me two sons. Genesis 44:27 One went out from me, and I said, “Surely he is torn in pieces;” and I haven’t seen him since. Genesis 44:28 If you take this one also from me, and harm happens to him, you will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to Sheol.’ Genesis 44:29 Now therefore when I come to your servant my father, and the boy is not with us; since his life is bound up in the boy’s life; Genesis 44:30 it will happen, when he sees that the boy is no more, that he will die. Your servants will bring down the gray hairs of your servant, our father, with sorrow to Sheol. Genesis 44:31 For your servant became collateral for the boy to my father, saying, ‘If I don’t bring him to you, then I will bear the blame to my father forever.’ Genesis 44:32 Now therefore, please let your servant stay instead of the boy, my lord’s slave; and let the boy go up with his brothers. Genesis 44:33 For how will I go up to my father, if the boy isn’t with me?—lest I see the evil that will come on my father.” Genesis 44:34

title: Genesis 45:1–15
context: After Judah’s plea in chapter 44, Joseph can no longer keep the mask. He clears the room, weeps, and names himself to the brothers who sold him—then reads their crime through God’s sending to preserve life, and calls them near for reconciliation.
text: Genesis 45:1–15 Genesis After Judah’s plea in chapter 44, Joseph can no longer keep the mask. He clears the room, weeps, and names himself to the brothers who sold him—then reads their crime through God’s sending to preserve life, and calls them near for reconciliation. Then Joseph couldn’t control himself before all those who stood before him, and he called out, “Cause everyone to go out from me!” No one else stood with him, while Joseph made himself known to his brothers. Genesis 45:1 He wept aloud. The Egyptians heard, and the house of Pharaoh heard. Genesis 45:2 Joseph said to his brothers, “I am Joseph! Does my father still live?” His brothers couldn’t answer him; for they were terrified at his presence. Genesis 45:3 Joseph said to his brothers, “Come near to me, please.” They came near. He said, “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. Genesis 45:4 Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life. Genesis 45:5 For these two years the famine has been in the land, and there are yet five years, in which there will be no plowing and no harvest. Genesis 45:6 God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant on the earth, and to save you alive by a great deliverance. Genesis 45:7 So now it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God, and he has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord of all his house, and ruler over all the land of Egypt. Genesis 45:8 Hurry, and go up to my father, and tell him, ‘This is what your son Joseph says, “God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me. Don’t wait. Genesis 45:9 You shall dwell in the land of Goshen, and you will be near to me, you, your children, your children’s children, your flocks, your herds, and all that you have. Genesis 45:10 There I will provide for you; for there are yet five years of famine; lest you come to poverty, you, and your household, and all that you have.”’ Genesis 45:11 Behold, your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin, that it is my mouth that speaks to you. Genesis 45:12 You shall tell my father of all my glory in Egypt, and of all that you have seen. You shall hurry and bring my father down here.” Genesis 45:13 He fell on his brother Benjamin’s neck and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck. Genesis 45:14 He kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him. Genesis 45:15

title: Genesis 45:16–28
context: News of the brothers reaches Pharaoh, who stocks the invitation with wagons and the fat of the land. The sons of Israel go home; Jacob’s heart goes numb at the report, then revives at Joseph’s words and wagons, and Israel says it is enough: he will go and see his son.
text: Genesis 45:16–28 Genesis News of the brothers reaches Pharaoh, who stocks the invitation with wagons and the fat of the land. The sons of Israel go home; Jacob’s heart goes numb at the report, then revives at Joseph’s words and wagons, and Israel says it is enough: he will go and see his son. The report of it was heard in Pharaoh’s house, saying, “Joseph’s brothers have come.” It pleased Pharaoh well, and his servants. Genesis 45:16 Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Tell your brothers, ‘Do this: Load your animals, and go, travel to the land of Canaan. Genesis 45:17 Take your father and your households, and come to me, and I will give you the good of the land of Egypt, and you will eat the fat of the land.’ Genesis 45:18 Now you are commanded to do this: Take wagons out of the land of Egypt for your little ones, and for your wives, and bring your father, and come. Genesis 45:19 Also, don’t concern yourselves about your belongings, for the good of all the land of Egypt is yours.” Genesis 45:20 The sons of Israel did so. Joseph gave them wagons, according to the commandment of Pharaoh, and gave them provision for the way. Genesis 45:21 He gave each one of them changes of clothing, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of clothing. Genesis 45:22 He sent the following to his father: ten donkeys loaded with the good things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain and bread and provision for his father by the way. Genesis 45:23 So he sent his brothers away, and they departed. He said to them, “See that you don’t quarrel on the way.” Genesis 45:24 They went up out of Egypt, and came into the land of Canaan, to Jacob their father. Genesis 45:25 They told him, saying, “Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt.” His heart fainted, for he didn’t believe them. Genesis 45:26 They told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said to them. When he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of Jacob, their father, revived. Genesis 45:27 Israel said, “It is enough. Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die.” Genesis 45:28

title: Genesis 46:1–27
context: Israel sets out with all he has, sacrifices at Beersheba to the God of his father, Isaac. God speaks in the visions of the night: do not be afraid to go down into Egypt; I will make you a great nation there; I will go down with you, bring you up again. Joseph’s hand will close your eyes. Then the household migrates, and the sons of Israel are listed by mothers—Leah, Zilpah, Rachel, and Bilhah—with Joseph’s two sons born in Egypt; all the persons of Jacob’s house who came into Egypt are seventy.
text: Genesis 46:1–27 Genesis Israel sets out with all he has, sacrifices at Beersheba to the God of his father, Isaac. God speaks in the visions of the night: do not be afraid to go down into Egypt; I will make you a great nation there; I will go down with you, bring you up again. Joseph’s hand will close your eyes. Then the household migrates, and the sons of Israel are listed by mothers—Leah, Zilpah, Rachel, and Bilhah—with Joseph’s two sons born in Egypt; all the persons of Jacob’s house who came into Egypt are seventy. Israel traveled with all that he had, and came to Beersheba, and offered sacrifices to the God of his father, Isaac. Genesis 46:1 God spoke to Israel in the visions of the night, and said, “Jacob, Jacob!” He said, “Here I am.” Genesis 46:2 He said, “I am God, the God of your father. Don’t be afraid to go down into Egypt, for there I will make of you a great nation. Genesis 46:3 I will go down with you into Egypt. I will also surely bring you up again. Joseph’s hand will close your eyes.” Genesis 46:4 Jacob rose up from Beersheba, and the sons of Israel carried Jacob, their father, their little ones, and their wives, in the wagons which Pharaoh had sent to carry him. Genesis 46:5 They took their livestock, and their goods, which they had gotten in the land of Canaan, and came into Egypt—Jacob, and all his offspring with him, Genesis 46:6 his sons, and his sons’ sons with him, his daughters, and his sons’ daughters, and he brought all his offspring with him into Egypt. Genesis 46:7 These are the names of the children of Israel, who came into Egypt, Jacob and his sons: Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn. Genesis 46:8 The sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. Genesis 46:9 The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanite woman. Genesis 46:10 The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Genesis 46:11 The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah; but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan. The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul. Genesis 46:12 The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Iob, and Shimron. Genesis 46:13 The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel. Genesis 46:14 These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan Aram, with his daughter Dinah. All the souls of his sons and his daughters were thirty-three. Genesis 46:15 The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli. Genesis 46:16 The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and Serah their sister. The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel. Genesis 46:17 These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to Leah, his daughter, and these she bore to Jacob, even sixteen souls. Genesis 46:18 The sons of Rachel, Jacob’s wife: Joseph and Benjamin. Genesis 46:19 To Joseph in the land of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore to him. Genesis 46:20 The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard. Genesis 46:21 These are the sons of Rachel, who were born to Jacob: all the souls were fourteen. Genesis 46:22 The son of Dan: Hushim. Genesis 46:23 The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem. Genesis 46:24 These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel, his daughter, and these she bore to Jacob: all the souls were seven. Genesis 46:25 All the souls who came with Jacob into Egypt, who were his direct offspring, in addition to Jacob’s sons’ wives, all the souls were sixty-six. Genesis 46:26 The sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were two souls. All the souls of the house of Jacob, who came into Egypt, were seventy. Genesis 46:27

title: Genesis 46:28–34
context: Judah is sent ahead to Joseph to show the way to Goshen. Joseph appears, falls on Israel’s neck, and weeps a good while; Israel says he can now die, having seen Joseph’s face. Joseph then coaches the brothers to tell Pharaoh they are shepherds and livestock keepers, so they may dwell in Goshen—every shepherd being an abomination to the Egyptians.
text: Genesis 46:28–34 Genesis Judah is sent ahead to Joseph to show the way to Goshen. Joseph appears, falls on Israel’s neck, and weeps a good while; Israel says he can now die, having seen Joseph’s face. Joseph then coaches the brothers to tell Pharaoh they are shepherds and livestock keepers, so they may dwell in Goshen—every shepherd being an abomination to the Egyptians. Jacob sent Judah before him to Joseph, to show the way before him to Goshen, and they came into the land of Goshen. Genesis 46:28 Joseph prepared his chariot, and went up to meet Israel, his father, in Goshen. He presented himself to him, and fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a good while. Genesis 46:29 Israel said to Joseph, “Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive.” Genesis 46:30 Joseph said to his brothers, and to his father’s house, “I will go up, and speak with Pharaoh, and will tell him, ‘My brothers, and my father’s house, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me. Genesis 46:31 These men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock, and they have brought their flocks, and their herds, and all that they have.’ Genesis 46:32 It will happen, when Pharaoh summons you, and will say, ‘What is your occupation?’ Genesis 46:33 that you shall say, ‘Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now, both we, and our fathers:’ that you may dwell in the land of Goshen; for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians.” Genesis 46:34

title: Genesis 47:1–12
context: After the reunion in chapter 46, Joseph presents his family to Pharaoh. Five brothers request Goshen as sojourners; Pharaoh grants the best of the land. Jacob blesses the king, names his life a 130-year sojourn, and Joseph settles and feeds the household in Rameses.
text: Genesis 47:1–12 Genesis After the reunion in chapter 46, Joseph presents his family to Pharaoh. Five brothers request Goshen as sojourners; Pharaoh grants the best of the land. Jacob blesses the king, names his life a 130-year sojourn, and Joseph settles and feeds the household in Rameses. Then Joseph went in and told Pharaoh, and said, “My father and my brothers, with their flocks, their herds, and all that they own, have come out of the land of Canaan; and behold, they are in the land of Goshen.” Genesis 47:1 From among his brothers he took five men, and presented them to Pharaoh. Genesis 47:2 Pharaoh said to his brothers, “What is your occupation?” They said to Pharaoh, “Your servants are shepherds, both we, and our fathers.” Genesis 47:3 They also said to Pharaoh, “We have come to live as foreigners in the land, for there is no pasture for your servants’ flocks. For the famine is severe in the land of Canaan. Now therefore, please let your servants dwell in the land of Goshen.” Genesis 47:4 Pharaoh spoke to Joseph, saying, “Your father and your brothers have come to you. Genesis 47:5 The land of Egypt is before you. Make your father and your brothers dwell in the best of the land. Let them dwell in the land of Goshen. If you know any able men among them, then put them in charge of my livestock.” Genesis 47:6 Joseph brought in Jacob, his father, and set him before Pharaoh; and Jacob blessed Pharaoh. Genesis 47:7 Pharaoh said to Jacob, “How old are you?” Genesis 47:8 Jacob said to Pharaoh, “The years of my pilgrimage are one hundred thirty years. The days of the years of my life have been few and evil. They have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their pilgrimage.” Genesis 47:9 Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and went out from the presence of Pharaoh. Genesis 47:10 Joseph placed his father and his brothers, and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded. Genesis 47:11 Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all of his father’s household with bread, according to the sizes of their families. Genesis 47:12

title: Genesis 47:13–26
context: While Israel eats in Goshen, the famine empties Egypt and Canaan of money, livestock, land, and finally personal freedom. Joseph buys all for Pharaoh, exempts priestly land, issues seed, and fixes a fifth as statute—the people calling it salvation even as they become servants.
text: Genesis 47:13–26 Genesis While Israel eats in Goshen, the famine empties Egypt and Canaan of money, livestock, land, and finally personal freedom. Joseph buys all for Pharaoh, exempts priestly land, issues seed, and fixes a fifth as statute—the people calling it salvation even as they become servants. There was no bread in all the land; for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan fainted by reason of the famine. Genesis 47:13 Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, for the grain which they bought: and Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh’s house. Genesis 47:14 When the money was all spent in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph, and said, “Give us bread, for why should we die in your presence? For our money fails.” Genesis 47:15 Joseph said, “Give me your livestock; and I will give you food for your livestock, if your money is gone.” Genesis 47:16 They brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them bread in exchange for the horses, and for the flocks, and for the herds, and for the donkeys: and he fed them with bread in exchange for all their livestock for that year. Genesis 47:17 When that year was ended, they came to him the second year, and said to him, “We will not hide from my lord how our money is all spent, and the herds of livestock are my lord’s. There is nothing left in the sight of my lord, but our bodies, and our lands. Genesis 47:18 Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land for bread, and we and our land will be servants to Pharaoh. Give us seed, that we may live, and not die, and that the land won’t be desolate.” Genesis 47:19 So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, for every man of the Egyptians sold his field, because the famine was severe on them, and the land became Pharaoh’s. Genesis 47:20 As for the people, he moved them to the cities from one end of the border of Egypt even to the other end of it. Genesis 47:21 Only he didn’t buy the land of the priests, for the priests had a portion from Pharaoh, and ate their portion which Pharaoh gave them. That is why they didn’t sell their land. Genesis 47:22 Then Joseph said to the people, “Behold, I have bought you and your land today for Pharaoh. Behold, here is seed for you, and you shall sow the land. Genesis 47:23 It will happen at the harvests, that you shall give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four parts will be your own, for seed of the field, for your food, for them of your households, and for food for your little ones.” Genesis 47:24 They said, “You have saved our lives! Let us find favor in the sight of my lord, and we will be Pharaoh’s servants.” Genesis 47:25 Joseph made it a statute concerning the land of Egypt to this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth. Only the land of the priests alone didn’t become Pharaoh’s. Genesis 47:26

title: Genesis 47:27–31
context: The famine policy ends; the camera returns to Israel in Goshen: possessions, fruitfulness, and Jacob’s remaining seventeen years. Near death he binds Joseph under oath not to bury him in Egypt but with the fathers, then bows on the bed.
text: Genesis 47:27–31 Genesis The famine policy ends; the camera returns to Israel in Goshen: possessions, fruitfulness, and Jacob’s remaining seventeen years. Near death he binds Joseph under oath not to bury him in Egypt but with the fathers, then bows on the bed. Israel lived in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen; and they got themselves possessions therein, and were fruitful, and multiplied exceedingly. Genesis 47:27 Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were one hundred forty-seven years. Genesis 47:28 The time came near that Israel must die, and he called his son Joseph, and said to him, “If now I have found favor in your sight, please put your hand under my thigh, and deal kindly and truly with me. Please don’t bury me in Egypt, Genesis 47:29 but when I sleep with my fathers, you shall carry me out of Egypt, and bury me in their burying place.” Joseph said, “I will do as you have said.” Genesis 47:30 Israel said, “Swear to me,” and he swore to him. Then Israel bowed himself on the bed’s head. Genesis 47:31

title: Genesis 48:1–7
context: Joseph hears that Jacob is ill and brings Manasseh and Ephraim. Israel sits up, recites El Shaddai’s Luz promise, and adopts the two Egyptian-born sons as his own—equal to Reuben and Simeon—then remembers Rachel’s burial on the way to Ephrath.
text: Genesis 48:1–7 Genesis Joseph hears that Jacob is ill and brings Manasseh and Ephraim. Israel sits up, recites El Shaddai’s Luz promise, and adopts the two Egyptian-born sons as his own—equal to Reuben and Simeon—then remembers Rachel’s burial on the way to Ephrath. After these things, someone said to Joseph, “Behold, your father is sick.” He took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. Genesis 48:1 Someone told Jacob, and said, “Behold, your son Joseph comes to you,” and Israel strengthened himself, and sat on the bed. Genesis 48:2 Jacob said to Joseph, “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and blessed me, Genesis 48:3 and said to me, ‘Behold, I will make you fruitful, and multiply you, and I will make of you a company of peoples, and will give this land to your offspring after you for an everlasting possession.’ Genesis 48:4 Now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you into Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh, even as Reuben and Simeon, will be mine. Genesis 48:5 Your offspring, whom you become the father of after them, will be yours. They will be called after the name of their brothers in their inheritance. Genesis 48:6 As for me, when I came from Paddan, Rachel died beside me in the land of Canaan on the way, when there was still some distance to come to Ephrath, and I buried her there on the way to Ephrath (also called Bethlehem).” Genesis 48:7

title: Genesis 48:8–22
context: Dim-eyed Israel blesses Joseph’s sons, crossing his hands so the right rests on Ephraim the younger. Joseph protests firstborn custom; Jacob refuses: “I know, my son, I know.” The blessing names God as shepherd and redeeming angel, sets Ephraim before Manasseh, and pledges return to the fathers’ land.
text: Genesis 48:8–22 Genesis Dim-eyed Israel blesses Joseph’s sons, crossing his hands so the right rests on Ephraim the younger. Joseph protests firstborn custom; Jacob refuses: “I know, my son, I know.” The blessing names God as shepherd and redeeming angel, sets Ephraim before Manasseh, and pledges return to the fathers’ land. Israel saw Joseph’s sons, and said, “Who are these?” Genesis 48:8 Joseph said to his father, “They are my sons, whom God has given me here.” He said, “Please bring them to me, and I will bless them.” Genesis 48:9 Now the eyes of Israel were dim for age, so that he couldn’t see well. Joseph brought them near to him; and he kissed them, and embraced them. Genesis 48:10 Israel said to Joseph, “I didn’t think I would see your face, and behold, God has let me see your offspring also.” Genesis 48:11 Joseph brought them out from between his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth. Genesis 48:12 Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand, and brought them near to him. Genesis 48:13 Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands knowingly, for Manasseh was the firstborn. Genesis 48:14 He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me all my life long to this day, Genesis 48:15 the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads, and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac. Let them grow into a multitude upon the earth.” Genesis 48:16 When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him. He held up his father’s hand, to remove it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s head. Genesis 48:17 Joseph said to his father, “Not so, my father, for this is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head.” Genesis 48:18 His father refused, and said, “I know, my son, I know. He also will become a people, and he also will be great. However, his younger brother will be greater than he, and his offspring will become a multitude of nations.” Genesis 48:19 He blessed them that day, saying, “Israel will bless in your name, saying, ‘God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh’” He set Ephraim before Manasseh. Genesis 48:20 Israel said to Joseph, “Behold, I am dying, but God will be with you, and bring you again to the land of your fathers. Genesis 48:21 Moreover I have given to you one portion above your brothers, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.” Genesis 48:22

title: Genesis 49:1–12
context: Dying Jacob gathers his sons to tell what will happen in days to come. Reuben loses preeminence; Simeon and Levi are divided for violence; Judah receives praise, the lion, the scepter, and the obedience of the peoples—the messianic hinge of the chapter.
text: Genesis 49:1–12 Genesis Dying Jacob gathers his sons to tell what will happen in days to come. Reuben loses preeminence; Simeon and Levi are divided for violence; Judah receives praise, the lion, the scepter, and the obedience of the peoples—the messianic hinge of the chapter. Jacob called to his sons, and said: “Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which will happen to you in the days to come. Genesis 49:1 Assemble yourselves, and hear, you sons of Jacob. Listen to Israel, your father. Genesis 49:2 “Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength, excelling in dignity, and excelling in power. Genesis 49:3 Boiling over like water, you shall not excel, because you went up to your father’s bed, then defiled it. He went up to my couch. Genesis 49:4 “Simeon and Levi are brothers. Their swords are weapons of violence. Genesis 49:5 My soul, don’t come into their council. My glory, don’t be united to their assembly; for in their anger they killed men. In their self-will they hamstrung cattle. Genesis 49:6 Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel. I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel. Genesis 49:7 “Judah, your brothers will praise you. Your hand will be on the neck of your enemies. Your father’s sons will bow down before you. Genesis 49:8 Judah is a lion’s cub. From the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down, he crouched as a lion, as a lioness. Who will rouse him up? Genesis 49:9 The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs. The obedience of the peoples will be to him. Genesis 49:10 Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine, he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood of grapes. Genesis 49:11 His eyes will be red with wine, his teeth white with milk. Genesis 49:12

title: Genesis 49:13–28
context: Jacob continues through Zebulun, Issachar, Dan (with a cry for the Lord’s salvation), Gad, Asher, Naphtali, a long blessing on attacked-yet-helped Joseph, and Benjamin the wolf. He then names the twelve tribes, assigns each a suitable blessing, and the speech turns toward burial at Machpelah.
text: Genesis 49:13–28 Genesis Jacob continues through Zebulun, Issachar, Dan (with a cry for the Lord’s salvation), Gad, Asher, Naphtali, a long blessing on attacked-yet-helped Joseph, and Benjamin the wolf. He then names the twelve tribes, assigns each a suitable blessing, and the speech turns toward burial at Machpelah. “Zebulun will dwell at the haven of the sea. He will be for a haven of ships. His border will be on Sidon. Genesis 49:13 “Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the saddlebags. Genesis 49:14 He saw a resting place, that it was good, the land, that it was pleasant. He bows his shoulder to the burden, and becomes a servant doing forced labor. Genesis 49:15 “Dan will judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel. Genesis 49:16 Dan will be a serpent on the trail, an adder in the path, that bites the horse’s heels, so that his rider falls backward. Genesis 49:17 I have waited for your salvation, LORD. Genesis 49:18 “A troop will press on Gad, but he will press on their heel. Genesis 49:19 “Asher’s food will be rich. He will produce royal dainties. Genesis 49:20 “Naphtali is a doe set free, who bears beautiful fawns. Genesis 49:21 “Joseph is a fruitful vine, a fruitful vine by a spring. His branches run over the wall. Genesis 49:22 The archers have severely grieved him, shot at him, and persecuted him: Genesis 49:23 But his bow remained strong. The arms of his hands were made strong, by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob, (from there is the shepherd, the stone of Israel), Genesis 49:24 even by the God of your father, who will help you, by the Almighty, who will bless you, with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that lies below, blessings of the breasts, and of the womb. Genesis 49:25 The blessings of your father have prevailed above the blessings of my ancestors, above the boundaries of the ancient hills. They will be on the head of Joseph, on the crown of the head of him who is separated from his brothers. Genesis 49:26 “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf. In the morning he will devour the prey. At evening he will divide the plunder.” Genesis 49:27 All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them, and blessed them. He blessed everyone according to his own blessing. Genesis 49:28

title: Genesis 49:29–33
context: After blessing the twelve, Jacob commands burial with his fathers in the cave at Machpelah—the plot Abraham bought in Canaan—then draws up his feet and is gathered to his people.
text: Genesis 49:29–33 Genesis After blessing the twelve, Jacob commands burial with his fathers in the cave at Machpelah—the plot Abraham bought in Canaan—then draws up his feet and is gathered to his people. He instructed them, and said to them, “I am to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, Genesis 49:29 in the cave that is in the field of Machpelah, which is before Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place. Genesis 49:30 There they buried Abraham and Sarah, his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah, his wife, and there I buried Leah: Genesis 49:31 the field and the cave that is therein, which was purchased from the children of Heth.” Genesis 49:32 When Jacob finished charging his sons, he gathered up his feet into the bed, breathed his last breath, and was gathered to his people. Genesis 49:33

title: Genesis 5:1–20
context: After Cain’s line in chapter 4, Genesis 5 opens the “book of the generations of Adam”—image-bearing humanity named Man, then the Sethite succession marching toward Noah. The refrain “then he died” sounds the curse after Eden; the long years still display God’s patience preserving a people.
text: Genesis 5:1–20 Genesis After Cain’s line in chapter 4, Genesis 5 opens the “book of the generations of Adam”—image-bearing humanity named Man, then the Sethite succession marching toward Noah. The refrain “then he died” sounds the curse after Eden; the long years still display God’s patience preserving a people. This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, he made him in God’s likeness. Genesis 5:1 He created them male and female, and blessed them. On the day they were created, he named them Adam. Genesis 5:2 Adam lived one hundred thirty years, and became the father of a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. Genesis 5:3 The days of Adam after he became the father of Seth were eight hundred years, and he became the father of other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:4 All the days that Adam lived were nine hundred thirty years, then he died. Genesis 5:5 Seth lived one hundred five years, then became the father of Enosh. Genesis 5:6 Seth lived after he became the father of Enosh eight hundred seven years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:7 All of the days of Seth were nine hundred twelve years, then he died. Genesis 5:8 Enosh lived ninety years, and became the father of Kenan. Genesis 5:9 Enosh lived after he became the father of Kenan eight hundred fifteen years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:10 All of the days of Enosh were nine hundred five years, then he died. Genesis 5:11 Kenan lived seventy years, then became the father of Mahalalel. Genesis 5:12 Kenan lived after he became the father of Mahalalel eight hundred forty years, and became the father of other sons and daughters Genesis 5:13 and all of the days of Kenan were nine hundred ten years, then he died. Genesis 5:14 Mahalalel lived sixty-five years, then became the father of Jared. Genesis 5:15 Mahalalel lived after he became the father of Jared eight hundred thirty years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:16 All of the days of Mahalalel were eight hundred ninety-five years, then he died. Genesis 5:17 Jared lived one hundred sixty-two years, then became the father of Enoch. Genesis 5:18 Jared lived after he became the father of Enoch eight hundred years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:19 All of the days of Jared were nine hundred sixty-two years, then he died. Genesis 5:20

title: Genesis 5:21–32
context: The genealogy breaks its death-refrain for Enoch, who walked with God and was taken. Methuselah’s long life, Lamech’s naming of Noah as hoped relief from the cursed ground, and Noah’s three sons then carry the line God will preserve through the flood.
text: Genesis 5:21–32 Genesis The genealogy breaks its death-refrain for Enoch, who walked with God and was taken. Methuselah’s long life, Lamech’s naming of Noah as hoped relief from the cursed ground, and Noah’s three sons then carry the line God will preserve through the flood. Enoch lived sixty-five years, then became the father of Methuselah. Genesis 5:21 After Methuselah’s birth, Enoch walked with God for three hundred years, and became the father of more sons and daughters. Genesis 5:22 All the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty-five years. Genesis 5:23 Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him. Genesis 5:24 Methuselah lived one hundred eighty-seven years, then became the father of Lamech. Genesis 5:25 Methuselah lived after he became the father of Lamech seven hundred eighty-two years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:26 All the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty-nine years, then he died. Genesis 5:27 Lamech lived one hundred eighty-two years, then became the father of a son. Genesis 5:28 He named him Noah, saying, “This one will comfort us in our work and in the toil of our hands, caused by the ground which the LORD has cursed.” Genesis 5:29 Lamech lived after he became the father of Noah five hundred ninety-five years, and became the father of other sons and daughters. Genesis 5:30 All the days of Lamech were seven hundred seventy-seven years, then he died. Genesis 5:31 Noah was five hundred years old, then Noah became the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Genesis 5:32

title: Genesis 50:1–14
context: Joseph weeps over Jacob, has Israel embalmed, and Egypt mourns seventy days. With Pharaoh’s leave a great company goes up to Canaan, laments at Atad, and buries him in Machpelah—Abraham’s purchased cave—then Joseph and his brothers return to Egypt.
text: Genesis 50:1–14 Genesis Joseph weeps over Jacob, has Israel embalmed, and Egypt mourns seventy days. With Pharaoh’s leave a great company goes up to Canaan, laments at Atad, and buries him in Machpelah—Abraham’s purchased cave—then Joseph and his brothers return to Egypt. Joseph fell on his father’s face, wept on him, and kissed him. Genesis 50:1 Joseph commanded his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father; and the physicians embalmed Israel. Genesis 50:2 Forty days were used for him, for that is how many days it takes to embalm. The Egyptians wept for Israel for seventy days. Genesis 50:3 When the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph spoke to Pharaoh’s staff, saying, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, please speak in the ears of Pharaoh, saying, Genesis 50:4 ‘My father made me swear, saying, “Behold, I am dying. Bury me in my grave which I have dug for myself in the land of Canaan.” Now therefore, please let me go up and bury my father, and I will come again.’” Genesis 50:5 Pharaoh said, “Go up, and bury your father, just like he made you swear.” Genesis 50:6 Joseph went up to bury his father; and with him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house, all the elders of the land of Egypt, Genesis 50:7 all the house of Joseph, his brothers, and his father’s house. Only their little ones, their flocks, and their herds, they left in the land of Goshen. Genesis 50:8 Both chariots and horsemen went up with him. It was a very great company. Genesis 50:9 They came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, and there they lamented with a very great and severe lamentation. He mourned for his father seven days. Genesis 50:10 When the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning in the floor of Atad, they said, “This is a grievous mourning by the Egyptians.” Therefore its name was called Abel Mizraim, which is beyond the Jordan. Genesis 50:11 His sons did to him just as he commanded them, Genesis 50:12 for his sons carried him into the land of Canaan, and buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham bought with the field, as a possession for a burial site, from Ephron the Hittite, near Mamre. Genesis 50:13 Joseph returned into Egypt—he, and his brothers, and all that went up with him to bury his father, after he had buried his father. Genesis 50:14

title: Genesis 50:15–26
context: After Jacob’s burial, Joseph’s brothers fear that with their father gone he will finally repay the evil they did. They send a plea for forgiveness; Joseph weeps, refuses to take God’s place, and reads the sale through providence: they meant evil, God meant it for good, that many people should live. He provides for them, lives 110 years, and dies in Egypt under oath that God will visit them and that his bones will go up—hope aimed at the Exodus.
text: Genesis 50:15–26 Genesis After Jacob’s burial, Joseph’s brothers fear that with their father gone he will finally repay the evil they did. They send a plea for forgiveness; Joseph weeps, refuses to take God’s place, and reads the sale through providence: they meant evil, God meant it for good, that many people should live. He provides for them, lives 110 years, and dies in Egypt under oath that God will visit them and that his bones will go up—hope aimed at the Exodus. When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.” Genesis 50:15 They sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father commanded before he died, saying, Genesis 50:16 ‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him. Genesis 50:17 His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.” Genesis 50:18 Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God? Genesis 50:19 As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today. Genesis 50:20 Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them. Genesis 50:21 Joseph lived in Egypt, he, and his father’s house. Joseph lived one hundred ten years. Genesis 50:22 Joseph saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation. The children also of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born on Joseph’s knees. Genesis 50:23 Joseph said to his brothers, “I am dying, but God will surely visit you, and bring you up out of this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.” Genesis 50:24 Joseph took an oath from the children of Israel, saying, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.” Genesis 50:25 So Joseph died, being one hundred ten years old, and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt. Genesis 50:26

title: Genesis 6:1–8
context: As humanity multiplies, boundaries blur and violence ripens. The Lord limits His Spirit’s striving with flesh, names the earth’s great wickedness—every intention only evil continually—and grieves to His heart. Judgment is announced: He will blot out man and creature from the land. Yet the dark paragraph ends with a door: Noah found favor in the LORD’s eyes of the Lord.
text: Genesis 6:1–8 Genesis As humanity multiplies, boundaries blur and violence ripens. The Lord limits His Spirit’s striving with flesh, names the earth’s great wickedness—every intention only evil continually—and grieves to His heart. Judgment is announced: He will blot out man and creature from the land. Yet the dark paragraph ends with a door: Noah found favor in the LORD’s eyes of the Lord. When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them, Genesis 6:1 God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives. Genesis 6:2 The LORD said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.” Genesis 6:3 The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also after that, when God’s sons came in to men’s daughters and had children with them. Those were the mighty men who were of old, men of renown. Genesis 6:4 The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great on the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil. Genesis 6:5 The LORD was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him in his heart. Genesis 6:6 The LORD said, “I will destroy man whom I have created from the surface of the ground—man, along with animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky—for I am sorry that I have made them.” Genesis 6:7 But Noah found favor in the LORD’s eyes. Genesis 6:8

title: Genesis 6:9–22
context: A new toledoth names Noah: righteous, blameless in his generation, a man who walked with God. The earth is corrupt and violent; God tells Noah He will end all flesh and commands an ark—precise, pitched, three-decked—then pledges covenant, a household inside, and pairs of living things preserved. Noah does all that God commanded him.
text: Genesis 6:9–22 Genesis A new toledoth names Noah: righteous, blameless in his generation, a man who walked with God. The earth is corrupt and violent; God tells Noah He will end all flesh and commands an ark—precise, pitched, three-decked—then pledges covenant, a household inside, and pairs of living things preserved. Noah does all that God commanded him. This is the history of the generations of Noah: Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time. Noah walked with God. Genesis 6:9 Noah became the father of three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Genesis 6:10 The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence. Genesis 6:11 God saw the earth, and saw that it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth. Genesis 6:12 God said to Noah, “I will bring an end to all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them and the earth. Genesis 6:13 Make a ship of gopher wood. You shall make rooms in the ship, and shall seal it inside and outside with pitch. Genesis 6:14 This is how you shall make it. The length of the ship shall be three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits. Genesis 6:15 You shall make a roof in the ship, and you shall finish it to a cubit upward. You shall set the door of the ship in its side. You shall make it with lower, second, and third levels. Genesis 6:16 I, even I, will bring the flood of waters on this earth, to destroy all flesh having the breath of life from under the sky. Everything that is on the earth will die. Genesis 6:17 But I will establish my covenant with you. You shall come into the ship, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you. Genesis 6:18 Of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ship, to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female. Genesis 6:19 Of the birds after their kind, of the livestock after their kind, of every creeping thing of the ground after its kind, two of every sort will come to you, to keep them alive. Genesis 6:20 Take with you some of all food that is eaten, and gather it to yourself; and it will be for food for you, and for them.” Genesis 6:21 Thus Noah did. He did all that God commanded him. Genesis 6:22

title: Genesis 7:1–16
context: The LORD commands Noah to go into the ark with his household, for He has seen him righteous in this generation, and to take clean and unclean animals and birds so that offspring will live. In seven days rain will fall forty days and nights and blot out every living thing. Noah obeys. At six hundred years he and his family enter; after seven days the flood comes. On a dated day the fountains of the deep burst and the windows of heaven open; they enter two by two of all flesh, and the LORD shuts him in.
text: Genesis 7:1–16 Genesis The LORD commands Noah to go into the ark with his household, for He has seen him righteous in this generation, and to take clean and unclean animals and birds so that offspring will live. In seven days rain will fall forty days and nights and blot out every living thing. Noah obeys. At six hundred years he and his family enter; after seven days the flood comes. On a dated day the fountains of the deep burst and the windows of heaven open; they enter two by two of all flesh, and the LORD shuts him in. The LORD said to Noah, “Come with all of your household into the ship, for I have seen your righteousness before me in this generation. Genesis 7:1 You shall take seven pairs of every clean animal with you, the male and his female. Of the animals that are not clean, take two, the male and his female. Genesis 7:2 Also of the birds of the sky, seven and seven, male and female, to keep seed alive on the surface of all the earth. Genesis 7:3 In seven days, I will cause it to rain on the earth for forty days and forty nights. I will destroy every living thing that I have made from the surface of the ground.” Genesis 7:4 Noah did everything that the LORD commanded him. Genesis 7:5 Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came on the earth. Genesis 7:6 Noah went into the ship with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives, because of the floodwaters. Genesis 7:7 Clean animals, unclean animals, birds, and everything that creeps on the ground Genesis 7:8 went by pairs to Noah into the ship, male and female, as God commanded Noah. Genesis 7:9 After the seven days, the floodwaters came on the earth. Genesis 7:10 In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst open, and the sky’s windows opened. Genesis 7:11 It rained on the earth forty days and forty nights. Genesis 7:12 In the same day Noah, and Shem, Ham, and Japheth—the sons of Noah—and Noah’s wife and the three wives of his sons with them, entered into the ship— Genesis 7:13 they, and every animal after its kind, all the livestock after their kind, every creeping thing that creeps on the earth after its kind, and every bird after its kind, every bird of every sort. Genesis 7:14 Pairs from all flesh with the breath of life in them went into the ship to Noah. Genesis 7:15 Those who went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God commanded him; then the LORD shut him in. Genesis 7:16

title: Genesis 7:17–24
context: Judgment falls as the Lord had said: waters increase forty days, lift the ark high above the earth, and cover even the high mountains. All flesh that moved on dry land dies—everything with the breath of life. God blots out every living thing on the ground; only Noah and those with him in the ark are left, and the waters prevail 150 days.
text: Genesis 7:17–24 Genesis Judgment falls as the Lord had said: waters increase forty days, lift the ark high above the earth, and cover even the high mountains. All flesh that moved on dry land dies—everything with the breath of life. God blots out every living thing on the ground; only Noah and those with him in the ark are left, and the waters prevail 150 days. The flood was forty days on the earth. The waters increased, and lifted up the ship, and it was lifted up above the earth. Genesis 7:17 The waters rose, and increased greatly on the earth; and the ship floated on the surface of the waters. Genesis 7:18 The waters rose very high on the earth. All the high mountains that were under the whole sky were covered. Genesis 7:19 The waters rose fifteen cubits higher, and the mountains were covered. Genesis 7:20 All flesh died that moved on the earth, including birds, livestock, animals, every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, and every man. Genesis 7:21 All on the dry land, in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life, died. Genesis 7:22 Every living thing was destroyed that was on the surface of the ground, including man, livestock, creeping things, and birds of the sky. They were destroyed from the earth.
