Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ship. Genesis 7:23 The waters flooded the earth one hundred fifty days. Genesis 7:24

title: Genesis 8:1–19
context: After the flood, God remembers Noah and the creatures in the ark; the waters recede, the ark rests on Ararat, and Noah waits with raven and dove until God commands the family and the animals to go out and fill the earth again.
text: Genesis 8:1–19 Genesis After the flood, God remembers Noah and the creatures in the ark; the waters recede, the ark rests on Ararat, and Noah waits with raven and dove until God commands the family and the animals to go out and fill the earth again. God remembered Noah, all the animals, and all the livestock that were with him in the ship; and God made a wind to pass over the earth. The waters subsided. Genesis 8:1 The deep’s fountains and the sky’s windows were also stopped, and the rain from the sky was restrained. Genesis 8:2 The waters continually receded from the earth. After the end of one hundred fifty days the waters receded. Genesis 8:3 The ship rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on Ararat’s mountains. Genesis 8:4 The waters receded continually until the tenth month. In the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were visible. Genesis 8:5 At the end of forty days, Noah opened the window of the ship which he had made, Genesis 8:6 and he sent out a raven. It went back and forth, until the waters were dried up from the earth. Genesis 8:7 He himself sent out a dove to see if the waters were abated from the surface of the ground, Genesis 8:8 but the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned into the ship to him, for the waters were on the surface of the whole earth. He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship. Genesis 8:9 He waited yet another seven days; and again he sent the dove out of the ship. Genesis 8:10 The dove came back to him at evening and, behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters were abated from the earth. Genesis 8:11 He waited yet another seven days, and sent out the dove; and she didn’t return to him any more. Genesis 8:12 In the six hundred first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried up from the earth. Noah removed the covering of the ship, and looked. He saw that the surface of the ground was dry. Genesis 8:13 In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry. Genesis 8:14 God spoke to Noah, saying, Genesis 8:15 “Go out of the ship, you, your wife, your sons, and your sons’ wives with you. Genesis 8:16 Bring out with you every living thing that is with you of all flesh, including birds, livestock, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, that they may breed abundantly on the earth, and be fruitful, and multiply on the earth.” Genesis 8:17 Noah went out, with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives with him. Genesis 8:18 Every animal, every creeping thing, and every bird, whatever moves on the earth, after their families, went out of the ship. Genesis 8:19

title: Genesis 8:20–22
context: Noah’s first act on dry ground is worship: he builds an altar and offers burnt offerings; the LORD smells the pleasing aroma and promises never again to curse the ground or strike every living thing, as in the flood, while earth’s seasons endure.
text: Genesis 8:20–22 Genesis Noah’s first act on dry ground is worship: he builds an altar and offers burnt offerings; the LORD smells the pleasing aroma and promises never again to curse the ground or strike every living thing, as in the flood, while earth’s seasons endure. Noah built an altar to the LORD, and took of every clean animal, and of every clean bird, and offered burnt offerings on the altar. Genesis 8:20 The LORD smelled the pleasant aroma. The LORD said in his heart, “I will not again curse the ground any more for man’s sake because the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth. I will never again strike every living thing, as I have done. Genesis 8:21 While the earth remains, seed time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night will not cease.” Genesis 8:22

title: Genesis 9:1–17
context: After the flood, God blesses Noah and his sons, restores the call to fill the earth, sets limits around blood and human life, and establishes a covenant with all flesh—signed by the bow in the clouds—that a flood will never again destroy the earth.
text: Genesis 9:1–17 Genesis After the flood, God blesses Noah and his sons, restores the call to fill the earth, sets limits around blood and human life, and establishes a covenant with all flesh—signed by the bow in the clouds—that a flood will never again destroy the earth. God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, and replenish the earth. Genesis 9:1 The fear of you and the dread of you will be on every animal of the earth, and on every bird of the sky. Everything that moves along the ground, and all the fish of the sea, are delivered into your hand. Genesis 9:2 Every moving thing that lives will be food for you. As I gave you the green herb, I have given everything to you. Genesis 9:3 But flesh with its life, that is, its blood, you shall not eat. Genesis 9:4 I will surely require accounting for your life’s blood. At the hand of every animal I will require it. At the hand of man, even at the hand of every man’s brother, I will require the life of man. Genesis 9:5 Whoever sheds man’s blood, his blood will be shed by man, for God made man in his own image. Genesis 9:6 Be fruitful and multiply. Increase abundantly on the earth, and multiply in it.” Genesis 9:7 God spoke to Noah and to his sons with him, saying, Genesis 9:8 “As for me, behold, I establish my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you, Genesis 9:9 and with every living creature that is with you: the birds, the livestock, and every animal of the earth with you, of all that go out of the ship, even every animal of the earth. Genesis 9:10 I will establish my covenant with you: All flesh will not be cut off any more by the waters of the flood. There will never again be a flood to destroy the earth.” Genesis 9:11 God said, “This is the token of the covenant which I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for perpetual generations: Genesis 9:12 I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth. Genesis 9:13 When I bring a cloud over the earth, that the rainbow will be seen in the cloud, Genesis 9:14 I will remember my covenant, which is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh, and the waters will no more become a flood to destroy all flesh. Genesis 9:15 The rainbow will be in the cloud. I will look at it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth.” Genesis 9:16 God said to Noah, “This is the token of the covenant which I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth.” Genesis 9:17

title: Genesis 9:18–29
context: Noah’s three sons go forth from the ark to people the earth; then the rescued patriarch plants a vineyard, falls in shameful drunkenness, and a family crisis ends in curse on Canaan and blessing on Shem and Japheth—before Noah’s long life closes.
text: Genesis 9:18–29 Genesis Noah’s three sons go forth from the ark to people the earth; then the rescued patriarch plants a vineyard, falls in shameful drunkenness, and a family crisis ends in curse on Canaan and blessing on Shem and Japheth—before Noah’s long life closes. The sons of Noah who went out from the ship were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Ham is the father of Canaan. Genesis 9:18 These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the whole earth was populated. Genesis 9:19 Noah began to be a farmer, and planted a vineyard. Genesis 9:20 He drank of the wine and got drunk. He was uncovered within his tent. Genesis 9:21 Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father, and told his two brothers outside. Genesis 9:22 Shem and Japheth took a garment, and laid it on both their shoulders, went in backwards, and covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were backwards, and they didn’t see their father’s nakedness. Genesis 9:23 Noah awoke from his wine, and knew what his youngest son had done to him. Genesis 9:24 He said, “Canaan is cursed. He will be a servant of servants to his brothers.” Genesis 9:25 He said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem. Let Canaan be his servant. Genesis 9:26 May God enlarge Japheth. Let him dwell in the tents of Shem. Let Canaan be his servant.” Genesis 9:27 Noah lived three hundred fifty years after the flood. Genesis 9:28 All the days of Noah were nine hundred fifty years, and then he died. Genesis 9:29

title: Hebrews 1:1–4
context: Hebrews opens without a greeting, going straight to its theme: God, who spoke in many ways through the prophets, has now spoken finally in his Son. The Son is heir of all things, agent of creation, the radiance of God’s glory and exact imprint of his nature, who upholds the universe by his word. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, as superior to angels as his name is greater. Arminian and Reformed readers share this high Christology almost entirely. Their emphases differ only in how they apply the finished purification.
text: Hebrews 1:1–4 Hebrews Hebrews opens without a greeting, going straight to its theme: God, who spoke in many ways through the prophets, has now spoken finally in his Son. The Son is heir of all things, agent of creation, the radiance of God’s glory and exact imprint of his nature, who upholds the universe by his word. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, as superior to angels as his name is greater. Arminian and Reformed readers share this high Christology almost entirely. Their emphases differ only in how they apply the finished purification. God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, Hebrews 1:1 has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds. Hebrews 1:2 His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power, who, when he had by himself purified us of our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high, Hebrews 1:3 having become as much better than the angels as the more excellent name he has inherited is better than theirs. Hebrews 1:4

title: Hebrews 1:5–14
context: A chain of Old Testament quotations proves that the Son is greater than the angels. God never said to an angel, “You are my Son,” and he commands the angels to worship the firstborn. The angels are servants, but the Son is addressed as God, whose throne is forever and who laid the foundations of the earth and remains unchanged when creation wears out. The Son sits at God’s right hand, while angels are ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation. Both traditions use this passage as a key witness to the deity of Christ. They differ slightly on who “those who will inherit salvation” are.
text: Hebrews 1:5–14 Hebrews A chain of Old Testament quotations proves that the Son is greater than the angels. God never said to an angel, “You are my Son,” and he commands the angels to worship the firstborn. The angels are servants, but the Son is addressed as God, whose throne is forever and who laid the foundations of the earth and remains unchanged when creation wears out. The Son sits at God’s right hand, while angels are ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation. Both traditions use this passage as a key witness to the deity of Christ. They differ slightly on who “those who will inherit salvation” are. For to which of the angels did he say at any time, “You are my Son. Today I have become your father?” and again, “I will be to him a Father, and he will be to me a Son?” Hebrews 1:5 When he again brings in the firstborn into the world he says, “Let all the angels of God worship him.” Hebrews 1:6 Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his servants a flame of fire.” Hebrews 1:7 But of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. The scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your Kingdom. Hebrews 1:8 You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows.” Hebrews 1:9 And, “You, Lord, in the beginning, laid the foundation of the earth. The heavens are the works of your hands. Hebrews 1:10 They will perish, but you continue. They all will grow old like a garment does. Hebrews 1:11 You will roll them up like a mantle, and they will be changed; but you are the same. Your years won’t fail.” Hebrews 1:12 But which of the angels has he told at any time, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet?” Hebrews 1:13 Aren’t they all serving spirits, sent out to do service for the sake of those who will inherit salvation? Hebrews 1:14

title: Hebrews 10:1–10
context: The writer brings his argument about sacrifice to a climax. The law was only a shadow of the good things to come, and its repeated sacrifices could never perfect worshipers or take away sins. They served as a yearly reminder of sin. Quoting Psalm 40, he shows Christ coming to do God’s will in a prepared body, setting aside the old sacrifices to establish the new. By that will believers have been sanctified through the offering of Jesus’ body once for all. Both traditions affirm the sufficiency of Christ’s single sacrifice. They differ on what it actually secures, and for whom.
text: Hebrews 10:1–10 Hebrews The writer brings his argument about sacrifice to a climax. The law was only a shadow of the good things to come, and its repeated sacrifices could never perfect worshipers or take away sins. They served as a yearly reminder of sin. Quoting Psalm 40, he shows Christ coming to do God’s will in a prepared body, setting aside the old sacrifices to establish the new. By that will believers have been sanctified through the offering of Jesus’ body once for all. Both traditions affirm the sufficiency of Christ’s single sacrifice. They differ on what it actually secures, and for whom. For the law, having a shadow of the good to come, not the very image of the things, can never with the same sacrifices year by year, which they offer continually, make perfect those who draw near. Hebrews 10:1 Or else wouldn’t they have ceased to be offered, because the worshipers, having been once cleansed, would have had no more consciousness of sins? Hebrews 10:2 But in those sacrifices there is a yearly reminder of sins. Hebrews 10:3 For it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins. Hebrews 10:4 Therefore when he comes into the world, he says, “You didn’t desire sacrifice and offering, but you prepared a body for me. Hebrews 10:5 You had no pleasure in whole burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin. Hebrews 10:6 Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come (in the scroll of the book it is written of me) to do your will, O God.’” Hebrews 10:7 Previously saying, “Sacrifices and offerings and whole burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin you didn’t desire, neither had pleasure in them” (those which are offered according to the law), Hebrews 10:8 then he has said, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He takes away the first, that he may establish the second, Hebrews 10:9 by which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. Hebrews 10:10

title: Hebrews 10:11–18
context: The writer contrasts the standing priests of the old covenant, offering the same sacrifices daily, with Christ, who offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and sat down at God’s right hand. By that single offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified. The Holy Spirit confirms it through Jeremiah’s new covenant promise: God will write his laws on hearts and remember sins no more. Where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin. Verse 14 is a key text for the Reformed doctrine of definite atonement and is read differently by Arminians.
text: Hebrews 10:11–18 Hebrews The writer contrasts the standing priests of the old covenant, offering the same sacrifices daily, with Christ, who offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and sat down at God’s right hand. By that single offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified. The Holy Spirit confirms it through Jeremiah’s new covenant promise: God will write his laws on hearts and remember sins no more. Where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin. Verse 14 is a key text for the Reformed doctrine of definite atonement and is read differently by Arminians. Every priest indeed stands day by day serving and offering often the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins, Hebrews 10:11 but he, when he had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down on the right hand of God, Hebrews 10:12 from that time waiting until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet. Hebrews 10:13 For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified. Hebrews 10:14 The Holy Spirit also testifies to us, for after saying, Hebrews 10:15 “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days,” says the Lord, “I will put my laws on their heart, I will also write them on their mind;” then he says, Hebrews 10:16 “I will remember their sins and their iniquities no more.” Hebrews 10:17 Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin. Hebrews 10:18

title: Hebrews 10:19–25
context: Having shown that Christ’s single sacrifice has accomplished what the old sacrifices never could, the writer turns to exhortation. Believers have confidence to enter God’s presence by the blood of Jesus through a new and living way, and they have a great priest over God’s house. So they should draw near with a true heart, hold fast their confession without wavering, and stir one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together. Both traditions treasure this passage. They differ mainly on how the call to hold fast relates to God’s faithfulness.
text: Hebrews 10:19–25 Hebrews Having shown that Christ’s single sacrifice has accomplished what the old sacrifices never could, the writer turns to exhortation. Believers have confidence to enter God’s presence by the blood of Jesus through a new and living way, and they have a great priest over God’s house. So they should draw near with a true heart, hold fast their confession without wavering, and stir one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together. Both traditions treasure this passage. They differ mainly on how the call to hold fast relates to God’s faithfulness. Having therefore, brothers, boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus, Hebrews 10:19 by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh, Hebrews 10:20 and having a great priest over God’s house, Hebrews 10:21 let’s draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and having our body washed with pure water, Hebrews 10:22 let’s hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering; for he who promised is faithful. Hebrews 10:23 Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works, Hebrews 10:24 not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching. Hebrews 10:25

title: Hebrews 10:26–31
context: This is the fourth and sharpest warning in Hebrews. If someone sins deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, only a fearful expectation of judgment. The writer argues from the lesser to the greater: if rejecting Moses’ law brought death, how much worse for one who has trampled the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace. This passage is central to the debate over whether true believers can finally fall away.
text: Hebrews 10:26–31 Hebrews This is the fourth and sharpest warning in Hebrews. If someone sins deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, only a fearful expectation of judgment. The writer argues from the lesser to the greater: if rejecting Moses’ law brought death, how much worse for one who has trampled the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace. This passage is central to the debate over whether true believers can finally fall away. For if we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more a sacrifice for sins, Hebrews 10:26 but a certain fearful expectation of judgment, and a fierceness of fire which will devour the adversaries. Hebrews 10:27 A man who disregards Moses’ law dies without compassion on the word of two or three witnesses. Hebrews 10:28 How much worse punishment do you think he will be judged worthy of who has trodden under foot the Son of God, and has counted the blood of the covenant with which he was sanctified an unholy thing, and has insulted the Spirit of grace? Hebrews 10:29 For we know him who said, “Vengeance belongs to me. I will repay,” says the Lord. Again, “The Lord will judge his people.” Hebrews 10:30 It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. Hebrews 10:31

title: Hebrews 10:32–39
context: The writer balances the warning with encouragement. He reminds the readers of their early days, when they endured suffering and public shame, showed compassion to prisoners, and joyfully accepted the loss of property, knowing they had a better possession. So they must not throw away their confidence but endure, because the coming one will not delay. The righteous will live by faith, and God has no pleasure in anyone who shrinks back. The writer concludes that “we” are not of those who shrink back to destruction but of those who believe and preserve their souls. Both traditions read the closing verse as confidence. They differ on whether it is a certainty or an expectation.
text: Hebrews 10:32–39 Hebrews The writer balances the warning with encouragement. He reminds the readers of their early days, when they endured suffering and public shame, showed compassion to prisoners, and joyfully accepted the loss of property, knowing they had a better possession. So they must not throw away their confidence but endure, because the coming one will not delay. The righteous will live by faith, and God has no pleasure in anyone who shrinks back. The writer concludes that “we” are not of those who shrink back to destruction but of those who believe and preserve their souls. Both traditions read the closing verse as confidence. They differ on whether it is a certainty or an expectation. But remember the former days, in which, after you were enlightened, you endured a great struggle with sufferings: Hebrews 10:32 partly, being exposed to both reproaches and oppressions, and partly, becoming partakers with those who were treated so. Hebrews 10:33 For you both had compassion on me in my chains and joyfully accepted the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you have for yourselves a better possession and an enduring one in the heavens. Hebrews 10:34 Therefore don’t throw away your boldness, which has a great reward. Hebrews 10:35 For you need endurance so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise. Hebrews 10:36 “In a very little while, he who comes will come and will not wait. Hebrews 10:37 But the righteous one will live by faith. If he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.” Hebrews 10:38 But we are not of those who shrink back to destruction, but of those who have faith to the saving of the soul. Hebrews 10:39

title: Hebrews 11:1–7
context: Hebrews 11 begins its great roll call of faith. Faith is the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen, and by it the people of old received God’s approval. By faith we understand that God made the world by his word. Abel offered a better sacrifice, Enoch was taken up because he pleased God, and Noah built the ark in reverent fear. Without faith it is impossible to please God, because whoever comes to him must believe that he exists and rewards those who seek him. Both traditions celebrate this chapter. They differ on where faith comes from.
text: Hebrews 11:1–7 Hebrews Hebrews 11 begins its great roll call of faith. Faith is the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen, and by it the people of old received God’s approval. By faith we understand that God made the world by his word. Abel offered a better sacrifice, Enoch was taken up because he pleased God, and Noah built the ark in reverent fear. Without faith it is impossible to please God, because whoever comes to him must believe that he exists and rewards those who seek him. Both traditions celebrate this chapter. They differ on where faith comes from. Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen. Hebrews 11:1 For by this, the elders obtained approval. Hebrews 11:2 By faith we understand that the universe has been framed by the word of God, so that what is seen has not been made out of things which are visible. Hebrews 11:3 By faith Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, through which he had testimony given to him that he was righteous, God testifying with respect to his gifts; and through it he, being dead, still speaks. Hebrews 11:4 By faith Enoch was taken away, so that he wouldn’t see death, and he was not found, because God translated him. For he has had testimony given to him that before his translation he had been well pleasing to God. Hebrews 11:5 Without faith it is impossible to be well pleasing to him, for he who comes to God must believe that he exists, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him. Hebrews 11:6 By faith Noah, being warned about things not yet seen, moved with godly fear, prepared a ship for the saving of his house, through which he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness which is according to faith. Hebrews 11:7

title: Hebrews 11:17–22
context: Abraham, when tested, offered up Isaac, the son through whom the promise was to come, reasoning that God could raise him from the dead. Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph then acted by faith regarding things to come, blessing their sons and looking ahead to Israel’s exodus. Both traditions see faith that trusts God’s promise beyond death. They draw different lessons about testing.
text: Hebrews 11:17–22 Hebrews Abraham, when tested, offered up Isaac, the son through whom the promise was to come, reasoning that God could raise him from the dead. Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph then acted by faith regarding things to come, blessing their sons and looking ahead to Israel’s exodus. Both traditions see faith that trusts God’s promise beyond death. They draw different lessons about testing. By faith, Abraham, being tested, offered up Isaac. Yes, he who had gladly received the promises was offering up his only born son, Hebrews 11:17 to whom it was said, “Your offspring will be accounted as from Isaac,” Hebrews 11:18 concluding that God is able to raise up even from the dead. Figuratively speaking, he also did receive him back from the dead. Hebrews 11:19 By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau, even concerning things to come. Hebrews 11:20 By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshiped, leaning on the top of his staff. Hebrews 11:21 By faith Joseph, when his end was near, made mention of the departure of the children of Israel, and gave instructions concerning his bones. Hebrews 11:22

title: Hebrews 11:23–31
context: Moses’ parents hid him by faith, unafraid of the king’s edict. Moses himself refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing ill-treatment with God’s people over the passing pleasures of sin, because he considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures. By faith he left Egypt, kept the Passover, and led the people through the Red Sea. By faith the walls of Jericho fell, and Rahab was spared. Both traditions see faith making real choices. They frame those choices differently.
text: Hebrews 11:23–31 Hebrews Moses’ parents hid him by faith, unafraid of the king’s edict. Moses himself refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing ill-treatment with God’s people over the passing pleasures of sin, because he considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures. By faith he left Egypt, kept the Passover, and led the people through the Red Sea. By faith the walls of Jericho fell, and Rahab was spared. Both traditions see faith making real choices. They frame those choices differently. By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that he was a beautiful child; and they were not afraid of the king’s commandment. Hebrews 11:23 By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, Hebrews 11:24 choosing rather to share ill treatment with God’s people than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a time, Hebrews 11:25 considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked to the reward. Hebrews 11:26 By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible. Hebrews 11:27 By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of the blood, that the destroyer of the firstborn should not touch them. Hebrews 11:28 By faith they passed through the Red Sea as on dry land. When the Egyptians tried to do so, they were swallowed up. Hebrews 11:29 By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. Hebrews 11:30 By faith Rahab the prostitute didn’t perish with those who were disobedient, having received the spies in peace. Hebrews 11:31

title: Hebrews 11:32–40
context: The writer runs out of time to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets. Through faith some conquered kingdoms, shut lions’ mouths, and escaped the sword. Others were tortured, mocked, imprisoned, stoned, sawn in two, and killed, refusing release to gain a better resurrection. The world was not worthy of them. All were commended for their faith but did not receive what was promised, because God had provided something better, so that they would not be made perfect apart from us. Both traditions see faith vindicated whether it leads to triumph or to suffering.
text: Hebrews 11:32–40 Hebrews The writer runs out of time to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets. Through faith some conquered kingdoms, shut lions’ mouths, and escaped the sword. Others were tortured, mocked, imprisoned, stoned, sawn in two, and killed, refusing release to gain a better resurrection. The world was not worthy of them. All were commended for their faith but did not receive what was promised, because God had provided something better, so that they would not be made perfect apart from us. Both traditions see faith vindicated whether it leads to triumph or to suffering. What more shall I say? For the time would fail me if I told of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets— Hebrews 11:32 who through faith subdued kingdoms, worked out righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, Hebrews 11:33 quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, from weakness were made strong, grew mighty in war, and caused foreign armies to flee. Hebrews 11:34 Women received their dead by resurrection. Others were tortured, not accepting their deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Hebrews 11:35 Others were tried by mocking and scourging, yes, moreover by bonds and imprisonment. Hebrews 11:36 They were stoned. They were sawn apart. They were tempted. They were slain with the sword. They went around in sheep skins and in goat skins; being destitute, afflicted, ill-treated— Hebrews 11:37 of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and the holes of the earth. Hebrews 11:38 These all, having been commended for their faith, didn’t receive the promise, Hebrews 11:39 God having provided some better thing concerning us, so that apart from us they should not be made perfect. Hebrews 11:40

title: Hebrews 11:8–16
context: Abraham obeyed God’s call to go out, not knowing where he was going, and lived as a foreigner in the land of promise, looking for the city whose designer and builder is God. By faith Sarah received power to conceive, and from one man as good as dead came descendants as many as the stars. These all died in faith without receiving the promises, confessing that they were strangers on the earth, seeking a better, heavenly country. So God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them. Both traditions draw from the passage a picture of pilgrim faith.
text: Hebrews 11:8–16 Hebrews Abraham obeyed God’s call to go out, not knowing where he was going, and lived as a foreigner in the land of promise, looking for the city whose designer and builder is God. By faith Sarah received power to conceive, and from one man as good as dead came descendants as many as the stars. These all died in faith without receiving the promises, confessing that they were strangers on the earth, seeking a better, heavenly country. So God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them. Both traditions draw from the passage a picture of pilgrim faith. By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went. Hebrews 11:8 By faith he lived as an alien in the land of promise, as in a land not his own, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise. Hebrews 11:9 For he was looking for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God. Hebrews 11:10 By faith even Sarah herself received power to conceive, and she bore a child when she was past age, since she counted him faithful who had promised. Hebrews 11:11 Therefore as many as the stars of the sky in multitude, and as innumerable as the sand which is by the sea shore, were fathered by one man, and him as good as dead. Hebrews 11:12 These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar, and having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. Hebrews 11:13 For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a country of their own. Hebrews 11:14 If indeed they had been thinking of that country from which they went out, they would have had enough time to return. Hebrews 11:15 But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them. Hebrews 11:16

title: Hebrews 12:1–13
context: Surrounded by the great cloud of faithful witnesses from chapter 11, believers are to lay aside every weight and sin and run their race with endurance, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith, who endured the cross. The readers’ hardships are God’s fatherly discipline, a sign that they are true children. Discipline is painful for a time, but it produces the peaceful fruit of righteousness. So they should strengthen weak hands and make straight paths. Both traditions draw deep comfort here. They differ on the meaning of “founder and perfecter of faith.”
text: Hebrews 12:1–13 Hebrews Surrounded by the great cloud of faithful witnesses from chapter 11, believers are to lay aside every weight and sin and run their race with endurance, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith, who endured the cross. The readers’ hardships are God’s fatherly discipline, a sign that they are true children. Discipline is painful for a time, but it produces the peaceful fruit of righteousness. So they should strengthen weak hands and make straight paths. Both traditions draw deep comfort here. They differ on the meaning of “founder and perfecter of faith.” Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us, Hebrews 12:1 looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. Hebrews 12:2 For consider him who has endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, that you don’t grow weary, fainting in your souls. Hebrews 12:3 You have not yet resisted to blood, striving against sin. Hebrews 12:4 You have forgotten the exhortation which reasons with you as with children, “My son, don’t take lightly the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when you are reproved by him; Hebrews 12:5 for whom the Lord loves, he disciplines, and chastises every son whom he receives.” Hebrews 12:6 It is for discipline that you endure. God deals with you as with children, for what son is there whom his father doesn’t discipline? Hebrews 12:7 But if you are without discipline, of which all have been made partakers, then you are illegitimate, and not children. Hebrews 12:8 Furthermore, we had the fathers of our flesh to chasten us, and we paid them respect. Shall we not much rather be in subjection to the Father of spirits and live? Hebrews 12:9 For they indeed for a few days disciplined us as seemed good to them, but he for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness. Hebrews 12:10 All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it. Hebrews 12:11 Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees, Hebrews 12:12 and make straight paths for your feet, so what is lame may not be dislocated, but rather be healed. Hebrews 12:13

title: Hebrews 12:14–17
context: The writer urges the readers to pursue peace with everyone and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord. They must see to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God, that no bitter root springs up, and that no one is sexually immoral or godless like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal and afterward could not reverse it. Verse 14 is a key text in Wesleyan teaching on holiness, and verse 15 raises the question of falling short of grace.
text: Hebrews 12:14–17 Hebrews The writer urges the readers to pursue peace with everyone and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord. They must see to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God, that no bitter root springs up, and that no one is sexually immoral or godless like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal and afterward could not reverse it. Verse 14 is a key text in Wesleyan teaching on holiness, and verse 15 raises the question of falling short of grace. Follow after peace with all men, and the sanctification without which no man will see the Lord, Hebrews 12:14 looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it, Hebrews 12:15 lest there be any sexually immoral person or profane person, like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal. Hebrews 12:16 For you know that even when he afterward desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no place for a change of mind though he sought it diligently with tears. Hebrews 12:17

title: Hebrews 12:18–29
context: The writer contrasts two mountains. Believers have not come to Sinai, with its fire, darkness, and terrifying voice, but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, with innumerable angels, the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, God the judge, the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. They must not refuse the one who speaks from heaven. God will shake earth and heaven once more, leaving only what cannot be shaken. Receiving an unshakable kingdom, believers should worship God with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire. Both traditions see the glory of the new covenant here. They differ on the force of the closing warning.
text: Hebrews 12:18–29 Hebrews The writer contrasts two mountains. Believers have not come to Sinai, with its fire, darkness, and terrifying voice, but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, with innumerable angels, the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, God the judge, the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. They must not refuse the one who speaks from heaven. God will shake earth and heaven once more, leaving only what cannot be shaken. Receiving an unshakable kingdom, believers should worship God with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire. Both traditions see the glory of the new covenant here. They differ on the force of the closing warning. For you have not come to a mountain that might be touched and that burned with fire, and to blackness, darkness, storm, Hebrews 12:18 the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words; which those who heard it begged that not one more word should be spoken to them, Hebrews 12:19 for they could not stand that which was commanded, “If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned”. Hebrews 12:20 So fearful was the appearance that Moses said, “I am terrified and trembling.” Hebrews 12:21 But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable multitudes of angels, Hebrews 12:22 to the festal gathering and assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of just men made perfect, Hebrews 12:23 to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel. Hebrews 12:24 See that you don’t refuse him who speaks. For if they didn’t escape when they refused him who warned on the earth, how much more will we not escape who turn away from him who warns from heaven, Hebrews 12:25 whose voice shook the earth then, but now he has promised, saying, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth, but also the heavens.” Hebrews 12:26 This phrase, “Yet once more” signifies the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that have been made, that those things which are not shaken may remain. Hebrews 12:27 Therefore, receiving a Kingdom that can’t be shaken, let’s have grace, through which we serve God acceptably, with reverence and awe, Hebrews 12:28 for our God is a consuming fire. Hebrews 12:29

title: Hebrews 13:1–6
context: The final chapter turns to practical exhortations. Brotherly love must continue. Believers are to show hospitality, remember prisoners and the mistreated, honor marriage and keep it pure, and stay free from the love of money, content with what they have. God has promised never to leave or forsake them, so they can say with confidence that the Lord is their helper. Both traditions read these instructions as the fruit of grace. They find different comfort in God’s promise in verse 5.
text: Hebrews 13:1–6 Hebrews The final chapter turns to practical exhortations. Brotherly love must continue. Believers are to show hospitality, remember prisoners and the mistreated, honor marriage and keep it pure, and stay free from the love of money, content with what they have. God has promised never to leave or forsake them, so they can say with confidence that the Lord is their helper. Both traditions read these instructions as the fruit of grace. They find different comfort in God’s promise in verse 5. Let brotherly love continue. Hebrews 13:1 Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it. Hebrews 13:2 Remember those who are in bonds, as bound with them, and those who are ill-treated, since you are also in the body. Hebrews 13:3 Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the bed be undefiled; but God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers. Hebrews 13:4 Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.” Hebrews 13:5 So that with good courage we say, “The Lord is my helper. I will not fear. What can man do to me?” Hebrews 13:6

title: Hebrews 13:18–25
context: The writer asks for prayer, confident that he has a clear conscience, and urges them to pray that he may be restored to them soon. He then offers one of the great benedictions of the New Testament: may the God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip them with everything good to do his will, working in them what pleases him. He asks them to bear with his word of exhortation, shares news of Timothy, and sends greetings. Both traditions see the benediction joining God’s work and human obedience.
text: Hebrews 13:18–25 Hebrews The writer asks for prayer, confident that he has a clear conscience, and urges them to pray that he may be restored to them soon. He then offers one of the great benedictions of the New Testament: may the God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip them with everything good to do his will, working in them what pleases him. He asks them to bear with his word of exhortation, shares news of Timothy, and sends greetings. Both traditions see the benediction joining God’s work and human obedience. Pray for us, for we are persuaded that we have a good conscience, desiring to live honorably in all things. Hebrews 13:18 I strongly urge you to do this, that I may be restored to you sooner. Hebrews 13:19 Now may the God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep with the blood of an eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus, Hebrews 13:20 make you complete in every good work to do his will, working in you that which is well pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen. Hebrews 13:21 But I exhort you, brothers, endure the word of exhortation, for I have written to you in few words. Hebrews 13:22 Know that our brother Timothy has been freed, with whom, if he comes shortly, I will see you. Hebrews 13:23 Greet all of your leaders and all the saints. The Italians greet you. Hebrews 13:24 Grace be with you all. Amen. Hebrews 13:25

title: Hebrews 13:7–17
context: The readers are to remember their former leaders and imitate their faith, because Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. They should not be carried away by strange teachings about foods, since the heart is strengthened by grace. Believers have an altar the old priests cannot share. As Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people by his blood, so believers should go to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach, seeking the city to come. They are to offer a sacrifice of praise and do good, and to obey their present leaders, who watch over their souls. Both traditions draw rich teaching here, with differences on the sacraments and church order.
text: Hebrews 13:7–17 Hebrews The readers are to remember their former leaders and imitate their faith, because Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. They should not be carried away by strange teachings about foods, since the heart is strengthened by grace. Believers have an altar the old priests cannot share. As Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people by his blood, so believers should go to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach, seeking the city to come. They are to offer a sacrifice of praise and do good, and to obey their present leaders, who watch over their souls. Both traditions draw rich teaching here, with differences on the sacraments and church order. Remember your leaders, men who spoke to you the word of God, and considering the results of their conduct, imitate their faith. Hebrews 13:7 Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Hebrews 13:8 Don’t be carried away by various and strange teachings, for it is good that the heart be established by grace, not by foods, through which those who were so occupied were not benefited. Hebrews 13:9 We have an altar from which those who serve the holy tabernacle have no right to eat. Hebrews 13:10 For the bodies of those animals, whose blood is brought into the holy place by the high priest as an offering for sin, are burned outside of the camp. Hebrews 13:11 Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside of the gate. Hebrews 13:12 Let’s therefore go out to him outside of the camp, bearing his reproach. Hebrews 13:13 For we don’t have here an enduring city, but we seek that which is to come. Hebrews 13:14 Through him, then, let’s offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of lips which proclaim allegiance to his name. Hebrews 13:15 But don’t forget to be doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased. Hebrews 13:16 Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch on behalf of your souls, as those who will give account, that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be unprofitable for you. Hebrews 13:17

title: Hebrews 2:1–4
context: This is the first of the warning passages in Hebrews. Having shown that the Son is greater than the angels, the writer draws the practical conclusion: listeners must pay closer attention to what they have heard, so they do not drift away. If the message delivered through angels at Sinai carried just penalties, there will be no escape for those who neglect so great a salvation, first spoken by the Lord and confirmed by those who heard him and by God’s signs. Both traditions take the warning seriously. They differ on whether drifting away could end in final loss for a true believer.
text: Hebrews 2:1–4 Hebrews This is the first of the warning passages in Hebrews. Having shown that the Son is greater than the angels, the writer draws the practical conclusion: listeners must pay closer attention to what they have heard, so they do not drift away. If the message delivered through angels at Sinai carried just penalties, there will be no escape for those who neglect so great a salvation, first spoken by the Lord and confirmed by those who heard him and by God’s signs. Both traditions take the warning seriously. They differ on whether drifting away could end in final loss for a true believer. Therefore we ought to pay greater attention to the things that were heard, lest perhaps we drift away. Hebrews 2:1 For if the word spoken through angels proved steadfast, and every transgression and disobedience received a just penalty, Hebrews 2:2 how will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation—which at the first having been spoken through the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard, Hebrews 2:3 God also testifying with them, both by signs and wonders, by various works of power, and by gifts of the Holy Spirit, according to his own will? Hebrews 2:4

title: Hebrews 2:10–18
context: The writer explains why the Son had to share in human nature and suffering. It was fitting for God to make the founder of salvation perfect through suffering, as he brings many sons to glory. Christ is not ashamed to call them brothers. He shared flesh and blood so that through death he might destroy the devil and free those enslaved by fear of death. He became like his brothers in every respect so that he could be a merciful and faithful high priest, making atonement for the people’s sins, and able to help those who are tempted. Both traditions treasure the passage. They read its references to “children” and “the people” differently.
text: Hebrews 2:10–18 Hebrews The writer explains why the Son had to share in human nature and suffering. It was fitting for God to make the founder of salvation perfect through suffering, as he brings many sons to glory. Christ is not ashamed to call them brothers. He shared flesh and blood so that through death he might destroy the devil and free those enslaved by fear of death. He became like his brothers in every respect so that he could be a merciful and faithful high priest, making atonement for the people’s sins, and able to help those who are tempted. Both traditions treasure the passage. They read its references to “children” and “the people” differently. For it became him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, in bringing many children to glory, to make the author of their salvation perfect through sufferings. Hebrews 2:10 For both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one, for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brothers, Hebrews 2:11 saying, “I will declare your name to my brothers. Among the congregation I will sing your praise.” Hebrews 2:12 Again, “I will put my trust in him.” Again, “Behold, here I am with the children whom God has given me.” Hebrews 2:13 Since then the children have shared in flesh and blood, he also himself in the same way partook of the same, that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, Hebrews 2:14 and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. Hebrews 2:15 For most certainly, he doesn’t give help to angels, but he gives help to the offspring of Abraham. Hebrews 2:16 Therefore he was obligated in all things to be made like his brothers, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. Hebrews 2:17 For in that he himself has suffered being tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted. Hebrews 2:18

title: Hebrews 2:5–9
context: The writer turns to Psalm 8, which marvels that God made humanity a little lower than the angels and put all things under its feet. We do not yet see everything subject to humanity, but we do see Jesus, made lower than the angels for a little while and now crowned with glory because he suffered death, so that by God’s grace he might taste death for everyone. Verse 9 is a central text in the debate over the extent of the atonement.
text: Hebrews 2:5–9 Hebrews The writer turns to Psalm 8, which marvels that God made humanity a little lower than the angels and put all things under its feet. We do not yet see everything subject to humanity, but we do see Jesus, made lower than the angels for a little while and now crowned with glory because he suffered death, so that by God’s grace he might taste death for everyone. Verse 9 is a central text in the debate over the extent of the atonement. For he didn’t subject the world to come, of which we speak, to angels. Hebrews 2:5 But one has somewhere testified, saying, “What is man, that you think of him? Or the son of man, that you care for him? Hebrews 2:6 You made him a little lower than the angels. You crowned him with glory and honor. Hebrews 2:7 You have put all things in subjection under his feet.” For in that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing that is not subject to him. But now we don’t yet see all things subjected to him. Hebrews 2:8 But we see him who has been made a little lower than the angels, Jesus, because of the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor, that by the grace of God he should taste of death for everyone. Hebrews 2:9

title: Hebrews 3:1–6
context: The writer calls “holy brothers” to consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of their confession. Moses was faithful as a servant in God’s house, but Jesus is faithful as a Son over the house, and is worthy of greater glory as the builder is greater than the house. Believers are his house, if they hold fast their confidence and hope. The conditional “if” in verse 6 introduces a theme that runs through the next chapter. The two traditions read it differently.
text: Hebrews 3:1–6 Hebrews The writer calls “holy brothers” to consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of their confession. Moses was faithful as a servant in God’s house, but Jesus is faithful as a Son over the house, and is worthy of greater glory as the builder is greater than the house. Believers are his house, if they hold fast their confidence and hope. The conditional “if” in verse 6 introduces a theme that runs through the next chapter. The two traditions read it differently. Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our confession: Jesus, Hebrews 3:1 who was faithful to him who appointed him, as also Moses was in all his house. Hebrews 3:2 For he has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses, because he who built the house has more honor than the house. Hebrews 3:3 For every house is built by someone; but he who built all things is God. Hebrews 3:4 Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were afterward to be spoken, Hebrews 3:5 but Christ is faithful as a Son over his house. We are his house, if we hold fast our confidence and the glorying of our hope firm to the end. Hebrews 3:6

title: Hebrews 3:7–19
context: Quoting Psalm 95, the writer urges the readers not to harden their hearts as Israel did in the wilderness. That generation saw God’s works for forty years yet tested him, and God swore they would not enter his rest. The readers must take care that none of them has an evil, unbelieving heart that leads them to fall away from the living God, and must exhort one another daily. We have come to share in Christ, if we hold our original confidence firm to the end. Israel failed to enter because of unbelief. This passage is central to the warning theme of Hebrews.
text: Hebrews 3:7–19 Hebrews Quoting Psalm 95, the writer urges the readers not to harden their hearts as Israel did in the wilderness. That generation saw God’s works for forty years yet tested him, and God swore they would not enter his rest. The readers must take care that none of them has an evil, unbelieving heart that leads them to fall away from the living God, and must exhort one another daily. We have come to share in Christ, if we hold our original confidence firm to the end. Israel failed to enter because of unbelief. This passage is central to the warning theme of Hebrews. Therefore, even as the Holy Spirit says, “Today if you will hear his voice, Hebrews 3:7 don’t harden your hearts as in the rebellion, in the day of the trial in the wilderness, Hebrews 3:8 where your fathers tested me and tried me, and saw my deeds for forty years. Hebrews 3:9 Therefore I was displeased with that generation, and said, ‘They always err in their heart, but they didn’t know my ways.’ Hebrews 3:10 As I swore in my wrath, ‘They will not enter into my rest.’” Hebrews 3:11 Beware, brothers, lest perhaps there might be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, in falling away from the living God; Hebrews 3:12 but exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called “today”, lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. Hebrews 3:13 For we have become partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence firm to the end, Hebrews 3:14 while it is said, “Today if you will hear his voice, don’t harden your hearts, as in the rebellion.” Hebrews 3:15 For who, when they heard, rebelled? Wasn’t it all those who came out of Egypt led by Moses? Hebrews 3:16 With whom was he displeased forty years? Wasn’t it with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? Hebrews 3:17 To whom did he swear that they wouldn’t enter into his rest, but to those who were disobedient? Hebrews 3:18 We see that they weren’t able to enter in because of unbelief. Hebrews 3:19

title: Hebrews 4:1–13
context: The writer applies the wilderness story to his readers. Since the promise of entering God’s rest still stands, they should fear lest any of them fail to reach it. The good news came to Israel as it has come to us, but it did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith. A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, so believers must strive to enter it, lest anyone fall by the same disobedience. The passage ends with the word of God, living and active, which exposes the heart to the God to whom all must give account. Both traditions see faith as the way into God’s rest. They differ on the meaning of the warning to fall.
text: Hebrews 4:1–13 Hebrews The writer applies the wilderness story to his readers. Since the promise of entering God’s rest still stands, they should fear lest any of them fail to reach it. The good news came to Israel as it has come to us, but it did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith. A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, so believers must strive to enter it, lest anyone fall by the same disobedience. The passage ends with the word of God, living and active, which exposes the heart to the God to whom all must give account. Both traditions see faith as the way into God’s rest. They differ on the meaning of the warning to fall. Let’s fear therefore, lest perhaps anyone of you should seem to have come short of a promise of entering into his rest. Hebrews 4:1 For indeed we have had good news preached to us, even as they also did, but the word they heard didn’t profit them, because it wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard. Hebrews 4:2 For we who have believed do enter into that rest, even as he has said, “As I swore in my wrath, they will not enter into my rest;” although the works were finished from the foundation of the world. Hebrews 4:3 For he has said this somewhere about the seventh day, “God rested on the seventh day from all his works;” Hebrews 4:4 and in this place again, “They will not enter into my rest.” Hebrews 4:5 Seeing therefore it remains that some should enter into it, and they to whom the good news was preached before failed to enter in because of disobedience, Hebrews 4:6 he again defines a certain day, “today”, saying through David so long a time afterward (just as has been said), “Today if you will hear his voice, don’t harden your hearts.” Hebrews 4:7 For if Joshua had given them rest, he would not have spoken afterward of another day. Hebrews 4:8 There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God. Hebrews 4:9 For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his. Hebrews 4:10 Let’s therefore give diligence to enter into that rest, lest anyone fall after the same example of disobedience. Hebrews 4:11 For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Hebrews 4:12 There is no creature that is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid open before the eyes of him to whom we must give an account. Hebrews 4:13

title: Hebrews 4:14–16
context: After describing God’s word as able to search every heart, the writer turns to comfort. Believers have a great high priest, Jesus the Son of God, who has passed through the heavens, who sympathizes with human weakness, and who was tempted in every way without sinning. So they are to hold fast their confession and come boldly to the throne of grace. These verses are mostly common ground for Arminian and Reformed readers, with a difference in how they hear the command to hold fast.
text: Hebrews 4:14–16 Hebrews After describing God’s word as able to search every heart, the writer turns to comfort. Believers have a great high priest, Jesus the Son of God, who has passed through the heavens, who sympathizes with human weakness, and who was tempted in every way without sinning. So they are to hold fast their confession and come boldly to the throne of grace. These verses are mostly common ground for Arminian and Reformed readers, with a difference in how they hear the command to hold fast. Having then a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let’s hold tightly to our confession. Hebrews 4:14 For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin. Hebrews 4:15 Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need. Hebrews 4:16

title: Hebrews 5:1–10
context: The writer explains what makes a true high priest. A priest is taken from among men, deals gently with the ignorant and wayward because he shares their weakness, and does not take the honor on himself but is called by God. So too Christ was appointed by the Father, who declared him a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. In the days of his flesh he offered prayers with loud cries and tears, learned obedience through suffering, and, being made perfect, became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him. Verse 9 is read differently by the two traditions.
text: Hebrews 5:1–10 Hebrews The writer explains what makes a true high priest. A priest is taken from among men, deals gently with the ignorant and wayward because he shares their weakness, and does not take the honor on himself but is called by God. So too Christ was appointed by the Father, who declared him a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. In the days of his flesh he offered prayers with loud cries and tears, learned obedience through suffering, and, being made perfect, became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him. Verse 9 is read differently by the two traditions. For every high priest, being taken from among men, is appointed for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins. Hebrews 5:1 The high priest can deal gently with those who are ignorant and going astray, because he himself is also surrounded with weakness. Hebrews 5:2 Because of this, he must offer sacrifices for sins for the people, as well as for himself. Hebrews 5:3 Nobody takes this honor on himself, but he is called by God, just like Aaron was. Hebrews 5:4 So also Christ didn’t glorify himself to be made a high priest, but it was he who said to him, “You are my Son. Today I have become your father.” Hebrews 5:5 As he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.” Hebrews 5:6 He, in the days of his flesh, having offered up prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard for his godly fear, Hebrews 5:7 though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered. Hebrews 5:8 Having been made perfect, he became to all of those who obey him the author of eternal salvation, Hebrews 5:9 named by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek. Hebrews 5:10

title: Hebrews 5:11–14
context: The writer pauses before explaining Melchizedek, because his readers have become dull of hearing. By now they should be teachers, but they need milk again rather than solid food. Those who live on milk are unskilled in the word of righteousness, while the mature have trained their powers of discernment by constant practice. This rebuke leads into the warning of chapter 6. Both traditions see a call to spiritual growth, and they differ on how serious the danger of stagnation is.
text: Hebrews 5:11–14 Hebrews The writer pauses before explaining Melchizedek, because his readers have become dull of hearing. By now they should be teachers, but they need milk again rather than solid food. Those who live on milk are unskilled in the word of righteousness, while the mature have trained their powers of discernment by constant practice. This rebuke leads into the warning of chapter 6. Both traditions see a call to spiritual growth, and they differ on how serious the danger of stagnation is. About him we have many words to say, and hard to interpret, seeing you have become dull of hearing. Hebrews 5:11 For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God. You have come to need milk, and not solid food. Hebrews 5:12 For everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a baby. Hebrews 5:13 But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil. Hebrews 5:14

title: Hebrews 6:1–8
context: Hebrews 6 holds the letter’s hardest warning. The writer has just told his readers they are slow to learn, and now urges them past the basics toward maturity before describing people who were enlightened, tasted God’s gifts, shared in the Holy Spirit, and then fell away. Arminian and Reformed readers agree that the warning is severe and meant to be felt. They disagree about who is being described: believers who can finally fall, or people whose experience of grace never became saving faith.
text: Hebrews 6:1–8 Hebrews Hebrews 6 holds the letter’s hardest warning. The writer has just told his readers they are slow to learn, and now urges them past the basics toward maturity before describing people who were enlightened, tasted God’s gifts, shared in the Holy Spirit, and then fell away. Arminian and Reformed readers agree that the warning is severe and meant to be felt. They disagree about who is being described: believers who can finally fall, or people whose experience of grace never became saving faith. Therefore leaving the teaching of the first principles of Christ, let’s press on to perfection—not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works, of faith toward God, Hebrews 6:1 of the teaching of baptisms, of laying on of hands, of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. Hebrews 6:2 This will we do, if God permits. Hebrews 6:3 For concerning those who were once enlightened and tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, Hebrews 6:4 and tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, Hebrews 6:5 and then fell away, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance; seeing they crucify the Son of God for themselves again, and put him to open shame. Hebrews 6:6 For the land which has drunk the rain that comes often on it and produces a crop suitable for them for whose sake it is also tilled, receives blessing from God; Hebrews 6:7 but if it bears thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near being cursed, whose end is to be burned. Hebrews 6:8

title: Hebrews 6:9–20
context: After the severe warning of 6:4–8, the writer turns to confidence. He is persuaded of better things for his readers, things that belong to salvation, because God will not forget their love and service. He urges them to show the same diligence to the end and to imitate those who inherit the promises through faith and patience. Then he grounds their hope in God’s promise to Abraham, confirmed by an oath, so that by two unchangeable things the heirs of the promise have strong encouragement. This hope is a sure and steady anchor, fastened where Jesus has entered as forerunner. Both traditions read this section alongside the warning. They differ on whether the anchor guarantees the outcome or secures those who keep holding on.
text: Hebrews 6:9–20 Hebrews After the severe warning of 6:4–8, the writer turns to confidence. He is persuaded of better things for his readers, things that belong to salvation, because God will not forget their love and service. He urges them to show the same diligence to the end and to imitate those who inherit the promises through faith and patience. Then he grounds their hope in God’s promise to Abraham, confirmed by an oath, so that by two unchangeable things the heirs of the promise have strong encouragement. This hope is a sure and steady anchor, fastened where Jesus has entered as forerunner. Both traditions read this section alongside the warning. They differ on whether the anchor guarantees the outcome or secures those who keep holding on. But, beloved, we are persuaded of better things for you, and things that accompany salvation, even though we speak like this. Hebrews 6:9 For God is not unrighteous, so as to forget your work and the labor of love which you showed toward his name, in that you served the saints, and still do serve them. Hebrews 6:10 We desire that each one of you may show the same diligence to the fullness of hope even to the end, Hebrews 6:11 that you won’t be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and perseverance inherited the promises. Hebrews 6:12 For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he could swear by no one greater, he swore by himself, Hebrews 6:13 saying, “Surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.” Hebrews 6:14 Thus, having patiently endured, he obtained the promise. Hebrews 6:15 For men indeed swear by a greater one, and in every dispute of theirs the oath is final for confirmation. Hebrews 6:16 In this way God, being determined to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the immutability of his counsel, interposed with an oath, Hebrews 6:17 that by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have a strong encouragement, who have fled for refuge to take hold of the hope set before us. Hebrews 6:18 This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast and entering into that which is within the veil, Hebrews 6:19 where as a forerunner Jesus entered for us, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. Hebrews 6:20

title: Hebrews 7:1–10
context: The writer explains the mysterious Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who met Abraham, blessed him, and received a tenth of the spoils. His name means king of righteousness, and his title means king of peace. Scripture records no genealogy for him, which makes him a fitting picture of the Son, who has a priesthood without end. Because the lesser is blessed by the greater, and Levi in a sense paid tithes through Abraham, Melchizedek’s priesthood is superior to Levi’s. The passage is common ground for both traditions.
text: Hebrews 7:1–10 Hebrews The writer explains the mysterious Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who met Abraham, blessed him, and received a tenth of the spoils. His name means king of righteousness, and his title means king of peace. Scripture records no genealogy for him, which makes him a fitting picture of the Son, who has a priesthood without end. Because the lesser is blessed by the greater, and Levi in a sense paid tithes through Abraham, Melchizedek’s priesthood is superior to Levi’s. The passage is common ground for both traditions. For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of God Most High, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, Hebrews 7:1 to whom also Abraham divided a tenth part of all (being first, by interpretation, “king of righteousness”, and then also “king of Salem”, which means “king of peace”, Hebrews 7:2 without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God), remains a priest continually. Hebrews 7:3 Now consider how great this man was, to whom even Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth out of the best plunder. Hebrews 7:4 They indeed of the sons of Levi who receive the priest’s office have a commandment to take tithes from the people according to the law, that is, of their brothers, though these have come out of the body of Abraham, Hebrews 7:5 but he whose genealogy is not counted from them has accepted tithes from Abraham, and has blessed him who has the promises. Hebrews 7:6 But without any dispute the lesser is blessed by the greater. Hebrews 7:7 Here people who die receive tithes, but there one receives tithes of whom it is testified that he lives. Hebrews 7:8 We can say that through Abraham even Levi, who receives tithes, has paid tithes, Hebrews 7:9 for he was yet in the body of his father when Melchizedek met him. Hebrews 7:10

title: Hebrews 7:11–19
context: If perfection could have come through the Levitical priesthood, there would have been no need for another priest after the order of Melchizedek. A change of priesthood requires a change of law. Jesus came from Judah, not Levi, and became a priest by the power of an indestructible life, not by a legal requirement about descent. The former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness, since the law made nothing perfect, and a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God. Both traditions agree on the substance. They differ on how far the law is changed.
text: Hebrews 7:11–19 Hebrews If perfection could have come through the Levitical priesthood, there would have been no need for another priest after the order of Melchizedek. A change of priesthood requires a change of law. Jesus came from Judah, not Levi, and became a priest by the power of an indestructible life, not by a legal requirement about descent. The former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness, since the law made nothing perfect, and a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God. Both traditions agree on the substance. They differ on how far the law is changed. Now if perfection was through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people have received the law), what further need was there for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, and not be called after the order of Aaron? Hebrews 7:11 For the priesthood being changed, there is of necessity a change made also in the law. Hebrews 7:12 For he of whom these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one has officiated at the altar. Hebrews 7:13 For it is evident that our Lord has sprung out of Judah, about which tribe Moses spoke nothing concerning priesthood. Hebrews 7:14 This is yet more abundantly evident, if after the likeness of Melchizedek there arises another priest, Hebrews 7:15 who has been made, not after the law of a fleshly commandment, but after the power of an endless life; Hebrews 7:16 for it is testified, “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.” Hebrews 7:17 For there is an annulling of a foregoing commandment because of its weakness and uselessness Hebrews 7:18 (for the law made nothing perfect), and a bringing in of a better hope, through which we draw near to God. Hebrews 7:19

title: Hebrews 7:20–28
context: Jesus’ priesthood was confirmed with God’s oath, which makes him the guarantor of a better covenant. The old priests were many because death prevented them from continuing, but Jesus holds his priesthood permanently because he lives forever. So he is able to save completely those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them. He is holy, innocent, and exalted, and he does not need to offer daily sacrifices, because he offered himself once for all.
