Verse 25 is treasured by both traditions as a promise of Christ’s saving power.
text: Hebrews 7:20–28 Hebrews Jesus’ priesthood was confirmed with God’s oath, which makes him the guarantor of a better covenant. The old priests were many because death prevented them from continuing, but Jesus holds his priesthood permanently because he lives forever. So he is able to save completely those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them. He is holy, innocent, and exalted, and he does not need to offer daily sacrifices, because he offered himself once for all. Verse 25 is treasured by both traditions as a promise of Christ’s saving power. Inasmuch as he was not made priest without the taking of an oath Hebrews 7:20 (for they indeed have been made priests without an oath), but he with an oath by him that says of him, “The Lord swore and will not change his mind, ‘You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.’” Hebrews 7:21 By so much, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant. Hebrews 7:22 Many, indeed, have been made priests, because they are hindered from continuing by death. Hebrews 7:23 But he, because he lives forever, has his priesthood unchangeable. Hebrews 7:24 Therefore he is also able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, seeing that he lives forever to make intercession for them. Hebrews 7:25 For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, guiltless, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens; Hebrews 7:26 who doesn’t need, like those high priests, to offer up sacrifices daily, first for his own sins, and then for the sins of the people. For he did this once for all, when he offered up himself. Hebrews 7:27 For the law appoints men as high priests who have weakness, but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints a Son forever who has been perfected. Hebrews 7:28

title: Hebrews 8:1–13
context: The writer states his main point: believers have a high priest seated at the right hand of God, serving in the true tabernacle set up by the Lord. The earthly priests serve a copy and shadow. Christ’s ministry is far better, because he mediates a better covenant enacted on better promises. The writer quotes Jeremiah 31 in full: God will make a new covenant, write his laws on hearts, be their God, and remember their sins no more, so that all will know him. The new covenant makes the first obsolete. The two traditions read the new covenant promises differently, especially the scope of “they shall all know me.”
text: Hebrews 8:1–13 Hebrews The writer states his main point: believers have a high priest seated at the right hand of God, serving in the true tabernacle set up by the Lord. The earthly priests serve a copy and shadow. Christ’s ministry is far better, because he mediates a better covenant enacted on better promises. The writer quotes Jeremiah 31 in full: God will make a new covenant, write his laws on hearts, be their God, and remember their sins no more, so that all will know him. The new covenant makes the first obsolete. The two traditions read the new covenant promises differently, especially the scope of “they shall all know me.” Now in the things which we are saying, the main point is this: we have such a high priest, who sat down on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens, Hebrews 8:1 a servant of the sanctuary and of the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched, not man. Hebrews 8:2 For every high priest is appointed to offer both gifts and sacrifices. Therefore it is necessary that this high priest also have something to offer. Hebrews 8:3 For if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, seeing there are priests who offer the gifts according to the law, Hebrews 8:4 who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, even as Moses was warned by God when he was about to make the tabernacle, for he said, “See, you shall make everything according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain.” Hebrews 8:5 But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, by as much as he is also the mediator of a better covenant, which on better promises has been given as law. Hebrews 8:6 For if that first covenant had been faultless, then no place would have been sought for a second. Hebrews 8:7 For finding fault with them, he said, “Behold, the days are coming”, says the Lord, “that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah; Hebrews 8:8 not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they didn’t continue in my covenant, and I disregarded them,” says the Lord. Hebrews 8:9 “For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days,” says the Lord: “I will put my laws into their mind; I will also write them on their heart. I will be their God, and they will be my people. Hebrews 8:10 They will not teach every man his fellow citizen and every man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all will know me, from their least to their greatest. Hebrews 8:11 For I will be merciful to their unrighteousness. I will remember their sins and lawless deeds no more.” Hebrews 8:12 In that he says, “A new covenant”, he has made the first obsolete. But that which is becoming obsolete and grows aged is near to vanishing away. Hebrews 8:13

title: Hebrews 9:1–10
context: The writer describes the earthly tabernacle of the first covenant: the holy place with its lampstand and table, and the Most Holy Place with the ark and mercy seat. Priests entered the first room regularly, but only the high priest entered the second, once a year, and never without blood. The Holy Spirit signified by this that the way into God’s presence had not yet been opened while the first tent stood. Its gifts and sacrifices could not perfect the worshiper’s conscience. Both traditions read the tabernacle as a picture fulfilled in Christ, and they largely agree on this passage.
text: Hebrews 9:1–10 Hebrews The writer describes the earthly tabernacle of the first covenant: the holy place with its lampstand and table, and the Most Holy Place with the ark and mercy seat. Priests entered the first room regularly, but only the high priest entered the second, once a year, and never without blood. The Holy Spirit signified by this that the way into God’s presence had not yet been opened while the first tent stood. Its gifts and sacrifices could not perfect the worshiper’s conscience. Both traditions read the tabernacle as a picture fulfilled in Christ, and they largely agree on this passage. Now indeed even the first covenant had ordinances of divine service and an earthly sanctuary. Hebrews 9:1 For a tabernacle was prepared. In the first part were the lamp stand, the table, and the show bread, which is called the Holy Place. Hebrews 9:2 After the second veil was the tabernacle which is called the Holy of Holies, Hebrews 9:3 having a golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant overlaid on all sides with gold, in which was a golden pot holding the manna, Aaron’s rod that budded, and the tablets of the covenant; Hebrews 9:4 and above it cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat, of which things we can’t speak now in detail. Hebrews 9:5 Now these things having been thus prepared, the priests go in continually into the first tabernacle, accomplishing the services, Hebrews 9:6 but into the second the high priest alone, once in the year, not without blood, which he offers for himself and for the errors of the people. Hebrews 9:7 The Holy Spirit is indicating this, that the way into the Holy Place wasn’t yet revealed while the first tabernacle was still standing. Hebrews 9:8 This is a symbol of the present age, where gifts and sacrifices are offered that are incapable, concerning the conscience, of making the worshiper perfect, Hebrews 9:9 being only (with foods and drinks and various washings) fleshly ordinances, imposed until a time of reformation. Hebrews 9:10

title: Hebrews 9:11–22
context: Christ has come as high priest of the good things that have come. Through a greater tent not made with hands, and by his own blood rather than the blood of animals, he entered the holy places once for all, securing eternal redemption. If animal blood purified the flesh, how much more will Christ’s blood, offered through the eternal Spirit, purify the conscience to serve the living God. He is the mediator of a new covenant, whose death redeems from transgressions so that the called may receive the eternal inheritance. Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. Both traditions see substitutionary atonement here. They differ on what “eternal redemption” secures and for whom.
text: Hebrews 9:11–22 Hebrews Christ has come as high priest of the good things that have come. Through a greater tent not made with hands, and by his own blood rather than the blood of animals, he entered the holy places once for all, securing eternal redemption. If animal blood purified the flesh, how much more will Christ’s blood, offered through the eternal Spirit, purify the conscience to serve the living God. He is the mediator of a new covenant, whose death redeems from transgressions so that the called may receive the eternal inheritance. Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. Both traditions see substitutionary atonement here. They differ on what “eternal redemption” secures and for whom. But Christ having come as a high priest of the coming good things, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this creation, Hebrews 9:11 nor yet through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, entered in once for all into the Holy Place, having obtained eternal redemption. Hebrews 9:12 For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling those who have been defiled, sanctify to the cleanness of the flesh, Hebrews 9:13 how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without defect to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? Hebrews 9:14 For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, since a death has occurred for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first covenant, that those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. Hebrews 9:15 For where a last will and testament is, there must of necessity be the death of him who made it. Hebrews 9:16 For a will is in force where there has been death, for it is never in force while he who made it lives. Hebrews 9:17 Therefore even the first covenant has not been dedicated without blood. Hebrews 9:18 For when every commandment had been spoken by Moses to all the people according to the law, he took the blood of the calves and the goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, Hebrews 9:19 saying, “This is the blood of the covenant which God has commanded you.” Hebrews 9:20 He sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry in the same way with the blood. Hebrews 9:21 According to the law, nearly everything is cleansed with blood, and apart from shedding of blood there is no remission. Hebrews 9:22

title: Hebrews 9:23–28
context: The heavenly things required better sacrifices than the earthly copies. Christ entered heaven itself to appear in God’s presence for us, not to offer himself repeatedly as the high priest did each year, but once at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. As people die once and then face judgment, so Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those eagerly waiting for him. Verse 28’s “many” is read differently by the two traditions.
text: Hebrews 9:23–28 Hebrews The heavenly things required better sacrifices than the earthly copies. Christ entered heaven itself to appear in God’s presence for us, not to offer himself repeatedly as the high priest did each year, but once at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. As people die once and then face judgment, so Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those eagerly waiting for him. Verse 28’s “many” is read differently by the two traditions. It was necessary therefore that the copies of the things in the heavens should be cleansed with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. Hebrews 9:23 For Christ hasn’t entered into holy places made with hands, which are representations of the true, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us; Hebrews 9:24 nor yet that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters into the holy place year by year with blood not his own, Hebrews 9:25 or else he must have suffered often since the foundation of the world. But now once at the end of the ages, he has been revealed to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. Hebrews 9:26 Inasmuch as it is appointed for men to die once, and after this, judgment, Hebrews 9:27 so Christ also, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him. Hebrews 9:28

title: Isaiah 1:1–9
context: Isaiah son of Amoz sees concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Heaven and earth are summoned: the Lord has reared children who rebel. Ox and donkey know; Israel does not. A sinful nation is struck from head to foot. Country and cities lie desolate before foreigners. Zion is left like a shelter. Unless the LORD of Armies had left a few survivors, they would have been Sodom.
text: Isaiah 1:1–9 Isaiah Isaiah son of Amoz sees concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Heaven and earth are summoned: the Lord has reared children who rebel. Ox and donkey know; Israel does not. A sinful nation is struck from head to foot. Country and cities lie desolate before foreigners. Zion is left like a shelter. Unless the LORD of Armies had left a few survivors, they would have been Sodom. The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. Isaiah 1:1 Hear, heavens, and listen, earth; for the LORD has spoken: “I have nourished and brought up children and they have rebelled against me. Isaiah 1:2 The ox knows his owner, and the donkey his master’s crib; but Israel doesn’t know. My people don’t consider.” Isaiah 1:3 Ah sinful nation, a people loaded with iniquity, offspring of evildoers, children who deal corruptly! They have forsaken the LORD. They have despised the Holy One of Israel. They are estranged and backward. Isaiah 1:4 Why should you be beaten more, that you revolt more and more? The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint. Isaiah 1:5 From the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness in it, but wounds, welts, and open sores. They haven’t been closed, bandaged, or soothed with oil. Isaiah 1:6 Your country is desolate. Your cities are burned with fire. Strangers devour your land in your presence and it is desolate, as overthrown by strangers. Isaiah 1:7 The daughter of Zion is left like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a field of melons, like a besieged city. Isaiah 1:8 Unless the LORD of Armies had left to us a very small remnant, we would have been as Sodom. We would have been like Gomorrah. Isaiah 1:9

title: Isaiah 1:10–20
context: The remnant of 1:9 does not void the charge. Rulers of Judah are named Sodom, the people Gomorrah: hear the word. Multitudes of sacrifice, new moons, and spread hands cannot cover blood. Wash; cease evil; learn good; seek justice for fatherless and widow. Come, let us reason: scarlet may be snow. If willing and obedient, eat the good of the land; if they refuse, the sword; for the LORD’s mouth has spoken.
text: Isaiah 1:10–20 Isaiah The remnant of 1:9 does not void the charge. Rulers of Judah are named Sodom, the people Gomorrah: hear the word. Multitudes of sacrifice, new moons, and spread hands cannot cover blood. Wash; cease evil; learn good; seek justice for fatherless and widow. Come, let us reason: scarlet may be snow. If willing and obedient, eat the good of the land; if they refuse, the sword; for the LORD’s mouth has spoken. Hear the LORD’s word, you rulers of Sodom! Listen to the law of our God, you people of Gomorrah! Isaiah 1:10 “What are the multitude of your sacrifices to me?”, says the LORD. “I have had enough of the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fed animals. I don’t delight in the blood of bulls, or of lambs, or of male goats. Isaiah 1:11 When you come to appear before me, who has required this at your hand, to trample my courts? Isaiah 1:12 Bring no more vain offerings. Incense is an abomination to me. New moons, Sabbaths, and convocations— I can’t stand evil assemblies. Isaiah 1:13 My soul hates your New Moons and your appointed feasts. They are a burden to me. I am weary of bearing them. Isaiah 1:14 When you spread out your hands, I will hide my eyes from you. Yes, when you make many prayers, I will not hear. Your hands are full of blood. Isaiah 1:15 Wash yourselves. Make yourself clean. Put away the evil of your doings from before my eyes. Cease to do evil. Isaiah 1:16 Learn to do well. Seek justice. Relieve the oppressed. Defend the fatherless. Plead for the widow.” Isaiah 1:17 “Come now, and let’s reason together,” says the LORD: “Though your sins are as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they are red like crimson, they shall be as wool. Isaiah 1:18 If you are willing and obedient, you will eat the good of the land; Isaiah 1:19 but if you refuse and rebel, you will be devoured with the sword; for the LORD’s mouth has spoken it.” Isaiah 1:20

title: Isaiah 1:21–31
context: After the offer of snow, the charge turns to the city: faithful Jerusalem has become a whore; silver is dross; princes love bribes and ignore widow and fatherless. The Mighty One of Israel will get relief from foes, smelt dross, restore judges, and name her righteous again. Zion is redeemed by justice; those who repent, by righteousness. Rebels are broken. Oaks and gardens of idolatry wither; the strong and his work burn, with none to quench.
text: Isaiah 1:21–31 Isaiah After the offer of snow, the charge turns to the city: faithful Jerusalem has become a whore; silver is dross; princes love bribes and ignore widow and fatherless. The Mighty One of Israel will get relief from foes, smelt dross, restore judges, and name her righteous again. Zion is redeemed by justice; those who repent, by righteousness. Rebels are broken. Oaks and gardens of idolatry wither; the strong and his work burn, with none to quench. How the faithful city has become a prostitute! She was full of justice. Righteousness lodged in her, but now there are murderers. Isaiah 1:21 Your silver has become dross, your wine mixed with water. Isaiah 1:22 Your princes are rebellious and companions of thieves. Everyone loves bribes and follows after rewards. They don’t defend the fatherless, neither does the cause of the widow come to them. Isaiah 1:23 Therefore the Lord, GOD of Armies, the Mighty One of Israel, says: “Ah, I will get relief from my adversaries, and avenge myself on my enemies. Isaiah 1:24 I will turn my hand on you, thoroughly purge away your dross, and will take away all your tin. Isaiah 1:25 I will restore your judges as at the first, and your counselors as at the beginning. Afterward you shall be called ‘The city of righteousness, a faithful town.’ Isaiah 1:26 Zion shall be redeemed with justice, and her converts with righteousness. Isaiah 1:27 But the destruction of transgressors and sinners shall be together, and those who forsake the LORD shall be consumed. Isaiah 1:28 For they shall be ashamed of the oaks which you have desired, and you shall be confounded for the gardens that you have chosen. Isaiah 1:29 For you shall be as an oak whose leaf fades, and as a garden that has no water. Isaiah 1:30 The strong will be like tinder, and his work like a spark. They will both burn together, and no one will quench them.” Isaiah 1:31

title: Isaiah 10:1–4
context: The last in a series of woes targets officials who write unjust laws to rob widows, orphans, and the poor. When the day of punishment comes, their wealth will offer no refuge. The chapter’s refrain returns: God’s anger has not turned away, and his hand is still stretched out.
text: Isaiah 10:1–4 Isaiah The last in a series of woes targets officials who write unjust laws to rob widows, orphans, and the poor. When the day of punishment comes, their wealth will offer no refuge. The chapter’s refrain returns: God’s anger has not turned away, and his hand is still stretched out. Woe to those who decree unrighteous decrees, and to the writers who write oppressive decrees Isaiah 10:1 to deprive the needy of justice, and to rob the poor among my people of their rights, that widows may be their plunder, and that they may make the fatherless their prey! Isaiah 10:2 What will you do in the day of visitation, and in the desolation which will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth? Isaiah 10:3 They will only bow down under the prisoners, and will fall under the slain. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still. Isaiah 10:4

title: Isaiah 10:20–34
context: A remnant of Israel will stop leaning on the Assyrian who struck them and will rely truly on the LORD. Only a remnant will return, but Zion need not fear. The Assyrian army marches town by town toward Jerusalem, only to be felled like a forest by the LORD.
text: Isaiah 10:20–34 Isaiah A remnant of Israel will stop leaning on the Assyrian who struck them and will rely truly on the LORD. Only a remnant will return, but Zion need not fear. The Assyrian army marches town by town toward Jerusalem, only to be felled like a forest by the LORD. It will come to pass in that day that the remnant of Israel, and those who have escaped from the house of Jacob will no more again lean on him who struck them, but shall lean on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. Isaiah 10:20 A remnant will return, even the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God. Isaiah 10:21 For though your people, Israel, are like the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. A destruction is determined, overflowing with righteousness. Isaiah 10:22 For the Lord, GOD of Armies, will make a full end, and that determined, throughout all the earth. Isaiah 10:23 Therefore the Lord, GOD of Armies, says, “My people who dwell in Zion, don’t be afraid of the Assyrian, though he strike you with the rod, and lift up his staff against you, as Egypt did. Isaiah 10:24 For yet a very little while, and the indignation against you will be accomplished, and my anger will be directed to his destruction.” Isaiah 10:25 The LORD of Armies will stir up a scourge against him, as in the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb. His rod will be over the sea, and he will lift it up like he did against Egypt. Isaiah 10:26 It will happen in that day that his burden will depart from off your shoulder, and his yoke from off your neck, and the yoke shall be destroyed because of the anointing oil. Isaiah 10:27 He has come to Aiath. He has passed through Migron. At Michmash he stores his baggage. Isaiah 10:28 They have gone over the pass. They have taken up their lodging at Geba. Ramah trembles. Gibeah of Saul has fled. Isaiah 10:29 Cry aloud with your voice, daughter of Gallim! Listen, Laishah! You poor Anathoth! Isaiah 10:30 Madmenah is a fugitive. The inhabitants of Gebim flee for safety. Isaiah 10:31 This very day he will halt at Nob. He shakes his hand at the mountain of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem. Isaiah 10:32 Behold, the Lord, GOD of Armies, will lop the boughs with terror. The tall will be cut down, and the lofty will be brought low. Isaiah 10:33 He will cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon will fall by the Mighty One. Isaiah 10:34

title: Isaiah 10:5–19
context: Alas Assyrian, the rod of the Lord’s anger, the staff in whose hand is His fury. He sends him against a godless nation, to spoil and tread them like mire. But Assyria does not so intend: his heart is to destroy nations. He boasts his commanders are kings; Calno, Hamath, Samaria like the rest; he will do to Jerusalem’s idols as to Samaria’s. When the Lord has finished His work on Zion, He punishes the arrogant heart. The axe must not boast over the hewer. Therefore wasting and fire: the light of Israel becomes a flame; the forest’s remnant so few a child could write their.
text: Isaiah 10:5–19 Isaiah Alas Assyrian, the rod of the Lord’s anger, the staff in whose hand is His fury. He sends him against a godless nation, to spoil and tread them like mire. But Assyria does not so intend: his heart is to destroy nations. He boasts his commanders are kings; Calno, Hamath, Samaria like the rest; he will do to Jerusalem’s idols as to Samaria’s. When the Lord has finished His work on Zion, He punishes the arrogant heart. The axe must not boast over the hewer. Therefore wasting and fire: the light of Israel becomes a flame; the forest’s remnant so few a child could write their. Alas Assyrian, the rod of my anger, the staff in whose hand is my indignation! Isaiah 10:5 I will send him against a profane nation, and against the people who anger me I will give him a command to take the plunder and to take the prey, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. Isaiah 10:6 However, he doesn’t mean so, neither does his heart think so; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off not a few nations. Isaiah 10:7 For he says, “Aren’t all of my princes kings? Isaiah 10:8 Isn’t Calno like Carchemish? Isn’t Hamath like Arpad? Isn’t Samaria like Damascus?” Isaiah 10:9 As my hand has found the kingdoms of the idols, whose engraved images exceeded those of Jerusalem and of Samaria, Isaiah 10:10 shall I not, as I have done to Samaria and her idols, so do to Jerusalem and her idols? Isaiah 10:11 Therefore it will happen that when the Lord has performed his whole work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the willful proud heart of the king of Assyria, and the insolence of his arrogant looks. Isaiah 10:12 For he has said, “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I have understanding. I have removed the boundaries of the peoples, and have robbed their treasures. Like a valiant man I have brought down their rulers. Isaiah 10:13 My hand has found the riches of the peoples like a nest, and like one gathers eggs that are abandoned, I have gathered all the earth. There was no one who moved their wing, or that opened their mouth, or chirped.” Isaiah 10:14 Should an ax brag against him who chops with it? Should a saw exalt itself above him who saws with it? As if a rod should lift those who lift it up, or as if a staff should lift up someone who is not wood. Isaiah 10:15 Therefore the Lord, GOD of Armies, will send among his fat ones leanness; and under his glory a burning will be kindled like the burning of fire. Isaiah 10:16 The light of Israel will be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame; and it will burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day. Isaiah 10:17 He will consume the glory of his forest and of his fruitful field, both soul and body. It will be as when a standard bearer faints. Isaiah 10:18 The remnant of the trees of his forest shall be few, so that a child could write their number. Isaiah 10:19

title: Isaiah 11:1–9
context: A shoot comes from the stump of Jesse; a branch out of his roots bears fruit. The Spirit of the Lord rests on him: wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, fear of the Lord. His delight is that fear. He does not judge by eyes or ears, but in righteousness for the poor and meek. He strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth; the breath of his lips kills the wicked. Righteousness and faithfulness are his belt. Wolf with lamb, leopard with goat, calf and lion together; a little child leads them. Cow and bear graze; the lion eats straw. The nursing child plays at the cobra’s hole. They shall not hurt in all my holy mountain: the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord as waters cover the sea.
text: Isaiah 11:1–9 Isaiah A shoot comes from the stump of Jesse; a branch out of his roots bears fruit. The Spirit of the Lord rests on him: wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, fear of the Lord. His delight is that fear. He does not judge by eyes or ears, but in righteousness for the poor and meek. He strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth; the breath of his lips kills the wicked. Righteousness and faithfulness are his belt. Wolf with lamb, leopard with goat, calf and lion together; a little child leads them. Cow and bear graze; the lion eats straw. The nursing child plays at the cobra’s hole. They shall not hurt in all my holy mountain: the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord as waters cover the sea. A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit. Isaiah 11:1 The LORD’s Spirit will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD. Isaiah 11:2 His delight will be in the fear of the LORD. He will not judge by the sight of his eyes, neither decide by the hearing of his ears; Isaiah 11:3 but he will judge the poor with righteousness, and decide with equity for the humble of the earth. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth; and with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked. Isaiah 11:4 Righteousness will be the belt around his waist, and faithfulness the belt around his waist. Isaiah 11:5 The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the young goat, the calf, the young lion, and the fattened calf together; and a little child will lead them. Isaiah 11:6 The cow and the bear will graze. Their young ones will lie down together. The lion will eat straw like the ox. Isaiah 11:7 The nursing child will play near a cobra’s hole, and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper’s den. Isaiah 11:8 They will not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea. Isaiah 11:9

title: Isaiah 11:10–16
context: In that day that the nations will seek the root of Jesse stands as a banner of the peoples; the nations inquire of him; his resting place is glorious. The Lord extends his hand the second time to recover the remnant from Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath, and the coastlands. He raises a signal, assembles the banished of Israel, gathers the dispersed of Judah from the four corners. Ephraim’s jealousy departs; they shall not harass one another. They swoop on Philistia and the east; Edom, Moab, Ammon. The Lord dries the Egyptian sea and the River into seven channels; a highway for the remnant, as when Israel came up from Egypt.
text: Isaiah 11:10–16 Isaiah In that day that the nations will seek the root of Jesse stands as a banner of the peoples; the nations inquire of him; his resting place is glorious. The Lord extends his hand the second time to recover the remnant from Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath, and the coastlands. He raises a signal, assembles the banished of Israel, gathers the dispersed of Judah from the four corners. Ephraim’s jealousy departs; they shall not harass one another. They swoop on Philistia and the east; Edom, Moab, Ammon. The Lord dries the Egyptian sea and the River into seven channels; a highway for the remnant, as when Israel came up from Egypt. It will happen in that day that the nations will seek the root of Jesse, who stands as a banner of the peoples; and his resting place will be glorious. Isaiah 11:10 It will happen in that day that the Lord will set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant that is left of his people from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. Isaiah 11:11 He will set up a banner for the nations, and will assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth. Isaiah 11:12 The envy also of Ephraim will depart, and those who persecute Judah will be cut off. Ephraim won’t envy Judah, and Judah won’t persecute Ephraim. Isaiah 11:13 They will fly down on the shoulders of the Philistines on the west. Together they will plunder the children of the east. They will extend their power over Edom and Moab, and the children of Ammon will obey them. Isaiah 11:14 The LORD will utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea; and with his scorching wind he will wave his hand over the River, and will split it into seven streams, and cause men to march over in sandals. Isaiah 11:15 There will be a highway for the remnant that is left of his people from Assyria, like there was for Israel in the day that he came up out of the land of Egypt. Isaiah 11:16

title: Isaiah 12:1–6
context: A short hymn that closes Isaiah’s first major section. After the promise of the shoot from Jesse’s stump and the gathering of the remnant in chapter 11, the redeemed give thanks that God’s anger has turned to comfort. God himself is their salvation, strength, and song, and they draw water with joy from the wells of salvation. The song then turns outward, calling them to make his deeds known among the nations, and ends with Zion shouting because the Holy One of Israel is great in her midst.
text: Isaiah 12:1–6 Isaiah A short hymn that closes Isaiah’s first major section. After the promise of the shoot from Jesse’s stump and the gathering of the remnant in chapter 11, the redeemed give thanks that God’s anger has turned to comfort. God himself is their salvation, strength, and song, and they draw water with joy from the wells of salvation. The song then turns outward, calling them to make his deeds known among the nations, and ends with Zion shouting because the Holy One of Israel is great in her midst. In that day you will say, “I will give thanks to you, the LORD; for though you were angry with me, your anger has turned away and you comfort me. Isaiah 12:1 Behold, God is my salvation. I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD, the LORD, is my strength and song; and he has become my salvation.” Isaiah 12:2 Therefore with joy you will draw water out of the wells of salvation. Isaiah 12:3 In that day you will say, “Give thanks to the LORD! Call on his name! Declare his doings among the peoples! Proclaim that his name is exalted! Isaiah 12:4 Sing to the LORD, for he has done excellent things! Let this be known in all the earth! Isaiah 12:5 Cry aloud and shout, you inhabitant of Zion, for the Holy One of Israel is great among you!” Isaiah 12:6

title: Isaiah 13:1–16
context: Isaiah the son of Amoz sees the oracle concerning Babylon: a signal on a bare hill, the LORD of hosts mustering a host from a distant land, the day of the LORD near as destruction from the Almighty. Hands go feeble and hearts melt; the land is made a desolation and its sinners destroyed from it. Sun, moon, and stars go dark in the overthrow of proud Babylon; people become rarer than gold; fugitives flee like a hunted gazelle; the sword and the atrocities of ancient siege fall on the city.
text: Isaiah 13:1–16 Isaiah Isaiah the son of Amoz sees the oracle concerning Babylon: a signal on a bare hill, the LORD of hosts mustering a host from a distant land, the day of the LORD near as destruction from the Almighty. Hands go feeble and hearts melt; the land is made a desolation and its sinners destroyed from it. Sun, moon, and stars go dark in the overthrow of proud Babylon; people become rarer than gold; fugitives flee like a hunted gazelle; the sword and the atrocities of ancient siege fall on the city. The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw. Isaiah 13:1 Set up a banner on the bare mountain! Lift up your voice to them! Wave your hand, that they may go into the gates of the nobles. Isaiah 13:2 I have commanded my consecrated ones; yes, I have called my mighty men for my anger, even my proudly exulting ones. Isaiah 13:3 The noise of a multitude is in the mountains, as of a great people; the noise of an uproar of the kingdoms of the nations gathered together! The LORD of Armies is mustering the army for the battle. Isaiah 13:4 They come from a far country, from the uttermost part of heaven, even the LORD, and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land. Isaiah 13:5 Wail, for the LORD’s day is at hand! It will come as destruction from the Almighty. Isaiah 13:6 Therefore all hands will be feeble, and everyone’s heart will melt. Isaiah 13:7 They will be dismayed. Pangs and sorrows will seize them. They will be in pain like a woman in labor. They will look in amazement one at another. Their faces will be faces of flame. Isaiah 13:8 Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger; to make the land a desolation, and to destroy its sinners out of it. Isaiah 13:9 For the stars of the sky and its constellations will not give their light. The sun will be darkened in its going out, and the moon will not cause its light to shine. Isaiah 13:10 I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity. I will cause the arrogance of the proud to cease, and will humble the arrogance of the terrible. Isaiah 13:11 I will make people more rare than fine gold, even a person than the pure gold of Ophir. Isaiah 13:12 Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place in the LORD of Armies’ wrath, and in the day of his fierce anger. Isaiah 13:13 It will happen that like a hunted gazelle and like sheep that no one gathers, they will each turn to their own people, and will each flee to their own land. Isaiah 13:14 Everyone who is found will be thrust through. Everyone who is captured will fall by the sword. Isaiah 13:15 Their infants also will be dashed in pieces before their eyes. Their houses will be ransacked, and their wives raped. Isaiah 13:16

title: Isaiah 13:17–22
context: The LORD stirs up the Medes against Babylon: they have no regard for silver, and as for gold, they will not delight in it. Their bows slaughter the young men, and they have no pity on the fruit of the womb. Babylon, the glory of kingdoms and the pride of the Chaldeans, falls as Sodom and Gomorrah did when God overthrew them; the site is never inhabited, tents and shepherds gone, wild animals and howling creatures in the houses, ostriches and wild goats, hyenas in the fortresses, and jackals in the palaces. Her time is near to come, and her days will not be prolonged.
text: Isaiah 13:17–22 Isaiah The LORD stirs up the Medes against Babylon: they have no regard for silver, and as for gold, they will not delight in it. Their bows slaughter the young men, and they have no pity on the fruit of the womb. Babylon, the glory of kingdoms and the pride of the Chaldeans, falls as Sodom and Gomorrah did when God overthrew them; the site is never inhabited, tents and shepherds gone, wild animals and howling creatures in the houses, ostriches and wild goats, hyenas in the fortresses, and jackals in the palaces. Her time is near to come, and her days will not be prolonged. Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, who will not value silver, and as for gold, they will not delight in it. Isaiah 13:17 Their bows will dash the young men in pieces; and they shall have no pity on the fruit of the womb. Their eyes will not spare children. Isaiah 13:18 Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldeans’ pride, will be like when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. Isaiah 13:19 It will never be inhabited, neither will it be lived in from generation to generation. The Arabian will not pitch a tent there, neither will shepherds make their flocks lie down there. Isaiah 13:20 But wild animals of the desert will lie there, and their houses will be full of jackals. Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will frolic there. Isaiah 13:21 Hyenas will cry in their fortresses, and jackals in the pleasant palaces. Her time is near to come, and her days will not be prolonged. Isaiah 13:22

title: Isaiah 14:1–11
context: The LORD has compassion on Jacob and again chooses Israel, setting them in their own land; sojourners join them, and they possess their former captors in the LORD’s land. After rest from pain, turmoil, and hard service they take up a parable against the king of Babylon: the oppressor has ceased, the staff of the wicked is broken; the earth is quiet and the cedars of Lebanon rejoice; Sheol stirs the shades of dead kings to greet him, and his pomp is brought down to maggots and worms.
text: Isaiah 14:1–11 Isaiah The LORD has compassion on Jacob and again chooses Israel, setting them in their own land; sojourners join them, and they possess their former captors in the LORD’s land. After rest from pain, turmoil, and hard service they take up a parable against the king of Babylon: the oppressor has ceased, the staff of the wicked is broken; the earth is quiet and the cedars of Lebanon rejoice; Sheol stirs the shades of dead kings to greet him, and his pomp is brought down to maggots and worms. For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and set them in their own land. The foreigner will join himself with them, and they will unite with the house of Jacob. Isaiah 14:1 The peoples will take them, and bring them to their place. The house of Israel will possess them in the LORD’s land for servants and for handmaids. They will take as captives those whose captives they were; and they shall rule over their oppressors. Isaiah 14:2 It will happen in the day that the LORD will give you rest from your sorrow, from your trouble, and from the hard service in which you were made to serve, Isaiah 14:3 that you will take up this parable against the king of Babylon, and say, “How the oppressor has ceased! The golden city has ceased!” Isaiah 14:4 The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers, Isaiah 14:5 who struck the peoples in wrath with a continual stroke, who ruled the nations in anger, with a persecution that no one restrained. Isaiah 14:6 The whole earth is at rest, and is quiet. They break out in song. Isaiah 14:7 Yes, the cypress trees rejoice with you, with the cedars of Lebanon, saying, “Since you are humbled, no lumberjack has come up against us.” Isaiah 14:8 Sheol from beneath has moved for you to meet you at your coming. It stirs up the departed spirits for you, even all the rulers of the earth. It has raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations. Isaiah 14:9 They all will answer and ask you, “Have you also become as weak as we are? Have you become like us?” Isaiah 14:10 Your pomp is brought down to Sheol, with the sound of your stringed instruments. Maggots are spread out under you, and worms cover you. Isaiah 14:11

title: Isaiah 14:12–23
context: The taunt against the king of Babylon continues: the Day Star, son of Dawn, is fallen from heaven and cut down to the ground; he said in his heart he would ascend and make himself like the Most High! Yet he is brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit. Those who see him stare and ponder: Is this the man who made the earth to tremble? Kings of the nations sleep in their tombs; he is cast out like a loathed branch, denied burial for destroying his land and slaying his people. The LORD of hosts cuts off from Babylon name and remnant and sweeps it with the broom of destruction.
text: Isaiah 14:12–23 Isaiah The taunt against the king of Babylon continues: the Day Star, son of Dawn, is fallen from heaven and cut down to the ground; he said in his heart he would ascend and make himself like the Most High! Yet he is brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit. Those who see him stare and ponder: Is this the man who made the earth to tremble? Kings of the nations sleep in their tombs; he is cast out like a loathed branch, denied burial for destroying his land and slaying his people. The LORD of hosts cuts off from Babylon name and remnant and sweeps it with the broom of destruction. How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low! Isaiah 14:12 You said in your heart, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! Isaiah 14:13 I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” Isaiah 14:14 Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit. Isaiah 14:15 Those who see you will stare at you. They will ponder you, saying, “Is this the man who made the earth to tremble, who shook kingdoms, Isaiah 14:16 who made the world like a wilderness, and overthrew its cities, who didn’t release his prisoners to their home?” Isaiah 14:17 All the kings of the nations sleep in glory, everyone in his own house. Isaiah 14:18 But you are cast away from your tomb like an abominable branch, clothed with the slain who are thrust through with the sword, who go down to the stones of the pit; like a dead body trodden under foot. Isaiah 14:19 You will not join them in burial, because you have destroyed your land. You have killed your people. The offspring of evildoers will not be named forever. Isaiah 14:20 Prepare for slaughter of his children because of the iniquity of their fathers, that they not rise up and possess the earth, and fill the surface of the world with cities. Isaiah 14:21 “I will rise up against them,” says the LORD of Armies, “and cut off from Babylon name and remnant, and son and son’s son,” says the LORD. Isaiah 14:22 “I will also make it a possession for the porcupine, and pools of water. I will sweep it with the broom of destruction,” says the LORD of Armies. Isaiah 14:23

title: Isaiah 14:24–27
context: A short oracle sealed with an oath: what the LORD has planned will surely happen. Assyria will be broken on the LORD’s own mountains and its yoke lifted from Judah. The plan concerns the whole earth, and no one can turn back the hand stretched out to accomplish it.
text: Isaiah 14:24–27 Isaiah A short oracle sealed with an oath: what the LORD has planned will surely happen. Assyria will be broken on the LORD’s own mountains and its yoke lifted from Judah. The plan concerns the whole earth, and no one can turn back the hand stretched out to accomplish it. The LORD of Armies has sworn, saying, “Surely, as I have thought, so shall it happen; and as I have purposed, so shall it stand: Isaiah 14:24 that I will break the Assyrian in my land, and tread him under foot on my mountains. Then his yoke will leave them, and his burden leave their shoulders. Isaiah 14:25 This is the plan that is determined for the whole earth. This is the hand that is stretched out over all the nations. Isaiah 14:26 For the LORD of Armies has planned, and who can stop it? His hand is stretched out, and who can turn it back?” Isaiah 14:27

title: Isaiah 14:28–32
context: A short oracle dated to the year King Ahaz died. Philistia is warned not to celebrate the breaking of the rod that struck it, because a worse serpent will rise from that root. The poor of God’s people will graze in safety while Philistia’s root dies by famine and smoke comes from the north. When foreign envoys ask for news, the answer is that the LORD has founded Zion and his afflicted people will find refuge there.
text: Isaiah 14:28–32 Isaiah A short oracle dated to the year King Ahaz died. Philistia is warned not to celebrate the breaking of the rod that struck it, because a worse serpent will rise from that root. The poor of God’s people will graze in safety while Philistia’s root dies by famine and smoke comes from the north. When foreign envoys ask for news, the answer is that the LORD has founded Zion and his afflicted people will find refuge there. This burden was in the year that King Ahaz died. Isaiah 14:28 Don’t rejoice, O Philistia, all of you, because the rod that struck you is broken; for out of the serpent’s root an adder will emerge, and his fruit will be a fiery flying serpent. Isaiah 14:29 The firstborn of the poor will eat, and the needy will lie down in safety; and I will kill your root with famine, and your remnant will be killed. Isaiah 14:30 Howl, gate! Cry, city! You are melted away, Philistia, all of you; for smoke comes out of the north, and there is no straggler in his ranks. Isaiah 14:31 What will they answer the messengers of the nation? That the LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people will take refuge. Isaiah 14:32

title: Isaiah 15:1–9
context: Isaiah’s oracle against Moab, the first of a pair of chapters. In a single night Ar and Kir of Moab are laid waste. The people go up to their high places to weep; heads are shaved and beards cut off, and wailing fills the streets and rooftops from Heshbon and Elealeh to Jahaz. The prophet’s own heart cries out for Moab as refugees flee toward Zoar, the waters of Nimrim dry up, and the waters of Dimon run with blood, with a lion still waiting for those who escape.
text: Isaiah 15:1–9 Isaiah Isaiah’s oracle against Moab, the first of a pair of chapters. In a single night Ar and Kir of Moab are laid waste. The people go up to their high places to weep; heads are shaved and beards cut off, and wailing fills the streets and rooftops from Heshbon and Elealeh to Jahaz. The prophet’s own heart cries out for Moab as refugees flee toward Zoar, the waters of Nimrim dry up, and the waters of Dimon run with blood, with a lion still waiting for those who escape. The burden of Moab. For in a night, Ar of Moab is laid waste, and brought to nothing. For in a night Kir of Moab is laid waste, and brought to nothing. Isaiah 15:1 They have gone up to Bayith, and to Dibon, to the high places, to weep. Moab wails over Nebo and over Medeba. Baldness is on all of their heads. Every beard is cut off. Isaiah 15:2 In their streets, they clothe themselves in sackcloth. In their streets and on their housetops, everyone wails, weeping abundantly. Isaiah 15:3 Heshbon cries out with Elealeh. Their voice is heard even to Jahaz. Therefore the armed men of Moab cry aloud. Their souls tremble within them. Isaiah 15:4 My heart cries out for Moab! Her nobles flee to Zoar, to Eglath Shelishiyah; for they go up by the ascent of Luhith with weeping; for on the way to Horonaim, they raise up a cry of destruction. Isaiah 15:5 For the waters of Nimrim will be desolate; for the grass has withered away, the tender grass fails, there is no green thing. Isaiah 15:6 Therefore they will carry away the abundance they have gotten, and that which they have stored up, over the brook of the willows. Isaiah 15:7 For the cry has gone around the borders of Moab, its wailing to Eglaim, and its wailing to Beer Elim. Isaiah 15:8 For the waters of Dimon are full of blood; for I will bring yet more on Dimon, a lion on those of Moab who escape, and on the remnant of the land. Isaiah 15:9

title: Isaiah 16:1–14
context: The Moab oracle continues from chapter 15. Moab’s refugees are told to send tribute to Zion and to seek shelter there, and Judah is urged to hide the fugitives. A throne established in loving kindness in David’s tent stands over against Moab’s pride, which Isaiah says has emptied its boasting. The prophet weeps for the ruined vineyards of Heshbon and Sibmah, and the chapter closes with a dated sentence: within three years Moab’s glory will be brought low and only a small, feeble remnant left.
text: Isaiah 16:1–14 Isaiah The Moab oracle continues from chapter 15. Moab’s refugees are told to send tribute to Zion and to seek shelter there, and Judah is urged to hide the fugitives. A throne established in loving kindness in David’s tent stands over against Moab’s pride, which Isaiah says has emptied its boasting. The prophet weeps for the ruined vineyards of Heshbon and Sibmah, and the chapter closes with a dated sentence: within three years Moab’s glory will be brought low and only a small, feeble remnant left. Send the lambs for the ruler of the land from Selah to the wilderness, to the mountain of the daughter of Zion. Isaiah 16:1 For it will be that as wandering birds, as a scattered nest, so will the daughters of Moab be at the fords of the Arnon. Isaiah 16:2 Give counsel! Execute justice! Make your shade like the night in the middle of the noonday! Hide the outcasts! Don’t betray the fugitive! Isaiah 16:3 Let my outcasts dwell with you! As for Moab, be a hiding place for him from the face of the destroyer. For the extortionist is brought to nothing. Destruction ceases. The oppressors are consumed out of the land. Isaiah 16:4 A throne will be established in loving kindness. One will sit on it in truth, in the tent of David, judging, seeking justice, and swift to do righteousness. Isaiah 16:5 We have heard of the pride of Moab, that he is very proud; even of his arrogance, his pride, and his wrath. His boastings are nothing. Isaiah 16:6 Therefore Moab will wail for Moab. Everyone will wail. You will mourn for the raisin cakes of Kir Hareseth, utterly stricken. Isaiah 16:7 For the fields of Heshbon languish with the vine of Sibmah. The lords of the nations have broken down its choice branches, which reached even to Jazer, which wandered into the wilderness. Its shoots were spread abroad. They passed over the sea. Isaiah 16:8 Therefore I will weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah. I will water you with my tears, Heshbon, and Elealeh: for on your summer fruits and on your harvest the battle shout has fallen. Isaiah 16:9 Gladness is taken away, and joy out of the fruitful field; and in the vineyards there will be no singing, neither joyful noise. Nobody will tread out wine in the presses. I have made the shouting stop. Isaiah 16:10 Therefore my heart sounds like a harp for Moab, and my inward parts for Kir Heres. Isaiah 16:11 It will happen that when Moab presents himself, when he wearies himself on the high place, and comes to his sanctuary to pray, that he will not prevail. Isaiah 16:12 This is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Moab in time past. Isaiah 16:13 But now the LORD has spoken, saying, “Within three years, as a worker bound by contract would count them, the glory of Moab shall be brought into contempt, with all his great multitude; and the remnant will be very small and feeble.” Isaiah 16:14

title: Isaiah 17:1–14
context: An oracle against Damascus and its ally Ephraim, the northern kingdom, which had joined Syria against Judah. Both will be stripped bare, leaving only a few gleanings like olives left on a beaten tree. In that day people will look to their Maker instead of their altars. The chapter ends with roaring nations scattered overnight by God’s rebuke.
text: Isaiah 17:1–14 Isaiah An oracle against Damascus and its ally Ephraim, the northern kingdom, which had joined Syria against Judah. Both will be stripped bare, leaving only a few gleanings like olives left on a beaten tree. In that day people will look to their Maker instead of their altars. The chapter ends with roaring nations scattered overnight by God’s rebuke. The burden of Damascus. “Behold, Damascus is taken away from being a city, and it will be a ruinous heap. Isaiah 17:1 The cities of Aroer are forsaken. They will be for flocks, which shall lie down, and no one shall make them afraid. Isaiah 17:2 The fortress shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus, and the remnant of Syria. They will be as the glory of the children of Israel,” says the LORD of Armies. Isaiah 17:3 “It will happen in that day that the glory of Jacob will be made thin, and the fatness of his flesh will become lean. Isaiah 17:4 It will be like when the harvester gathers the wheat, and his arm reaps the grain. Yes, it will be like when one gleans grain in the valley of Rephaim. Isaiah 17:5 Yet gleanings will be left there, like the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives in the top of the uppermost bough, four or five in the outermost branches of a fruitful tree,” says the LORD, the God of Israel. Isaiah 17:6 In that day, people will look to their Maker, and their eyes will have respect for the Holy One of Israel. Isaiah 17:7 They will not look to the altars, the work of their hands; neither shall they respect that which their fingers have made, either the Asherah poles or the incense altars. Isaiah 17:8 In that day, their strong cities will be like the forsaken places in the woods and on the mountain top, which were forsaken from before the children of Israel; and it will be a desolation. Isaiah 17:9 For you have forgotten the God of your salvation, and have not remembered the rock of your strength. Therefore you plant pleasant plants, and set out foreign seedlings. Isaiah 17:10 In the day of your planting, you hedge it in. In the morning, you make your seed blossom, but the harvest flees away in the day of grief and of desperate sorrow. Isaiah 17:11 Ah, the uproar of many peoples who roar like the roaring of the seas; and the rushing of nations that rush like the rushing of mighty waters! Isaiah 17:12 The nations will rush like the rushing of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far off, and will be chased like the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like the whirling dust before the storm. Isaiah 17:13 At evening, behold, terror! Before the morning, they are no more. This is the portion of those who plunder us, and the lot of those who rob us. Isaiah 17:14

title: Isaiah 18:1–7
context: Isaiah addresses Cush, the land beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, whose envoys travel the Nile in papyrus boats. The LORD watches calmly from his dwelling and will prune the invader before the harvest. In the end this distant, feared nation will bring a gift to the LORD on Mount Zion.
text: Isaiah 18:1–7 Isaiah Isaiah addresses Cush, the land beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, whose envoys travel the Nile in papyrus boats. The LORD watches calmly from his dwelling and will prune the invader before the harvest. In the end this distant, feared nation will bring a gift to the LORD on Mount Zion. Ah, the land of the rustling of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia; Isaiah 18:1 that sends ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of papyrus on the waters, saying, “Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people awesome from their beginning onward, a nation that measures out and treads down, whose land the rivers divide!” Isaiah 18:2 All you inhabitants of the world, and you dwellers on the earth, when a banner is lifted up on the mountains, look! When the trumpet is blown, listen! Isaiah 18:3 For the LORD said to me, “I will be still, and I will see in my dwelling place, like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” Isaiah 18:4 For before the harvest, when the blossom is over, and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he will cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and he will cut down and take away the spreading branches. Isaiah 18:5 They will be left together for the ravenous birds of the mountains, and for the animals of the earth. The ravenous birds will eat them in the summer, and all the animals of the earth will eat them in the winter. Isaiah 18:6 In that time, a present will be brought to the LORD of Armies from a people tall and smooth, even from a people awesome from their beginning onward, a nation that measures out and treads down, whose land the rivers divide, to the place of the name of the LORD of Armies, Mount Zion. Isaiah 18:7

title: Isaiah 19:1–15
context: The LORD rides a swift cloud into Egypt, and its idols tremble. Civil war, failed counsel, a dried-up Nile, and collapsing industries follow. The famous wise men of Zoan and Memphis are exposed as fools. Judah, tempted to trust Egypt, learns how fragile that refuge is.
text: Isaiah 19:1–15 Isaiah The LORD rides a swift cloud into Egypt, and its idols tremble. Civil war, failed counsel, a dried-up Nile, and collapsing industries follow. The famous wise men of Zoan and Memphis are exposed as fools. Judah, tempted to trust Egypt, learns how fragile that refuge is. The burden of Egypt. “Behold, the LORD rides on a swift cloud, and comes to Egypt. The idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence; and the heart of Egypt will melt within it. Isaiah 19:1 I will stir up the Egyptians against the Egyptians, and they will fight everyone against his brother, and everyone against his neighbor; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom. Isaiah 19:2 The spirit of the Egyptians will fail within them. I will destroy their counsel. They will seek the idols, the charmers, those who have familiar spirits, and the wizards. Isaiah 19:3 I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a cruel lord. A fierce king will rule over them,” says the Lord, GOD of Armies. Isaiah 19:4 The waters will fail from the sea, and the river will be wasted and become dry. Isaiah 19:5 The rivers will become foul. The streams of Egypt will be diminished and dried up. The reeds and flags will wither away. Isaiah 19:6 The meadows by the Nile, by the brink of the Nile, and all the sown fields of the Nile, will become dry, be driven away, and be no more. Isaiah 19:7 The fishermen will lament, and all those who fish in the Nile will mourn, and those who spread nets on the waters will languish. Isaiah 19:8 Moreover those who work in combed flax, and those who weave white cloth, will be confounded. Isaiah 19:9 The pillars will be broken in pieces. All those who work for hire will be grieved in soul. Isaiah 19:10 The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish. The counsel of the wisest counselors of Pharaoh has become stupid. How do you say to Pharaoh, “I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings”? Isaiah 19:11 Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you now; and let them know what the LORD of Armies has purposed concerning Egypt. Isaiah 19:12 The princes of Zoan have become fools. The princes of Memphis are deceived. They have caused Egypt to go astray, those who are the cornerstone of her tribes. Isaiah 19:13 The LORD has mixed a spirit of perverseness in the middle of her; and they have caused Egypt to go astray in all of its works, like a drunken man staggers in his vomit. Isaiah 19:14 Neither shall there be any work for Egypt, which head or tail, palm branch or rush, may do. Isaiah 19:15

title: Isaiah 19:16–25
context: The oracle against Egypt turns into one of Isaiah’s most astonishing promises. Egypt will fear the LORD, then build an altar to him, cry to him, and be healed. A highway will link Egypt and Assyria in worship, and God will call them “my people” and “the work of my hands” alongside Israel his inheritance.
text: Isaiah 19:16–25 Isaiah The oracle against Egypt turns into one of Isaiah’s most astonishing promises. Egypt will fear the LORD, then build an altar to him, cry to him, and be healed. A highway will link Egypt and Assyria in worship, and God will call them “my people” and “the work of my hands” alongside Israel his inheritance. In that day the Egyptians will be like women. They will tremble and fear because of the shaking of the LORD of Armies’s hand, which he shakes over them. Isaiah 19:16 The land of Judah will become a terror to Egypt. Everyone to whom mention is made of it will be afraid, because of the plans of the LORD of Armies, which he determines against it. Isaiah 19:17 In that day, there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan, and swear to the LORD of Armies. One will be called “The city of destruction.” Isaiah 19:18 In that day, there will be an altar to the LORD in the middle of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border. Isaiah 19:19 It will be for a sign and for a witness to the LORD of Armies in the land of Egypt; for they will cry to the LORD because of oppressors, and he will send them a savior and a defender, and he will deliver them. Isaiah 19:20 The LORD will be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day. Yes, they will worship with sacrifice and offering, and will vow a vow to the LORD, and will perform it. Isaiah 19:21 The LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing. They will return to the LORD, and he will be entreated by them, and will heal them. Isaiah 19:22 In that day there will be a highway out of Egypt to Assyria, and the Assyrian shall come into Egypt, and the Egyptian into Assyria; and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians. Isaiah 19:23 In that day, Israel will be the third with Egypt and with Assyria, a blessing within the earth; Isaiah 19:24 because the LORD of Armies has blessed them, saying, “Blessed be Egypt my people, Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.” Isaiah 19:25

title: Isaiah 2:1–5
context: After Zion’s dross and a restored name, Isaiah sees a word concerning Judah and Jerusalem: in the latter days the mountain of the Lord’s house is established above the hills, and nations flow to it. Peoples say, Come, let’s go up, and he will teach us of his ways. Law goes out from Zion; He judges; swords become plowshares. House of Jacob is told to walk in that light.
text: Isaiah 2:1–5 Isaiah After Zion’s dross and a restored name, Isaiah sees a word concerning Judah and Jerusalem: in the latter days the mountain of the Lord’s house is established above the hills, and nations flow to it. Peoples say, Come, let’s go up, and he will teach us of his ways. Law goes out from Zion; He judges; swords become plowshares. House of Jacob is told to walk in that light. This is what Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem. Isaiah 2:1 It shall happen in the latter days, that the mountain of the LORD’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it. Isaiah 2:2 Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For the law shall go out of Zion, and the LORD’s word from Jerusalem. Isaiah 2:3 He will judge between the nations, and will decide concerning many peoples. They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more. Isaiah 2:4 House of Jacob, come, and let’s walk in the light of the LORD. Isaiah 2:5

title: Isaiah 2:6–22
context: After nations streaming to the word, the house of Jacob is full of eastern rites, Philistine fortune-tellers, silver, horses, and handmade idols. Man is brought low. Hide in the rock from the Lord’s terror. A day of the Lord of hosts against all that is proud—cedars, hills, towers, ships of Tarshish. The Lord alone is exalted; idols pass away; silver gods go to moles and bats. Stop trusting in man, whose breath is in his nostrils is breath.
text: Isaiah 2:6–22 Isaiah After nations streaming to the word, the house of Jacob is full of eastern rites, Philistine fortune-tellers, silver, horses, and handmade idols. Man is brought low. Hide in the rock from the Lord’s terror. A day of the Lord of hosts against all that is proud—cedars, hills, towers, ships of Tarshish. The Lord alone is exalted; idols pass away; silver gods go to moles and bats. Stop trusting in man, whose breath is in his nostrils is breath. For you have forsaken your people, the house of Jacob, because they are filled from the east, with those who practice divination like the Philistines, and they clasp hands with the children of foreigners. Isaiah 2:6 Their land is full of silver and gold, neither is there any end of their treasures. Their land also is full of horses, neither is there any end of their chariots. Isaiah 2:7 Their land also is full of idols. They worship the work of their own hands, that which their own fingers have made. Isaiah 2:8 Man is brought low, and mankind is humbled; therefore don’t forgive them. Isaiah 2:9 Enter into the rock, and hide in the dust, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the glory of his majesty. Isaiah 2:10 The lofty looks of man will be brought low, the arrogance of men will be bowed down, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day. Isaiah 2:11 For there will be a day of the LORD of Armies for all that is proud and arrogant, and for all that is lifted up, and it shall be brought low— Isaiah 2:12 for all the cedars of Lebanon, that are high and lifted up, for all the oaks of Bashan, Isaiah 2:13 for all the high mountains, for all the hills that are lifted up, Isaiah 2:14 for every lofty tower, for every fortified wall, Isaiah 2:15 for all the ships of Tarshish, and for all pleasant imagery. Isaiah 2:16 The loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the arrogance of men shall be brought low; and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day. Isaiah 2:17 The idols shall utterly pass away. Isaiah 2:18 Men shall go into the caves of the rocks, and into the holes of the earth, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the glory of his majesty, when he arises to shake the earth mightily. Isaiah 2:19 In that day, men shall cast away their idols of silver and their idols of gold, which have been made for themselves to worship, to the moles and to the bats, Isaiah 2:20 to go into the caverns of the rocks, and into the clefts of the ragged rocks, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the glory of his majesty, when he arises to shake the earth mightily. Isaiah 2:21 Stop trusting in man, whose breath is in his nostrils; for of what account is he? Isaiah 2:22

title: Isaiah 20:1–6
context: When Assyria captures Ashdod (around 711 BC), Isaiah is told to walk stripped and barefoot for three years. The sign acts out the fate of Egypt and Cush, whose captives will be led away the same way. Those who trusted them for rescue will be left asking where to turn.
text: Isaiah 20:1–6 Isaiah When Assyria captures Ashdod (around 711 BC), Isaiah is told to walk stripped and barefoot for three years. The sign acts out the fate of Egypt and Cush, whose captives will be led away the same way. Those who trusted them for rescue will be left asking where to turn. In the year that Tartan came to Ashdod, when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him, and he fought against Ashdod and took it; Isaiah 20:1 at that time the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, “Go, and loosen the sackcloth from off your waist, and take your sandals from off your feet.” He did so, walking naked and barefoot. Isaiah 20:2 The LORD said, “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and a wonder concerning Egypt and concerning Ethiopia, Isaiah 20:3 so the king of Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot, and with buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt. Isaiah 20:4 They will be dismayed and confounded, because of Ethiopia their expectation, and of Egypt their glory. Isaiah 20:5 The inhabitants of this coast land will say in that day, ‘Behold, this is our expectation, where we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria. And we, how will we escape?’” Isaiah 20:6

title: Isaiah 21:1–10
context: A dark oracle against Babylon, called ‘the wilderness of the sea.’ The vision is so harsh that the prophet is doubled over in anguish. Elam and Media attack while Babylon’s leaders feast, and a watchman finally reports: ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon!’ Revelation 14:8 and 18:2 echo the cry.
text: Isaiah 21:1–10 Isaiah A dark oracle against Babylon, called ‘the wilderness of the sea.’ The vision is so harsh that the prophet is doubled over in anguish. Elam and Media attack while Babylon’s leaders feast, and a watchman finally reports: ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon!’ Revelation 14:8 and 18:2 echo the cry. The burden of the wilderness of the sea. As whirlwinds in the South sweep through, it comes from the wilderness, from an awesome land. Isaiah 21:1 A grievous vision is declared to me. The treacherous man deals treacherously, and the destroyer destroys. Go up, Elam; attack! I have stopped all of Media’s sighing. Isaiah 21:2 Therefore my thighs are filled with anguish. Pains have seized me, like the pains of a woman in labor. I am in so much pain that I can’t hear. I am so dismayed that I can’t see. Isaiah 21:3 My heart flutters. Horror has frightened me. The twilight that I desired has been turned into trembling for me. Isaiah 21:4 They prepare the table. They set the watch. They eat. They drink. Rise up, you princes, oil the shield! Isaiah 21:5 For the Lord said to me, “Go, set a watchman. Let him declare what he sees. Isaiah 21:6 When he sees a troop, horsemen in pairs, a troop of donkeys, a troop of camels, he shall listen diligently with great attentiveness.” Isaiah 21:7 He cried like a lion: “Lord, I stand continually on the watchtower in the daytime, and every night I stay at my post. Isaiah 21:8 Behold, here comes a troop of men, horsemen in pairs.” He answered, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the engraved images of her gods are broken to the ground. Isaiah 21:9 You are my threshing, and the grain of my floor!” That which I have heard from the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, I have declared to you. Isaiah 21:10

title: Isaiah 21:11–17
context: Two short oracles. From Edom someone calls to the watchman, asking how much of the night is left; the answer is that morning comes, but so does night, so keep asking. Then Arabian caravans flee the sword, and within a year the glory of Kedar will fade.
text: Isaiah 21:11–17 Isaiah Two short oracles. From Edom someone calls to the watchman, asking how much of the night is left; the answer is that morning comes, but so does night, so keep asking. Then Arabian caravans flee the sword, and within a year the glory of Kedar will fade. The burden of Dumah. One calls to me out of Seir, “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” Isaiah 21:11 The watchman said, “The morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire. Come back again.” Isaiah 21:12 The burden on Arabia. You will lodge in the thickets in Arabia, you caravans of Dedanites. Isaiah 21:13 They brought water to him who was thirsty. The inhabitants of the land of Tema met the fugitives with their bread. Isaiah 21:14 For they fled away from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the heat of battle. Isaiah 21:15 For the Lord said to me, “Within a year, as a worker bound by contract would count it, all the glory of Kedar will fail, Isaiah 21:16 and the residue of the number of the archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, will be few; for the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken it.” Isaiah 21:17

title: Isaiah 22:1–14
context: While the city celebrates on its rooftops, Isaiah weeps. Jerusalem has prepared for siege—checking weapons, repairing walls, storing water—but never looked to the God who planned its history. When he called for mourning, they feasted: “Let’s eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die.”
text: Isaiah 22:1–14 Isaiah While the city celebrates on its rooftops, Isaiah weeps. Jerusalem has prepared for siege—checking weapons, repairing walls, storing water—but never looked to the God who planned its history. When he called for mourning, they feasted: “Let’s eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die.” The burden of the valley of vision. What ails you now, that you have all gone up to the housetops? Isaiah 22:1 You that are full of shouting, a tumultuous city, a joyous town, your slain are not slain with the sword, neither are they dead in battle. Isaiah 22:2 All your rulers fled away together. They were bound by the archers. All who were found by you were bound together. They fled far away. Isaiah 22:3 Therefore I said, “Look away from me. I will weep bitterly. Don’t labor to comfort me for the destruction of the daughter of my people. Isaiah 22:4 For it is a day of confusion, and of treading down, and of perplexity from the Lord, GOD of Armies, in the valley of vision, a breaking down of the walls, and a crying to the mountains.” Isaiah 22:5 Elam carried his quiver, with chariots of men and horsemen; and Kir uncovered the shield. Isaiah 22:6 Your choicest valleys were full of chariots, and the horsemen set themselves in array at the gate. Isaiah 22:7 He took away the covering of Judah; and you looked in that day to the armor in the house of the forest. Isaiah 22:8 You saw the breaches of David’s city, that they were many; and you gathered together the waters of the lower pool. Isaiah 22:9 You counted the houses of Jerusalem, and you broke down the houses to fortify the wall. Isaiah 22:10 You also made a reservoir between the two walls for the water of the old pool. But you didn’t look to him who had done this, neither did you have respect for him who planned it long ago. Isaiah 22:11 In that day, the Lord, GOD of Armies, called to weeping, to mourning, to baldness, and to dressing in sackcloth; Isaiah 22:12 and behold, there is joy and gladness, killing cattle and killing sheep, eating meat and drinking wine: “Let’s eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die.” Isaiah 22:13 The LORD of Armies revealed himself in my ears, “Surely this iniquity will not be forgiven you until you die,” says the Lord, GOD of Armies. Isaiah 22:14

title: Isaiah 22:15–25
context: In Hezekiah’s court, the steward Shebna is building himself a showy tomb while Jerusalem faces danger. Isaiah announces his removal and the promotion of Eliakim, who will receive the key of David’s house and be a father to the city. Even Eliakim, fastened like a peg in a firm place, will eventually give way under the weight his family hangs on him. Revelation 3:7 borrows the image of the key for Christ.
text: Isaiah 22:15–25 Isaiah In Hezekiah’s court, the steward Shebna is building himself a showy tomb while Jerusalem faces danger. Isaiah announces his removal and the promotion of Eliakim, who will receive the key of David’s house and be a father to the city. Even Eliakim, fastened like a peg in a firm place, will eventually give way under the weight his family hangs on him. Revelation 3:7 borrows the image of the key for Christ. The Lord, GOD of Armies says, “Go, get yourself to this treasurer, even to Shebna, who is over the house, and say, Isaiah 22:15 ‘What are you doing here? Who has you here, that you have dug out a tomb here?’ Cutting himself out a tomb on high, chiseling a habitation for himself in the rock!” Isaiah 22:16 Behold, the LORD will overcome you and hurl you away violently. Yes, he will grasp you firmly. Isaiah 22:17 He will surely wind you around and around, and throw you like a ball into a large country. There you will die, and there the chariots of your glory will be, you disgrace of your lord’s house. Isaiah 22:18 I will thrust you from your office. You will be pulled down from your station. Isaiah 22:19 It will happen in that day that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, Isaiah 22:20 and I will clothe him with your robe, and strengthen him with your belt. I will commit your government into his hand; and he will be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah. Isaiah 22:21 I will lay the key of David’s house on his shoulder.
