John 8:27 Jesus therefore said to them, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and I do nothing of myself, but as my Father taught me, I say these things. John 8:28 He who sent me is with me. The Father hasn’t left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him.” John 8:29 As he spoke these things, many believed in him. John 8:30

title: John 8:31–47
context: Jesus turns to Jews who had believed him, If you remain in my word, then you are truly disciples; you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free. They protest Abrahamic freedom. He answers that everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin; a bondservant doesn’t live in the house forever, but a son does; if therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed. Offspring of Abraham still seek to kill him because his word finds no place in them. Abraham’s children would do Abraham’s works; instead they do their father’s. They claim God as Father; he says if God were their Father they would love him. They cannot bear to hear his word because they are of their father the devil, a murderer and liar. Whoever is of God hears God’s words; the reason they do not hear is that they are not of God.
text: John 8:31–47 John Jesus turns to Jews who had believed him, If you remain in my word, then you are truly disciples; you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free. They protest Abrahamic freedom. He answers that everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin; a bondservant doesn’t live in the house forever, but a son does; if therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed. Offspring of Abraham still seek to kill him because his word finds no place in them. Abraham’s children would do Abraham’s works; instead they do their father’s. They claim God as Father; he says if God were their Father they would love him. They cannot bear to hear his word because they are of their father the devil, a murderer and liar. Whoever is of God hears God’s words; the reason they do not hear is that they are not of God. Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. John 8:31 You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” John 8:32 They answered him, “We are Abraham’s offspring, and have never been in bondage to anyone. How do you say, ‘You will be made free’?” John 8:33 Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin. John 8:34 A bondservant doesn’t live in the house forever. A son remains forever. John 8:35 If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed. John 8:36 I know that you are Abraham’s offspring, yet you seek to kill me, because my word finds no place in you. John 8:37 I say the things which I have seen with my Father; and you also do the things which you have seen with your father.” John 8:38 They answered him, “Our father is Abraham.” Jesus said to them, “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham. John 8:39 But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth which I heard from God. Abraham didn’t do this. John 8:40 You do the works of your father.” They said to him, “We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father, God.” John 8:41 Therefore Jesus said to them, “If God were your father, you would love me, for I came out and have come from God. For I haven’t come of myself, but he sent me. John 8:42 Why don’t you understand my speech? Because you can’t hear my word. John 8:43 You are of your father the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and doesn’t stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks on his own; for he is a liar, and the father of lies. John 8:44 But because I tell the truth, you don’t believe me. John 8:45 Which of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me? John 8:46 He who is of God hears the words of God. For this cause you don’t hear, because you are not of God.” John 8:47

title: John 8:48–59
context: The dispute turns to insult and then to glory. They call Jesus a Samaritan and say he has a demon. He denies the demon, honors the Father, and does not seek his own glory. If anyone keeps his word, he will never see death. They hear bodily immortality, invoke Abraham and the prophets who died, and ask who he makes himself. He answers that the Father glorifies him; they have not known God; Abraham rejoiced to see his day. They scoff that he is not yet fifty. He answers with the divine present: before Abraham came into existence, I AM. They pick up stones; he hides himself and goes out of the temple.
text: John 8:48–59 John The dispute turns to insult and then to glory. They call Jesus a Samaritan and say he has a demon. He denies the demon, honors the Father, and does not seek his own glory. If anyone keeps his word, he will never see death. They hear bodily immortality, invoke Abraham and the prophets who died, and ask who he makes himself. He answers that the Father glorifies him; they have not known God; Abraham rejoiced to see his day. They scoff that he is not yet fifty. He answers with the divine present: before Abraham came into existence, I AM. They pick up stones; he hides himself and goes out of the temple. Then the Jews answered him, “Don’t we say well that you are a Samaritan, and have a demon?” John 8:48 Jesus answered, “I don’t have a demon, but I honor my Father and you dishonor me. John 8:49 But I don’t seek my own glory. There is one who seeks and judges. John 8:50 Most certainly, I tell you, if a person keeps my word, he will never see death.” John 8:51 Then the Jews said to him, “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, as did the prophets; and you say, ‘If a man keeps my word, he will never taste of death.’ John 8:52 Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? The prophets died. Who do you make yourself out to be?” John 8:53 Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say that he is our God. John 8:54 You have not known him, but I know him. If I said, ‘I don’t know him,’ I would be like you, a liar. But I know him and keep his word. John 8:55 Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day. He saw it and was glad.” John 8:56 The Jews therefore said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old! Have you seen Abraham?” John 8:57 Jesus said to them, “Most certainly, I tell you, before Abraham came into existence, I AM. ” John 8:58 Therefore they took up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple, having gone through the middle of them, and so passed by. John 8:59

title: John 9:1–12
context: As he passes by, Jesus sees a man blind from birth. The disciples ask who sinned. Jesus refuses the dilemma: it was not that this man or his parents sinned, but that the works of God might be revealed in him. Night is coming; while he is in the world he is the light. He makes mud with spit, anoints the man’s eyes, and sends him to Siloam (Sent). The man goes, washes, and comes seeing. Neighbors dispute his identity; he testifies that he is the man, and that he does not know where Jesus is.
text: John 9:1–12 John As he passes by, Jesus sees a man blind from birth. The disciples ask who sinned. Jesus refuses the dilemma: it was not that this man or his parents sinned, but that the works of God might be revealed in him. Night is coming; while he is in the world he is the light. He makes mud with spit, anoints the man’s eyes, and sends him to Siloam (Sent). The man goes, washes, and comes seeing. Neighbors dispute his identity; he testifies that he is the man, and that he does not know where Jesus is. As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. John 9:1 His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” John 9:2 Jesus answered, “This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents, but that the works of God might be revealed in him. John 9:3 I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. The night is coming, when no one can work. John 9:4 While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” John 9:5 When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, anointed the blind man’s eyes with the mud, John 9:6 and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So he went away, washed, and came back seeing. John 9:7 Therefore the neighbors and those who saw that he was blind before said, “Isn’t this he who sat and begged?” John 9:8 Others were saying, “It is he.” Still others were saying, “He looks like him.” He said, “I am he.” John 9:9 They therefore were asking him, “How were your eyes opened?” John 9:10 He answered, “A man called Jesus made mud, anointed my eyes, and said to me, ‘Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.’ So I went away and washed, and I received sight.” John 9:11 Then they asked him, “Where is he?” He said, “I don’t know.” John 9:12

title: John 9:13–34
context: Neighbors bring the healed man to the Pharisees. It was Sabbath when Jesus made the mud. Division follows: this man is not from God, because he doesn’t keep the Sabbath—or how can a sinner do such signs? The man says he is a prophet. Leaders will not believe he had been blind until they grill the parents, who fear synagogue-expulsion and defer: he is of age. A second interrogation demands, Give glory to God; we know this man is a sinner. One thing I know: I was blind, now I see. They revile him; he reasons from the unprecedented sign; they say he was born in sins, and cast him out.
text: John 9:13–34 John Neighbors bring the healed man to the Pharisees. It was Sabbath when Jesus made the mud. Division follows: this man is not from God, because he doesn’t keep the Sabbath—or how can a sinner do such signs? The man says he is a prophet. Leaders will not believe he had been blind until they grill the parents, who fear synagogue-expulsion and defer: he is of age. A second interrogation demands, Give glory to God; we know this man is a sinner. One thing I know: I was blind, now I see. They revile him; he reasons from the unprecedented sign; they say he was born in sins, and cast him out. They brought him who had been blind to the Pharisees. John 9:13 It was a Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. John 9:14 Again therefore the Pharisees also asked him how he received his sight. He said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, I washed, and I see.” John 9:15 Some therefore of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, because he doesn’t keep the Sabbath.” Others said, “How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?” So there was division among them. John 9:16 Therefore they asked the blind man again, “What do you say about him, because he opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.” John 9:17 The Jews therefore didn’t believe concerning him, that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of him who had received his sight, John 9:18 and asked them, “Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?” John 9:19 His parents answered them, “We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind; John 9:20 but how he now sees, we don’t know; or who opened his eyes, we don’t know. He is of age. Ask him. He will speak for himself.” John 9:21 His parents said these things because they feared the Jews; for the Jews had already agreed that if any man would confess him as Christ, he would be put out of the synagogue. John 9:22 Therefore his parents said, “He is of age. Ask him.” John 9:23 So they called the man who was blind a second time, and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.” John 9:24 He therefore answered, “I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.” John 9:25 They said to him again, “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” John 9:26 He answered them, “I told you already, and you didn’t listen. Why do you want to hear it again? You don’t also want to become his disciples, do you?” John 9:27 They insulted him and said, “You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. John 9:28 We know that God has spoken to Moses. But as for this man, we don’t know where he comes from.” John 9:29 The man answered them, “How amazing! You don’t know where he comes from, yet he opened my eyes. John 9:30 We know that God doesn’t listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, he listens to him. John 9:31 Since the world began it has never been heard of that anyone opened the eyes of someone born blind. John 9:32 If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.” John 9:33 They answered him, “You were altogether born in sins, and do you teach us?” Then they threw him out. John 9:34

title: John 9:35–41
context: After the healed man is thrown out of the synagogue, Jesus seeks him out and reveals himself as the Son of Man, and the man believes and worships. Jesus then declares that he came so the blind might see and those who claim to see might become blind. The Pharisees’ question, ‘Are we also blind?’, exposes the sin of refusing light while claiming to have it.
text: John 9:35–41 John After the healed man is thrown out of the synagogue, Jesus seeks him out and reveals himself as the Son of Man, and the man believes and worships. Jesus then declares that he came so the blind might see and those who claim to see might become blind. The Pharisees’ question, ‘Are we also blind?’, exposes the sin of refusing light while claiming to have it. Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and finding him, he said, “Do you believe in the Son of God?” John 9:35 He answered, “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” John 9:36 Jesus said to him, “You have both seen him, and it is he who speaks with you.” John 9:37 He said, “Lord, I believe!” and he worshiped him. John 9:38 Jesus said, “I came into this world for judgment, that those who don’t see may see; and that those who see may become blind.” John 9:39 Those of the Pharisees who were with him heard these things, and said to him, “Are we also blind?” John 9:40 Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, ‘We see.’ Therefore your sin remains. John 9:41

title: Matthew 1:1–17
context: Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy of Jesus Christ—tracing the Messiah from Abraham and David through exile to Joseph and Mary—so that readers see promise fulfilled and a Savior who belongs to Israel’s story.
text: Matthew 1:1–17 Matthew Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy of Jesus Christ—tracing the Messiah from Abraham and David through exile to Joseph and Mary—so that readers see promise fulfilled and a Savior who belongs to Israel’s story. The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Matthew 1:1 Abraham became the father of Isaac. Isaac became the father of Jacob. Jacob became the father of Judah and his brothers. Matthew 1:2 Judah became the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar. Perez became the father of Hezron. Hezron became the father of Ram. Matthew 1:3 Ram became the father of Amminadab. Amminadab became the father of Nahshon. Nahshon became the father of Salmon. Matthew 1:4 Salmon became the father of Boaz by Rahab. Boaz became the father of Obed by Ruth. Obed became the father of Jesse. Matthew 1:5 Jesse became the father of King David. David the king became the father of Solomon by her who had been Uriah’s wife. Matthew 1:6 Solomon became the father of Rehoboam. Rehoboam became the father of Abijah. Abijah became the father of Asa. Matthew 1:7 Asa became the father of Jehoshaphat. Jehoshaphat became the father of Joram. Joram became the father of Uzziah. Matthew 1:8 Uzziah became the father of Jotham. Jotham became the father of Ahaz. Ahaz became the father of Hezekiah. Matthew 1:9 Hezekiah became the father of Manasseh. Manasseh became the father of Amon. Amon became the father of Josiah. Matthew 1:10 Josiah became the father of Jechoniah and his brothers at the time of the exile to Babylon. Matthew 1:11 After the exile to Babylon, Jechoniah became the father of Shealtiel. Shealtiel became the father of Zerubbabel. Matthew 1:12 Zerubbabel became the father of Abiud. Abiud became the father of Eliakim. Eliakim became the father of Azor. Matthew 1:13 Azor became the father of Zadok. Zadok became the father of Achim. Achim became the father of Eliud. Matthew 1:14 Eliud became the father of Eleazar. Eleazar became the father of Matthan. Matthan became the father of Jacob. Matthew 1:15 Jacob became the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ. Matthew 1:16 So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; from David to the exile to Babylon fourteen generations; and from the carrying away to Babylon to the Christ, fourteen generations. Matthew 1:17

title: Matthew 1:18–25
context: After the genealogy, Matthew narrates Jesus’ birth: Mary’s virginal conception by the Holy Spirit, Joseph’s righteous struggle and obedience, the naming of Jesus as Savior, and the fulfillment of Isaiah’s Immanuel promise.
text: Matthew 1:18–25 Matthew After the genealogy, Matthew narrates Jesus’ birth: Mary’s virginal conception by the Holy Spirit, Joseph’s righteous struggle and obedience, the naming of Jesus as Savior, and the fulfillment of Isaiah’s Immanuel promise. Now the birth of Jesus Christ was like this: After his mother, Mary, was engaged to Joseph, before they came together, she was found pregnant by the Holy Spirit. Matthew 1:18 Joseph, her husband, being a righteous man, and not willing to make her a public example, intended to put her away secretly. Matthew 1:19 But when he thought about these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, “Joseph, son of David, don’t be afraid to take to yourself Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit. Matthew 1:20 She shall give birth to a son. You shall name him Jesus, for it is he who shall save his people from their sins.” Matthew 1:21 Now all this has happened that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying, Matthew 1:22 “Behold, the virgin shall be with child, and shall give birth to a son. They shall call his name Immanuel,” which is, being interpreted, “God with us.” Matthew 1:23 Joseph arose from his sleep, and did as the angel of the Lord commanded him, and took his wife to himself; Matthew 1:24 and didn’t know her sexually until she had given birth to her firstborn son. He named him Jesus. Matthew 1:25

title: Matthew 10:1–4
context: After mercy and conflict in Galilee, Jesus calls the Twelve, gives them authority over spirits and sickness, and names them as apostles. The mission discourse begins with a named circle—ordinary men under the King’s delegated power, including the one who will betray Him.
text: Matthew 10:1–4 Matthew After mercy and conflict in Galilee, Jesus calls the Twelve, gives them authority over spirits and sickness, and names them as apostles. The mission discourse begins with a named circle—ordinary men under the King’s delegated power, including the one who will betray Him. He called to himself his twelve disciples, and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every sickness. Matthew 10:1 Now the names of the twelve apostles are these. The first, Simon, who is called Peter; Andrew, his brother; James the son of Zebedee; John, his brother; Matthew 10:2 Philip; Bartholomew; Thomas; Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus; Lebbaeus, who was also called Thaddaeus; Matthew 10:3 Simon the Zealot; and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him. Matthew 10:4

title: Matthew 10:16–23
context: Jesus widens the mission charge into realism: sheep among wolves, courts and kings, family betrayal, hatred for His name, endurance unto salvation, and flight from town to town until the Son of Man comes. Courage here is Spirit-supplied witness, not naïveté.
text: Matthew 10:16–23 Matthew Jesus widens the mission charge into realism: sheep among wolves, courts and kings, family betrayal, hatred for His name, endurance unto salvation, and flight from town to town until the Son of Man comes. Courage here is Spirit-supplied witness, not naïveté. “Behold, I send you out as sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and harmless as doves. Matthew 10:16 But beware of men, for they will deliver you up to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you. Matthew 10:17 Yes, and you will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony to them and to the nations. Matthew 10:18 But when they deliver you up, don’t be anxious how or what you will say, for it will be given you in that hour what you will say. Matthew 10:19 For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. Matthew 10:20 “Brother will deliver up brother to death, and the father his child. Children will rise up against parents and cause them to be put to death. Matthew 10:21 You will be hated by all men for my name’s sake, but he who endures to the end will be saved. Matthew 10:22 But when they persecute you in this city, flee into the next, for most certainly I tell you, you will not have gone through the cities of Israel until the Son of Man has come. Matthew 10:23

title: Matthew 10:24–33
context: Jesus reframes fear: disciples share the Master’s mistreatment, yet must proclaim openly. Fear God rather than body-killers; trust the Father who numbers hairs and values sparrows; acknowledge Christ before people, for He will acknowledge or deny before the Father.
text: Matthew 10:24–33 Matthew Jesus reframes fear: disciples share the Master’s mistreatment, yet must proclaim openly. Fear God rather than body-killers; trust the Father who numbers hairs and values sparrows; acknowledge Christ before people, for He will acknowledge or deny before the Father. “A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord. Matthew 10:24 It is enough for the disciple that he be like his teacher, and the servant like his lord. If they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more those of his household! Matthew 10:25 Therefore don’t be afraid of them, for there is nothing covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. Matthew 10:26 What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear whispered in the ear, proclaim on the housetops. Matthew 10:27 Don’t be afraid of those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul. Rather, fear him who is able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. Matthew 10:28 “Aren’t two sparrows sold for an assarion coin? Not one of them falls to the ground apart from your Father’s will. Matthew 10:29 But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Matthew 10:30 Therefore don’t be afraid. You are of more value than many sparrows. Matthew 10:31 Everyone therefore who confesses me before men, I will also confess him before my Father who is in heaven. Matthew 10:32 But whoever denies me before men, I will also deny him before my Father who is in heaven. Matthew 10:33

title: Matthew 10:34–39
context: Jesus corrects false expectations of easy peace: His coming divides households, demands supreme love, requires the cross, and inverts life’s calculus—finding life by losing it for His sake. Allegiance to the King outranks every natural bond.
text: Matthew 10:34–39 Matthew Jesus corrects false expectations of easy peace: His coming divides households, demands supreme love, requires the cross, and inverts life’s calculus—finding life by losing it for His sake. Allegiance to the King outranks every natural bond. “Don’t think that I came to send peace on the earth. I didn’t come to send peace, but a sword. Matthew 10:34 For I came to set a man at odds against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Matthew 10:35 A man’s foes will be those of his own household. Matthew 10:36 He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me isn’t worthy of me. Matthew 10:37 He who doesn’t take his cross and follow after me isn’t worthy of me. Matthew 10:38 He who seeks his life will lose it; and he who loses his life for my sake will find it. Matthew 10:39

title: Matthew 10:40–42
context: The discourse closes with hospitality theology: receiving messengers is receiving Christ and the Father; prophetic and righteous welcome carry matching reward; just a cup of cold water to a little disciple is remembered. Mission hardship is matched by kingdom honor for those who welcome the sent.
text: Matthew 10:40–42 Matthew The discourse closes with hospitality theology: receiving messengers is receiving Christ and the Father; prophetic and righteous welcome carry matching reward; just a cup of cold water to a little disciple is remembered. Mission hardship is matched by kingdom honor for those who welcome the sent. “He who receives you receives me, and he who receives me receives him who sent me. Matthew 10:40 He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. He who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward. Matthew 10:41 Whoever gives one of these little ones just a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, most certainly I tell you, he will in no way lose his reward.” Matthew 10:42

title: Matthew 10:5–15
context: Jesus sends the Twelve on a time-bound mission to Israel’s lost sheep: proclaim the kingdom, heal freely, travel light, seek worthy houses, and treat rejection with solemn witness. Priority to Israel here does not annul later Gentile mission; it honors covenant order as the King advances.
text: Matthew 10:5–15 Matthew Jesus sends the Twelve on a time-bound mission to Israel’s lost sheep: proclaim the kingdom, heal freely, travel light, seek worthy houses, and treat rejection with solemn witness. Priority to Israel here does not annul later Gentile mission; it honors covenant order as the King advances. Jesus sent these twelve out and commanded them, saying, “Don’t go among the Gentiles, and don’t enter into any city of the Samaritans. Matthew 10:5 Rather, go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Matthew 10:6 As you go, preach, saying, ‘The Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!’ Matthew 10:7 Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, and cast out demons. Freely you received, so freely give. Matthew 10:8 Don’t take any gold, silver, or brass in your money belts. Matthew 10:9 Take no bag for your journey, neither two coats, nor sandals, nor staff: for the laborer is worthy of his food. Matthew 10:10 Into whatever city or village you enter, find out who in it is worthy, and stay there until you go on. Matthew 10:11 As you enter into the household, greet it. Matthew 10:12 If the household is worthy, let your peace come on it, but if it isn’t worthy, let your peace return to you. Matthew 10:13 Whoever doesn’t receive you or hear your words, as you go out of that house or that city, shake the dust off your feet. Matthew 10:14 Most certainly I tell you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city. Matthew 10:15

title: Matthew 11:1–6
context: After commissioning the Twelve (ch. 10), Jesus resumes His own ministry while John the Baptist—now in prison—sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the Coming One. Jesus answers with Isaiah-shaped messianic works and a beatitude for those not offended by Him.
text: Matthew 11:1–6 Matthew After commissioning the Twelve (ch. 10), Jesus resumes His own ministry while John the Baptist—now in prison—sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the Coming One. Jesus answers with Isaiah-shaped messianic works and a beatitude for those not offended by Him. When Jesus had finished directing his twelve disciples, he departed from there to teach and preach in their cities. Matthew 11:1 Now when John heard in the prison the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples Matthew 11:2 and said to him, “Are you he who comes, or should we look for another?” Matthew 11:3 Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John the things which you hear and see: Matthew 11:4 the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. Matthew 11:5 Blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me.” Matthew 11:6

title: Matthew 11:16–19
context: After honoring John before the crowds (vv. 7–15), Jesus turns to diagnose “this generation”: like quarrelsome children in the marketplaces, it refuses both John’s austere call and the Son of Man’s table fellowship—But wisdom is justified by her children.
text: Matthew 11:16–19 Matthew After honoring John before the crowds (vv. 7–15), Jesus turns to diagnose “this generation”: like quarrelsome children in the marketplaces, it refuses both John’s austere call and the Son of Man’s table fellowship—But wisdom is justified by her children. “But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces, who call to their companions Matthew 11:16 and say, ‘We played the flute for you, and you didn’t dance. We mourned for you, and you didn’t lament.’ Matthew 11:17 For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ Matthew 11:18 The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ But wisdom is justified by her children.” Matthew 11:19

title: Matthew 11:20–24
context: After exposing this generation’s refusal of both John’s austerity and the Son of Man’s table fellowship (vv. 16–19), Jesus denounces the Galilean cities in which most of his mighty works had been done—Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum—comparing their unrepentance with Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom.
text: Matthew 11:20–24 Matthew After exposing this generation’s refusal of both John’s austerity and the Son of Man’s table fellowship (vv. 16–19), Jesus denounces the Galilean cities in which most of his mighty works had been done—Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum—comparing their unrepentance with Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom. Then he began to denounce the cities in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they didn’t repent. Matthew 11:20 “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon which were done in you, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Matthew 11:21 But I tell you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you. Matthew 11:22 You, Capernaum, who are exalted to heaven, you will go down to Hades. For if the mighty works had been done in Sodom which were done in you, it would have remained until today. Matthew 11:23 But I tell you that it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment, than for you.” Matthew 11:24

title: Matthew 11:25–27
context: After pronouncing woes on unrepentant cities (vv. 20–24), Jesus turns from indictment to thanksgiving. He praises the Father—Lord of heaven and earth—for a revelatory will that hides kingdom truth from the self-wise and discloses it to little children, then speaks of the Son’s exclusive knowledge of the Father and of those to whom the Son desires to reveal him.
text: Matthew 11:25–27 Matthew After pronouncing woes on unrepentant cities (vv. 20–24), Jesus turns from indictment to thanksgiving. He praises the Father—Lord of heaven and earth—for a revelatory will that hides kingdom truth from the self-wise and discloses it to little children, then speaks of the Son’s exclusive knowledge of the Father and of those to whom the Son desires to reveal him. At that time, Jesus answered, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants. Matthew 11:25 Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight. Matthew 11:26 All things have been delivered to me by my Father. No one knows the Son, except the Father; neither does anyone know the Father, except the Son and he to whom the Son desires to reveal him. Matthew 11:27

title: Matthew 11:28–30
context: From thanksgiving over the Father’s revelatory will (vv. 25–27), Jesus turns outward to the weary. He invites all you who labor and are heavily burdened to come to Him for rest, to take His yoke, learn from His gentleness and lowliness, and find that His yoke is easy and His burden light.
text: Matthew 11:28–30 Matthew From thanksgiving over the Father’s revelatory will (vv. 25–27), Jesus turns outward to the weary. He invites all you who labor and are heavily burdened to come to Him for rest, to take His yoke, learn from His gentleness and lowliness, and find that His yoke is easy and His burden light. “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Matthew 11:28 Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. Matthew 11:29 For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” Matthew 11:30

title: Matthew 11:7–15
context: After John’s disciples leave with Jesus’ answer (vv. 2–6), Jesus turns to the crowds and interprets John’s ministry: the Baptist is no reed or soft courtier but more than a prophet—Malachi’s messenger, Elijah who is to come—yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
text: Matthew 11:7–15 Matthew After John’s disciples leave with Jesus’ answer (vv. 2–6), Jesus turns to the crowds and interprets John’s ministry: the Baptist is no reed or soft courtier but more than a prophet—Malachi’s messenger, Elijah who is to come—yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. As these went their way, Jesus began to say to the multitudes concerning John, “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? Matthew 11:7 But what did you go out to see? A man in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. Matthew 11:8 But why did you go out? To see a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and much more than a prophet. Matthew 11:9 For this is he, of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ Matthew 11:10 Most certainly I tell you, among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer; yet he who is least in the Kingdom of Heaven is greater than he. Matthew 11:11 From the days of John the Baptizer until now, the Kingdom of Heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force. Matthew 11:12 For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John. Matthew 11:13 If you are willing to receive it, this is Elijah, who is to come. Matthew 11:14 He who has ears to hear, let him hear. Matthew 11:15

title: Matthew 12:1–8
context: Following Jesus’ invitation to the weary (11:28–30), Matthew narrates a Sabbath controversy: the disciples pluck grain, the Pharisees accuse, and Jesus answers from Scripture—David, the temple priests, Hosea’s “mercy,” and His own lordship of the Sabbath.
text: Matthew 12:1–8 Matthew Following Jesus’ invitation to the weary (11:28–30), Matthew narrates a Sabbath controversy: the disciples pluck grain, the Pharisees accuse, and Jesus answers from Scripture—David, the temple priests, Hosea’s “mercy,” and His own lordship of the Sabbath. At that time, Jesus went on the Sabbath day through the grain fields. His disciples were hungry and began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. Matthew 12:1 But the Pharisees, when they saw it, said to him, “Behold, your disciples do what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.” Matthew 12:2 But he said to them, “Haven’t you read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: Matthew 12:3 how he entered into God’s house and ate the show bread, which was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests? Matthew 12:4 Or have you not read in the law that on the Sabbath day the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? Matthew 12:5 But I tell you that one greater than the temple is here. Matthew 12:6 But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you wouldn’t have condemned the guiltless. Matthew 12:7 For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.” Matthew 12:8

title: Matthew 12:15–21
context: After the Pharisees conspire to destroy Him (12:14), Jesus withdraws; crowds follow and He heals them all, charging silence. Matthew reads the scene as Isaiah 42 fulfilled—the chosen Servant who will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick until he leads justice to victory. In whose name the nations hope.
text: Matthew 12:15–21 Matthew After the Pharisees conspire to destroy Him (12:14), Jesus withdraws; crowds follow and He heals them all, charging silence. Matthew reads the scene as Isaiah 42 fulfilled—the chosen Servant who will not break a bruised reed or quench a smoldering wick until he leads justice to victory. In whose name the nations hope. Jesus, perceiving that, withdrew from there. Great multitudes followed him; and he healed them all, Matthew 12:15 and commanded them that they should not make him known, Matthew 12:16 that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying, Matthew 12:17 “Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit on him. He will proclaim justice to the nations. Matthew 12:18 He will not strive, nor shout, neither will anyone hear his voice in the streets. Matthew 12:19 He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a smoking flax, until he leads justice to victory. Matthew 12:20 In his name, the nations will hope.” Matthew 12:21

title: Matthew 12:22–32
context: After Sabbath controversy and Isaiah’s Servant song (12:1–21), Matthew narrates a Spirit-worked deliverance: Jesus heals a demon, blind and mute. Crowds wonder about the Son of David; Pharisees attribute the exorcism to Beelzebul. Jesus answers with kingdom logic, the strong man bound, and a solemn warning about blasphemy against the Spirit.
text: Matthew 12:22–32 Matthew After Sabbath controversy and Isaiah’s Servant song (12:1–21), Matthew narrates a Spirit-worked deliverance: Jesus heals a demon, blind and mute. Crowds wonder about the Son of David; Pharisees attribute the exorcism to Beelzebul. Jesus answers with kingdom logic, the strong man bound, and a solemn warning about blasphemy against the Spirit. Then one possessed by a demon, blind and mute, was brought to him; and he healed him, so that the blind and mute man both spoke and saw. Matthew 12:22 All the multitudes were amazed, and said, “Can this be the son of David?” Matthew 12:23 But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons.” Matthew 12:24 Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand. Matthew 12:25 If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? Matthew 12:26 If I by Beelzebul cast out demons, by whom do your children cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. Matthew 12:27 But if I by the Spirit of God cast out demons, then God’s Kingdom has come upon you. Matthew 12:28 Or how can one enter into the house of the strong man and plunder his goods, unless he first bind the strong man? Then he will plunder his house. Matthew 12:29 “He who is not with me is against me, and he who doesn’t gather with me, scatters. Matthew 12:30 Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven men. Matthew 12:31 Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, either in this age, or in that which is to come. Matthew 12:32

title: Matthew 12:33–37
context: After the Beelzebul charge and the warning about blasphemy against the Spirit (12:22–32), Jesus presses the Pharisees with tree-and-fruit logic: speech flows from the heart’s treasure, and on judgment day careless words will justify or condemn.
text: Matthew 12:33–37 Matthew After the Beelzebul charge and the warning about blasphemy against the Spirit (12:22–32), Jesus presses the Pharisees with tree-and-fruit logic: speech flows from the heart’s treasure, and on judgment day careless words will justify or condemn. “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree corrupt and its fruit corrupt; for the tree is known by its fruit. Matthew 12:33 You offspring of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak good things? For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks. Matthew 12:34 The good man out of his good treasure brings out good things, and the evil man out of his evil treasure brings out evil things. Matthew 12:35 I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment. Matthew 12:36 For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” Matthew 12:37

title: Matthew 12:38–42
context: After tree-and-fruit warnings and the accounting of careless words (12:33–37), some scribes and Pharisees answer Jesus by asking for a sign. He refuses spectacle to unbelief, promises only the sign of Jonah—His own death and rising—and warns that Nineveh and the queen of the South will condemn this generation, for something greater than Jonah and Solomon is here.
text: Matthew 12:38–42 Matthew After tree-and-fruit warnings and the accounting of careless words (12:33–37), some scribes and Pharisees answer Jesus by asking for a sign. He refuses spectacle to unbelief, promises only the sign of Jonah—His own death and rising—and warns that Nineveh and the queen of the South will condemn this generation, for something greater than Jonah and Solomon is here. Then certain of the scribes and Pharisees answered, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from you.” Matthew 12:38 But he answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks after a sign, but no sign will be given to it but the sign of Jonah the prophet. Matthew 12:39 For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the huge fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. Matthew 12:40 The men of Nineveh will stand up in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, someone greater than Jonah is here. Matthew 12:41 The Queen of the South will rise up in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and behold, someone greater than Solomon is here. Matthew 12:42

title: Matthew 12:43–45
context: After the demand for a sign and Jesus’ reply from Jonah, Nineveh, and the queen of the South (12:38–42), He warns with a brief parable: an unclean spirit departs, returns to an empty house, and the last state is worse—applied to “this evil generation.”
text: Matthew 12:43–45 Matthew After the demand for a sign and Jesus’ reply from Jonah, Nineveh, and the queen of the South (12:38–42), He warns with a brief parable: an unclean spirit departs, returns to an empty house, and the last state is worse—applied to “this evil generation.” “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he passes through waterless places seeking rest, and doesn’t find it. Matthew 12:43 Then he says, ‘I will return into my house from which I came;’ and when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order. Matthew 12:44 Then he goes and takes with himself seven other spirits more evil than he is, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first. Even so will it be also to this evil generation.” Matthew 12:45

title: Matthew 12:46–50
context: After the demand for a sign and the warning about the returning unclean spirit (12:38–45), Matthew closes the chapter with a family interruption: while Jesus is still speaking, His mother and brothers stand outside asking to speak with Him—and He redefines true kinship around discipleship and the Father’s will.
text: Matthew 12:46–50 Matthew After the demand for a sign and the warning about the returning unclean spirit (12:38–45), Matthew closes the chapter with a family interruption: while Jesus is still speaking, His mother and brothers stand outside asking to speak with Him—and He redefines true kinship around discipleship and the Father’s will. While he was yet speaking to the multitudes, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, seeking to speak to him. Matthew 12:46 One said to him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside, seeking to speak to you.” Matthew 12:47 But he answered him who spoke to him, “Who is my mother? Who are my brothers?” Matthew 12:48 He stretched out his hand toward his disciples, and said, “Behold, my mother and my brothers! Matthew 12:49 For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.” Matthew 12:50

title: Matthew 12:9–14
context: Continuing the Sabbath controversy (12:1–8), Jesus enters the synagogue, faces a trap question over a man with a withered hand, answers with mercy’s logic, heals, and draws the Pharisees into a plot to destroy Him.
text: Matthew 12:9–14 Matthew Continuing the Sabbath controversy (12:1–8), Jesus enters the synagogue, faces a trap question over a man with a withered hand, answers with mercy’s logic, heals, and draws the Pharisees into a plot to destroy Him. He departed from there and went into their synagogue. Matthew 12:9 And behold, there was a man with a withered hand. They asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath day?” so that they might accuse him. Matthew 12:10 He said to them, “What man is there among you who has one sheep, and if this one falls into a pit on the Sabbath day, won’t he grab on to it and lift it out? Matthew 12:11 Of how much more value then is a man than a sheep! Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath day.” Matthew 12:12 Then he told the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out; and it was restored whole, just like the other. Matthew 12:13 But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how they might destroy him. Matthew 12:14

title: Matthew 13:1–9
context: On the same day as the conflicts of chapter 12, Jesus leaves the house, sits beside the sea, and teaches great crowds from a boat. Matthew opens a concentrated block of kingdom teaching in parables—beginning with the Sower—where hearing the word becomes the hinge of discipleship.
text: Matthew 13:1–9 Matthew On the same day as the conflicts of chapter 12, Jesus leaves the house, sits beside the sea, and teaches great crowds from a boat. Matthew opens a concentrated block of kingdom teaching in parables—beginning with the Sower—where hearing the word becomes the hinge of discipleship. On that day Jesus went out of the house and sat by the seaside. Matthew 13:1 Great multitudes gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat and sat; and all the multitude stood on the beach. Matthew 13:2 He spoke to them many things in parables, saying, “Behold, a farmer went out to sow. Matthew 13:3 As he sowed, some seeds fell by the roadside, and the birds came and devoured them. Matthew 13:4 Others fell on rocky ground, where they didn’t have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, because they had no depth of earth. Matthew 13:5 When the sun had risen, they were scorched. Because they had no root, they withered away. Matthew 13:6 Others fell among thorns. The thorns grew up and choked them. Matthew 13:7 Others fell on good soil and yielded fruit: some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty. Matthew 13:8 He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” Matthew 13:9

title: Matthew 13:10–17
context: After the Sower parable, the disciples ask why Jesus teaches the crowds in parables. He answers with the gift of kingdom secrets, Isaiah’s judgment oracle on dull hearts, and a blessing on eyes and ears that truly see and hear—framing how the word divides hearers.
text: Matthew 13:10–17 Matthew After the Sower parable, the disciples ask why Jesus teaches the crowds in parables. He answers with the gift of kingdom secrets, Isaiah’s judgment oracle on dull hearts, and a blessing on eyes and ears that truly see and hear—framing how the word divides hearers. The disciples came, and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?” Matthew 13:10 He answered them, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven, but it is not given to them. Matthew 13:11 For whoever has, to him will be given, and he will have abundance; but whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he has. Matthew 13:12 Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they don’t see, and hearing, they don’t hear, neither do they understand. Matthew 13:13 In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, which says, ‘By hearing you will hear, and will in no way understand; Seeing you will see, and will in no way perceive; Matthew 13:14 for this people’s heart has grown callous, their ears are dull of hearing, and they have closed their eyes; or else perhaps they might perceive with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again, and I would heal them.’ Matthew 13:15 “But blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear. Matthew 13:16 For most certainly I tell you that many prophets and righteous men desired to see the things which you see, and didn’t see them; and to hear the things which you hear, and didn’t hear them. Matthew 13:17

title: Matthew 13:18–23
context: Jesus explains the Sower to the disciples: four soils picture four hearings of the kingdom word—snatched, shallow, choked, and fruitful. Understanding and endurance become the pastoral hinge of the parable’s meaning.
text: Matthew 13:18–23 Matthew Jesus explains the Sower to the disciples: four soils picture four hearings of the kingdom word—snatched, shallow, choked, and fruitful. Understanding and endurance become the pastoral hinge of the parable’s meaning. “Hear, then, the parable of the farmer. Matthew 13:18 When anyone hears the word of the Kingdom and doesn’t understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away that which has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown by the roadside. Matthew 13:19 What was sown on the rocky places, this is he who hears the word and immediately with joy receives it; Matthew 13:20 yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while. When oppression or persecution arises because of the word, immediately he stumbles. Matthew 13:21 What was sown among the thorns, this is he who hears the word, but the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful. Matthew 13:22 What was sown on the good ground, this is he who hears the word and understands it, who most certainly bears fruit and produces, some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty.” Matthew 13:23

title: Matthew 13:24–30
context: Jesus sets another kingdom parable before the crowds: good seed sown in a field, an enemy’s weeds mixed among the wheat, and a master’s patience until harvest. Premature uprooting is refused; final separation is reserved for the reapers.
text: Matthew 13:24–30 Matthew Jesus sets another kingdom parable before the crowds: good seed sown in a field, an enemy’s weeds mixed among the wheat, and a master’s patience until harvest. Premature uprooting is refused; final separation is reserved for the reapers. He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field, Matthew 13:24 but while people slept, his enemy came and sowed darnel weeds also among the wheat, and went away. Matthew 13:25 But when the blade sprang up and produced grain, then the darnel weeds appeared also. Matthew 13:26 The servants of the householder came and said to him, ‘Sir, didn’t you sow good seed in your field? Where did these darnel weeds come from?’ Matthew 13:27 “He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ “The servants asked him, ‘Do you want us to go and gather them up?’ Matthew 13:28 “But he said, ‘No, lest perhaps while you gather up the darnel weeds, you root up the wheat with them. Matthew 13:29 Let both grow together until the harvest, and in the harvest time I will tell the reapers, “First, gather up the darnel weeds, and bind them in bundles to burn them; but gather the wheat into my barn.”’” Matthew 13:30

title: Matthew 13:31–35
context: Jesus adds twin kingdom images—mustard seed and leaven—then Matthew explains His parable method as fulfillment of prophetic speech that utters what has been hidden.
text: Matthew 13:31–35 Matthew Jesus adds twin kingdom images—mustard seed and leaven—then Matthew explains His parable method as fulfillment of prophetic speech that utters what has been hidden. He set another parable before them, saying, “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a grain of mustard seed which a man took, and sowed in his field, Matthew 13:31 which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches.” Matthew 13:32 He spoke another parable to them. “The Kingdom of Heaven is like yeast which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until it was all leavened.” Matthew 13:33 Jesus spoke all these things in parables to the multitudes; and without a parable, he didn’t speak to them, Matthew 13:34 that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet, saying, “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.” Matthew 13:35

title: Matthew 13:36–43
context: Leaving the crowds, Jesus enters the house and explains the weeds parable to the disciples: Son of Man, world-field, sons of kingdom and of the evil one, end-of-age harvest by angels, fiery judgment, and the righteous shining in the Father’s kingdom.
text: Matthew 13:36–43 Matthew Leaving the crowds, Jesus enters the house and explains the weeds parable to the disciples: Son of Man, world-field, sons of kingdom and of the evil one, end-of-age harvest by angels, fiery judgment, and the righteous shining in the Father’s kingdom. Then Jesus sent the multitudes away, and went into the house. His disciples came to him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the darnel weeds of the field.” Matthew 13:36 He answered them, “He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man, Matthew 13:37 the field is the world, the good seeds are the children of the Kingdom, and the darnel weeds are the children of the evil one. Matthew 13:38 The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. Matthew 13:39 As therefore the darnel weeds are gathered up and burned with fire; so will it be at the end of this age. Matthew 13:40 The Son of Man will send out his angels, and they will gather out of his Kingdom all things that cause stumbling and those who do iniquity, Matthew 13:41 and will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Matthew 13:42 Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the Kingdom of their Father. He who has ears to hear, let him hear. Matthew 13:43

title: Matthew 13:44–46
context: Jesus pairs two brief kingdom images: treasure hidden in the field and a merchant found one pearl of great value—both ending in joyful, total exchange for what is found.
text: Matthew 13:44–46 Matthew Jesus pairs two brief kingdom images: treasure hidden in the field and a merchant found one pearl of great value—both ending in joyful, total exchange for what is found. “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. Matthew 13:44 “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a merchant seeking fine pearls, Matthew 13:45 who having found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had and bought it. Matthew 13:46

title: Matthew 13:47–52
context: Jesus adds the dragnet parable of final separation, then asks whether the disciples understand and compares the trained kingdom scribe to a householder bringing out new and old treasure.
text: Matthew 13:47–52 Matthew Jesus adds the dragnet parable of final separation, then asks whether the disciples understand and compares the trained kingdom scribe to a householder bringing out new and old treasure. “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a dragnet that was cast into the sea and gathered some fish of every kind, Matthew 13:47 which, when it was filled, fishermen drew up on the beach. They sat down and gathered the good into containers, but the bad they threw away. Matthew 13:48 So it will be in the end of the world. The angels will come and separate the wicked from among the righteous, Matthew 13:49 and will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Matthew 13:50 Jesus said to them, “Have you understood all these things?” They answered him, “Yes, Lord.” Matthew 13:51 He said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been made a disciple in the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a householder, who brings out of his treasure new and old things.” Matthew 13:52

title: Matthew 13:53–58
context: After the parable discourse, Jesus returns to His hometown synagogue. Familiarity breeds offense: neighbors name His family, stumble over His wisdom and works, and unbelief limits the mighty works done there.
text: Matthew 13:53–58 Matthew After the parable discourse, Jesus returns to His hometown synagogue. Familiarity breeds offense: neighbors name His family, stumble over His wisdom and works, and unbelief limits the mighty works done there. When Jesus had finished these parables, he departed from there. Matthew 13:53 Coming into his own country, he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? Matthew 13:54 Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t his mother called Mary, and his brothers James, Joses, Simon, and Judas? Matthew 13:55 Aren’t all of his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all of these things?” Matthew 13:56 They were offended by him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor, except in his own country and in his own house.” Matthew 13:57 He didn’t do many mighty works there because of their unbelief. Matthew 13:58

title: Matthew 14:1–12
context: After Nazareth’s unbelief closes Matthew 13, the narrative turns to Herod Antipas: rumors of Jesus’ fame reopen the story of John’s imprisonment and beheading. The flashback ends as John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus—immediately before the feeding of the five thousand.
text: Matthew 14:1–12 Matthew After Nazareth’s unbelief closes Matthew 13, the narrative turns to Herod Antipas: rumors of Jesus’ fame reopen the story of John’s imprisonment and beheading. The flashback ends as John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus—immediately before the feeding of the five thousand. At that time, Herod the tetrarch heard the report concerning Jesus, Matthew 14:1 and said to his servants, “This is John the Baptizer. He is risen from the dead. That is why these powers work in him.” Matthew 14:2 For Herod had arrested John, bound him, and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife. Matthew 14:3 For John said to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” Matthew 14:4 When he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet. Matthew 14:5 But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced among them and pleased Herod. Matthew 14:6 Therefore he promised with an oath to give her whatever she should ask. Matthew 14:7 She, being prompted by her mother, said, “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptizer.” Matthew 14:8 The king was grieved, but for the sake of his oaths and of those who sat at the table with him, he commanded it to be given, Matthew 14:9 and he sent and beheaded John in the prison. Matthew 14:10 His head was brought on a platter and given to the young lady; and she brought it to her mother. Matthew 14:11 His disciples came, took the body, and buried it. Then they went and told Jesus. Matthew 14:12

title: Matthew 14:13–21
context: After John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus (14:1–12), Jesus withdraws by boat to a deserted place—yet the crowds follow on foot. Evening brings the disciples’ scarcity report, five loaves and two fish placed in His hands, a blessing, broken bread, satisfied multitudes, and twelve baskets left over.
text: Matthew 14:13–21 Matthew After John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus (14:1–12), Jesus withdraws by boat to a deserted place—yet the crowds follow on foot. Evening brings the disciples’ scarcity report, five loaves and two fish placed in His hands, a blessing, broken bread, satisfied multitudes, and twelve baskets left over. Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a deserted place apart. When the multitudes heard it, they followed him on foot from the cities. Matthew 14:13 Jesus went out, and he saw a great multitude. He had compassion on them and healed their sick. Matthew 14:14 When evening had come, his disciples came to him, saying, “This place is deserted, and the hour is already late. Send the multitudes away, that they may go into the villages, and buy themselves food.” Matthew 14:15 But Jesus said to them, “They don’t need to go away. You give them something to eat.” Matthew 14:16 They told him, “We only have here five loaves and two fish.” Matthew 14:17 He said, “Bring them here to me.” Matthew 14:18 He commanded the multitudes to sit down on the grass; and he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, broke and gave the loaves to the disciples; and the disciples gave to the multitudes. Matthew 14:19 They all ate and were filled. They took up twelve baskets full of that which remained left over from the broken pieces. Matthew 14:20 Those who ate were about five thousand men, in addition to women and children. Matthew 14:21

title: Matthew 14:22–33
context: After the five thousand eat and twelve baskets remain (14:13–21), Jesus immediately sends the disciples ahead by boat, dismisses the crowds, and prays alone on the mountain. In the night storm He walks on the sea, steadies their fear—“It is I”—receives Peter’s venture of faith, rescues him when fear sinks him, stills the wind, and hears the boat’s worship: “You are truly the Son of God.”
text: Matthew 14:22–33 Matthew After the five thousand eat and twelve baskets remain (14:13–21), Jesus immediately sends the disciples ahead by boat, dismisses the crowds, and prays alone on the mountain. In the night storm He walks on the sea, steadies their fear—“It is I”—receives Peter’s venture of faith, rescues him when fear sinks him, stills the wind, and hears the boat’s worship: “You are truly the Son of God.” Immediately Jesus made the disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the multitudes away. Matthew 14:22 After he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into the mountain by himself to pray. When evening had come, he was there alone. Matthew 14:23 But the boat was now in the middle of the sea, distressed by the waves, for the wind was contrary. Matthew 14:24 In the fourth watch of the night, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea. Matthew 14:25 When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, “It’s a ghost!” and they cried out for fear. Matthew 14:26 But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Cheer up! It is I! Don’t be afraid.” Matthew 14:27 Peter answered him and said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.” Matthew 14:28 He said, “Come!” Peter stepped down from the boat and walked on the waters to come to Jesus. Matthew 14:29 But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, “Lord, save me!” Matthew 14:30 Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” Matthew 14:31 When they got up into the boat, the wind ceased. Matthew 14:32 Those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, “You are truly the Son of God!” Matthew 14:33

title: Matthew 14:34–36
context: After the storm stills and the disciples worship Jesus as the Son of God (14:22–33), they land at Gennesaret. Recognition spreads through the region: the sick are brought, the fringe of His garment is sought, and all who touch are made well—mercy continuing on shore after glory on the sea.
text: Matthew 14:34–36 Matthew After the storm stills and the disciples worship Jesus as the Son of God (14:22–33), they land at Gennesaret. Recognition spreads through the region: the sick are brought, the fringe of His garment is sought, and all who touch are made well—mercy continuing on shore after glory on the sea. When they had crossed over, they came to the land of Gennesaret. Matthew 14:34 When the people of that place recognized him, they sent into all that surrounding region and brought to him all who were sick; Matthew 14:35 and they begged him that they might just touch the fringe of his garment. As many as touched it were made whole. Matthew 14:36

title: Matthew 15:1–9
context: Pharisees and scribes arrive from Jerusalem and accuse Jesus’ disciples of breaking the tradition of the elders by eating with unwashed hands. Jesus turns the charge: their Corban practice voids God’s command to honor father and mother, and Isaiah’s word exposes lip-service worship that teaches human commandments as doctrine.
text: Matthew 15:1–9 Matthew Pharisees and scribes arrive from Jerusalem and accuse Jesus’ disciples of breaking the tradition of the elders by eating with unwashed hands. Jesus turns the charge: their Corban practice voids God’s command to honor father and mother, and Isaiah’s word exposes lip-service worship that teaches human commandments as doctrine. Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem, saying, Matthew 15:1 “Why do your disciples disobey the tradition of the elders? For they don’t wash their hands when they eat bread.” Matthew 15:2 He answered them, “Why do you also disobey the commandment of God because of your tradition? Matthew 15:3 For God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him be put to death.’ Matthew 15:4 But you say, ‘Whoever may tell his father or his mother, “Whatever help you might otherwise have gotten from me is a gift devoted to God,” Matthew 15:5 he shall not honor his father or mother.’ You have made the commandment of God void because of your tradition. Matthew 15:6 You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, saying, Matthew 15:7 ‘These people draw near to me with their mouth, and honor me with their lips; but their heart is far from me. Matthew 15:8 And they worship me in vain, teaching as doctrine rules made by men.’” Matthew 15:9

title: Matthew 15:10–20
context: Jesus turns from the Jerusalem challengers to the crowd: defilement is not what enters the mouth but what comes out of it. When the disciples report Pharisaic offense, He speaks of unplanted plants, blind guides, and—answering Peter—evil that proceeds from the heart. Unwashed hands do not defile; the heart’s overflow does.
text: Matthew 15:10–20 Matthew Jesus turns from the Jerusalem challengers to the crowd: defilement is not what enters the mouth but what comes out of it. When the disciples report Pharisaic offense, He speaks of unplanted plants, blind guides, and—answering Peter—evil that proceeds from the heart. Unwashed hands do not defile; the heart’s overflow does. He summoned the multitude, and said to them, “Hear, and understand. Matthew 15:10 That which enters into the mouth doesn’t defile the man; but that which proceeds out of the mouth, this defiles the man.” Matthew 15:11 Then the disciples came and said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” Matthew 15:12 But he answered, “Every plant which my heavenly Father didn’t plant will be uprooted. Matthew 15:13 Leave them alone. They are blind guides of the blind. If the blind guide the blind, both will fall into a pit.” Matthew 15:14 Peter answered him, “Explain the parable to us.” Matthew 15:15 So Jesus said, “Do you also still not understand? Matthew 15:16 Don’t you understand that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the belly and then out of the body? Matthew 15:17 But the things which proceed out of the mouth come out of the heart, and they defile the man. Matthew 15:18 For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies. Matthew 15:19 These are the things which defile the man; but to eat with unwashed hands doesn’t defile the man.” Matthew 15:20

title: Matthew 15:21–28
context: Jesus withdraws into the region of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman cries for mercy to the Son of David for her demon-oppressed daughter. After silence, a word about Israel’s lost sheep, and a hard saying about children’s bread, her faith answers with crumbs from the masters’ table. Jesus praises her great faith; her daughter is healed instantly.
text: Matthew 15:21–28 Matthew Jesus withdraws into the region of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman cries for mercy to the Son of David for her demon-oppressed daughter. After silence, a word about Israel’s lost sheep, and a hard saying about children’s bread, her faith answers with crumbs from the masters’ table. Jesus praises her great faith; her daughter is healed instantly. Jesus went out from there and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. Matthew 15:21 Behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those borders and cried, saying, “Have mercy on me, Lord, you son of David! My daughter is severely possessed by a demon!” Matthew 15:22 But he answered her not a word. His disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away; for she cries after us.” Matthew 15:23 But he answered, “I wasn’t sent to anyone but the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” Matthew 15:24 But she came and worshiped him, saying, “Lord, help me.” Matthew 15:25 But he answered, “It is not appropriate to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” Matthew 15:26 But she said, “Yes, Lord, but even the dogs eat the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.” Matthew 15:27 Then Jesus answered her, “Woman, great is your faith! Be it done to you even as you desire.” And her daughter was healed from that hour. Matthew 15:28

title: Matthew 15:29–39
context: From the coast Jesus returns beside the Sea of Galilee, sits on the mountain, and heals crowds of lame, blind, crippled, mute, and many others; they glorify the God of Israel. He then has compassion on a three-day crowd with nothing to eat, multiplies seven loaves and a few fish, satisfies about four thousand men, in addition to women and children, gathers seven baskets of leftovers, and departs by boat into the borders of Magdala.
text: Matthew 15:29–39 Matthew From the coast Jesus returns beside the Sea of Galilee, sits on the mountain, and heals crowds of lame, blind, crippled, mute, and many others; they glorify the God of Israel. He then has compassion on a three-day crowd with nothing to eat, multiplies seven loaves and a few fish, satisfies about four thousand men, in addition to women and children, gathers seven baskets of leftovers, and departs by boat into the borders of Magdala. Jesus departed from there and came near to the sea of Galilee; and he went up on the mountain and sat there. Matthew 15:29 Great multitudes came to him, having with them the lame, blind, mute, maimed, and many others, and they put them down at his feet. He healed them, Matthew 15:30 so that the multitude wondered when they saw the mute speaking, the injured healed, the lame walking, and the blind seeing—and they glorified the God of Israel. Matthew 15:31 Jesus summoned his disciples and said, “I have compassion on the multitude, because they have continued with me now three days and have nothing to eat. I don’t want to send them away fasting, or they might faint on the way.” Matthew 15:32 The disciples said to him, “Where could we get so many loaves in a deserted place as to satisfy so great a multitude?” Matthew 15:33 Jesus said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.” Matthew 15:34 He commanded the multitude to sit down on the ground; Matthew 15:35 and he took the seven loaves and the fish. He gave thanks and broke them, and gave to the disciples, and the disciples to the multitudes. Matthew 15:36 They all ate and were filled. They took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces that were left over. Matthew 15:37 Those who ate were four thousand men, in addition to women and children. Matthew 15:38 Then he sent away the multitudes, got into the boat, and came into the borders of Magdala. Matthew 15:39

title: Matthew 16:1–4
context: After feeding multitudes and healing, Jesus is confronted by Pharisees and Sadducees who demand a sign from heaven. But he exposes their spiritual blindness, refuses a spectacle, and points them to the sign of Jonah—then leaves them.
text: Matthew 16:1–4 Matthew After feeding multitudes and healing, Jesus is confronted by Pharisees and Sadducees who demand a sign from heaven. But he exposes their spiritual blindness, refuses a spectacle, and points them to the sign of Jonah—then leaves them. The Pharisees and Sadducees came, and testing him, asked him to show them a sign from heaven. Matthew 16:1 But he answered them, “When it is evening, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.’ Matthew 16:2 In the morning, ‘It will be foul weather today, for the sky is red and threatening.’ Hypocrites! You know how to discern the appearance of the sky, but you can’t discern the signs of the times! Matthew 16:3 An evil and adulterous generation seeks after a sign, and there will be no sign given to it, except the sign of the prophet Jonah.” He left them and departed. Matthew 16:4

title: Matthew 16:13–20
context: At Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks who He is. Peter confesses Him as the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus blesses this as the Father’s revelation, promises to build His church on this rock, grants keys of the kingdom, and charges silence for now.
text: Matthew 16:13–20 Matthew At Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks who He is. Peter confesses Him as the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus blesses this as the Father’s revelation, promises to build His church on this rock, grants keys of the kingdom, and charges silence for now. Now when Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?” Matthew 16:13 They said, “Some say John the Baptizer, some, Elijah, and others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” Matthew 16:14 He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” Matthew 16:15 Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Matthew 16:16 Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. Matthew 16:17 I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. Matthew 16:18 I will give to you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven; and whatever you release on earth will have been released in heaven.” Matthew 16:19 Then he commanded the disciples that they should tell no one that he was Jesus the Christ. Matthew 16:20

title: Matthew 16:21–23
context: Immediately after Peter’s confession, Jesus begins to show the necessity of His suffering, death, and resurrection. Peter rebukes Him; Jesus rebukes Peter as a satanic hindrance for setting his mind on human things rather than God’s.
text: Matthew 16:21–23 Matthew Immediately after Peter’s confession, Jesus begins to show the necessity of His suffering, death, and resurrection. Peter rebukes Him; Jesus rebukes Peter as a satanic hindrance for setting his mind on human things rather than God’s. From that time, Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up. Matthew 16:21 Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you.” Matthew 16:22 But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” Matthew 16:23

title: Matthew 16:24–28
context: Jesus applies the cross to every disciple: deny self, take up the cross, follow Him. He contrasts saving and losing life, warns against gaining the world at the soul’s cost, and promises the Son of Man’s coming in glory—with a pledge that some present will see Him coming in His kingdom.
text: Matthew 16:24–28 Matthew Jesus applies the cross to every disciple: deny self, take up the cross, follow Him. He contrasts saving and losing life, warns against gaining the world at the soul’s cost, and promises the Son of Man’s coming in glory—with a pledge that some present will see Him coming in His kingdom. Then Jesus said to his disciples, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. Matthew 16:24 For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it. Matthew 16:25 For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his life? Or what will a man give in exchange for his life? Matthew 16:26 For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will give to everyone according to his deeds. Matthew 16:27 Most certainly I tell you, there are some standing here who will in no way taste of death until they see the Son of Man coming in his Kingdom.” Matthew 16:28

title: Matthew 16:5–12
context: Crossing the lake, the disciples fret about forgotten bread while Jesus warns them of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees. He recalls the feedings, exposes their little faith, and clarifies that the danger is false teaching, not empty baskets.
text: Matthew 16:5–12 Matthew Crossing the lake, the disciples fret about forgotten bread while Jesus warns them of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees. He recalls the feedings, exposes their little faith, and clarifies that the danger is false teaching, not empty baskets. The disciples came to the other side and had forgotten to take bread. Matthew 16:5 Jesus said to them, “Take heed and beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” Matthew 16:6 They reasoned among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread.” Matthew 16:7 Jesus, perceiving it, said, “Why do you reason among yourselves, you of little faith, because you have brought no bread? Matthew 16:8 Don’t you yet perceive or remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you took up, Matthew 16:9 or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you took up?
