Matthew 16:10 How is it that you don’t perceive that I didn’t speak to you concerning bread? But beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” Matthew 16:11 Then they understood that he didn’t tell them to beware of the yeast of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. Matthew 16:12

title: Matthew 17:1–8
context: Six days after Peter’s confession and the first passion prediction, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. He is transfigured; Moses and Elijah appear; the Father’s voice from the bright cloud commands them to listen to the beloved Son. The disciples fall in fear; Jesus touches them, and they see Jesus only.
text: Matthew 17:1–8 Matthew Six days after Peter’s confession and the first passion prediction, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. He is transfigured; Moses and Elijah appear; the Father’s voice from the bright cloud commands them to listen to the beloved Son. The disciples fall in fear; Jesus touches them, and they see Jesus only. After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves. Matthew 17:1 He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light. Matthew 17:2 Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them talking with him. Matthew 17:3 Peter answered and said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” Matthew 17:4 While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” Matthew 17:5 When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces, and were very afraid. Matthew 17:6 Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.” Matthew 17:7 Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone. Matthew 17:8

title: Matthew 17:14–20
context: At the foot of the mountain a desperate father kneels for his demon-afflicted son after the disciples failed to heal him. Jesus laments the faithless generation, casts out the demon, and privately explains the failure as little faith—then promises mountain-moving power to mustard-seed faith.
text: Matthew 17:14–20 Matthew At the foot of the mountain a desperate father kneels for his demon-afflicted son after the disciples failed to heal him. Jesus laments the faithless generation, casts out the demon, and privately explains the failure as little faith—then promises mountain-moving power to mustard-seed faith. When they came to the multitude, a man came to him, kneeling down to him and saying, Matthew 17:14 “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he is epileptic and suffers grievously; for he often falls into the fire, and often into the water. Matthew 17:15 So I brought him to your disciples, and they could not cure him.” Matthew 17:16 Jesus answered, “Faithless and perverse generation! How long will I be with you? How long will I bear with you? Bring him here to me.” Matthew 17:17 Jesus rebuked the demon, and it went out of him, and the boy was cured from that hour. Matthew 17:18 Then the disciples came to Jesus privately, and said, “Why weren’t we able to cast it out?” Matthew 17:19 He said to them, “Because of your unbelief. For most certainly I tell you, if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will tell this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you. Matthew 17:20

title: Matthew 17:22–23
context: Gathering in Galilee, Jesus again announces that the Son of Man will be delivered, killed, and raised on the third day. The disciples are greatly distressed—hearing the suffering more clearly than the promise of rising.
text: Matthew 17:22–23 Matthew Gathering in Galilee, Jesus again announces that the Son of Man will be delivered, killed, and raised on the third day. The disciples are greatly distressed—hearing the suffering more clearly than the promise of rising. While they were staying in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered up into the hands of men, Matthew 17:22 and they will kill him, and the third day he will be raised up.” They were exceedingly sorry. Matthew 17:23

title: Matthew 17:24–27
context: In Capernaum collectors ask Peter whether Jesus pays the two-drachma temple tax. Jesus teaches Peter that sons are free, yet provides a miraculous shekel from a fish’s mouth so as not to give offense—paying for Himself and for Peter.
text: Matthew 17:24–27 Matthew In Capernaum collectors ask Peter whether Jesus pays the two-drachma temple tax. Jesus teaches Peter that sons are free, yet provides a miraculous shekel from a fish’s mouth so as not to give offense—paying for Himself and for Peter. When they had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma coins came to Peter, and said, “Doesn’t your teacher pay the didrachma?” Matthew 17:24 He said, “Yes.” When he came into the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying, “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive toll or tribute? From their children, or from strangers?” Matthew 17:25 Peter said to him, “From strangers.” Jesus said to him, “Therefore the children are exempt. Matthew 17:26 But, lest we cause them to stumble, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take up the first fish that comes up. When you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater coin. Take that, and give it to them for me and you.” Matthew 17:27

title: Matthew 17:9–13
context: Coming down from the mountain, Jesus forbids reporting the vision until the resurrection. The disciples ask about Elijah’s expected coming; Jesus teaches that Elijah has already come in John the Baptist’s rejected ministry, and that the Son of Man will likewise suffer.
text: Matthew 17:9–13 Matthew Coming down from the mountain, Jesus forbids reporting the vision until the resurrection. The disciples ask about Elijah’s expected coming; Jesus teaches that Elijah has already come in John the Baptist’s rejected ministry, and that the Son of Man will likewise suffer. As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying, “Don’t tell anyone what you saw, until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.” Matthew 17:9 His disciples asked him, saying, “Then why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” Matthew 17:10 Jesus answered them, “Elijah indeed comes first, and will restore all things; Matthew 17:11 but I tell you that Elijah has come already, and they didn’t recognize him, but did to him whatever they wanted to. Even so the Son of Man will also suffer by them.” Matthew 17:12 Then the disciples understood that he spoke to them of John the Baptizer. Matthew 17:13

title: Matthew 18:1–5
context: After teaching on the temple tax, the disciples ask who ranks highest in the kingdom. Jesus places a child in their midst and redefines greatness as humility and welcome—entrance itself depends on turning to become like children.
text: Matthew 18:1–5 Matthew After teaching on the temple tax, the disciples ask who ranks highest in the kingdom. Jesus places a child in their midst and redefines greatness as humility and welcome—entrance itself depends on turning to become like children. In that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Who then is greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven?” Matthew 18:1 Jesus called a little child to himself, and set him in the middle of them Matthew 18:2 and said, “Most certainly I tell you, unless you turn and become as little children, you will in no way enter into the Kingdom of Heaven. Matthew 18:3 Whoever therefore humbles himself as this little child is the greatest in the Kingdom of Heaven. Matthew 18:4 Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me, Matthew 18:5

title: Matthew 18:10–14
context: After warning against causing little ones who believe to stumble, Jesus forbids despising them and roots their dignity in the Father’s heavenly care. The parable of the lost sheep follows at once, showing His searching joy over recovering even one who has gone astray.
text: Matthew 18:10–14 Matthew After warning against causing little ones who believe to stumble, Jesus forbids despising them and roots their dignity in the Father’s heavenly care. The parable of the lost sheep follows at once, showing His searching joy over recovering even one who has gone astray. See that you don’t despise one of these little ones, for I tell you that in heaven their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven. Matthew 18:10 “What do you think? If a man has one hundred sheep, and one of them goes astray, doesn’t he leave the ninety-nine, go to the mountains, and seek that which has gone astray? Matthew 18:12 If he finds it, most certainly I tell you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine which have not gone astray. Matthew 18:13 Even so it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish. Matthew 18:14

title: Matthew 18:15–20
context: Jesus moves from seeking the stray sheep to ordered restoration among brothers. He maps private confrontation, witnesses, and church involvement—aimed at gaining the offender—then grounds the process in binding and loosing, corporate prayer, and His own presence with the gathered few.
text: Matthew 18:15–20 Matthew Jesus moves from seeking the stray sheep to ordered restoration among brothers. He maps private confrontation, witnesses, and church involvement—aimed at gaining the offender—then grounds the process in binding and loosing, corporate prayer, and His own presence with the gathered few. “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother. Matthew 18:15 But if he doesn’t listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established. Matthew 18:16 If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly. If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector. Matthew 18:17 Most certainly I tell you, whatever things you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever things you release on earth will have been released in heaven. Matthew 18:18 Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. Matthew 18:19 For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.” Matthew 18:20

title: Matthew 18:21–35
context: Peter asks how often a brother must be forgiven—seven times?—and Jesus answers with unlimited pardon, then tells the parable of the unmerciful servant. A king cancels an unpayable debt; the forgiven man throttles a fellow servant over a tiny sum; the master reverses mercy and warns that the heavenly Father will do likewise to those who will not forgive from the heart.
text: Matthew 18:21–35 Matthew Peter asks how often a brother must be forgiven—seven times?—and Jesus answers with unlimited pardon, then tells the parable of the unmerciful servant. A king cancels an unpayable debt; the forgiven man throttles a fellow servant over a tiny sum; the master reverses mercy and warns that the heavenly Father will do likewise to those who will not forgive from the heart. Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?” Matthew 18:21 Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven. Matthew 18:22 Therefore the Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants. Matthew 18:23 When he had begun to settle, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents. Matthew 18:24 But because he couldn’t pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, with his wife, his children, and all that he had, and payment to be made. Matthew 18:25 The servant therefore fell down and knelt before him, saying, ‘Lord, have patience with me, and I will repay you all!’ Matthew 18:26 The lord of that servant, being moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the debt. Matthew 18:27 “But that servant went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him one hundred denarii, and he grabbed him and took him by the throat, saying, ‘Pay me what you owe!’ Matthew 18:28 “So his fellow servant fell down at his feet and begged him, saying, ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you!’ Matthew 18:29 He would not, but went and cast him into prison until he should pay back that which was due. Matthew 18:30 So when his fellow servants saw what was done, they were exceedingly sorry, and came and told their lord all that was done. Matthew 18:31 Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me. Matthew 18:32 Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’ Matthew 18:33 His lord was angry, and delivered him to the tormentors until he should pay all that was due to him. Matthew 18:34 So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds.” Matthew 18:35

title: Matthew 18:6–9
context: Having set a child before the disciples and tied greatness to humble welcome, Jesus turns to those who harm “little ones who believe.” He pronounces severe judgment on causing them to stumble and calls His hearers to radical, costly dealing with whatever in themselves leads to sin.
text: Matthew 18:6–9 Matthew Having set a child before the disciples and tied greatness to humble welcome, Jesus turns to those who harm “little ones who believe.” He pronounces severe judgment on causing them to stumble and calls His hearers to radical, costly dealing with whatever in themselves leads to sin. but whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a huge millstone were hung around his neck and that he were sunk in the depths of the sea. Matthew 18:6 “Woe to the world because of occasions of stumbling! For it must be that the occasions come, but woe to that person through whom the occasion comes! Matthew 18:7 If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter into life maimed or crippled, rather than having two hands or two feet to be cast into the eternal fire. Matthew 18:8 If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you. It is better for you to enter into life with one eye, rather than having two eyes to be cast into the Gehenna of fire. Matthew 18:9

title: Matthew 19:1–12
context: Leaving Galilee for Judea beyond the Jordan, Jesus faces a Pharisee trap about divorce. He answers from creation’s one-flesh design, names hardness of heart behind Moses’ concession, and then speaks of kingdom celibacy as a gift not all can receive.
text: Matthew 19:1–12 Matthew Leaving Galilee for Judea beyond the Jordan, Jesus faces a Pharisee trap about divorce. He answers from creation’s one-flesh design, names hardness of heart behind Moses’ concession, and then speaks of kingdom celibacy as a gift not all can receive. When Jesus had finished these words, he departed from Galilee and came into the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan. Matthew 19:1 Great multitudes followed him, and he healed them there. Matthew 19:2 Pharisees came to him, testing him and saying, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?” Matthew 19:3 He answered, “Haven’t you read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, Matthew 19:4 and said, ‘For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall be joined to his wife; and the two shall become one flesh’? Matthew 19:5 So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.” Matthew 19:6 They asked him, “Why then did Moses command us to give her a certificate of divorce and divorce her?” Matthew 19:7 He said to them, “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it has not been so. Matthew 19:8 I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery; and he who marries her when she is divorced commits adultery.” Matthew 19:9 His disciples said to him, “If this is the case of the man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.” Matthew 19:10 But he said to them, “Not all men can receive this saying, but those to whom it is given. Matthew 19:11 For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the Kingdom of Heaven’s sake. He who is able to receive it, let him receive it.” Matthew 19:12

title: Matthew 19:13–15
context: Right after the hard word on marriage and kingdom celibacy, parents bring children for Jesus’ hands and prayer. The disciples push them back; Jesus welcomes the little ones and names them as kingdom people.
text: Matthew 19:13–15 Matthew Right after the hard word on marriage and kingdom celibacy, parents bring children for Jesus’ hands and prayer. The disciples push them back; Jesus welcomes the little ones and names them as kingdom people. Then little children were brought to him that he should lay his hands on them and pray; and the disciples rebuked them. Matthew 19:13 But Jesus said, “Allow the little children, and don’t forbid them to come to me; for the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to ones like these.” Matthew 19:14 He laid his hands on them, and departed from there. Matthew 19:15

title: Matthew 19:16–22
context: A wealthy young man asks Jesus what good deed wins eternal life. Jesus points him to the one who is good, rehearses neighbor-love commandments, exposes the lack beneath his claim of full obedience, and calls him to sell, give, and follow—after which he leaves sorrowful.
text: Matthew 19:16–22 Matthew A wealthy young man asks Jesus what good deed wins eternal life. Jesus points him to the one who is good, rehearses neighbor-love commandments, exposes the lack beneath his claim of full obedience, and calls him to sell, give, and follow—after which he leaves sorrowful. Behold, one came to him and said, “Good teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?” Matthew 19:16 He said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, that is, God. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.” Matthew 19:17 He said to him, “Which ones?” Jesus said, “‘You shall not murder.’ ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ ‘You shall not steal.’ ‘You shall not offer false testimony.’ Matthew 19:18 ‘Honor your father and your mother.’ And, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” Matthew 19:19 The young man said to him, “All these things I have observed from my youth. What do I still lack?” Matthew 19:20 Jesus said to him, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” Matthew 19:21 But when the young man heard this, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions. Matthew 19:22

title: Matthew 19:23–30
context: After the rich young man leaves, Jesus warns how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom, heightens the image to camel and needle, and answers the disciples’ despair: with man impossible, with God possible. Peter asks about their reward; Jesus promises thrones, hundredfold return, eternal life—and the reversal of first and last.
text: Matthew 19:23–30 Matthew After the rich young man leaves, Jesus warns how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom, heightens the image to camel and needle, and answers the disciples’ despair: with man impossible, with God possible. Peter asks about their reward; Jesus promises thrones, hundredfold return, eternal life—and the reversal of first and last. Jesus said to his disciples, “Most certainly I say to you, a rich man will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven with difficulty. Matthew 19:23 Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through a needle’s eye than for a rich man to enter into God’s Kingdom.” Matthew 19:24 When the disciples heard it, they were exceedingly astonished, saying, “Who then can be saved?” Matthew 19:25 Looking at them, Jesus said, “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” Matthew 19:26 Then Peter answered, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?” Matthew 19:27 Jesus said to them, “Most certainly I tell you that you who have followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of Man will sit on the throne of his glory, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. Matthew 19:28 Everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name’s sake, will receive one hundred times, and will inherit eternal life. Matthew 19:29 But many will be last who are first, and first who are last. Matthew 19:30

title: Matthew 2:1–12
context: After Jesus’ birth in Bethlehem, Gentile wise men follow a star to Jerusalem seeking the newborn King; Scripture points them to Bethlehem, Herod schemes, and the Magi worship the child with gifts before being warned home by another way.
text: Matthew 2:1–12 Matthew After Jesus’ birth in Bethlehem, Gentile wise men follow a star to Jerusalem seeking the newborn King; Scripture points them to Bethlehem, Herod schemes, and the Magi worship the child with gifts before being warned home by another way. Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, behold, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem, saying, Matthew 2:1 “Where is he who is born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east, and have come to worship him.” Matthew 2:2 When King Herod heard it, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. Matthew 2:3 Gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where the Christ would be born. Matthew 2:4 They said to him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for this is written through the prophet, Matthew 2:5 ‘You Bethlehem, land of Judah, are in no way least among the princes of Judah; for out of you shall come a governor who shall shepherd my people, Israel.’” Matthew 2:6 Then Herod secretly called the wise men, and learned from them exactly what time the star appeared. Matthew 2:7 He sent them to Bethlehem, and said, “Go and search diligently for the young child. When you have found him, bring me word, so that I also may come and worship him.” Matthew 2:8 They, having heard the king, went their way; and behold, the star, which they saw in the east, went before them until it came and stood over where the young child was. Matthew 2:9 When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. Matthew 2:10 They came into the house and saw the young child with Mary, his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Opening their treasures, they offered to him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Matthew 2:11 Being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country another way. Matthew 2:12

title: Matthew 2:13–15
context: After the Magi leave, an angel warns Joseph in a dream to flee to Egypt with the child and Mary; Joseph obeys by night, and Matthew hears in their sojourn the fulfillment of “Out of Egypt I called my son.”
text: Matthew 2:13–15 Matthew After the Magi leave, an angel warns Joseph in a dream to flee to Egypt with the child and Mary; Joseph obeys by night, and Matthew hears in their sojourn the fulfillment of “Out of Egypt I called my son.” Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying, “Arise and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.” Matthew 2:13 He arose and took the young child and his mother by night and departed into Egypt, Matthew 2:14 and was there until the death of Herod, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying, “Out of Egypt I called my son.” Matthew 2:15

title: Matthew 2:16–18
context: When Herod realizes the Magi will not return, he erupts in rage and slaughters the boys of Bethlehem; Matthew frames the horror with Jeremiah’s lament of Rachel weeping for her children.
text: Matthew 2:16–18 Matthew When Herod realizes the Magi will not return, he erupts in rage and slaughters the boys of Bethlehem; Matthew frames the horror with Jeremiah’s lament of Rachel weeping for her children. Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked by the wise men, was exceedingly angry, and sent out and killed all the male children who were in Bethlehem and in all the surrounding countryside, from two years old and under, according to the exact time which he had learned from the wise men. Matthew 2:16 Then that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled, saying, Matthew 2:17 “A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children; she wouldn’t be comforted, because they are no more.” Matthew 2:18

title: Matthew 2:19–23
context: After Herod’s death, an angel tells Joseph to return to Israel; fearing Archelaus, Joseph is warned again and settles in Nazareth, fulfilling the word that the Messiah will be called a Nazarene.
text: Matthew 2:19–23 Matthew After Herod’s death, an angel tells Joseph to return to Israel; fearing Archelaus, Joseph is warned again and settles in Nazareth, fulfilling the word that the Messiah will be called a Nazarene. But when Herod was dead, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying, Matthew 2:19 “Arise and take the young child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel, for those who sought the young child’s life are dead.” Matthew 2:20 He arose and took the young child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel. Matthew 2:21 But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in the place of his father, Herod, he was afraid to go there. Being warned in a dream, he withdrew into the region of Galilee, Matthew 2:22 and came and lived in a city called Nazareth; that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophets that he will be called a Nazarene. Matthew 2:23

title: Matthew 20:1–16
context: After promising reward to those who left all to follow Him, Jesus tells the vineyard parable: a Master hires laborers at every hour and pays the last the same as the first. The point lands on grace, generosity, and the warning that the last will be first—and the first last.
text: Matthew 20:1–16 Matthew After promising reward to those who left all to follow Him, Jesus tells the vineyard parable: a Master hires laborers at every hour and pays the last the same as the first. The point lands on grace, generosity, and the warning that the last will be first—and the first last. “For the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who was the master of a household, who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. Matthew 20:1 When he had agreed with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. Matthew 20:2 He went out about the third hour, and saw others standing idle in the marketplace. Matthew 20:3 He said to them, ‘You also go into the vineyard, and whatever is right I will give you.’ So they went their way. Matthew 20:4 Again he went out about the sixth and the ninth hour, and did likewise. Matthew 20:5 About the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing idle. He said to them, ‘Why do you stand here all day idle?’ Matthew 20:6 “They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’ “He said to them, ‘You also go into the vineyard, and you will receive whatever is right.’ Matthew 20:7 “When evening had come, the lord of the vineyard said to his manager, ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning from the last to the first.’ Matthew 20:8 “When those who were hired at about the eleventh hour came, they each received a denarius. Matthew 20:9 When the first came, they supposed that they would receive more; and they likewise each received a denarius. Matthew 20:10 When they received it, they murmured against the master of the household, Matthew 20:11 saying, ‘These last have spent one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat!’ Matthew 20:12 “But he answered one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Didn’t you agree with me for a denarius? Matthew 20:13 Take that which is yours, and go your way. It is my desire to give to this last just as much as to you. Matthew 20:14 Isn’t it lawful for me to do what I want to with what I own? Or is your eye evil, because I am good?’ Matthew 20:15 So the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.” Matthew 20:16

title: Matthew 20:17–19
context: On the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus takes the Twelve aside for a third, sharper passion prediction: delivery to Jewish leaders, Gentile mockery and crucifixion, and resurrection on the third day—setting the cross before the disciples’ ambitions that follow.
text: Matthew 20:17–19 Matthew On the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus takes the Twelve aside for a third, sharper passion prediction: delivery to Jewish leaders, Gentile mockery and crucifixion, and resurrection on the third day—setting the cross before the disciples’ ambitions that follow. As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, Matthew 20:17 “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death, Matthew 20:18 and will hand him over to the Gentiles to mock, to scourge, and to crucify; and the third day he will be raised up.” Matthew 20:19

title: Matthew 20:20–28
context: Right after the third passion prediction, the mother of Zebedee’s sons seeks thrones beside Jesus. He answers with the cup, the Father’s preparation of places, and a call to servant greatness—climaxing in the Son of Man who came to serve and give His life as a ransom for many.
text: Matthew 20:20–28 Matthew Right after the third passion prediction, the mother of Zebedee’s sons seeks thrones beside Jesus. He answers with the cup, the Father’s preparation of places, and a call to servant greatness—climaxing in the Son of Man who came to serve and give His life as a ransom for many. Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, kneeling and asking a certain thing of him. Matthew 20:20 He said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Command that these, my two sons, may sit, one on your right hand and one on your left hand, in your Kingdom.” Matthew 20:21 But Jesus answered, “You don’t know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink, and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with?” They said to him, “We are able.” Matthew 20:22 He said to them, “You will indeed drink my cup, and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with; but to sit on my right hand and on my left hand is not mine to give, but it is for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” Matthew 20:23 When the ten heard it, they were indignant with the two brothers. Matthew 20:24 But Jesus summoned them, and said, “You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. Matthew 20:25 It shall not be so among you; but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Matthew 20:26 Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, Matthew 20:27 even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” Matthew 20:28

title: Matthew 20:29–34
context: Leaving Jericho with a great crowd, Jesus meets two blind men who cry out for mercy as Son of David. Rebuked by the crowd, they cry louder; He stops, asks what they want, touches their eyes in pity, and they see and follow Him.
text: Matthew 20:29–34 Matthew Leaving Jericho with a great crowd, Jesus meets two blind men who cry out for mercy as Son of David. Rebuked by the crowd, they cry louder; He stops, asks what they want, touches their eyes in pity, and they see and follow Him. As they went out from Jericho, a great multitude followed him. Matthew 20:29 Behold, two blind men sitting by the road, when they heard that Jesus was passing by, cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, you son of David!” Matthew 20:30 The multitude rebuked them, telling them that they should be quiet, but they cried out even more, “Lord, have mercy on us, you son of David!” Matthew 20:31 Jesus stood still and called them, and asked, “What do you want me to do for you?” Matthew 20:32 They told him, “Lord, that our eyes may be opened.” Matthew 20:33 Jesus, being moved with compassion, touched their eyes; and immediately their eyes received their sight, and they followed him. Matthew 20:34

title: Matthew 21:1–11
context: Jesus draws near Jerusalem from Bethphage and the Mount of Olives at the start of Passion Week. He enters the city as Zechariah’s humble King—hailed by crowds, soon to confront the temple—so that readers see royal claim and cross-bound purpose together.
text: Matthew 21:1–11 Matthew Jesus draws near Jerusalem from Bethphage and the Mount of Olives at the start of Passion Week. He enters the city as Zechariah’s humble King—hailed by crowds, soon to confront the temple—so that readers see royal claim and cross-bound purpose together. When they came near to Jerusalem and came to Bethsphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, Matthew 21:1 saying to them, “Go into the village that is opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me. Matthew 21:2 If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, ‘The Lord needs them,’ and immediately he will send them.” Matthew 21:3 All this was done that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet, saying, Matthew 21:4 “Tell the daughter of Zion, behold, your King comes to you, humble, and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.” Matthew 21:5 The disciples went and did just as Jesus commanded them, Matthew 21:6 and brought the donkey and the colt and laid their clothes on them; and he sat on them. Matthew 21:7 A very great multitude spread their clothes on the road. Others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. Matthew 21:8 The multitudes who went in front of him, and those who followed, kept shouting, “Hosanna to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!” Matthew 21:9 When he had come into Jerusalem, all the city was stirred up, saying, “Who is this?” Matthew 21:10 The multitudes said, “This is the prophet, Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.” Matthew 21:11

title: Matthew 21:12–17
context: After entering Jerusalem as Zechariah’s King, Jesus goes straight to the temple. He drives out commerce, heals the blind and lame, and receives the children’s Hosanna—while priests and scribes grow indignant—so Passion Week begins with cleansing, mercy, and contested praise.
text: Matthew 21:12–17 Matthew After entering Jerusalem as Zechariah’s King, Jesus goes straight to the temple. He drives out commerce, heals the blind and lame, and receives the children’s Hosanna—while priests and scribes grow indignant—so Passion Week begins with cleansing, mercy, and contested praise. Jesus entered into the temple of God and drove out all of those who sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the money changers’ tables and the seats of those who sold the doves. Matthew 21:12 He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers!” Matthew 21:13 The lame and the blind came to him in the temple, and he healed them. Matthew 21:14 But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children who were crying in the temple and saying, “Hosanna to the son of David!” they were indignant, Matthew 21:15 and said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” Jesus said to them, “Yes. Did you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of children and nursing babies, you have perfected praise’?” Matthew 21:16 He left them and went out of the city to Bethany, and camped there. Matthew 21:17

title: Matthew 21:18–22
context: The morning after the temple confrontation, Jesus returns toward Jerusalem hungry, curses a leafy but fruitless fig tree, and teaches the marveling disciples about faith that does not doubt and prayer that receives—linking judgment on barren religion with a call to living trust.
text: Matthew 21:18–22 Matthew The morning after the temple confrontation, Jesus returns toward Jerusalem hungry, curses a leafy but fruitless fig tree, and teaches the marveling disciples about faith that does not doubt and prayer that receives—linking judgment on barren religion with a call to living trust. Now in the morning, as he returned to the city, he was hungry. Matthew 21:18 Seeing a fig tree by the road, he came to it and found nothing on it but leaves. He said to it, “Let there be no fruit from you forever!” Immediately the fig tree withered away. Matthew 21:19 When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, “How did the fig tree immediately wither away?” Matthew 21:20 Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, if you have faith and don’t doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you told this mountain, ‘Be taken up and cast into the sea,’ it would be done. Matthew 21:21 All things, whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive.” Matthew 21:22

title: Matthew 21:23–27
context: Back in the temple, chief priests and elders challenge Jesus’ authority while He teaches. He answers with a question about John’s baptism; trapped between heaven’s claim and fear of the crowd, they plead ignorance—and He withholds further disclosure of His authority.
text: Matthew 21:23–27 Matthew Back in the temple, chief priests and elders challenge Jesus’ authority while He teaches. He answers with a question about John’s baptism; trapped between heaven’s claim and fear of the crowd, they plead ignorance—and He withholds further disclosure of His authority. When he had come into the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came to him as he was teaching, and said, “By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?” Matthew 21:23 Jesus answered them, “I also will ask you one question, which if you tell me, I likewise will tell you by what authority I do these things. Matthew 21:24 The baptism of John, where was it from? From heaven or from men?” They reasoned with themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will ask us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ Matthew 21:25 But if we say, ‘From men,’ we fear the multitude, for all hold John as a prophet.” Matthew 21:26 They answered Jesus, and said, “We don’t know.” He also said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. Matthew 21:27

title: Matthew 21:28–32
context: Still answering the temple leaders, Jesus tells the parable of the two sons: one refuses then goes; the other agrees then stays away. Saying yes is not the same as doing the Father’s will—and surprising repentant sinners enter the kingdom ahead of those who refused John’s light.
text: Matthew 21:28–32 Matthew Still answering the temple leaders, Jesus tells the parable of the two sons: one refuses then goes; the other agrees then stays away. Saying yes is not the same as doing the Father’s will—and surprising repentant sinners enter the kingdom ahead of those who refused John’s light. But what do you think? A man had two sons, and he came to the first, and said, ‘Son, go work today in my vineyard.’ Matthew 21:28 He answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind, and went. Matthew 21:29 He came to the second, and said the same thing. He answered, ‘I’m going, sir,’ but he didn’t go. Matthew 21:30 Which of the two did the will of his father?” They said to him, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Most certainly I tell you that the tax collectors and the prostitutes are entering into God’s Kingdom before you. Matthew 21:31 For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you didn’t believe him; but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. When you saw it, you didn’t even repent afterward, that you might believe him. Matthew 21:32

title: Matthew 21:33–46
context: Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants: a master plants a vineyard, leases it, and sends servants—then his son—for fruit. The tenants beat, kill, and finally murder the heir. Citing Psalm 118, Jesus warns that the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, and the kingdom will be taken from fruitless leaders and will be given to a nation who produce its fruits.
text: Matthew 21:33–46 Matthew Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants: a master plants a vineyard, leases it, and sends servants—then his son—for fruit. The tenants beat, kill, and finally murder the heir. Citing Psalm 118, Jesus warns that the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, and the kingdom will be taken from fruitless leaders and will be given to a nation who produce its fruits. “Hear another parable. There was a man who was a master of a household who planted a vineyard, set a hedge about it, dug a wine press in it, built a tower, leased it out to farmers, and went into another country. Matthew 21:33 When the season for the fruit came near, he sent his servants to the farmers to receive his fruit. Matthew 21:34 The farmers took his servants, beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Matthew 21:35 Again, he sent other servants more than the first; and they treated them the same way. Matthew 21:36 But afterward he sent to them his son, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ Matthew 21:37 But the farmers, when they saw the son, said among themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let’s kill him and seize his inheritance.’ Matthew 21:38 So they took him and threw him out of the vineyard, then killed him. Matthew 21:39 When therefore the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those farmers?” Matthew 21:40 They told him, “He will miserably destroy those miserable men, and will lease out the vineyard to other farmers who will give him the fruit in its season.” Matthew 21:41 Jesus said to them, “Did you never read in the Scriptures, ‘The stone which the builders rejected was made the head of the corner. This was from the Lord. It is marvelous in our eyes’? Matthew 21:42 “Therefore I tell you, God’s Kingdom will be taken away from you and will be given to a nation producing its fruit. Matthew 21:43 He who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but on whomever it will fall, it will scatter him as dust.” Matthew 21:44 When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he spoke about them. Matthew 21:45 When they sought to seize him, they feared the multitudes, because they considered him to be a prophet. Matthew 21:46

title: Matthew 22:1–14
context: Still in the temple courts after the vineyard parable, Jesus answers hostile leaders with another kingdom parable: a royal wedding feast. Refusal, judgment, wide invitation, and the wedding garment press both the sincerity of the call and the seriousness of coming on the King’s terms.
text: Matthew 22:1–14 Matthew Still in the temple courts after the vineyard parable, Jesus answers hostile leaders with another kingdom parable: a royal wedding feast. Refusal, judgment, wide invitation, and the wedding garment press both the sincerity of the call and the seriousness of coming on the King’s terms. Jesus answered and spoke to them again in parables, saying, Matthew 22:1 “The Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king, who made a wedding feast for his son, Matthew 22:2 and sent out his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. Matthew 22:3 Again he sent out other servants, saying, ‘Tell those who are invited, “Behold, I have prepared my dinner. My cattle and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready. Come to the wedding feast!”’ Matthew 22:4 But they made light of it, and went their ways, one to his own farm, another to his merchandise; Matthew 22:5 and the rest grabbed his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them. Matthew 22:6 When the king heard that, he was angry, and sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city. Matthew 22:7 “Then he said to his servants, ‘The wedding is ready, but those who were invited weren’t worthy. Matthew 22:8 Go therefore to the intersections of the highways, and as many as you may find, invite to the wedding feast.’ Matthew 22:9 Those servants went out into the highways and gathered together as many as they found, both bad and good. The wedding was filled with guests. Matthew 22:10 “But when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man who didn’t have on wedding clothing, Matthew 22:11 and he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you come in here not wearing wedding clothing?’ He was speechless. Matthew 22:12 Then the king said to the servants, ‘Bind him hand and foot, take him away, and throw him into the outer darkness. That is where the weeping and grinding of teeth will be.’ Matthew 22:13 For many are called, but few chosen.” Matthew 22:14

title: Matthew 22:15–22
context: Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus on the poll tax. His answer—“render to Caesar… and to God”—exposes bad faith, affirms civil duty without surrendering worship, and leaves opponents marveling as Passion Week tension rises.
text: Matthew 22:15–22 Matthew Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus on the poll tax. His answer—“render to Caesar… and to God”—exposes bad faith, affirms civil duty without surrendering worship, and leaves opponents marveling as Passion Week tension rises. Then the Pharisees went and took counsel how they might entrap him in his talk. Matthew 22:15 They sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that you are honest, and teach the way of God in truth, no matter whom you teach; for you aren’t partial to anyone. Matthew 22:16 Tell us therefore, what do you think? Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?” Matthew 22:17 But Jesus perceived their wickedness, and said, “Why do you test me, you hypocrites? Matthew 22:18 Show me the tax money.” They brought to him a denarius. Matthew 22:19 He asked them, “Whose is this image and inscription?” Matthew 22:20 They said to him, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Matthew 22:21 When they heard it, they marveled, and left him and went away. Matthew 22:22

title: Matthew 22:23–33
context: Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a levirate-marriage riddle to discredit life after death. Jesus corrects their view of the age to come, grounds hope in God’s power and the Scriptures, and silences them before the listening crowds.
text: Matthew 22:23–33 Matthew Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a levirate-marriage riddle to discredit life after death. Jesus corrects their view of the age to come, grounds hope in God’s power and the Scriptures, and silences them before the listening crowds. On that day Sadducees (those who say that there is no resurrection) came to him. They asked him, Matthew 22:23 saying, “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife and raise up offspring for his brother.’ Matthew 22:24 Now there were with us seven brothers. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. Matthew 22:25 In the same way, the second also, and the third, to the seventh. Matthew 22:26 After them all, the woman died. Matthew 22:27 In the resurrection therefore, whose wife will she be of the seven? For they all had her.” Matthew 22:28 But Jesus answered them, “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God. Matthew 22:29 For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like God’s angels in heaven. Matthew 22:30 But concerning the resurrection of the dead, haven’t you read that which was spoken to you by God, saying, Matthew 22:31 ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” Matthew 22:32 When the multitudes heard it, they were astonished at his teaching. Matthew 22:33

title: Matthew 22:34–40
context: After Jesus silences the Sadducees, Pharisees test Him with the greatest-commandment question. He answers with whole-person love for God (Deut 6:5) and neighbor-love like self (Lev 19:18), hanging all the Law and the Prophets on these two.
text: Matthew 22:34–40 Matthew After Jesus silences the Sadducees, Pharisees test Him with the greatest-commandment question. He answers with whole-person love for God (Deut 6:5) and neighbor-love like self (Lev 19:18), hanging all the Law and the Prophets on these two. But the Pharisees, when they heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, gathered themselves together. Matthew 22:34 One of them, a lawyer, asked him a question, testing him. Matthew 22:35 “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?” Matthew 22:36 Jesus said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ Matthew 22:37 This is the first and great commandment. Matthew 22:38 A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Matthew 22:39 The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.” Matthew 22:40

title: Matthew 22:41–46
context: Jesus turns the examination on the Pharisees: whose son is the Christ? Psalm 110:1 shows David calling the Messiah “Lord,” so the Son of David is more than a mere descendant. No one dares ask Him another question.
text: Matthew 22:41–46 Matthew Jesus turns the examination on the Pharisees: whose son is the Christ? Psalm 110:1 shows David calling the Messiah “Lord,” so the Son of David is more than a mere descendant. No one dares ask Him another question. Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, Matthew 22:41 saying, “What do you think of the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “Of David.” Matthew 22:42 He said to them, “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying, Matthew 22:43 ‘The Lord said to my Lord, sit on my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet’? Matthew 22:44 “If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” Matthew 22:45 No one was able to answer him a word, neither did any man dare ask him any more questions from that day forward. Matthew 22:46

title: Matthew 23:1–12
context: Still in the temple courts during Passion Week, Jesus turns from sparring with leaders to address the crowds and His disciples. Before the seven woes, He names the scribes’ and Pharisees’ teaching seat, exposes hypocrisy and honor-seeking, and sets the church’s posture: one Teacher, one Father, greatness as service, exaltation through humility.
text: Matthew 23:1–12 Matthew Still in the temple courts during Passion Week, Jesus turns from sparring with leaders to address the crowds and His disciples. Before the seven woes, He names the scribes’ and Pharisees’ teaching seat, exposes hypocrisy and honor-seeking, and sets the church’s posture: one Teacher, one Father, greatness as service, exaltation through humility. Then Jesus spoke to the multitudes and to his disciples, Matthew 23:1 saying, “The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Matthew 23:2 All things therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do, but don’t do their works; for they say, and don’t do. Matthew 23:3 For they bind heavy burdens that are grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not lift a finger to help them. Matthew 23:4 But they do all their works to be seen by men. They make their phylacteries broad and enlarge the fringes of their garments, Matthew 23:5 and love the place of honor at feasts, the best seats in the synagogues, Matthew 23:6 the salutations in the marketplaces, and to be called ‘Rabbi, Rabbi’ by men. Matthew 23:7 But you are not to be called ‘Rabbi’, for one is your teacher, the Christ, and all of you are brothers. Matthew 23:8 Call no man on the earth your father, for one is your Father, he who is in heaven. Matthew 23:9 Neither be called masters, for one is your master, the Christ. Matthew 23:10 But he who is greatest among you will be your servant. Matthew 23:11 Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Matthew 23:12

title: Matthew 23:13–15
context: After exposing honor-seeking religion, Jesus opens the seven woes. The first strike hypocrisy that blocks the kingdom and mission that multiplies ruin. (Verse 14, the widows’-houses woe found in many later manuscripts, is not treated in these notes.)
text: Matthew 23:13–15 Matthew After exposing honor-seeking religion, Jesus opens the seven woes. The first strike hypocrisy that blocks the kingdom and mission that multiplies ruin. (Verse 14, the widows’-houses woe found in many later manuscripts, is not treated in these notes.) “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you devour widows’ houses, and as a pretense you make long prayers. Therefore you will receive greater condemnation. Matthew 23:13 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel around by sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves. Matthew 23:15

title: Matthew 23:16–22
context: Jesus continues the woes against casuistry that ranks oaths by gold and gifts while sidelining temple, altar, and God. Blind guides invent loopholes; He restores the sacred order that ends at the throne.
text: Matthew 23:16–22 Matthew Jesus continues the woes against casuistry that ranks oaths by gold and gifts while sidelining temple, altar, and God. Blind guides invent loopholes; He restores the sacred order that ends at the throne. “Woe to you, you blind guides, who say, ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple, he is obligated.’ Matthew 23:16 You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? Matthew 23:17 And, ‘Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is on it, he is obligated.’ Matthew 23:18 You blind fools! For which is greater, the gift, or the altar that sanctifies the gift? Matthew 23:19 He therefore who swears by the altar, swears by it and by everything on it. Matthew 23:20 He who swears by the temple, swears by it and by him who has been living in it. Matthew 23:21 He who swears by heaven, swears by the throne of God and by him who sits on it. Matthew 23:22

title: Matthew 23:23–28
context: Mid-woes: tithing herbs while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness; cleaning cups and tombs while greed and lawlessness fill the inside. Jesus demands weightier obedience and inward purity, not cosmetic religion.
text: Matthew 23:23–28 Matthew Mid-woes: tithing herbs while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness; cleaning cups and tombs while greed and lawlessness fill the inside. Jesus demands weightier obedience and inward purity, not cosmetic religion. “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have left undone the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith. But you ought to have done these, and not to have left the other undone. Matthew 23:23 You blind guides, who strain out a gnat, and swallow a camel! Matthew 23:24 “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and unrighteousness. Matthew 23:25 You blind Pharisee, first clean the inside of the cup and of the platter, that its outside may become clean also. Matthew 23:26 “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitened tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones and of all uncleanness. Matthew 23:27 Even so you also outwardly appear righteous to men, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity. Matthew 23:28

title: Matthew 23:29–36
context: Final woe: decorating prophets’ tombs while sharing the fathers’ murderous line. Jesus sends prophets, wise men, and scribes they will kill; righteous blood from Abel to Zechariah comes on this generation.
text: Matthew 23:29–36 Matthew Final woe: decorating prophets’ tombs while sharing the fathers’ murderous line. Jesus sends prophets, wise men, and scribes they will kill; righteous blood from Abel to Zechariah comes on this generation. “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the tombs of the righteous, Matthew 23:29 and say, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we wouldn’t have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets.’ Matthew 23:30 Therefore you testify to yourselves that you are children of those who killed the prophets. Matthew 23:31 Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers. Matthew 23:32 You serpents, you offspring of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna? Matthew 23:33 Therefore, behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes. Some of them you will kill and crucify; and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city, Matthew 23:34 that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zachariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the sanctuary and the altar. Matthew 23:35 Most certainly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation. Matthew 23:36

title: Matthew 23:37–39
context: After the woes, Jesus laments Jerusalem: prophetic killers whom He longed to gather as a hen gathers her chicks—yet they were not willing. The house is left desolate until the city blesses the Coming One.
text: Matthew 23:37–39 Matthew After the woes, Jesus laments Jerusalem: prophetic killers whom He longed to gather as a hen gathers her chicks—yet they were not willing. The house is left desolate until the city blesses the Coming One. “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her! How often I would have gathered your children together, even as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not! Matthew 23:37 Behold, your house is left to you desolate. Matthew 23:38 For I tell you, you will not see me from now on, until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’” Matthew 23:39

title: Matthew 24:1–14
context: Leaving the temple after the woes of chapter 23, Jesus predicts its total ruin. On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask about timing, His coming, and the end of the age. He answers first with pastoral warnings: deception, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, cold love—and the gospel’s worldwide witness. These are birth pains, not yet the end; endurance and proclamation mark His people until the end comes.
text: Matthew 24:1–14 Matthew Leaving the temple after the woes of chapter 23, Jesus predicts its total ruin. On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask about timing, His coming, and the end of the age. He answers first with pastoral warnings: deception, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, cold love—and the gospel’s worldwide witness. These are birth pains, not yet the end; endurance and proclamation mark His people until the end comes. Jesus went out from the temple, and was going on his way. His disciples came to him to show him the buildings of the temple. Matthew 24:1 But he answered them, “You see all of these things, don’t you? Most certainly I tell you, there will not be left here one stone on another, that will not be thrown down.” Matthew 24:2 As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately, saying, “Tell us, when will these things be? What is the sign of your coming, and of the end of the age?” Matthew 24:3 Jesus answered them, “Be careful that no one leads you astray. Matthew 24:4 For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and will lead many astray. Matthew 24:5 You will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you aren’t troubled, for all this must happen, but the end is not yet. Matthew 24:6 For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there will be famines, plagues, and earthquakes in various places. Matthew 24:7 But all these things are the beginning of birth pains. Matthew 24:8 “Then they will deliver you up to oppression and will kill you. You will be hated by all of the nations for my name’s sake. Matthew 24:9 Then many will stumble, and will deliver up one another, and will hate one another. Matthew 24:10 Many false prophets will arise and will lead many astray. Matthew 24:11 Because iniquity will be multiplied, the love of many will grow cold. Matthew 24:12 But he who endures to the end will be saved. Matthew 24:13 This Good News of the Kingdom will be preached in the whole world for a testimony to all the nations, and then the end will come. Matthew 24:14

title: Matthew 24:15–28
context: Still on Olivet, Jesus turns from birth pains to a sharper crisis: Daniel’s abomination in the holy place, urgent flight from Judea, unmatched tribulation shortened for the elect, and a fresh wave of false christs with signs. He tells them beforehand so they will not chase wilderness rumors or inner-room sightings. His own coming will be as public as lightning from east to west.
text: Matthew 24:15–28 Matthew Still on Olivet, Jesus turns from birth pains to a sharper crisis: Daniel’s abomination in the holy place, urgent flight from Judea, unmatched tribulation shortened for the elect, and a fresh wave of false christs with signs. He tells them beforehand so they will not chase wilderness rumors or inner-room sightings. His own coming will be as public as lightning from east to west. “When, therefore, you see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of through Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), Matthew 24:15 then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Matthew 24:16 Let him who is on the housetop not go down to take out the things that are in his house. Matthew 24:17 Let him who is in the field not return back to get his clothes. Matthew 24:18 But woe to those who are with child and to nursing mothers in those days! Matthew 24:19 Pray that your flight will not be in the winter nor on a Sabbath, Matthew 24:20 for then there will be great suffering, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, no, nor ever will be. Matthew 24:21 Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would have been saved. But for the sake of the chosen ones, those days will be shortened. Matthew 24:22 “Then if any man tells you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ!’ or, ‘There!’ don’t believe it. Matthew 24:23 For false christs and false prophets will arise, and they will show great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the chosen ones. Matthew 24:24 “Behold, I have told you beforehand. Matthew 24:25 “If therefore they tell you, ‘Behold, he is in the wilderness,’ don’t go out; or ‘Behold, he is in the inner rooms,’ don’t believe it. Matthew 24:26 For as the lightning flashes from the east, and is seen even to the west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be. Matthew 24:27 For wherever the carcass is, that is where the vultures gather together. Matthew 24:28

title: Matthew 24:29–31
context: After the suffering of those days, Jesus describes cosmic shaking, the sign of the Son of Man, worldwide mourning, and His cloud-coming in power and glory. Angels with trumpet gather together his chosen ones from the four winds—public, royal, and final for the hope of His people.
text: Matthew 24:29–31 Matthew After the suffering of those days, Jesus describes cosmic shaking, the sign of the Son of Man, worldwide mourning, and His cloud-coming in power and glory. Angels with trumpet gather together his chosen ones from the four winds—public, royal, and final for the hope of His people. “But immediately after the suffering of those days, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken; Matthew 24:29 and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the sky. Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of the sky with power and great glory. Matthew 24:30 He will send out his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they will gather together his chosen ones from the four winds, from one end of the sky to the other. Matthew 24:31

title: Matthew 24:32–35
context: Jesus adds the fig-tree lesson: tender branch and leaves mean summer is near; likewise “all these things” mean He is near, even at the gates. He seals it with a solemn “Certainly” about this generation and the unmatched permanence of His words over heaven and earth.
text: Matthew 24:32–35 Matthew Jesus adds the fig-tree lesson: tender branch and leaves mean summer is near; likewise “all these things” mean He is near, even at the gates. He seals it with a solemn “Certainly” about this generation and the unmatched permanence of His words over heaven and earth. “Now from the fig tree learn this parable: When its branch has now become tender and produces its leaves, you know that the summer is near. Matthew 24:32 Even so you also, when you see all these things, know that he is near, even at the doors. Matthew 24:33 Most certainly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things are accomplished. Matthew 24:34 Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. Matthew 24:35

title: Matthew 24:36–44
context: Jesus turns to the unknown day and hour: angels do not know it, nor the Son, but the Father only. The days of Noah picture ordinary life interrupted by sudden judgment. Separation scenes and a thief-in-the-night image press one charge—stay awake and be ready, for in an hour that you don’t expect, the Son of Man comes at an unexpected hour.
text: Matthew 24:36–44 Matthew Jesus turns to the unknown day and hour: angels do not know it, nor the Son, but the Father only. The days of Noah picture ordinary life interrupted by sudden judgment. Separation scenes and a thief-in-the-night image press one charge—stay awake and be ready, for in an hour that you don’t expect, the Son of Man comes at an unexpected hour. “But no one knows of that day and hour, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father only. Matthew 24:36 As the days of Noah were, so will the coming of the Son of Man be. Matthew 24:37 For as in those days which were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ship, Matthew 24:38 and they didn’t know until the flood came and took them all away, so will the coming of the Son of Man be. Matthew 24:39 Then two men will be in the field: one will be taken and one will be left. Matthew 24:40 Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken and one will be left. Matthew 24:41 Watch therefore, for you don’t know in what hour your Lord comes. Matthew 24:42 But know this, that if the master of the house had known in what watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have watched, and would not have allowed his house to be broken into. Matthew 24:43 Therefore also be ready, for in an hour that you don’t expect, the Son of Man will come. Matthew 24:44

title: Matthew 24:45–51
context: Jesus closes the chapter with the faithful and wise servant set over the household to feed others in season, versus the wicked servant who assumes delay, abuses peers, and joins drunkards. Blessing and promotion meet the found-doing servant; sudden return, dismembering judgment, and hypocrites’ weeping meet the wicked one—bridge into chapter 25’s readiness parables.
text: Matthew 24:45–51 Matthew Jesus closes the chapter with the faithful and wise servant set over the household to feed others in season, versus the wicked servant who assumes delay, abuses peers, and joins drunkards. Blessing and promotion meet the found-doing servant; sudden return, dismembering judgment, and hypocrites’ weeping meet the wicked one—bridge into chapter 25’s readiness parables. “Who then is the faithful and wise servant, whom his lord has set over his household, to give them their food in due season? Matthew 24:45 Blessed is that servant whom his lord finds doing so when he comes. Matthew 24:46 Most certainly I tell you that he will set him over all that he has. Matthew 24:47 But if that evil servant should say in his heart, ‘My lord is delaying his coming,’ Matthew 24:48 and begins to beat his fellow servants, and eat and drink with the drunkards, Matthew 24:49 the lord of that servant will come in a day when he doesn’t expect it and in an hour when he doesn’t know it, Matthew 24:50 and will cut him in pieces and appoint his portion with the hypocrites. That is where the weeping and grinding of teeth will be. Matthew 24:51

title: Matthew 25:1–13
context: Still answering the disciples’ watchfulness questions from chapter 24, Jesus pictures the kingdom as ten virgins awaiting a delayed bridegroom. Wisdom and folly turn on oil ready before the midnight cry; those prepared enter the feast, the door shuts, and the refrain returns: watch, for you don’t know the day nor the hour.
text: Matthew 25:1–13 Matthew Still answering the disciples’ watchfulness questions from chapter 24, Jesus pictures the kingdom as ten virgins awaiting a delayed bridegroom. Wisdom and folly turn on oil ready before the midnight cry; those prepared enter the feast, the door shuts, and the refrain returns: watch, for you don’t know the day nor the hour. “Then the Kingdom of Heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. Matthew 25:1 Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. Matthew 25:2 Those who were foolish, when they took their lamps, took no oil with them, Matthew 25:3 but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps. Matthew 25:4 Now while the bridegroom delayed, they all slumbered and slept. Matthew 25:5 But at midnight there was a cry, ‘Behold! The bridegroom is coming! Come out to meet him!’ Matthew 25:6 Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps. Matthew 25:7 The foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’ Matthew 25:8 But the wise answered, saying, ‘What if there isn’t enough for us and you? You go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.’ Matthew 25:9 While they went away to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut. Matthew 25:10 Afterward the other virgins also came, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’ Matthew 25:11 But he answered, ‘Most certainly I tell you, I don’t know you.’ Matthew 25:12 Watch therefore, for you don’t know the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming. Matthew 25:13

title: Matthew 25:14–30
context: Jesus continues the readiness theme with a journeying master who entrusts unequal talents according to ability, then returns after a long time to settle accounts. Faithful servants enter the master’s joy; the fearful, idle servant loses even what he hid and is cast into outer darkness—stewardship under delayed return.
text: Matthew 25:14–30 Matthew Jesus continues the readiness theme with a journeying master who entrusts unequal talents according to ability, then returns after a long time to settle accounts. Faithful servants enter the master’s joy; the fearful, idle servant loses even what he hid and is cast into outer darkness—stewardship under delayed return. “For it is like a man going into another country, who called his own servants and entrusted his goods to them. Matthew 25:14 To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his own ability. Then he went on his journey. Matthew 25:15 Immediately he who received the five talents went and traded with them, and made another five talents. Matthew 25:16 In the same way, he also who got the two gained another two. Matthew 25:17 But he who received the one talent went away and dug in the earth and hid his lord’s money. Matthew 25:18 “Now after a long time the lord of those servants came, and settled accounts with them. Matthew 25:19 He who received the five talents came and brought another five talents, saying, ‘Lord, you delivered to me five talents. Behold, I have gained another five talents in addition to them.’ Matthew 25:20 “His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’ Matthew 25:21 “He also who got the two talents came and said, ‘Lord, you delivered to me two talents. Behold, I have gained another two talents in addition to them.’ Matthew 25:22 “His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things. I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’ Matthew 25:23 “He also who had received the one talent came and said, ‘Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man, reaping where you didn’t sow, and gathering where you didn’t scatter. Matthew 25:24 I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.’ Matthew 25:25 “But his lord answered him, ‘You wicked and slothful servant. You knew that I reap where I didn’t sow, and gather where I didn’t scatter. Matthew 25:26 You ought therefore to have deposited my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received back my own with interest. Matthew 25:27 Take away therefore the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten talents. Matthew 25:28 For to everyone who has will be given, and he will have abundance, but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away. Matthew 25:29 Throw out the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ Matthew 25:30

title: Matthew 25:31–46
context: Jesus ends the discourse with the Son of Man in glory, angels, and a throne of judgment over all nations. Sheep and goats are separated; the King identifies with ‘the least of these’ in hunger, thirst, strangerhood, nakedness, sickness, and prison. Eternal punishment and eternal life close the chapter—mercy’s fruit revealed, not a rival gospel.
text: Matthew 25:31–46 Matthew Jesus ends the discourse with the Son of Man in glory, angels, and a throne of judgment over all nations. Sheep and goats are separated; the King identifies with ‘the least of these’ in hunger, thirst, strangerhood, nakedness, sickness, and prison. Eternal punishment and eternal life close the chapter—mercy’s fruit revealed, not a rival gospel. “But when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory. Matthew 25:31 Before him all the nations will be gathered, and he will separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. Matthew 25:32 He will set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left. Matthew 25:33 Then the King will tell those on his right hand, ‘Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the Kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; Matthew 25:34 for I was hungry and you gave me food to eat. I was thirsty and you gave me drink. I was a stranger and you took me in. Matthew 25:35 I was naked and you clothed me. I was sick and you visited me. I was in prison and you came to me.’ Matthew 25:36 “Then the righteous will answer him, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you a drink? Matthew 25:37 When did we see you as a stranger and take you in, or naked and clothe you? Matthew 25:38 When did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?’ Matthew 25:39 “The King will answer them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’ Matthew 25:40 Then he will say also to those on the left hand, ‘Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels; Matthew 25:41 for I was hungry, and you didn’t give me food to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me no drink; Matthew 25:42 I was a stranger, and you didn’t take me in; naked, and you didn’t clothe me; sick, and in prison, and you didn’t visit me.’ Matthew 25:43 “Then they will also answer, saying, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry, or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and didn’t help you?’ Matthew 25:44 “Then he will answer them, saying, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you didn’t do it to one of the least of these, you didn’t do it to me.’ Matthew 25:45 These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” Matthew 25:46

title: Matthew 26:1–5
context: After the Olivet Discourse (chs. 24–25), Matthew opens the Passion narrative. Jesus announces that Passover is two days away and that the Son of Man will be delivered up to crucifixion, while the chief priests and elders plot a stealthy arrest—yet delay it for fear of the people.
text: Matthew 26:1–5 Matthew After the Olivet Discourse (chs. 24–25), Matthew opens the Passion narrative. Jesus announces that Passover is two days away and that the Son of Man will be delivered up to crucifixion, while the chief priests and elders plot a stealthy arrest—yet delay it for fear of the people. When Jesus had finished all these words, he said to his disciples, Matthew 26:1 “You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified.” Matthew 26:2 Then the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders of the people were gathered together in the court of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas. Matthew 26:3 They took counsel together that they might take Jesus by deceit and kill him. Matthew 26:4 But they said, “Not during the feast, lest a riot occur among the people.” Matthew 26:5

title: Matthew 26:14–16
context: Immediately after the anointing at Bethany, Judas Iscariot goes to the chief priests, bargains to deliver Jesus for silver, and from then on seeks an opportunity to betray Him.
text: Matthew 26:14–16 Matthew Immediately after the anointing at Bethany, Judas Iscariot goes to the chief priests, bargains to deliver Jesus for silver, and from then on seeks an opportunity to betray Him. Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests Matthew 26:14 and said, “What are you willing to give me if I deliver him to you?” So they weighed out for him thirty pieces of silver. Matthew 26:15 From that time he sought opportunity to betray him. Matthew 26:16

title: Matthew 26:17–25
context: On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples ask where to prepare the Passover. Jesus directs them to a certain man in the city; they prepare the meal. At table He announces that one of them will betray Him, identifies the traitor by the dipped morsel exchange with Judas, and Judas answers with a feigned question.
