text: Matthew 26:17–25 Matthew On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples ask where to prepare the Passover. Jesus directs them to a certain man in the city; they prepare the meal. At table He announces that one of them will betray Him, identifies the traitor by the dipped morsel exchange with Judas, and Judas answers with a feigned question. Now on the first day of unleavened bread, the disciples came to Jesus, saying to him, “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” Matthew 26:17 He said, “Go into the city to a certain person, and tell him, ‘The Teacher says, “My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.”’” Matthew 26:18 The disciples did as Jesus commanded them, and they prepared the Passover. Matthew 26:19 Now when evening had come, he was reclining at the table with the twelve disciples. Matthew 26:20 As they were eating, he said, “Most certainly I tell you that one of you will betray me.” Matthew 26:21 They were exceedingly sorrowful, and each began to ask him, “It isn’t me, is it, Lord?” Matthew 26:22 He answered, “He who dipped his hand with me in the dish will betray me. Matthew 26:23 The Son of Man goes even as it is written of him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would be better for that man if he had not been born.” Matthew 26:24 Judas, who betrayed him, answered, “It isn’t me, is it, Rabbi?” He said to him, “You said it.” Matthew 26:25

title: Matthew 26:26–30
context: During the Passover meal Jesus institutes the Lord’s Supper: bread as His body, the cup of the covenant in His blood poured out for many for the remission of sins. He points ahead to drinking new with them in His Father’s kingdom, then they sing a hymn and go out to the Mount of Olives. (Key text: default Voices now; passage-specific quotes later as assigned.)
text: Matthew 26:26–30 Matthew During the Passover meal Jesus institutes the Lord’s Supper: bread as His body, the cup of the covenant in His blood poured out for many for the remission of sins. He points ahead to drinking new with them in His Father’s kingdom, then they sing a hymn and go out to the Mount of Olives. (Key text: default Voices now; passage-specific quotes later as assigned.) As they were eating, Jesus took bread, gave thanks for it, and broke it. He gave to the disciples and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.” Matthew 26:26 He took the cup, gave thanks, and gave to them, saying, “All of you drink it, Matthew 26:27 for this is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins. Matthew 26:28 But I tell you that I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on, until that day when I drink it anew with you in my Father’s Kingdom.” Matthew 26:29 When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Matthew 26:30

title: Matthew 26:31–35
context: On the way Jesus cites Zechariah: the shepherd will be struck and the sheep scattered, yet promises to go before them to Galilee after He is raised. Peter vows loyalty even to death; Jesus foretells a threefold denial before the rooster crows; the others echo Peter’s boast.
text: Matthew 26:31–35 Matthew On the way Jesus cites Zechariah: the shepherd will be struck and the sheep scattered, yet promises to go before them to Galilee after He is raised. Peter vows loyalty even to death; Jesus foretells a threefold denial before the rooster crows; the others echo Peter’s boast. Then Jesus said to them, “All of you will be made to stumble because of me tonight, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ Matthew 26:31 But after I am raised up, I will go before you into Galilee.” Matthew 26:32 But Peter answered him, “Even if all will be made to stumble because of you, I will never be made to stumble.” Matthew 26:33 Jesus said to him, “Most certainly I tell you that tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” Matthew 26:34 Peter said to him, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” All of the disciples also said likewise. Matthew 26:35

title: Matthew 26:36–46
context: At Gethsemane Jesus takes Peter, James, and John aside, grieves to the point of death, and thrice prays that the cup pass if possible—yet submits to the Father’s will. The disciples sleep despite His call to watch and pray; He returns the third time announcing the hour and the betrayer’s arrival. (Key text: default Voices now; passage-specific quotes later as assigned.)
text: Matthew 26:36–46 Matthew At Gethsemane Jesus takes Peter, James, and John aside, grieves to the point of death, and thrice prays that the cup pass if possible—yet submits to the Father’s will. The disciples sleep despite His call to watch and pray; He returns the third time announcing the hour and the betrayer’s arrival. (Key text: default Voices now; passage-specific quotes later as assigned.) Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go there and pray.” Matthew 26:36 He took with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, and began to be sorrowful and severely troubled. Matthew 26:37 Then Jesus said to them, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with me.” Matthew 26:38 He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” Matthew 26:39 He came to the disciples and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, “What, couldn’t you watch with me for one hour? Matthew 26:40 Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Matthew 26:41 Again, a second time he went away and prayed, saying, “My Father, if this cup can’t pass away from me unless I drink it, your desire be done.” Matthew 26:42 He came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. Matthew 26:43 He left them again, went away, and prayed a third time, saying the same words. Matthew 26:44 Then he came to his disciples and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Matthew 26:45 Arise, let’s be going. Behold, he who betrays me is at hand.” Matthew 26:46

title: Matthew 26:47–56
context: Judas arrives with a crowd from the chief priests and elders, betrays Jesus with a kiss, and the arrest follows. A disciple strikes with the sword; Jesus rebukes violence, affirms He could call legions of angels, and submits so the Scriptures are fulfilled. The disciples flee.
text: Matthew 26:47–56 Matthew Judas arrives with a crowd from the chief priests and elders, betrays Jesus with a kiss, and the arrest follows. A disciple strikes with the sword; Jesus rebukes violence, affirms He could call legions of angels, and submits so the Scriptures are fulfilled. The disciples flee. While he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great multitude with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and elders of the people. Matthew 26:47 Now he who betrayed him had given them a sign, saying, “Whoever I kiss, he is the one. Seize him.” Matthew 26:48 Immediately he came to Jesus, and said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kissed him. Matthew 26:49 Jesus said to him, “Friend, why are you here?” Then they came and laid hands on Jesus, and took him. Matthew 26:50 Behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand and drew his sword, and struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear. Matthew 26:51 Then Jesus said to him, “Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword. Matthew 26:52 Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels? Matthew 26:53 How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that it must be so?” Matthew 26:54 In that hour Jesus said to the multitudes, “Have you come out as against a robber with swords and clubs to seize me? I sat daily in the temple teaching, and you didn’t arrest me. Matthew 26:55 But all this has happened that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples left him and fled. Matthew 26:56

title: Matthew 26:57–68
context: Jesus is led to Caiaphas; the scribes and elders gather. Peter follows at a distance into the courtyard. The council seeks false testimony, finally charges Jesus under the temple saying and His confession as the Christ, the Son of God. The high priest declares blasphemy; they condemn Him as deserving death and begin to mock and strike Him.
text: Matthew 26:57–68 Matthew Jesus is led to Caiaphas; the scribes and elders gather. Peter follows at a distance into the courtyard. The council seeks false testimony, finally charges Jesus under the temple saying and His confession as the Christ, the Son of God. The high priest declares blasphemy; they condemn Him as deserving death and begin to mock and strike Him. Those who had taken Jesus led him away to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders were gathered together. Matthew 26:57 But Peter followed him from a distance to the court of the high priest, and entered in and sat with the officers, to see the end. Matthew 26:58 Now the chief priests, the elders, and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus, that they might put him to death, Matthew 26:59 and they found none. Even though many false witnesses came forward, they found none. But at last two false witnesses came forward Matthew 26:60 and said, “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to build it in three days.’” Matthew 26:61 The high priest stood up and said to him, “Have you no answer? What is this that these testify against you?” Matthew 26:62 But Jesus stayed silent. The high priest answered him, “I adjure you by the living God that you tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.” Matthew 26:63 Jesus said to him, “You have said so. Nevertheless, I tell you, after this you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming on the clouds of the sky.” Matthew 26:64 Then the high priest tore his clothing, saying, “He has spoken blasphemy! Why do we need any more witnesses? Behold, now you have heard his blasphemy. Matthew 26:65 What do you think?” They answered, “He is worthy of death!” Matthew 26:66 Then they spat in his face and beat him with their fists, and some slapped him, Matthew 26:67 saying, “Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who hit you?” Matthew 26:68

title: Matthew 26:6–13
context: While leaders plot in Jerusalem, Jesus is in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman anoints Him with costly ointment; the disciples call it waste; Jesus defends her act as beautiful preparation for His burial and promises that the gospel will remember her wherever it is proclaimed.
text: Matthew 26:6–13 Matthew While leaders plot in Jerusalem, Jesus is in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman anoints Him with costly ointment; the disciples call it waste; Jesus defends her act as beautiful preparation for His burial and promises that the gospel will remember her wherever it is proclaimed. Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, Matthew 26:6 a woman came to him having an alabaster jar of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he sat at the table. Matthew 26:7 But when his disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying, “Why this waste? Matthew 26:8 For this ointment might have been sold for much and given to the poor.” Matthew 26:9 However, knowing this, Jesus said to them, “Why do you trouble the woman? She has done a good work for me. Matthew 26:10 For you always have the poor with you, but you don’t always have me. Matthew 26:11 For in pouring this ointment on my body, she did it to prepare me for burial. Matthew 26:12 Most certainly I tell you, wherever this Good News is preached in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be spoken of as a memorial of her.” Matthew 26:13

title: Matthew 26:69–75
context: In the courtyard a servant girl, then another, then bystanders confront Peter about being with Jesus. He denies with oath and curse that he does not know the man. The rooster crows; Peter remembers Jesus’ word, goes out, and weeps bitterly.
text: Matthew 26:69–75 Matthew In the courtyard a servant girl, then another, then bystanders confront Peter about being with Jesus. He denies with oath and curse that he does not know the man. The rooster crows; Peter remembers Jesus’ word, goes out, and weeps bitterly. Now Peter was sitting outside in the court, and a maid came to him, saying, “You were also with Jesus, the Galilean!” Matthew 26:69 But he denied it before them all, saying, “I don’t know what you are talking about.” Matthew 26:70 When he had gone out onto the porch, someone else saw him and said to those who were there, “This man also was with Jesus of Nazareth.” Matthew 26:71 Again he denied it with an oath, “I don’t know the man.” Matthew 26:72 After a little while those who stood by came and said to Peter, “Surely you are also one of them, for your speech makes you known.” Matthew 26:73 Then he began to curse and to swear, “I don’t know the man!” Immediately the rooster crowed. Matthew 26:74 Peter remembered the word which Jesus had said to him, “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” Then he went out and wept bitterly. Matthew 26:75

title: Matthew 27:1–2
context: After the night trial and Peter’s denial (ch. 26), morning comes. The chief priests and elders take formal counsel to put Jesus to death, then bind Him and deliver Him over to Pontius Pilate the governor.
text: Matthew 27:1–2 Matthew After the night trial and Peter’s denial (ch. 26), morning comes. The chief priests and elders take formal counsel to put Jesus to death, then bind Him and deliver Him over to Pontius Pilate the governor. Now when morning had come, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. Matthew 27:1 They bound him, led him away, and delivered him up to Pontius Pilate, the governor. Matthew 27:2

title: Matthew 27:11–14
context: Bound and delivered to Pilate (vv. 1–2), Jesus now stands before the Roman governor. Pilate asks about kingship; the chief priests and elders heap accusations; Jesus answers little, and the governor is greatly amazed.
text: Matthew 27:11–14 Matthew Bound and delivered to Pilate (vv. 1–2), Jesus now stands before the Roman governor. Pilate asks about kingship; the chief priests and elders heap accusations; Jesus answers little, and the governor is greatly amazed. Now Jesus stood before the governor; and the governor asked him, saying, “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus said to him, “So you say.” Matthew 27:11 When he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing. Matthew 27:12 Then Pilate said to him, “Don’t you hear how many things they testify against you?” Matthew 27:13 He gave him no answer, not even one word, so that the governor marveled greatly. Matthew 27:14

title: Matthew 27:15–26
context: After Jesus’ silence before Pilate (vv. 11–14), the feast custom of releasing a prisoner sets the stage. Pilate offers Barabbas or Jesus; the crowd, stirred by the priests, chooses Barabbas and demands crucifixion. Pilate washes his hands, the people accept bloodguilt, and Jesus is scourged and delivered to be crucified.
text: Matthew 27:15–26 Matthew After Jesus’ silence before Pilate (vv. 11–14), the feast custom of releasing a prisoner sets the stage. Pilate offers Barabbas or Jesus; the crowd, stirred by the priests, chooses Barabbas and demands crucifixion. Pilate washes his hands, the people accept bloodguilt, and Jesus is scourged and delivered to be crucified. Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release to the multitude one prisoner whom they desired. Matthew 27:15 They had then a notable prisoner called Barabbas. Matthew 27:16 When therefore they were gathered together, Pilate said to them, “Whom do you want me to release to you? Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” Matthew 27:17 For he knew that because of envy they had delivered him up. Matthew 27:18 While he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent to him, saying, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him.” Matthew 27:19 Now the chief priests and the elders persuaded the multitudes to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. Matthew 27:20 But the governor answered them, “Which of the two do you want me to release to you?” They said, “Barabbas!” Matthew 27:21 Pilate said to them, “What then shall I do to Jesus who is called Christ?” They all said to him, “Let him be crucified!” Matthew 27:22 But the governor said, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they cried out exceedingly, saying, “Let him be crucified!” Matthew 27:23 So when Pilate saw that nothing was being gained, but rather that a disturbance was starting, he took water and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous person. You see to it.” Matthew 27:24 All the people answered, “May his blood be on us and on our children!” Matthew 27:25 Then he released Barabbas to them, but Jesus he flogged and delivered to be crucified. Matthew 27:26

title: Matthew 27:27–31
context: After Barabbas is released and Jesus is scourged and delivered to be crucified (v. 26), the governor’s soldiers take Jesus into the headquarters, mock His kingship with robe, thorns, and reed, then lead Him away to the cross.
text: Matthew 27:27–31 Matthew After Barabbas is released and Jesus is scourged and delivered to be crucified (v. 26), the governor’s soldiers take Jesus into the headquarters, mock His kingship with robe, thorns, and reed, then lead Him away to the cross. Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the Praetorium, and gathered the whole garrison together against him. Matthew 27:27 They stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him. Matthew 27:28 They braided a crown of thorns and put it on his head, and a reed in his right hand; and they kneeled down before him and mocked him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” Matthew 27:29 They spat on him, and took the reed and struck him on the head. Matthew 27:30 When they had mocked him, they took the robe off him, and put his clothes on him, and led him away to crucify him. Matthew 27:31

title: Matthew 27:3–10
context: As Jesus is condemned and handed to Pilate, Judas the betrayer is seized with remorse, returns the silver, and dies in despair; the priests buy the potter’s field, and Matthew records Scripture’s fulfillment.
text: Matthew 27:3–10 Matthew As Jesus is condemned and handed to Pilate, Judas the betrayer is seized with remorse, returns the silver, and dies in despair; the priests buy the potter’s field, and Matthew records Scripture’s fulfillment. Then Judas, who betrayed him, when he saw that Jesus was condemned, felt remorse, and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, Matthew 27:3 saying, “I have sinned in that I betrayed innocent blood.” But they said, “What is that to us? You see to it.” Matthew 27:4 He threw down the pieces of silver in the sanctuary and departed. Then he went away and hanged himself. Matthew 27:5 The chief priests took the pieces of silver and said, “It’s not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is the price of blood.” Matthew 27:6 They took counsel, and bought the potter’s field with them to bury strangers in. Matthew 27:7 Therefore that field has been called “The Field of Blood” to this day. Matthew 27:8 Then that which was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled, saying, “They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him upon whom a price had been set, whom some of the children of Israel priced, Matthew 27:9 and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord commanded me.” Matthew 27:10

title: Matthew 27:32–44
context: On the way to Golgotha Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross. Jesus is crucified between robbers, titled King of the Jews, and mocked by passersby and leaders who dare Him to come down from the cross.
text: Matthew 27:32–44 Matthew On the way to Golgotha Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross. Jesus is crucified between robbers, titled King of the Jews, and mocked by passersby and leaders who dare Him to come down from the cross. As they came out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name, and they compelled him to go with them, that he might carry his cross. Matthew 27:32 When they came to a place called “Golgotha”, that is to say, “The place of a skull,” Matthew 27:33 they gave him sour wine to drink mixed with gall. When he had tasted it, he would not drink. Matthew 27:34 When they had crucified him, they divided his clothing among them, casting lots, Matthew 27:35 and they sat and watched him there. Matthew 27:36 They set up over his head the accusation against him written, “THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.” Matthew 27:37 Then there were two robbers crucified with him, one on his right hand and one on the left. Matthew 27:38 Those who passed by blasphemed him, wagging their heads Matthew 27:39 and saying, “You who destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross!” Matthew 27:40 Likewise the chief priests also mocking with the scribes, the Pharisees, and the elders, said, Matthew 27:41 “He saved others, but he can’t save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him come down from the cross now, and we will believe in him. Matthew 27:42 He trusts in God. Let God deliver him now, if he wants him; for he said, ‘I am the Son of God.’” Matthew 27:43 The robbers also who were crucified with him cast on him the same reproach. Matthew 27:44

title: Matthew 27:45–56
context: From the sixth to the ninth hour darkness covers the land. Jesus cries the forsaken cry of Psalm 22, yields up His spirit, the temple curtain tears, earth shakes, saints are raised, and a centurion confesses the Son of God while women watch from a distance.
text: Matthew 27:45–56 Matthew From the sixth to the ninth hour darkness covers the land. Jesus cries the forsaken cry of Psalm 22, yields up His spirit, the temple curtain tears, earth shakes, saints are raised, and a centurion confesses the Son of God while women watch from a distance. Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. Matthew 27:45 About the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, “Eli, Eli, lima sabachthani?” That is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Matthew 27:46 Some of them who stood there, when they heard it, said, “This man is calling Elijah.” Matthew 27:47 Immediately one of them ran and took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave him a drink. Matthew 27:48 The rest said, “Let him be. Let’s see whether Elijah comes to save him.” Matthew 27:49 Jesus cried again with a loud voice, and yielded up his spirit. Matthew 27:50 Behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom. The earth quaked and the rocks were split. Matthew 27:51 The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised; Matthew 27:52 and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered into the holy city and appeared to many. Matthew 27:53 Now the centurion and those who were with him watching Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were done, were terrified, saying, “Truly this was the Son of God!” Matthew 27:54 Many women were there watching from afar, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, serving him. Matthew 27:55 Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. Matthew 27:56

title: Matthew 27:57–61
context: Evening falls. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, asks Pilate for Jesus’ body, wraps it in clean linen, and lays it in his own new rock tomb; Mary Magdalene was there, and the other Mary sit opposite, watching.
text: Matthew 27:57–61 Matthew Evening falls. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, asks Pilate for Jesus’ body, wraps it in clean linen, and lays it in his own new rock tomb; Mary Magdalene was there, and the other Mary sit opposite, watching. When evening had come, a rich man from Arimathaea named Joseph, who himself was also Jesus’ disciple, came. Matthew 27:57 This man went to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body. Then Pilate commanded the body to be given up. Matthew 27:58 Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen cloth Matthew 27:59 and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut out in the rock. Then he rolled a large stone against the door of the tomb, and departed. Matthew 27:60 Mary Magdalene was there, and the other Mary, sitting opposite the tomb. Matthew 27:61

title: Matthew 27:62–66
context: After Preparation Day, chief priests and Pharisees ask Pilate to secure the tomb against a stolen-body story. Pilate grants a guard; they seal the stone—unwittingly strengthening the later witness of resurrection.
text: Matthew 27:62–66 Matthew After Preparation Day, chief priests and Pharisees ask Pilate to secure the tomb against a stolen-body story. Pilate grants a guard; they seal the stone—unwittingly strengthening the later witness of resurrection. Now on the next day, which was the day after the Preparation Day, the chief priests and the Pharisees were gathered together to Pilate, Matthew 27:62 saying, “Sir, we remember what that deceiver said while he was still alive: ‘After three days I will rise again.’ Matthew 27:63 Command therefore that the tomb be made secure until the third day, lest perhaps his disciples come at night and steal him away, and tell the people, ‘He is risen from the dead;’ and the last deception will be worse than the first.” Matthew 27:64 Pilate said to them, “You have a guard. Go, make it as secure as you can.” Matthew 27:65 So they went with the guard and made the tomb secure, sealing the stone. Matthew 27:66

title: Matthew 28:1–10
context: At dawn on the first day of the week the women come to the tomb. An angel of the Lord rolls back the stone, announces that Jesus has risen, and sends them to tell the disciples. As they go, the risen Jesus meets them; they worship Him, and He directs them—and His brothers—to Galilee.
text: Matthew 28:1–10 Matthew At dawn on the first day of the week the women come to the tomb. An angel of the Lord rolls back the stone, announces that Jesus has risen, and sends them to tell the disciples. As they go, the risen Jesus meets them; they worship Him, and He directs them—and His brothers—to Galilee. Now after the Sabbath, as it began to dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb. Matthew 28:1 Behold, there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from the sky and came and rolled away the stone from the door and sat on it. Matthew 28:2 His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. Matthew 28:3 For fear of him, the guards shook, and became like dead men. Matthew 28:4 The angel answered the women, “Don’t be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus, who has been crucified. Matthew 28:5 He is not here, for he has risen, just like he said. Come, see the place where the Lord was lying. Matthew 28:6 Go quickly and tell his disciples, ‘He has risen from the dead, and behold, he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him.’ Behold, I have told you.” Matthew 28:7 They departed quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy, and ran to bring his disciples word. Matthew 28:8 As they went to tell his disciples, behold, Jesus met them, saying, “Rejoice!” They came and took hold of his feet, and worshiped him. Matthew 28:9 Then Jesus said to them, “Don’t be afraid. Go tell my brothers that they should go into Galilee, and there they will see me.” Matthew 28:10

title: Matthew 28:11–15
context: While the women go with Easter news, some of the guard report to the chief priests. The leaders bribe the soldiers to spread a theft story, promise protection from the governor, and a rival account takes root that Matthew says persists to his day.
text: Matthew 28:11–15 Matthew While the women go with Easter news, some of the guard report to the chief priests. The leaders bribe the soldiers to spread a theft story, promise protection from the governor, and a rival account takes root that Matthew says persists to his day. Now while they were going, behold, some of the guards came into the city and told the chief priests all the things that had happened. Matthew 28:11 When they were assembled with the elders and had taken counsel, they gave a large amount of silver to the soldiers, Matthew 28:12 saying, “Say that his disciples came by night and stole him away while we slept. Matthew 28:13 If this comes to the governor’s ears, we will persuade him and make you free of worry.” Matthew 28:14 So they took the money and did as they were told. This saying was spread abroad among the Jews, and continues until today. Matthew 28:15

title: Matthew 28:16–20
context: The eleven meet Jesus on the mountain in Galilee. They worship—yet some doubt. The risen Lord claims all authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth, sends them to make disciples of all nations, commands Triune baptism and obedience-teaching, and promises His presence to the end of the age.
text: Matthew 28:16–20 Matthew The eleven meet Jesus on the mountain in Galilee. They worship—yet some doubt. The risen Lord claims all authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth, sends them to make disciples of all nations, commands Triune baptism and obedience-teaching, and promises His presence to the end of the age. But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had sent them. Matthew 28:16 When they saw him, they bowed down to him; but some doubted. Matthew 28:17 Jesus came to them and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Matthew 28:18 Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, Matthew 28:19 teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen. Matthew 28:20

title: Matthew 3:1–6
context: Years after the Nazareth settlement, Matthew jumps to John’s public ministry: a wilderness preacher calls Israel to repent because the kingdom of heaven is near, fulfills Isaiah’s voice, and baptizes confessing crowds in the Jordan.
text: Matthew 3:1–6 Matthew Years after the Nazareth settlement, Matthew jumps to John’s public ministry: a wilderness preacher calls Israel to repent because the kingdom of heaven is near, fulfills Isaiah’s voice, and baptizes confessing crowds in the Jordan. In those days, John the Baptizer came, preaching in the wilderness of Judea, saying, Matthew 3:1 “Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!” Matthew 3:2 For this is he who was spoken of by Isaiah the prophet, saying, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness, make the way of the Lord ready! Make his paths straight!” Matthew 3:3 Now John himself wore clothing made of camel’s hair with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey. Matthew 3:4 Then people from Jerusalem, all of Judea, and all the region around the Jordan went out to him. Matthew 3:5 They were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins. Matthew 3:6

title: Matthew 3:13–17
context: Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized by John; John hesitates, Jesus insists on fulfilling all righteousness, and after the baptism the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father’s voice names Jesus the beloved Son.
text: Matthew 3:13–17 Matthew Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized by John; John hesitates, Jesus insists on fulfilling all righteousness, and after the baptism the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father’s voice names Jesus the beloved Son. Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. Matthew 3:13 But John would have hindered him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” Matthew 3:14 But Jesus, answering, said to him, “Allow it now, for this is the fitting way for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him. Matthew 3:15 Jesus, when he was baptized, went up directly from the water: and behold, the heavens were opened to him. He saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove, and coming on him. Matthew 3:16 Behold, a voice out of the heavens said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” Matthew 3:17

title: Matthew 3:7–12
context: John confronts Pharisees and Sadducees seeking baptism without fruit: viper brood, Abrahamic presumption, axe at the root, and a Coming One who baptizes with Spirit and fire and separates wheat from chaff.
text: Matthew 3:7–12 Matthew John confronts Pharisees and Sadducees seeking baptism without fruit: viper brood, Abrahamic presumption, axe at the root, and a Coming One who baptizes with Spirit and fire and separates wheat from chaff. But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming for his baptism, he said to them, “You offspring of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Matthew 3:7 Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance! Matthew 3:8 Don’t think to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham for our father,’ for I tell you that God is able to raise up children to Abraham from these stones. Matthew 3:9 Even now the ax lies at the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that doesn’t produce good fruit is cut down, and cast into the fire. Matthew 3:10 “I indeed baptize you in water for repentance, but he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit. Matthew 3:11 His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor. He will gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn up with unquenchable fire.” Matthew 3:12

title: Matthew 4:1–11
context: After baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil; fasting forty days, He answers each assault with Scripture, refuses bread, spectacle, and false worship, and after Satan departs angels minister to Him.
text: Matthew 4:1–11 Matthew After baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil; fasting forty days, He answers each assault with Scripture, refuses bread, spectacle, and false worship, and after Satan departs angels minister to Him. Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. Matthew 4:1 When he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was hungry afterward. Matthew 4:2 The tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.” Matthew 4:3 But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’” Matthew 4:4 Then the devil took him into the holy city. He set him on the pinnacle of the temple, Matthew 4:5 and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and, ‘On their hands they will bear you up, so that you don’t dash your foot against a stone.’” Matthew 4:6 Jesus said to him, “Again, it is written, ‘You shall not test the Lord, your God.’” Matthew 4:7 Again, the devil took him to an exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. Matthew 4:8 He said to him, “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” Matthew 4:9 Then Jesus said to him, “Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.’” Matthew 4:10 Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and served him. Matthew 4:11

title: Matthew 4:12–17
context: Hearing of John’s arrest, Jesus withdraws to Galilee, settles in Capernaum, which is by the sea, in Zebulun and Naphtali, fulfills Isaiah’s light-for-darkness promise, and begins preaching: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”
text: Matthew 4:12–17 Matthew Hearing of John’s arrest, Jesus withdraws to Galilee, settles in Capernaum, which is by the sea, in Zebulun and Naphtali, fulfills Isaiah’s light-for-darkness promise, and begins preaching: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” Now when Jesus heard that John was delivered up, he withdrew into Galilee. Matthew 4:12 Leaving Nazareth, he came and lived in Capernaum, which is by the sea, in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali, Matthew 4:13 that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying, Matthew 4:14 “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, toward the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles, Matthew 4:15 the people who sat in darkness saw a great light; to those who sat in the region and shadow of death, to them light has dawned.” Matthew 4:16 From that time, Jesus began to preach, and to say, “Repent! For the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.” Matthew 4:17

title: Matthew 4:18–22
context: Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus calls Simon Peter and Andrew from their nets, then James and John from their boat with Zebedee; all four leave immediately and follow Him.
text: Matthew 4:18–22 Matthew Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus calls Simon Peter and Andrew from their nets, then James and John from their boat with Zebedee; all four leave immediately and follow Him. Walking by the sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers: Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew, his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen. Matthew 4:18 He said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.” Matthew 4:19 They immediately left their nets and followed him. Matthew 4:20 Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets. He called them. Matthew 4:21 They immediately left the boat and their father, and followed him. Matthew 4:22

title: Matthew 4:23–25
context: Jesus travels throughout Galilee teaching in synagogues, proclaiming the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and affliction; fame spreads to Syria, the sick are brought, and great crowds follow from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.
text: Matthew 4:23–25 Matthew Jesus travels throughout Galilee teaching in synagogues, proclaiming the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and affliction; fame spreads to Syria, the sick are brought, and great crowds follow from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan. Jesus went about in all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people. Matthew 4:23 The report about him went out into all Syria. They brought to him all who were sick, afflicted with various diseases and torments, possessed with demons, epileptics, and paralytics; and he healed them. Matthew 4:24 Great multitudes from Galilee, Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and from beyond the Jordan followed him. Matthew 4:25

title: Matthew 5:1–12
context: Jesus opens the Sermon on the Mount by sitting as Israel’s Teacher-King. Crowds gather; disciples draw near; and the Beatitudes announce who is truly blessed under the kingdom of heaven—not the self-secure, but the needy who receive God’s grace and walk in its fruit.
text: Matthew 5:1–12 Matthew Jesus opens the Sermon on the Mount by sitting as Israel’s Teacher-King. Crowds gather; disciples draw near; and the Beatitudes announce who is truly blessed under the kingdom of heaven—not the self-secure, but the needy who receive God’s grace and walk in its fruit. Seeing the multitudes, he went up onto the mountain. When he had sat down, his disciples came to him. Matthew 5:1 He opened his mouth and taught them, saying, Matthew 5:2 “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. Matthew 5:3 Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Matthew 5:4 Blessed are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth. Matthew 5:5 Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. Matthew 5:6 Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Matthew 5:7 Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Matthew 5:8 Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. Matthew 5:9 Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. Matthew 5:10 “Blessed are you when people reproach you, persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Matthew 5:11 Rejoice, and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven. For that is how they persecuted the prophets who were before you. Matthew 5:12

title: Matthew 5:13–16
context: After the Beatitudes name the blessed character of the kingdom, Jesus turns to identity: disciples are salt and light in the world. The Sermon moves from who they are under the King’s blessing to how that life preserves, flavors, and illuminates for the Father’s glory.
text: Matthew 5:13–16 Matthew After the Beatitudes name the blessed character of the kingdom, Jesus turns to identity: disciples are salt and light in the world. The Sermon moves from who they are under the King’s blessing to how that life preserves, flavors, and illuminates for the Father’s glory. “You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted? It is then good for nothing, but to be cast out and trodden under the feet of men. Matthew 5:13 “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden. Matthew 5:14 Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house. Matthew 5:15 Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. Matthew 5:16

title: Matthew 5:17–20
context: Still on the mountain, Jesus turns from salt and light to a charge many feared He meant to erase Moses: the Law and the Prophets. He refuses abolish and claims fulfill—then presses a kingdom righteousness that must go deeper than scribal and Pharisaic religion.
text: Matthew 5:17–20 Matthew Still on the mountain, Jesus turns from salt and light to a charge many feared He meant to erase Moses: the Law and the Prophets. He refuses abolish and claims fulfill—then presses a kingdom righteousness that must go deeper than scribal and Pharisaic religion. “Don’t think that I came to destroy the law or the prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill. Matthew 5:17 For most certainly, I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not even one smallest letter or one tiny pen stroke shall in any way pass away from the law, until all things are accomplished. Matthew 5:18 Therefore, whoever shall break one of these least commandments and teach others to do so, shall be called least in the Kingdom of Heaven; but whoever shall do and teach them shall be called great in the Kingdom of Heaven. Matthew 5:19 For I tell you that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, there is no way you will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven. Matthew 5:20

title: Matthew 5:21–26
context: In the Sermon’s first antithesis, Jesus takes the commandment against murder and presses it inward. The King who fulfills the Law exposes anger, contempt, and broken fellowship as matters of judgment—and calls disciples to reconcile before they worship and settle quickly before the court closes.
text: Matthew 5:21–26 Matthew In the Sermon’s first antithesis, Jesus takes the commandment against murder and presses it inward. The King who fulfills the Law exposes anger, contempt, and broken fellowship as matters of judgment—and calls disciples to reconcile before they worship and settle quickly before the court closes. “You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ and ‘Whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.’ Matthew 5:21 But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ will be in danger of the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna. Matthew 5:22 “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, Matthew 5:23 leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift. Matthew 5:24 Agree with your adversary quickly while you are with him on the way; lest perhaps the prosecutor deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Matthew 5:25 Most certainly I tell you, you shall by no means get out of there until you have paid the last penny. Matthew 5:26

title: Matthew 5:27–30
context: In the Sermon’s second antithesis, Jesus takes the commandment against adultery and presses it inward. The King who fulfills the Law exposes lustful intent as adultery of the heart—and calls disciples to radical, costly dealing with whatever draws them toward sin rather than risk the whole self under judgment.
text: Matthew 5:27–30 Matthew In the Sermon’s second antithesis, Jesus takes the commandment against adultery and presses it inward. The King who fulfills the Law exposes lustful intent as adultery of the heart—and calls disciples to radical, costly dealing with whatever draws them toward sin rather than risk the whole self under judgment. “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery;’ Matthew 5:27 but I tell you that everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart. Matthew 5:28 If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna. Matthew 5:29 If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off, and throw it away from you. For it is more profitable for you that one of your members should perish, than for your whole body to be cast into Gehenna. Matthew 5:30

title: Matthew 5:31–32
context: In another Sermon antithesis, Jesus takes the familiar permission of a divorce certificate and presses marriage toward the heart of the covenant. The King who fulfills the Law will not let disciples treat a spouse as disposable paper—and He names the adultery that casual divorce and remarriage can create, while marking sexual immorality as the stated exception.
text: Matthew 5:31–32 Matthew In another Sermon antithesis, Jesus takes the familiar permission of a divorce certificate and presses marriage toward the heart of the covenant. The King who fulfills the Law will not let disciples treat a spouse as disposable paper—and He names the adultery that casual divorce and remarriage can create, while marking sexual immorality as the stated exception. “It was also said, ‘Whoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorce,’ Matthew 5:31 but I tell you that whoever puts away his wife, except for the cause of sexual immorality, makes her an adulteress; and whoever marries her when she is put away commits adultery. Matthew 5:32

title: Matthew 5:33–37
context: In the Sermon’s antithesis on oaths, Jesus takes the old word against false swearing and presses speech toward simple truthfulness. The King who fulfills the Law will not let disciples prop up shaky words with heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or their own heads—and He calls for a Yes’ and No that need no sacred scaffolding, because anything more comes from evil.
text: Matthew 5:33–37 Matthew In the Sermon’s antithesis on oaths, Jesus takes the old word against false swearing and presses speech toward simple truthfulness. The King who fulfills the Law will not let disciples prop up shaky words with heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or their own heads—and He calls for a Yes’ and No that need no sacred scaffolding, because anything more comes from evil. “Again you have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not make false vows, but shall perform to the Lord your vows,’ Matthew 5:33 but I tell you, don’t swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God; Matthew 5:34 nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. Matthew 5:35 Neither shall you swear by your head, for you can’t make one hair white or black. Matthew 5:36 But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one. Matthew 5:37

title: Matthew 5:38–42
context: Jesus next addresses retaliation. The “eye for an eye” principle limited vengeance in Israel’s courts; the King now calls disciples to absorb insult and excess demand without returning blow for blow—kingdom generosity that breaks the cycle of payback.
text: Matthew 5:38–42 Matthew Jesus next addresses retaliation. The “eye for an eye” principle limited vengeance in Israel’s courts; the King now calls disciples to absorb insult and excess demand without returning blow for blow—kingdom generosity that breaks the cycle of payback. “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.’ Matthew 5:38 But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also. Matthew 5:39 If anyone sues you to take away your coat, let him have your cloak also. Matthew 5:40 Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two. Matthew 5:41 Give to him who asks you, and don’t turn away him who desires to borrow from you. Matthew 5:42

title: Matthew 5:43–48
context: The antitheses climax in love of enemies. Jesus corrects a shriveled reading of neighbor-love, roots disciple love in the Father’s common kindness to evil and good, and calls His people toward the Father’s own perfection—holy love that refuses a closed circle.
text: Matthew 5:43–48 Matthew The antitheses climax in love of enemies. Jesus corrects a shriveled reading of neighbor-love, roots disciple love in the Father’s common kindness to evil and good, and calls His people toward the Father’s own perfection—holy love that refuses a closed circle. “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ Matthew 5:43 But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you, Matthew 5:44 that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust. Matthew 5:45 For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same? Matthew 5:46 If you only greet your friends, what more do you do than others? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same? Matthew 5:47 Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect. Matthew 5:48

title: Matthew 6:1–4
context: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus turns from kingdom righteousness to the danger of performing piety for human applause—beginning with almsgiving that seeks the Father’s eye, not the crowd’s praise.
text: Matthew 6:1–4 Matthew In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus turns from kingdom righteousness to the danger of performing piety for human applause—beginning with almsgiving that seeks the Father’s eye, not the crowd’s praise. “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. Matthew 6:1 Therefore, when you do merciful deeds, don’t sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may get glory from men. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward. Matthew 6:2 But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, Matthew 6:3 so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly. Matthew 6:4

title: Matthew 6:16–18
context: Jesus completes the secret-piety triad—after alms and prayer—by reforming fasting: refuse gloomy display for human eyes; appear ordinary before people so that the Father who sees in secret is the true audience.
text: Matthew 6:16–18 Matthew Jesus completes the secret-piety triad—after alms and prayer—by reforming fasting: refuse gloomy display for human eyes; appear ordinary before people so that the Father who sees in secret is the true audience. “Moreover when you fast, don’t be like the hypocrites, with sad faces. For they disfigure their faces that they may be seen by men to be fasting. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward. Matthew 6:16 But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, Matthew 6:17 so that you are not seen by men to be fasting, but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you. Matthew 6:18

title: Matthew 6:19–24
context: Jesus turns from secret piety to the heart’s treasure: refuse perishable earthly stockpiles; store up in heaven; keep a healthy eye; and confess that no one can serve both God and money.
text: Matthew 6:19–24 Matthew Jesus turns from secret piety to the heart’s treasure: refuse perishable earthly stockpiles; store up in heaven; keep a healthy eye; and confess that no one can serve both God and money. “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal; Matthew 6:19 but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; Matthew 6:20 for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Matthew 6:21 “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. Matthew 6:22 But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! Matthew 6:23 “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon. Matthew 6:24

title: Matthew 6:25–34
context: Having unmasked mammon, Jesus addresses anxiety about food, drink, and clothing: the Father feeds birds and clothes lilies; disciples of little faith are worth more; seek first the kingdom and His righteousness, and leave tomorrow’s trouble to tomorrow.
text: Matthew 6:25–34 Matthew Having unmasked mammon, Jesus addresses anxiety about food, drink, and clothing: the Father feeds birds and clothes lilies; disciples of little faith are worth more; seek first the kingdom and His righteousness, and leave tomorrow’s trouble to tomorrow. Therefore I tell you, don’t be anxious for your life: what you will eat, or what you will drink; nor yet for your body, what you will wear. Isn’t life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Matthew 6:25 See the birds of the sky, that they don’t sow, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns. Your heavenly Father feeds them. Aren’t you of much more value than they? Matthew 6:26 “Which of you by being anxious, can add one moment to his lifespan? Matthew 6:27 Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don’t toil, neither do they spin, Matthew 6:28 yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these. Matthew 6:29 But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today exists and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, won’t he much more clothe you, you of little faith? Matthew 6:30 “Therefore don’t be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’, ‘What will we drink?’ or, ‘With what will we be clothed?’ Matthew 6:31 For the Gentiles seek after all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. Matthew 6:32 But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well. Matthew 6:33 Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient. Matthew 6:34

title: Matthew 6:5–15
context: Jesus next reforms prayer: reject hypocritical display and empty pagan wordiness; pray to the Father in secret; and learn the pattern of the Lord’s Prayer, with a sober word on forgiving others as we seek forgiveness.
text: Matthew 6:5–15 Matthew Jesus next reforms prayer: reject hypocritical display and empty pagan wordiness; pray to the Father in secret; and learn the pattern of the Lord’s Prayer, with a sober word on forgiving others as we seek forgiveness. “When you pray, you shall not be as the hypocrites, for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men. Most certainly, I tell you, they have received their reward. Matthew 6:5 But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly. Matthew 6:6 In praying, don’t use vain repetitions as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking. Matthew 6:7 Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need before you ask him. Matthew 6:8 Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Matthew 6:9 Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Matthew 6:10 Give us today our daily bread. Matthew 6:11 Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. Matthew 6:12 Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’ Matthew 6:13 “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. Matthew 6:14 But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. Matthew 6:15

title: Matthew 7:1–5
context: Still in the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus turns from anxiety and treasure to relationships in the kingdom community: a warning against hypocritical judgment, paired with the call to clear-eyed self-examination before helping a brother.
text: Matthew 7:1–5 Matthew Still in the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus turns from anxiety and treasure to relationships in the kingdom community: a warning against hypocritical judgment, paired with the call to clear-eyed self-examination before helping a brother. “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged. Matthew 7:1 For with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you. Matthew 7:2 Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye? Matthew 7:3 Or how will you tell your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye,’ and behold, the beam is in your own eye? Matthew 7:4 You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye. Matthew 7:5

title: Matthew 7:12–14
context: Jesus gathers the sermon’s ethic into the Golden Rule, then presses the urgency of the two ways: the narrow gate that leads to life and the wide, easy road that leads to destruction.
text: Matthew 7:12–14 Matthew Jesus gathers the sermon’s ethic into the Golden Rule, then presses the urgency of the two ways: the narrow gate that leads to life and the wide, easy road that leads to destruction. Therefore, whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets. Matthew 7:12 “Enter in by the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter in by it. Matthew 7:13 How narrow is the gate and the way is restricted that leads to life! There are few who find it. Matthew 7:14

title: Matthew 7:15–20
context: On the narrow way, Jesus warns of false prophets: charming exteriors, predatory hearts, and a simple test—fruit over fleece. Disciples must discern by what a life and teaching actually produce.
text: Matthew 7:15–20 Matthew On the narrow way, Jesus warns of false prophets: charming exteriors, predatory hearts, and a simple test—fruit over fleece. Disciples must discern by what a life and teaching actually produce. “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves. Matthew 7:15 By their fruits you will know them. Do you gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles? Matthew 7:16 Even so, every good tree produces good fruit, but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit. Matthew 7:17 A good tree can’t produce evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree produce good fruit. Matthew 7:18 Every tree that doesn’t grow good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Matthew 7:19 Therefore by their fruits you will know them. Matthew 7:20

title: Matthew 7:21–23
context: Jesus presses past religious speech and even impressive ministry claims to the heart of kingdom entry: doing the Father’s will—and the dread verdict for workers of lawlessness He never knew.
text: Matthew 7:21–23 Matthew Jesus presses past religious speech and even impressive ministry claims to the heart of kingdom entry: doing the Father’s will—and the dread verdict for workers of lawlessness He never knew. “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Matthew 7:21 Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Matthew 7:22 Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’ Matthew 7:23

title: Matthew 7:24–29
context: The Sermon on the Mount closes with two builders—hearing-and-doing versus hearing-without-doing—then Matthew’s narrator notes the crowds’ astonishment: Jesus taught with authority, not as their scribes.
text: Matthew 7:24–29 Matthew The Sermon on the Mount closes with two builders—hearing-and-doing versus hearing-without-doing—then Matthew’s narrator notes the crowds’ astonishment: Jesus taught with authority, not as their scribes. “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on the rock. Matthew 7:24 The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock. Matthew 7:25 Everyone who hears these words of mine and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. Matthew 7:26 The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house; and it fell—and its fall was great.” Matthew 7:27 When Jesus had finished saying these things, the multitudes were astonished at his teaching, Matthew 7:28 for he taught them with authority, and not like the scribes. Matthew 7:29

title: Matthew 7:6
context: Between the ban on hypocritical judgment and the invitation to ask, seek, and knock, Jesus adds a brief word of holy prudence: do not cast what is sacred before those who will only trample and turn violent.
text: Matthew 7:6 Matthew Between the ban on hypocritical judgment and the invitation to ask, seek, and knock, Jesus adds a brief word of holy prudence: do not cast what is sacred before those who will only trample and turn violent. “Don’t give that which is holy to the dogs, neither throw your pearls before the pigs, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet, and turn and tear you to pieces. Matthew 7:6

title: Matthew 7:7–11
context: After warnings about hypocritical judgment and holy things cast before the hostile, Jesus opens the door of prayer: ask, seek, knock—and trusts the Father’s goodness by comparing earthly parents’ gifts to heaven’s far greater generosity.
text: Matthew 7:7–11 Matthew After warnings about hypocritical judgment and holy things cast before the hostile, Jesus opens the door of prayer: ask, seek, knock—and trusts the Father’s goodness by comparing earthly parents’ gifts to heaven’s far greater generosity. “Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you. Matthew 7:7 For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened. Matthew 7:8 Or who is there among you who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Matthew 7:9 Or if he asks for a fish, who will give him a serpent? Matthew 7:10 If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! Matthew 7:11

title: Matthew 8:1–4
context: Jesus comes down from the Sermon on the Mount into concrete mercy: a leper kneels, Jesus touches the unclean, and Mosaic law is honored as the man is sent to the priest. Kingdom authority shown in word now appears in healing compassion.
text: Matthew 8:1–4 Matthew Jesus comes down from the Sermon on the Mount into concrete mercy: a leper kneels, Jesus touches the unclean, and Mosaic law is honored as the man is sent to the priest. Kingdom authority shown in word now appears in healing compassion. When he came down from the mountain, great multitudes followed him. Matthew 8:1 Behold, a leper came to him and worshiped him, saying, “Lord, if you want to, you can make me clean.” Matthew 8:2 Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I want to. Be made clean.” Immediately his leprosy was cleansed. Matthew 8:3 Jesus said to him, “See that you tell nobody; but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.” Matthew 8:4

title: Matthew 8:14–17
context: In Peter’s house Jesus heals a fevered mother-in-law who rises to serve; that evening He casts out demons with a word and heals all who are sick. Matthew reads the mercy as Isaiah 53:4 fulfilled—the Servant who takes illnesses and bears diseases.
text: Matthew 8:14–17 Matthew In Peter’s house Jesus heals a fevered mother-in-law who rises to serve; that evening He casts out demons with a word and heals all who are sick. Matthew reads the mercy as Isaiah 53:4 fulfilled—the Servant who takes illnesses and bears diseases. When Jesus came into Peter’s house, he saw his wife’s mother lying sick with a fever. Matthew 8:14 He touched her hand, and the fever left her. So she got up and served him. Matthew 8:15 When evening came, they brought to him many possessed with demons. He cast out the spirits with a word, and healed all who were sick, Matthew 8:16 that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying, “He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.” Matthew 8:17

title: Matthew 8:18–22
context: Seeing crowds, Jesus orders a crossing—and two would-be followers meet the cost of discipleship: the Son of Man’s homelessness and the demand that following Him outrank even sacred family duty.
text: Matthew 8:18–22 Matthew Seeing crowds, Jesus orders a crossing—and two would-be followers meet the cost of discipleship: the Son of Man’s homelessness and the demand that following Him outrank even sacred family duty. Now when Jesus saw great multitudes around him, he gave the order to depart to the other side. Matthew 8:18 A scribe came and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” Matthew 8:19 Jesus said to him, “The foxes have holes and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” Matthew 8:20 Another of his disciples said to him, “Lord, allow me first to go and bury my father.” Matthew 8:21 But Jesus said to him, “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.” Matthew 8:22

title: Matthew 8:23–27
context: Jesus embarks; a sudden storm terrifies the disciples while He sleeps. Their cry, His rebuke of wind and sea, and their wonder disclose both little faith and lordship over creation.
text: Matthew 8:23–27 Matthew Jesus embarks; a sudden storm terrifies the disciples while He sleeps. Their cry, His rebuke of wind and sea, and their wonder disclose both little faith and lordship over creation. When he got into a boat, his disciples followed him. Matthew 8:23 Behold, a violent storm came up on the sea, so much that the boat was covered with the waves; but he was asleep. Matthew 8:24 The disciples came to him and woke him up, saying, “Save us, Lord! We are dying!” Matthew 8:25 He said to them, “Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?” Then he got up, rebuked the wind and the sea, and there was a great calm. Matthew 8:26 The men marveled, saying, “What kind of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” Matthew 8:27

title: Matthew 8:28–34
context: On the other side, two demon-possessed men confront Jesus. The demons recognize the Son of God, beg, and enter a herd of pigs that perish—while the town asks Jesus to leave. Authority over hell meets human preference for pigs and peace over the Liberator.
text: Matthew 8:28–34 Matthew On the other side, two demon-possessed men confront Jesus. The demons recognize the Son of God, beg, and enter a herd of pigs that perish—while the town asks Jesus to leave. Authority over hell meets human preference for pigs and peace over the Liberator. When he came to the other side, into the country of the Gergesenes, two people possessed by demons met him there, coming out of the tombs, exceedingly fierce, so that nobody could pass that way. Matthew 8:28 Behold, they cried out, saying, “What do we have to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” Matthew 8:29 Now there was a herd of many pigs feeding far away from them. Matthew 8:30 The demons begged him, saying, “If you cast us out, permit us to go away into the herd of pigs.” Matthew 8:31 He said to them, “Go!” They came out and went into the herd of pigs; and behold, the whole herd of pigs rushed down the cliff into the sea and died in the water. Matthew 8:32 Those who fed them fled and went away into the city and told everything, including what happened to those who were possessed with demons. Matthew 8:33 Behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus. When they saw him, they begged that he would depart from their borders. Matthew 8:34

title: Matthew 8:5–13
context: In Capernaum a Roman centurion appeals for a paralyzed servant. His insight into authority draws Jesus’ marvel and opens a window onto Gentile inclusion and the danger of covenant presumption—faith that trusts the word, not proximity or pedigree.
text: Matthew 8:5–13 Matthew In Capernaum a Roman centurion appeals for a paralyzed servant. His insight into authority draws Jesus’ marvel and opens a window onto Gentile inclusion and the danger of covenant presumption—faith that trusts the word, not proximity or pedigree. When he came into Capernaum, a centurion came to him, asking him for help, Matthew 8:5 saying, “Lord, my servant lies in the house paralyzed, grievously tormented.” Matthew 8:6 Jesus said to him, “I will come and heal him.” Matthew 8:7 The centurion answered, “Lord, I’m not worthy for you to come under my roof. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed. Matthew 8:8 For I am also a man under authority, having under myself soldiers. I tell this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and tell another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and tell my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” Matthew 8:9 When Jesus heard it, he marveled and said to those who followed, “Most certainly I tell you, I haven’t found so great a faith, not even in Israel. Matthew 8:10 I tell you that many will come from the east and the west, and will sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the Kingdom of Heaven, Matthew 8:11 but the children of the Kingdom will be thrown out into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Matthew 8:12 Jesus said to the centurion, “Go your way. Let it be done for you as you have believed.” His servant was healed in that hour. Matthew 8:13

title: Matthew 9:1–8
context: Back in His own city, Jesus meets a paralytic brought by friends. He first forgives sins, then heals the body—proving the Son of Man’s authority on earth against scribal charges of blasphemy. Mercy that reaches the deeper need also vindicates itself in visible power.
text: Matthew 9:1–8 Matthew Back in His own city, Jesus meets a paralytic brought by friends. He first forgives sins, then heals the body—proving the Son of Man’s authority on earth against scribal charges of blasphemy. Mercy that reaches the deeper need also vindicates itself in visible power. He entered into a boat and crossed over, and came into his own city. Matthew 9:1 Behold, they brought to him a man who was paralyzed, lying on a bed. Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic, “Son, cheer up! Your sins are forgiven you.” Matthew 9:2 Behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man blasphemes.” Matthew 9:3 Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, “Why do you think evil in your hearts? Matthew 9:4 For which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven;’ or to say, ‘Get up, and walk’? Matthew 9:5 But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—” (then he said to the paralytic), “Get up, and take up your mat, and go to your house.” Matthew 9:6 He arose and departed to his house. Matthew 9:7 But when the multitudes saw it, they marveled and glorified God, who had given such authority to men. Matthew 9:8

title: Matthew 9:14–17
context: John’s disciples ask why they and the Pharisees fast while Jesus’ disciples do not. Jesus answers with wedding joy, a coming removal of the bridegroom, and twin images of new cloth and new wine—kingdom life that cannot be patched onto unreformed forms.
text: Matthew 9:14–17 Matthew John’s disciples ask why they and the Pharisees fast while Jesus’ disciples do not. Jesus answers with wedding joy, a coming removal of the bridegroom, and twin images of new cloth and new wine—kingdom life that cannot be patched onto unreformed forms. Then John’s disciples came to him, saying, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples don’t fast?” Matthew 9:14 Jesus said to them, “Can the friends of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast. Matthew 9:15 No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for the patch would tear away from the garment, and a worse hole is made. Matthew 9:16 Neither do people put new wine into old wineskins, or else the skins would burst, and the wine be spilled, and the skins ruined. No, they put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved.” Matthew 9:17

title: Matthew 9:18–26
context: While Jesus teaches, a ruler kneels for his dead daughter; on the way, a woman with a twelve-year hemorrhage touches His fringe and is healed. At the house, mockery yields to Jesus’ hand, and the girl arises—twin mercies of interrupted journey and restored life.
text: Matthew 9:18–26 Matthew While Jesus teaches, a ruler kneels for his dead daughter; on the way, a woman with a twelve-year hemorrhage touches His fringe and is healed. At the house, mockery yields to Jesus’ hand, and the girl arises—twin mercies of interrupted journey and restored life. While he told these things to them, behold, a ruler came and worshiped him, saying, “My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.” Matthew 9:18 Jesus got up and followed him, as did his disciples. Matthew 9:19 Behold, a woman who had a discharge of blood for twelve years came behind him, and touched the fringe of his garment; Matthew 9:20 for she said within herself, “If I just touch his garment, I will be made well.” Matthew 9:21 But Jesus, turning around and seeing her, said, “Daughter, cheer up! Your faith has made you well.” And the woman was made well from that hour. Matthew 9:22 When Jesus came into the ruler’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd in noisy disorder, Matthew 9:23 he said to them, “Make room, because the girl isn’t dead, but sleeping.” They were ridiculing him. Matthew 9:24 But when the crowd was sent out, he entered in, took her by the hand, and the girl arose. Matthew 9:25 The report of this went out into all that land. Matthew 9:26

title: Matthew 9:27–31
context: Two blind men follow Jesus, crying for mercy as Son of David. Indoors He probes their faith, touches their eyes, and opens them—then warns silence they cannot keep as fame spreads.
text: Matthew 9:27–31 Matthew Two blind men follow Jesus, crying for mercy as Son of David. Indoors He probes their faith, touches their eyes, and opens them—then warns silence they cannot keep as fame spreads. As Jesus passed by from there, two blind men followed him, calling out and saying, “Have mercy on us, son of David!” Matthew 9:27 When he had come into the house, the blind men came to him. Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They told him, “Yes, Lord.” Matthew 9:28 Then he touched their eyes, saying, “According to your faith be it done to you.” Matthew 9:29 Then their eyes were opened. Jesus strictly commanded them, saying, “See that no one knows about this.” Matthew 9:30 But they went out and spread abroad his fame in all that land. Matthew 9:31

title: Matthew 9:32–34
context: A mute, demon-oppressed man is brought; the demon is cast out and speech returns. Crowds marvel at unprecedented mercy in Israel, while Pharisees attribute the exorcism to the prince of demons—miracle meets blasphemous spin.
text: Matthew 9:32–34 Matthew A mute, demon-oppressed man is brought; the demon is cast out and speech returns. Crowds marvel at unprecedented mercy in Israel, while Pharisees attribute the exorcism to the prince of demons—miracle meets blasphemous spin. As they went out, behold, a mute man who was demon possessed was brought to him. Matthew 9:32 When the demon was cast out, the mute man spoke. The multitudes marveled, saying, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!” Matthew 9:33 But the Pharisees said, “By the prince of the demons, he casts out demons.” Matthew 9:34

title: Matthew 9:35–38
context: Jesus’ Galilean circuit—teaching, kingdom gospel, and healing—frames His compassion for harassed, shepherdless crowds. He turns disciples toward prayer: plentiful harvest, few laborers, ask the Lord of the harvest will send workers.
text: Matthew 9:35–38 Matthew Jesus’ Galilean circuit—teaching, kingdom gospel, and healing—frames His compassion for harassed, shepherdless crowds. He turns disciples toward prayer: plentiful harvest, few laborers, ask the Lord of the harvest will send workers. Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people. Matthew 9:35 But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd. Matthew 9:36 Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Matthew 9:37 Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers into his harvest.” Matthew 9:38

title: Matthew 9:9–13
