Romans 11:29 For as you in time past were disobedient to God, but now have obtained mercy by their disobedience, Romans 11:30 even so these also have now been disobedient, that by the mercy shown to you they may also obtain mercy. Romans 11:31 For God has bound all to disobedience, that he might have mercy on all. Romans 11:32 Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out! Romans 11:33 “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” Romans 11:34 “Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him again?” Romans 11:35 For of him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen. Romans 11:36

title: Romans 12:1–8
context: Paul turns from doctrine to practice. In view of God’s mercies, believers are to offer their bodies as living sacrifices and be transformed by the renewing of their minds. They should think soberly of themselves and use their varied gifts within the one body of Christ. Both traditions see this as the response of grateful worship to grace, and they largely agree on the passage.
text: Romans 12:1–8 Romans Paul turns from doctrine to practice. In view of God’s mercies, believers are to offer their bodies as living sacrifices and be transformed by the renewing of their minds. They should think soberly of themselves and use their varied gifts within the one body of Christ. Both traditions see this as the response of grateful worship to grace, and they largely agree on the passage. Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service. Romans 12:1 Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God. Romans 12:2 For I say through the grace that was given me, to everyone who is among you, not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith. Romans 12:3 For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function, Romans 12:4 so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another, Romans 12:5 having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith; Romans 12:6 or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching; Romans 12:7 or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness. Romans 12:8

title: Romans 12:9–21
context: Paul describes the shape of love in the Christian community and toward outsiders. Love is sincere, hates evil, and holds to good. It honors others, serves the Lord with zeal, rejoices in hope, endures trouble, prays, shares, and welcomes strangers. Toward enemies it blesses rather than curses, refuses revenge, and leaves judgment to God, overcoming evil with good. Both traditions read this as the fruit of grace. Wesleyan readers often see a picture of the perfect love they hope grace will produce. Reformed readers see the pattern of a life of gratitude.
text: Romans 12:9–21 Romans Paul describes the shape of love in the Christian community and toward outsiders. Love is sincere, hates evil, and holds to good. It honors others, serves the Lord with zeal, rejoices in hope, endures trouble, prays, shares, and welcomes strangers. Toward enemies it blesses rather than curses, refuses revenge, and leaves judgment to God, overcoming evil with good. Both traditions read this as the fruit of grace. Wesleyan readers often see a picture of the perfect love they hope grace will produce. Reformed readers see the pattern of a life of gratitude. Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good. Romans 12:9 In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another, Romans 12:10 not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, Romans 12:11 rejoicing in hope, enduring in troubles, continuing steadfastly in prayer, Romans 12:12 contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality. Romans 12:13 Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don’t curse. Romans 12:14 Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep. Romans 12:15 Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits. Romans 12:16 Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men. Romans 12:17 If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men. Romans 12:18 Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.” Romans 12:19 Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.” Romans 12:20 Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. Romans 12:21

title: Romans 13:1–7
context: Paul instructs believers to submit to governing authorities, because there is no authority except from God. Rulers are God’s servants to restrain evil and commend good, so believers should obey for conscience’s sake, pay taxes, and give honor and respect where due. The passage has shaped Christian political thought for centuries. The questions it raises, such as the limits of obedience and the right to resist tyranny, cut across both traditions rather than dividing them. Each still brings its own emphasis.
text: Romans 13:1–7 Romans Paul instructs believers to submit to governing authorities, because there is no authority except from God. Rulers are God’s servants to restrain evil and commend good, so believers should obey for conscience’s sake, pay taxes, and give honor and respect where due. The passage has shaped Christian political thought for centuries. The questions it raises, such as the limits of obedience and the right to resist tyranny, cut across both traditions rather than dividing them. Each still brings its own emphasis. Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God. Romans 13:1 Therefore he who resists the authority withstands the ordinance of God; and those who withstand will receive to themselves judgment. Romans 13:2 For rulers are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil. Do you desire to have no fear of the authority? Do that which is good, and you will have praise from the authority, Romans 13:3 for he is a servant of God to you for good. But if you do that which is evil, be afraid, for he doesn’t bear the sword in vain; for he is a servant of God, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil. Romans 13:4 Therefore you need to be in subjection, not only because of the wrath, but also for conscience’ sake. Romans 13:5 For this reason you also pay taxes, for they are servants of God’s service, continually doing this very thing. Romans 13:6 Therefore give everyone what you owe: if you owe taxes, pay taxes; if customs, then customs; if respect, then respect; if honor, then honor. Romans 13:7

title: Romans 13:8–14
context: Paul sums up the law in love. Believers should owe nothing except the continuing debt of love, because love fulfills the commandments. He then adds urgency: the night is nearly over and the day of salvation is near, so believers should wake up, put off the works of darkness, and put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Augustine’s conversion turned on verses 13–14. Both traditions embrace the passage, with different emphases on holiness and on how the law relates to love.
text: Romans 13:8–14 Romans Paul sums up the law in love. Believers should owe nothing except the continuing debt of love, because love fulfills the commandments. He then adds urgency: the night is nearly over and the day of salvation is near, so believers should wake up, put off the works of darkness, and put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Augustine’s conversion turned on verses 13–14. Both traditions embrace the passage, with different emphases on holiness and on how the law relates to love. Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. Romans 13:8 For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and whatever other commandments there are, are all summed up in this saying, namely, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Romans 13:9 Love doesn’t harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law. Romans 13:10 Do this, knowing the time, that it is already time for you to awaken out of sleep, for salvation is now nearer to us than when we first believed. Romans 13:11 The night is far gone, and the day is near. Let’s therefore throw off the deeds of darkness, and let’s put on the armor of light. Romans 13:12 Let’s walk properly, as in the day; not in reveling and drunkenness, not in sexual promiscuity and lustful acts, and not in strife and jealousy. Romans 13:13 But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts. Romans 13:14

title: Romans 14:1–12
context: Paul addresses tensions between the “weak,” who keep food laws and special days out of conscience, and the “strong,” who feel free from them. Neither group should despise or judge the other, because each lives and dies to the Lord, and each will give account to God. Both traditions read the passage as a guide to Christian liberty and charity on secondary matters. Each draws on it in its own way, Arminian readers stressing individual accountability and Reformed readers stressing the lordship of Christ over conscience.
text: Romans 14:1–12 Romans Paul addresses tensions between the “weak,” who keep food laws and special days out of conscience, and the “strong,” who feel free from them. Neither group should despise or judge the other, because each lives and dies to the Lord, and each will give account to God. Both traditions read the passage as a guide to Christian liberty and charity on secondary matters. Each draws on it in its own way, Arminian readers stressing individual accountability and Reformed readers stressing the lordship of Christ over conscience. Now accept one who is weak in faith, but not for disputes over opinions. Romans 14:1 One man has faith to eat all things, but he who is weak eats only vegetables. Romans 14:2 Don’t let him who eats despise him who doesn’t eat. Don’t let him who doesn’t eat judge him who eats, for God has accepted him. Romans 14:3 Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand. Romans 14:4 One man esteems one day as more important. Another esteems every day alike. Let each man be fully assured in his own mind. Romans 14:5 He who observes the day, observes it to the Lord; and he who does not observe the day, to the Lord he does not observe it. He who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives God thanks. He who doesn’t eat, to the Lord he doesn’t eat, and gives God thanks. Romans 14:6 For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. Romans 14:7 For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s. Romans 14:8 For to this end Christ died, rose, and lived again, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living. Romans 14:9 But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you again, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. Romans 14:10 For it is written, “‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘to me every knee will bow. Every tongue will confess to God.’” Romans 14:11 So then each one of us will give account of himself to God. Romans 14:12

title: Romans 14:13–23
context: Paul turns from the weak to the strong. Though no food is unclean in itself, believers should never use their liberty in a way that causes a brother to stumble or destroys someone for whom Christ died. The kingdom of God is about righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, not food and drink. Whatever is not from faith is sin. Both traditions draw ethical guidance from the passage. Verse 15, which warns against destroying a brother for whom Christ died, is a point of real debate between them.
text: Romans 14:13–23 Romans Paul turns from the weak to the strong. Though no food is unclean in itself, believers should never use their liberty in a way that causes a brother to stumble or destroys someone for whom Christ died. The kingdom of God is about righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, not food and drink. Whatever is not from faith is sin. Both traditions draw ethical guidance from the passage. Verse 15, which warns against destroying a brother for whom Christ died, is a point of real debate between them. Therefore let’s not judge one another any more, but judge this rather, that no man put a stumbling block in his brother’s way, or an occasion for falling. Romans 14:13 I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean of itself; except that to him who considers anything to be unclean, to him it is unclean. Romans 14:14 Yet if because of food your brother is grieved, you walk no longer in love. Don’t destroy with your food him for whom Christ died. Romans 14:15 Then don’t let your good be slandered, Romans 14:16 for God’s Kingdom is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Romans 14:17 For he who serves Christ in these things is acceptable to God and approved by men. Romans 14:18 So then, let’s follow after things which make for peace, and things by which we may build one another up. Romans 14:19 Don’t overthrow God’s work for food’s sake. All things indeed are clean, however it is evil for that man who creates a stumbling block by eating. Romans 14:20 It is good to not eat meat, drink wine, nor do anything by which your brother stumbles, is offended, or is made weak. Romans 14:21 Do you have faith? Have it to yourself before God. Happy is he who doesn’t judge himself in that which he approves. Romans 14:22 But he who doubts is condemned if he eats, because it isn’t of faith; and whatever is not of faith is sin. Romans 14:23

title: Romans 15:1–13
context: Paul finishes his appeal to the strong and the weak by pointing to Christ, who did not please himself. Scripture was written to give endurance and hope, and Paul prays that the church will glorify God with one voice. Believers are to welcome one another as Christ welcomed them, because Christ became a servant to Israel to confirm God’s promises and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. A chain of Old Testament quotations celebrates the nations praising God, and Paul closes with a prayer to the God of hope. Both traditions read the passage as a vision of one people of God drawn from every nation, with different emphases on how that people is gathered.
text: Romans 15:1–13 Romans Paul finishes his appeal to the strong and the weak by pointing to Christ, who did not please himself. Scripture was written to give endurance and hope, and Paul prays that the church will glorify God with one voice. Believers are to welcome one another as Christ welcomed them, because Christ became a servant to Israel to confirm God’s promises and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. A chain of Old Testament quotations celebrates the nations praising God, and Paul closes with a prayer to the God of hope. Both traditions read the passage as a vision of one people of God drawn from every nation, with different emphases on how that people is gathered. Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Romans 15:1 Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up. Romans 15:2 For even Christ didn’t please himself. But, as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.” Romans 15:3 For whatever things were written before were written for our learning, that through perseverance and through encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. Romans 15:4 Now the God of perseverance and of encouragement grant you to be of the same mind with one another according to Christ Jesus, Romans 15:5 that with one accord you may with one mouth glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Romans 15:6 Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God. Romans 15:7 Now I say that Christ has been made a servant of the circumcision for the truth of God, that he might confirm the promises given to the fathers, Romans 15:8 and that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, “Therefore I will give praise to you among the Gentiles and sing to your name.” Romans 15:9 Again he says, “Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.” Romans 15:10 Again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles! Let all the peoples praise him.” Romans 15:11 Again, Isaiah says, “There will be the root of Jesse, he who arises to rule over the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope.” Romans 15:12 Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope in the power of the Holy Spirit. Romans 15:13

title: Romans 15:14–33
context: Paul explains why he has written so boldly and shares his plans. His ministry is a priestly service of bringing the Gentiles as an offering to God, made acceptable by the Holy Spirit. He has preached from Jerusalem to Illyricum, aiming to go where Christ has not been named, and now plans to visit Rome on the way to Spain after delivering an offering to Jerusalem. He asks the Romans to pray for him. These are largely personal verses. Both traditions draw lessons about mission, prayer, and providence, with differing emphases on how God’s will relates to human plans.
text: Romans 15:14–33 Romans Paul explains why he has written so boldly and shares his plans. His ministry is a priestly service of bringing the Gentiles as an offering to God, made acceptable by the Holy Spirit. He has preached from Jerusalem to Illyricum, aiming to go where Christ has not been named, and now plans to visit Rome on the way to Spain after delivering an offering to Jerusalem. He asks the Romans to pray for him. These are largely personal verses. Both traditions draw lessons about mission, prayer, and providence, with differing emphases on how God’s will relates to human plans. I myself am also persuaded about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, able also to admonish others. Romans 15:14 But I write the more boldly to you in part as reminding you, because of the grace that was given to me by God, Romans 15:15 that I should be a servant of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, serving as a priest of the Good News of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles might be made acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. Romans 15:16 I have therefore my boasting in Christ Jesus in things pertaining to God. Romans 15:17 For I will not dare to speak of any things except those which Christ worked through me for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed, Romans 15:18 in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of God’s Spirit; so that from Jerusalem and around as far as to Illyricum, I have fully preached the Good News of Christ; Romans 15:19 yes, making it my aim to preach the Good News, not where Christ was already named, that I might not build on another’s foundation. Romans 15:20 But, as it is written, “They will see, to whom no news of him came. They who haven’t heard will understand.” Romans 15:21 Therefore also I was hindered these many times from coming to you, Romans 15:22 but now, no longer having any place in these regions, and having these many years a longing to come to you, Romans 15:23 whenever I travel to Spain, I will come to you. For I hope to see you on my journey, and to be helped on my way there by you, if first I may enjoy your company for a while. Romans 15:24 But now, I say, I am going to Jerusalem, serving the saints. Romans 15:25 For it has been the good pleasure of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor among the saints who are at Jerusalem. Romans 15:26 Yes, it has been their good pleasure, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, they owe it to them also to serve them in material things. Romans 15:27 When therefore I have accomplished this, and have sealed to them this fruit, I will go on by way of you to Spain. Romans 15:28 I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of the blessing of the Good News of Christ. Romans 15:29 Now I beg you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, that you strive together with me in your prayers to God for me, Romans 15:30 that I may be delivered from those who are disobedient in Judea, and that my service which I have for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints, Romans 15:31 that I may come to you in joy through the will of God, and together with you, find rest. Romans 15:32 Now the God of peace be with you all. Amen. Romans 15:33

title: Romans 16:1–16
context: Paul commends Phoebe, servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae and bearer of the letter, then greets coworkers and saints at Rome: Prisca and Aquila, Andronicus and Junia, household gatherings, and many named by love and labor. The list ends with a holy kiss and greeting from all the churches of Christ.
text: Romans 16:1–16 Romans Paul commends Phoebe, servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae and bearer of the letter, then greets coworkers and saints at Rome: Prisca and Aquila, Andronicus and Junia, household gatherings, and many named by love and labor. The list ends with a holy kiss and greeting from all the churches of Christ. I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae, Romans 16:1 that you receive her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and that you assist her in whatever matter she may need from you, for she herself also has been a helper of many, and of my own self. Romans 16:2 Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, Romans 16:3 who risked their own necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the assemblies of the Gentiles. Romans 16:4 Greet the assembly that is in their house. Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the first fruits of Achaia to Christ. Romans 16:5 Greet Mary, who labored much for us. Romans 16:6 Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and my fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles, who were also in Christ before me. Romans 16:7 Greet Amplias, my beloved in the Lord. Romans 16:8 Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and Stachys, my beloved. Romans 16:9 Greet Apelles, the approved in Christ. Greet those who are of the household of Aristobulus. Romans 16:10 Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet them of the household of Narcissus, who are in the Lord. Romans 16:11 Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. Greet Persis, the beloved, who labored much in the Lord. Romans 16:12 Greet Rufus, the chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine. Romans 16:13 Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Romans 16:14 Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them. Romans 16:15 Greet one another with a holy kiss. The assemblies of Christ greet you. Romans 16:16

title: Romans 16:17–27
context: Paul warns the Romans to watch those who cause divisions contrary to the doctrine they have been taught, promises that the God of peace will quickly crush Satan under their feet, sends greetings from his company, and closes with a doxology to the only wise God through Jesus Christ, who has now disclosed to every nation the mystery kept hidden for ages, so that they may believe and obey. (Verse 24, a grace benediction, is found in later manuscripts and printed in the WEB. The WEB places the closing doxology at 14:24–26, following the Majority Text; it is shown here as 16:25–27.)
text: Romans 16:17–27 Romans Paul warns the Romans to watch those who cause divisions contrary to the doctrine they have been taught, promises that the God of peace will quickly crush Satan under their feet, sends greetings from his company, and closes with a doxology to the only wise God through Jesus Christ, who has now disclosed to every nation the mystery kept hidden for ages, so that they may believe and obey. (Verse 24, a grace benediction, is found in later manuscripts and printed in the WEB. The WEB places the closing doxology at 14:24–26, following the Majority Text; it is shown here as 16:25–27.) Now I beg you, brothers, look out for those who are causing the divisions and occasions of stumbling, contrary to the doctrine which you learned, and turn away from them. Romans 16:17 For those who are such don’t serve our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly; and by their smooth and flattering speech they deceive the hearts of the innocent. Romans 16:18 For your obedience has become known to all. I rejoice therefore over you. But I desire to have you wise in that which is good, but innocent in that which is evil. Romans 16:19 And the God of peace will quickly crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Romans 16:20 Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you, as do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my relatives. Romans 16:21 I, Tertius, who write the letter, greet you in the Lord. Romans 16:22 Gaius, my host and host of the whole assembly, greets you. Erastus, the treasurer of the city, greets you, as does Quartus, the brother. Romans 16:23 The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all! Amen. Romans 16:24 Now to him who is able to establish you according to my Good News and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery which has been kept secret through long ages, Romans 16:25 but now is revealed, and by the Scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the eternal God, is made known for obedience of faith to all the nations; Romans 16:26 to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory forever! Amen. Romans 16:27

title: Romans 2:1–11
context: Paul turns to the person who condemns the sins of Romans 1 while doing the same things. God’s judgment is according to truth, and his kindness is meant to lead to repentance, not to be presumed upon. God will repay each person according to their works: eternal life to those who seek glory by patient well-doing, wrath to those who obey unrighteousness. There is no partiality with God. Both traditions agree that judgment is impartial. They differ on how verses 6–10 relate to justification by faith.
text: Romans 2:1–11 Romans Paul turns to the person who condemns the sins of Romans 1 while doing the same things. God’s judgment is according to truth, and his kindness is meant to lead to repentance, not to be presumed upon. God will repay each person according to their works: eternal life to those who seek glory by patient well-doing, wrath to those who obey unrighteousness. There is no partiality with God. Both traditions agree that judgment is impartial. They differ on how verses 6–10 relate to justification by faith. Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judge. For in that which you judge another, you condemn yourself. For you who judge practice the same things. Romans 2:1 We know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who practice such things. Romans 2:2 Do you think this, O man who judges those who practice such things, and do the same, that you will escape the judgment of God? Romans 2:3 Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? Romans 2:4 But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart you are treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath, revelation, and of the righteous judgment of God, Romans 2:5 who “will pay back to everyone according to their works:” Romans 2:6 to those who by perseverance in well-doing seek for glory, honor, and incorruptibility, eternal life; Romans 2:7 but to those who are self-seeking and don’t obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, will be wrath, indignation, Romans 2:8 oppression, and anguish on every soul of man who does evil, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. Romans 2:9 But glory, honor, and peace go to every man who does good, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. Romans 2:10 For there is no partiality with God. Romans 2:11

title: Romans 2:12–29
context: Paul continues to level the ground between Jew and Gentile. Those who sin without the law will perish without it, and those under the law will be judged by it, because it is doers of the law, not hearers, who are counted righteous. Gentiles who do what the law requires show that its work is written on their hearts. Paul then confronts the Jewish teacher who relies on the law but breaks it, and concludes that true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit. The passage raises two questions on which readers in both traditions differ among themselves: whether verse 13 describes a real or hypothetical standard, and who the Gentiles of verses 14–15 are.
text: Romans 2:12–29 Romans Paul continues to level the ground between Jew and Gentile. Those who sin without the law will perish without it, and those under the law will be judged by it, because it is doers of the law, not hearers, who are counted righteous. Gentiles who do what the law requires show that its work is written on their hearts. Paul then confronts the Jewish teacher who relies on the law but breaks it, and concludes that true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit. The passage raises two questions on which readers in both traditions differ among themselves: whether verse 13 describes a real or hypothetical standard, and who the Gentiles of verses 14–15 are. For as many as have sinned without the law will also perish without the law. As many as have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. Romans 2:12 For it isn’t the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified Romans 2:13 (for when Gentiles who don’t have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves, Romans 2:14 in that they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience testifying with them, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or else excusing them) Romans 2:15 in the day when God will judge the secrets of men, according to my Good News, by Jesus Christ. Romans 2:16 Indeed you bear the name of a Jew, rest on the law, glory in God, Romans 2:17 know his will, and approve the things that are excellent, being instructed out of the law, Romans 2:18 and are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, Romans 2:19 a corrector of the foolish, a teacher of babies, having in the law the form of knowledge and of the truth. Romans 2:20 You therefore who teach another, don’t you teach yourself? You who preach that a man shouldn’t steal, do you steal? Romans 2:21 You who say a man shouldn’t commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples? Romans 2:22 You who glory in the law, do you dishonor God by disobeying the law? Romans 2:23 For “the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you,” just as it is written. Romans 2:24 For circumcision indeed profits, if you are a doer of the law, but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. Romans 2:25 If therefore the uncircumcised keep the ordinances of the law, won’t his uncircumcision be accounted as circumcision? Romans 2:26 Won’t those who are physically uncircumcised, but fulfill the law, judge you, who with the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law? Romans 2:27 For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, neither is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; Romans 2:28 but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; whose praise is not from men, but from God. Romans 2:29

title: Romans 3:1–8
context: If Jews and Gentiles alike stand under judgment, what advantage does the Jew have? Paul answers that Israel was entrusted with the oracles of God, and that human unfaithfulness cannot cancel God’s faithfulness. He then rejects the twisted logic that human sin should be excused because it highlights God’s righteousness. Both traditions read this as a defense of God’s faithfulness and justice, with few points of disagreement.
text: Romans 3:1–8 Romans If Jews and Gentiles alike stand under judgment, what advantage does the Jew have? Paul answers that Israel was entrusted with the oracles of God, and that human unfaithfulness cannot cancel God’s faithfulness. He then rejects the twisted logic that human sin should be excused because it highlights God’s righteousness. Both traditions read this as a defense of God’s faithfulness and justice, with few points of disagreement. Then what advantage does the Jew have? Or what is the profit of circumcision? Romans 3:1 Much in every way! Because first of all, they were entrusted with the revelations of God. Romans 3:2 For what if some were without faith? Will their lack of faith nullify the faithfulness of God? Romans 3:3 May it never be! Yes, let God be found true, but every man a liar. As it is written, “that you might be justified in your words, and might prevail when you come into judgment.” Romans 3:4 But if our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, what will we say? Is God unrighteous who inflicts wrath? I speak like men do. Romans 3:5 May it never be! For then how will God judge the world? Romans 3:6 For if the truth of God through my lie abounded to his glory, why am I also still judged as a sinner? Romans 3:7 Why not (as we are slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say), “Let’s do evil, that good may come?” Those who say so are justly condemned. Romans 3:8

title: Romans 3:21–31
context: After showing that Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin (1:18–3:20), Paul announces the good news: God’s righteousness has been revealed apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. Sinners are justified freely by grace through the redemption in Christ, whom God set forth as an atoning sacrifice. Boasting is excluded, and God is shown to be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. This passage is shared ground for Protestant theology, with differences in how the two traditions describe the atonement and faith.
text: Romans 3:21–31 Romans After showing that Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin (1:18–3:20), Paul announces the good news: God’s righteousness has been revealed apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. Sinners are justified freely by grace through the redemption in Christ, whom God set forth as an atoning sacrifice. Boasting is excluded, and God is shown to be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. This passage is shared ground for Protestant theology, with differences in how the two traditions describe the atonement and faith. But now apart from the law, a righteousness of God has been revealed, being testified by the law and the prophets; Romans 3:21 even the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all and on all those who believe. For there is no distinction, Romans 3:22 for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God; Romans 3:23 being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, Romans 3:24 whom God sent to be an atoning sacrifice through faith in his blood, for a demonstration of his righteousness through the passing over of prior sins, in God’s forbearance; Romans 3:25 to demonstrate his righteousness at this present time, that he might himself be just and the justifier of him who has faith in Jesus. Romans 3:26 Where then is the boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? Of works? No, but by a law of faith. Romans 3:27 We maintain therefore that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law. Romans 3:28 Or is God the God of Jews only? Isn’t he the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, Romans 3:29 since indeed there is one God who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. Romans 3:30 Do we then nullify the law through faith? May it never be! No, we establish the law. Romans 3:31

title: Romans 3:9–20
context: Paul concludes his case: Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin. He strings together Old Testament texts to show that no one is righteous, no one seeks God, and no one does good. The law silences every mouth and brings knowledge of sin, so no one will be justified by works of the law. Both traditions affirm universal sinfulness. They differ on what “no one seeks God” implies about human ability and about the grace that precedes faith.
text: Romans 3:9–20 Romans Paul concludes his case: Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin. He strings together Old Testament texts to show that no one is righteous, no one seeks God, and no one does good. The law silences every mouth and brings knowledge of sin, so no one will be justified by works of the law. Both traditions affirm universal sinfulness. They differ on what “no one seeks God” implies about human ability and about the grace that precedes faith. What then? Are we better than they? No, in no way. For we previously warned both Jews and Greeks that they are all under sin. Romans 3:9 As it is written, “There is no one righteous; no, not one. Romans 3:10 There is no one who understands. There is no one who seeks after God. Romans 3:11 They have all turned away. They have together become unprofitable. There is no one who does good, no, not so much as one.” Romans 3:12 “Their throat is an open tomb. With their tongues they have used deceit.” “The poison of vipers is under their lips.” Romans 3:13 “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.” Romans 3:14 “Their feet are swift to shed blood. Romans 3:15 Destruction and misery are in their ways. Romans 3:16 The way of peace, they haven’t known.” Romans 3:17 “There is no fear of God before their eyes.” Romans 3:18 Now we know that whatever things the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, that every mouth may be closed, and all the world may be brought under the judgment of God. Romans 3:19 Because by the works of the law, no flesh will be justified in his sight; for through the law comes the knowledge of sin. Romans 3:20

title: Romans 4:1–12
context: Paul turns to Abraham to show that justification has always been by faith. Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness, before he was circumcised. David also speaks of the blessedness of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works. Both traditions treat this as foundational for justification by faith. They differ on the meaning of “counted” and on how faith itself relates to righteousness.
text: Romans 4:1–12 Romans Paul turns to Abraham to show that justification has always been by faith. Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness, before he was circumcised. David also speaks of the blessedness of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works. Both traditions treat this as foundational for justification by faith. They differ on the meaning of “counted” and on how faith itself relates to righteousness. What then will we say that Abraham, our forefather, has found according to the flesh? Romans 4:1 For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not toward God. Romans 4:2 For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.” Romans 4:3 Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed. Romans 4:4 But to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness. Romans 4:5 Even as David also pronounces blessing on the man to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: Romans 4:6 “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Romans 4:7 Blessed is the man whom the Lord will by no means charge with sin.” Romans 4:8 Is this blessing then pronounced only on the circumcised, or on the uncircumcised also? For we say that faith was accounted to Abraham for righteousness. Romans 4:9 How then was it counted? When he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. Romans 4:10 He received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while he was in uncircumcision, that he might be the father of all those who believe, though they might be in uncircumcision, that righteousness might also be accounted to them. Romans 4:11 He is the father of circumcision to those who not only are of the circumcision, but who also walk in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham, which he had in uncircumcision. Romans 4:12

title: Romans 4:13–25
context: Paul presses the Abraham argument further. The promise that Abraham would inherit the world came through the righteousness of faith, not the law, so that it rests on grace and is guaranteed to all his offspring. Abraham believed God who gives life to the dead, trusting the promise against all natural hope, and his faith was counted as righteousness. Paul says this was written for believers today as well. Both traditions read the passage as a celebration of faith resting on God’s promise. They differ on how faith arises and on what makes the promise “sure.”
text: Romans 4:13–25 Romans Paul presses the Abraham argument further. The promise that Abraham would inherit the world came through the righteousness of faith, not the law, so that it rests on grace and is guaranteed to all his offspring. Abraham believed God who gives life to the dead, trusting the promise against all natural hope, and his faith was counted as righteousness. Paul says this was written for believers today as well. Both traditions read the passage as a celebration of faith resting on God’s promise. They differ on how faith arises and on what makes the promise “sure.” For the promise to Abraham and to his offspring that he would be heir of the world wasn’t through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. Romans 4:13 For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void, and the promise is made of no effect. Romans 4:14 For the law produces wrath; for where there is no law, neither is there disobedience. Romans 4:15 For this cause it is of faith, that it may be according to grace, to the end that the promise may be sure to all the offspring, not to that only which is of the law, but to that also which is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all. Romans 4:16 As it is written, “I have made you a father of many nations.” This is in the presence of him whom he believed: God, who gives life to the dead, and calls the things that are not, as though they were. Romans 4:17 Against hope, Abraham in hope believed, to the end that he might become a father of many nations, according to that which had been spoken, “So will your offspring be.” Romans 4:18 Without being weakened in faith, he didn’t consider his own body, already having been worn out, (he being about a hundred years old), and the deadness of Sarah’s womb. Romans 4:19 Yet, looking to the promise of God, he didn’t waver through unbelief, but grew strong through faith, giving glory to God, Romans 4:20 and being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform. Romans 4:21 Therefore it also was “credited to him for righteousness.” Romans 4:22 Now it was not written that it was accounted to him for his sake alone, Romans 4:23 but for our sake also, to whom it will be accounted, who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, Romans 4:24 who was delivered up for our trespasses, and was raised for our justification. Romans 4:25

title: Romans 5:1–11
context: Justified by faith, believers have peace with God, access to grace, and hope of glory. Even suffering produces endurance, character, and hope, because God’s love has been poured into their hearts by the Spirit. Paul then shows the depth of that love: Christ died for the ungodly while we were still sinners, and if we were reconciled while enemies, much more will we be saved by his life. Both traditions treasure this passage as a basis for assurance; they differ slightly on how certain final salvation is for every justified person.
text: Romans 5:1–11 Romans Justified by faith, believers have peace with God, access to grace, and hope of glory. Even suffering produces endurance, character, and hope, because God’s love has been poured into their hearts by the Spirit. Paul then shows the depth of that love: Christ died for the ungodly while we were still sinners, and if we were reconciled while enemies, much more will we be saved by his life. Both traditions treasure this passage as a basis for assurance; they differ slightly on how certain final salvation is for every justified person. Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ; Romans 5:1 through whom we also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand. We rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Romans 5:2 Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance; Romans 5:3 and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope; Romans 5:4 and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us. Romans 5:5 For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. Romans 5:6 For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a good person someone would even dare to die. Romans 5:7 But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Romans 5:8 Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we will be saved from God’s wrath through him. Romans 5:9 For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life. Romans 5:10 Not only so, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation. Romans 5:11

title: Romans 5:12–21
context: Paul compares Adam and Christ. Sin and death entered the world through one man, and through one man’s obedience grace and righteousness abound to many. The passage underlies the doctrine of original sin and the representative work of Christ. Arminian and Reformed readers share much of this, while differing on how Adam’s sin passes to his descendants and on the scope of “all” in verse 18.
text: Romans 5:12–21 Romans Paul compares Adam and Christ. Sin and death entered the world through one man, and through one man’s obedience grace and righteousness abound to many. The passage underlies the doctrine of original sin and the representative work of Christ. Arminian and Reformed readers share much of this, while differing on how Adam’s sin passes to his descendants and on the scope of “all” in verse 18. Therefore, as sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin, so death passed to all men because all sinned. Romans 5:12 For until the law, sin was in the world; but sin is not charged when there is no law. Romans 5:13 Nevertheless death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those whose sins weren’t like Adam’s disobedience, who is a foreshadowing of him who was to come. Romans 5:14 But the free gift isn’t like the trespass. For if by the trespass of the one the many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many. Romans 5:15 The gift is not as through one who sinned; for the judgment came by one to condemnation, but the free gift followed many trespasses to justification. Romans 5:16 For if by the trespass of the one, death reigned through the one; so much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ. Romans 5:17 So then as through one trespass, all men were condemned; even so through one act of righteousness, all men were justified to life. Romans 5:18 For as through the one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, even so through the obedience of the one, many will be made righteous. Romans 5:19 The law came in that the trespass might abound; but where sin abounded, grace abounded more exceedingly, Romans 5:20 that as sin reigned in death, even so grace might reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. Romans 5:21

title: Romans 6:1–14
context: Paul anticipates an objection: if grace abounds where sin increased, should believers keep sinning? He answers that those united to Christ in baptism have died to sin and been raised to new life. They are to consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God, and not let sin reign in their bodies, because they are not under law but under grace. Both traditions treat this as central to the Christian life. Arminian readers, following Wesley, often see in it the hope of deliverance from the power of willful sin. Reformed readers see the definitive break with sin that begins a lifelong process of sanctification.
text: Romans 6:1–14 Romans Paul anticipates an objection: if grace abounds where sin increased, should believers keep sinning? He answers that those united to Christ in baptism have died to sin and been raised to new life. They are to consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God, and not let sin reign in their bodies, because they are not under law but under grace. Both traditions treat this as central to the Christian life. Arminian readers, following Wesley, often see in it the hope of deliverance from the power of willful sin. Reformed readers see the definitive break with sin that begins a lifelong process of sanctification. What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? Romans 6:1 May it never be! We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer? Romans 6:2 Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? Romans 6:3 We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life. Romans 6:4 For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will also be part of his resurrection; Romans 6:5 knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin. Romans 6:6 For he who has died has been freed from sin. Romans 6:7 But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him, Romans 6:8 knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more. Death no longer has dominion over him! Romans 6:9 For the death that he died, he died to sin one time; but the life that he lives, he lives to God. Romans 6:10 Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Romans 6:11 Therefore don’t let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts. Romans 6:12 Also, do not present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God. Romans 6:13 For sin will not have dominion over you, for you are not under law, but under grace. Romans 6:14

title: Romans 6:15–23
context: Paul raises the question again in a new form: should believers sin because they are under grace? He answers with the image of slavery. Everyone serves some master, either sin leading to death or obedience leading to righteousness. Believers have been set free from sin and become slaves of God, bearing fruit toward holiness and eternal life. The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ. Both traditions see this as a call to holiness grounded in grace. They differ somewhat on the relation of holiness to final salvation.
text: Romans 6:15–23 Romans Paul raises the question again in a new form: should believers sin because they are under grace? He answers with the image of slavery. Everyone serves some master, either sin leading to death or obedience leading to righteousness. Believers have been set free from sin and become slaves of God, bearing fruit toward holiness and eternal life. The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ. Both traditions see this as a call to holiness grounded in grace. They differ somewhat on the relation of holiness to final salvation. What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law but under grace? May it never be! Romans 6:15 Don’t you know that when you present yourselves as servants and obey someone, you are the servants of whomever you obey, whether of sin to death, or of obedience to righteousness? Romans 6:16 But thanks be to God that, whereas you were bondservants of sin, you became obedient from the heart to that form of teaching to which you were delivered. Romans 6:17 Being made free from sin, you became bondservants of righteousness. Romans 6:18 I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh; for as you presented your members as servants to uncleanness and to wickedness upon wickedness, even so now present your members as servants to righteousness for sanctification. Romans 6:19 For when you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness. Romans 6:20 What fruit then did you have at that time in the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. Romans 6:21 But now, being made free from sin and having become servants of God, you have your fruit of sanctification and the result of eternal life. Romans 6:22 For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Romans 6:23

title: Romans 7:1–6
context: Paul uses the analogy of marriage to explain the believer’s release from the law. Just as death ends a marriage bond, believers have died to the law through the body of Christ so that they belong to another, the risen Christ, and bear fruit for God. They now serve in the new way of the Spirit, not the old way of the written code. Both traditions read this as the believer’s freedom from the law’s condemnation. They differ on the continuing role of the moral law.
text: Romans 7:1–6 Romans Paul uses the analogy of marriage to explain the believer’s release from the law. Just as death ends a marriage bond, believers have died to the law through the body of Christ so that they belong to another, the risen Christ, and bear fruit for God. They now serve in the new way of the Spirit, not the old way of the written code. Both traditions read this as the believer’s freedom from the law’s condemnation. They differ on the continuing role of the moral law. Or don’t you know, brothers (for I speak to men who know the law), that the law has dominion over a man for as long as he lives? Romans 7:1 For the woman that has a husband is bound by law to the husband while he lives, but if the husband dies, she is discharged from the law of the husband. Romans 7:2 So then if, while the husband lives, she is joined to another man, she would be called an adulteress. But if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is no adulteress, though she is joined to another man. Romans 7:3 Therefore, my brothers, you also were made dead to the law through the body of Christ, that you would be joined to another, to him who was raised from the dead, that we might produce fruit to God. Romans 7:4 For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions which were through the law worked in our members to bring out fruit to death. Romans 7:5 But now we have been discharged from the law, having died to that in which we were held; so that we serve in newness of the spirit, and not in oldness of the letter. Romans 7:6

title: Romans 7:7–25
context: Paul defends the law: it is holy, righteous, and good, but sin used the commandment to deceive and kill. He then describes in the first person a struggle in which he wants to do good but does evil, delighting in God’s law inwardly while another law wars in his members. The passage ends with a cry for deliverance and thanks to God through Jesus Christ. Interpreters have long disputed who the “I” of verses 14–25 is. Wesley read it as an awakened person not yet freed by grace. Many Reformed readers, following Augustine’s later view and Calvin, read it as the regenerate Paul. The debate does not fall neatly along party lines.
text: Romans 7:7–25 Romans Paul defends the law: it is holy, righteous, and good, but sin used the commandment to deceive and kill. He then describes in the first person a struggle in which he wants to do good but does evil, delighting in God’s law inwardly while another law wars in his members. The passage ends with a cry for deliverance and thanks to God through Jesus Christ. Interpreters have long disputed who the “I” of verses 14–25 is. Wesley read it as an awakened person not yet freed by grace. Many Reformed readers, following Augustine’s later view and Calvin, read it as the regenerate Paul. The debate does not fall neatly along party lines. What shall we say then? Is the law sin? May it never be! However, I wouldn’t have known sin except through the law. For I wouldn’t have known coveting unless the law had said, “You shall not covet.” Romans 7:7 But sin, finding occasion through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of coveting. For apart from the law, sin is dead. Romans 7:8 I was alive apart from the law once, but when the commandment came, sin revived and I died. Romans 7:9 The commandment which was for life, this I found to be for death; Romans 7:10 for sin, finding occasion through the commandment, deceived me, and through it killed me. Romans 7:11 Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, righteous, and good. Romans 7:12 Did then that which is good become death to me? May it never be! But sin, that it might be shown to be sin, was producing death in me through that which is good; that through the commandment sin might become exceedingly sinful. Romans 7:13 For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am fleshly, sold under sin. Romans 7:14 For I don’t understand what I am doing. For I don’t practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do. Romans 7:15 But if what I don’t desire, that I do, I consent to the law that it is good. Romans 7:16 So now it is no more I that do it, but sin which dwells in me. Romans 7:17 For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwells no good thing. For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good. Romans 7:18 For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice. Romans 7:19 But if what I don’t desire, that I do, it is no more I that do it, but sin which dwells in me. Romans 7:20 I find then the law that, while I desire to do good, evil is present. Romans 7:21 For I delight in God’s law after the inward person, Romans 7:22 but I see a different law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity under the law of sin which is in my members. Romans 7:23 What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death? Romans 7:24 I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord! So then with the mind, I myself serve God’s law, but with the flesh, sin’s law. Romans 7:25

title: Romans 8:1–11
context: Romans 8 opens with no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. What the law could not do because of the flesh, God did by sending his Son, so that the law’s requirement is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit. Paul contrasts the mind set on the flesh, which is hostile to God and cannot please him, with the mind set on the Spirit, which is life and peace. Both traditions treasure this passage. They differ on what “cannot” in verses 7–8 says about human ability and on how the Spirit’s indwelling relates to perseverance.
text: Romans 8:1–11 Romans Romans 8 opens with no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. What the law could not do because of the flesh, God did by sending his Son, so that the law’s requirement is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit. Paul contrasts the mind set on the flesh, which is hostile to God and cannot please him, with the mind set on the Spirit, which is life and peace. Both traditions treasure this passage. They differ on what “cannot” in verses 7–8 says about human ability and on how the Spirit’s indwelling relates to perseverance. There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. Romans 8:1 For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death. Romans 8:2 For what the law couldn’t do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, Romans 8:3 that the ordinance of the law might be fulfilled in us who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. Romans 8:4 For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit. Romans 8:5 For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace; Romans 8:6 because the mind of the flesh is hostile toward God, for it is not subject to God’s law, neither indeed can it be. Romans 8:7 Those who are in the flesh can’t please God. Romans 8:8 But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if it is so that the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if any man doesn’t have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. Romans 8:9 If Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is alive because of righteousness. Romans 8:10 But if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised up Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you. Romans 8:11

title: Romans 8:12–17
context: Paul draws a practical conclusion from the Spirit’s work in Romans 8:1–11. Believers owe the flesh nothing; those who put sin to death by the Spirit will live, and those led by the Spirit are God’s children. The Spirit of adoption replaces fear with the cry “Abba! Father!” and testifies with our spirit that we are heirs with Christ. Both traditions find assurance here, and both notice the conditions: “if you live after the flesh, you must die” and “if indeed we suffer with him.”
text: Romans 8:12–17 Romans Paul draws a practical conclusion from the Spirit’s work in Romans 8:1–11. Believers owe the flesh nothing; those who put sin to death by the Spirit will live, and those led by the Spirit are God’s children. The Spirit of adoption replaces fear with the cry “Abba! Father!” and testifies with our spirit that we are heirs with Christ. Both traditions find assurance here, and both notice the conditions: “if you live after the flesh, you must die” and “if indeed we suffer with him.” So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live after the flesh. Romans 8:12 For if you live after the flesh, you must die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. Romans 8:13 For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God. Romans 8:14 For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” Romans 8:15 The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God; Romans 8:16 and if children, then heirs—heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him. Romans 8:17

title: Romans 8:18–30
context: Paul sets present suffering against future glory. Creation groans, believers groan, and the Spirit groans in prayer, all waiting for the redemption of the body. The passage ends with two of the most debated verses in the debate over election: God works all things for good for those called according to his purpose, and those he foreknew he predestined, called, justified, and glorified. Arminian and Reformed readers share the hope of these verses and divide over the meaning of “foreknew.”
text: Romans 8:18–30 Romans Paul sets present suffering against future glory. Creation groans, believers groan, and the Spirit groans in prayer, all waiting for the redemption of the body. The passage ends with two of the most debated verses in the debate over election: God works all things for good for those called according to his purpose, and those he foreknew he predestined, called, justified, and glorified. Arminian and Reformed readers share the hope of these verses and divide over the meaning of “foreknew.” For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us. Romans 8:18 For the creation waits with eager expectation for the children of God to be revealed. Romans 8:19 For the creation was subjected to vanity, not of its own will, but because of him who subjected it, in hope Romans 8:20 that the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of decay into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. Romans 8:21 For we know that the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now. Romans 8:22 Not only so, but ourselves also, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the redemption of our body. Romans 8:23 For we were saved in hope, but hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for that which he sees? Romans 8:24 But if we hope for that which we don’t see, we wait for it with patience. Romans 8:25 In the same way, the Spirit also helps our weaknesses, for we don’t know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can’t be uttered. Romans 8:26 He who searches the hearts knows what is on the Spirit’s mind, because he makes intercession for the saints according to God. Romans 8:27 We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose. Romans 8:28 For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Romans 8:29 Whom he predestined, those he also called. Whom he called, those he also justified. Whom he justified, those he also glorified. Romans 8:30

title: Romans 8:31–39
context: Paul closes Romans 8 with a series of questions and a hymn of confidence. If God is for us, who can be against us? Who can bring a charge against God’s chosen ones, or condemn them, or separate them from Christ’s love? Paul answers that nothing in all creation can separate believers from God’s love in Christ Jesus. Both traditions treasure the passage as a foundation of assurance; they differ on whether a believer can separate himself.
text: Romans 8:31–39 Romans Paul closes Romans 8 with a series of questions and a hymn of confidence. If God is for us, who can be against us? Who can bring a charge against God’s chosen ones, or condemn them, or separate them from Christ’s love? Paul answers that nothing in all creation can separate believers from God’s love in Christ Jesus. Both traditions treasure the passage as a foundation of assurance; they differ on whether a believer can separate himself. What then shall we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? Romans 8:31 He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things? Romans 8:32 Who could bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who justifies. Romans 8:33 Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, yes rather, who was raised from the dead, who is at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us. Romans 8:34 Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? Romans 8:35 Even as it is written, “For your sake we are killed all day long. We were accounted as sheep for the slaughter.” Romans 8:36 No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. Romans 8:37 For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, Romans 8:38 nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Romans 8:39

title: Romans 9:1–13
context: Romans 9 opens with grief, not doctrine. Paul is in anguish because most of his fellow Israelites have not believed in their Messiah, though theirs are the covenants, the promises, and Christ himself according to the flesh. Has God’s word failed? Paul answers that not all who descend from Israel are Israel, and he points to Isaac over Ishmael and Jacob over Esau. Reformed readers see personal, unconditional election in these examples; Arminian readers see God’s freedom to choose the line of promise and to define his people by promise and faith rather than by descent.
text: Romans 9:1–13 Romans Romans 9 opens with grief, not doctrine. Paul is in anguish because most of his fellow Israelites have not believed in their Messiah, though theirs are the covenants, the promises, and Christ himself according to the flesh. Has God’s word failed? Paul answers that not all who descend from Israel are Israel, and he points to Isaac over Ishmael and Jacob over Esau. Reformed readers see personal, unconditional election in these examples; Arminian readers see God’s freedom to choose the line of promise and to define his people by promise and faith rather than by descent. I tell the truth in Christ. I am not lying, my conscience testifying with me in the Holy Spirit Romans 9:1 that I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart. Romans 9:2 For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers’ sake, my relatives according to the flesh Romans 9:3 who are Israelites; whose is the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service, and the promises; Romans 9:4 of whom are the fathers, and from whom is Christ as concerning the flesh, who is over all, God, blessed forever. Amen. Romans 9:5 But it is not as though the word of God has come to nothing. For they are not all Israel that are of Israel. Romans 9:6 Neither, because they are Abraham’s offspring, are they all children. But, “your offspring will be accounted as from Isaac.” Romans 9:7 That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as heirs. Romans 9:8 For this is a word of promise: “At the appointed time I will come, and Sarah will have a son.” Romans 9:9 Not only so, but Rebekah also conceived by one, by our father Isaac. Romans 9:10 For being not yet born, neither having done anything good or bad, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him who calls, Romans 9:11 it was said to her, “The elder will serve the younger.” Romans 9:12 Even as it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” Romans 9:13

title: Romans 9:14–29
context: Having described God’s choice of Jacob over Esau, Paul answers the objection that God is unjust. God says he will have mercy on whom he has mercy; he raised up Pharaoh to show his power; the potter has a right over the clay. Paul then speaks of vessels of wrath and vessels of mercy and of a people called from Jews and Gentiles alike. This is the most debated passage in the Arminian and Reformed discussion. Both sides read it as Scripture that silences human complaint; they differ on whether it describes unconditional individual election or God’s right to set the terms of mercy and to shape the history of Israel and the nations.
text: Romans 9:14–29 Romans Having described God’s choice of Jacob over Esau, Paul answers the objection that God is unjust. God says he will have mercy on whom he has mercy; he raised up Pharaoh to show his power; the potter has a right over the clay. Paul then speaks of vessels of wrath and vessels of mercy and of a people called from Jews and Gentiles alike. This is the most debated passage in the Arminian and Reformed discussion. Both sides read it as Scripture that silences human complaint; they differ on whether it describes unconditional individual election or God’s right to set the terms of mercy and to shape the history of Israel and the nations. What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? May it never be! Romans 9:14 For he said to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” Romans 9:15 So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy. Romans 9:16 For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I caused you to be raised up, that I might show in you my power, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” Romans 9:17 So then, he has mercy on whom he desires, and he hardens whom he desires. Romans 9:18 You will say then to me, “Why does he still find fault? For who withstands his will?” Romans 9:19 But indeed, O man, who are you to reply against God? Will the thing formed ask him who formed it, “Why did you make me like this?” Romans 9:20 Or hasn’t the potter a right over the clay, from the same lump to make one part a vessel for honor, and another for dishonor? Romans 9:21 What if God, willing to show his wrath and to make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, Romans 9:22 and that he might make known the riches of his glory on vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand for glory— Romans 9:23 us, whom he also called, not from the Jews only, but also from the Gentiles? Romans 9:24 As he says also in Hosea, “I will call them ‘my people,’ which were not my people; and her ‘beloved,’ who was not beloved.” Romans 9:25 “It will be that in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called ‘children of the living God.’” Romans 9:26 Isaiah cries concerning Israel, “If the number of the children of Israel are as the sand of the sea, it is the remnant who will be saved; Romans 9:27 for he will finish the work and cut it short in righteousness, because the Lord will make a short work upon the earth.” Romans 9:28 As Isaiah has said before, “Unless the Lord of Armies had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and would have been made like Gomorrah.” Romans 9:29

title: Romans 9:30–33
context: After the hard sayings about election and the potter, Paul draws a surprising conclusion. Gentiles who were not seeking righteousness have obtained it by faith, while Israel, pursuing the law as a matter of works, missed it and stumbled over the stone God laid in Zion. These verses turn the argument from God’s choosing to human believing. Arminian readers see them as the key to the chapter; Reformed readers see them as describing how God’s purpose is carried out.
text: Romans 9:30–33 Romans After the hard sayings about election and the potter, Paul draws a surprising conclusion. Gentiles who were not seeking righteousness have obtained it by faith, while Israel, pursuing the law as a matter of works, missed it and stumbled over the stone God laid in Zion. These verses turn the argument from God’s choosing to human believing. Arminian readers see them as the key to the chapter; Reformed readers see them as describing how God’s purpose is carried out. What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, who didn’t follow after righteousness, attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith; Romans 9:30 but Israel, following after a law of righteousness, didn’t arrive at the law of righteousness. Romans 9:31 Why? Because they didn’t seek it by faith, but as it were by works of the law. They stumbled over the stumbling stone, Romans 9:32 even as it is written, “Behold, I lay in Zion a stumbling stone and a rock of offense; and no one who believes in him will be disappointed.” Romans 9:33

title: Titus 1:1–4
context: Paul opens his letter to Titus by describing his apostleship in terms of its purpose: to promote the faith and knowledge of God’s elect, resting on the hope of eternal life promised before time began. God has revealed that promise in the preaching entrusted to Paul. He greets Titus as a true son in their shared faith.
text: Titus 1:1–4 Titus Paul opens his letter to Titus by describing his apostleship in terms of its purpose: to promote the faith and knowledge of God’s elect, resting on the hope of eternal life promised before time began. God has revealed that promise in the preaching entrusted to Paul. He greets Titus as a true son in their shared faith. Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God’s chosen ones and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness, Titus 1:1 in hope of eternal life, which God, who can’t lie, promised before time began; Titus 1:2 but in his own time revealed his word in the message with which I was entrusted according to the commandment of God our Savior, Titus 1:3 to Titus, my true child according to a common faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior. Titus 1:4

title: Titus 1:10–16
context: Titus needs sound elders because Crete is full of rebellious talkers and deceivers, especially from the circumcision group, who are upsetting whole households for profit. Paul quotes a Cretan poet’s harsh verdict on his own people and tells Titus to rebuke them sharply. Such teachers claim to know God but deny him by what they do.
text: Titus 1:10–16 Titus Titus needs sound elders because Crete is full of rebellious talkers and deceivers, especially from the circumcision group, who are upsetting whole households for profit. Paul quotes a Cretan poet’s harsh verdict on his own people and tells Titus to rebuke them sharply. Such teachers claim to know God but deny him by what they do. For there are also many unruly men, vain talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision, Titus 1:10 whose mouths must be stopped: men who overthrow whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for dishonest gain’s sake. Titus 1:11 One of them, a prophet of their own, said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, and idle gluttons.” Titus 1:12 This testimony is true. For this cause, reprove them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, Titus 1:13 not paying attention to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn away from the truth. Titus 1:14 To the pure, all things are pure, but to those who are defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their mind and their conscience are defiled.
