Titus 1:15 They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him, being abominable, disobedient, and unfit for any good work. Titus 1:16

title: Titus 1:5–9
context: Paul left Titus in Crete to put what remained into order the things that were lacking and appoint elders in every city: men above reproach, the husband of one wife, with believing children not open to debauchery or insubordination. An overseer, as God’s steward, must not be arrogant, quick-tempered, a drunkard, violent, or greedy, but given to hospitality, a lover of good, sober minded, fair, holy, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined, holding firm the trustworthy word so as to instruct in sound doctrine and convict those who contradict him.
text: Titus 1:5–9 Titus Paul left Titus in Crete to put what remained into order the things that were lacking and appoint elders in every city: men above reproach, the husband of one wife, with believing children not open to debauchery or insubordination. An overseer, as God’s steward, must not be arrogant, quick-tempered, a drunkard, violent, or greedy, but given to hospitality, a lover of good, sober minded, fair, holy, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined, holding firm the trustworthy word so as to instruct in sound doctrine and convict those who contradict him. I left you in Crete for this reason, that you would set in order the things that were lacking and appoint elders in every city, as I directed you— Titus 1:5 if anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having children who believe, who are not accused of loose or unruly behavior. Titus 1:6 For the overseer must be blameless, as God’s steward, not self-pleasing, not easily angered, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for dishonest gain; Titus 1:7 but given to hospitality, a lover of good, sober minded, fair, holy, self-controlled, Titus 1:8 holding to the faithful word which is according to the teaching, that he may be able to exhort in the sound doctrine, and to convict those who contradict him. Titus 1:9

title: Titus 2:1–8
context: Paul turns from Crete’s empty talkers to the life that matches sound doctrine: older men; older women who train the young women in household love and order; younger men; and Titus himself as a visible pattern. The public aim is that God’s word may not be blasphemed and that an opponent may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say about believers.
text: Titus 2:1–8 Titus Paul turns from Crete’s empty talkers to the life that matches sound doctrine: older men; older women who train the young women in household love and order; younger men; and Titus himself as a visible pattern. The public aim is that God’s word may not be blasphemed and that an opponent may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say about believers. But say the things which fit sound doctrine, Titus 2:1 that older men should be temperate, sensible, sober minded, sound in faith, in love, and in perseverance, Titus 2:2 and that older women likewise be reverent in behavior, not slanderers nor enslaved to much wine, teachers of that which is good, Titus 2:3 that they may train the young wives to love their husbands, to love their children, Titus 2:4 to be sober minded, chaste, workers at home, kind, being in subjection to their own husbands, that God’s word may not be blasphemed. Titus 2:5 Likewise, exhort the younger men to be sober minded. Titus 2:6 In all things show yourself an example of good works. In your teaching, show integrity, seriousness, incorruptibility, Titus 2:7 and soundness of speech that can’t be condemned, that he who opposes you may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say about us. Titus 2:8

title: Titus 2:11–15
context: Paul grounds all his household instructions in the gospel. God’s grace has appeared for all people, and it trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live soberly while they wait for Christ’s appearing. Christ gave himself to redeem a people zealous for good works, so Titus is to teach this with full authority. Both Arminian and Reformed readers find their views of grace’s scope and power in these verses.
text: Titus 2:11–15 Titus Paul grounds all his household instructions in the gospel. God’s grace has appeared for all people, and it trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live soberly while they wait for Christ’s appearing. Christ gave himself to redeem a people zealous for good works, so Titus is to teach this with full authority. Both Arminian and Reformed readers find their views of grace’s scope and power in these verses. For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men, Titus 2:11 instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age; Titus 2:12 looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ, Titus 2:13 who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works. Titus 2:14 Say these things and exhort and reprove with all authority. Let no one despise you. Titus 2:15

title: Titus 2:9–10
context: Paul turns to slaves in Christian households, urging honest, submissive, trustworthy service. The aim is that their conduct would make the teaching about God our Savior attractive. The instruction addresses believers within the social structures of the first century.
text: Titus 2:9–10 Titus Paul turns to slaves in Christian households, urging honest, submissive, trustworthy service. The aim is that their conduct would make the teaching about God our Savior attractive. The instruction addresses believers within the social structures of the first century. Exhort servants to be in subjection to their own masters and to be well-pleasing in all things, not contradicting, Titus 2:9 not stealing, but showing all good fidelity, that they may adorn the doctrine of God, our Savior, in all things. Titus 2:10

title: Titus 3:1–8
context: Titus is to remind the church of civic gentleness and courtesy toward all people, because we were also once foolish and enslaved. The turn is mercy: when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared, not by works, but according to mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit, poured out richly through Jesus Christ, so that, justified by his grace, we might be made heirs. Those who have believed are to devote themselves to good works.
text: Titus 3:1–8 Titus Titus is to remind the church of civic gentleness and courtesy toward all people, because we were also once foolish and enslaved. The turn is mercy: when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared, not by works, but according to mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit, poured out richly through Jesus Christ, so that, justified by his grace, we might be made heirs. Those who have believed are to devote themselves to good works. Remind them to be in subjection to rulers and to authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, Titus 3:1 to speak evil of no one, not to be contentious, to be gentle, showing all humility toward all men. Titus 3:2 For we were also once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another. Titus 3:3 But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared, Titus 3:4 not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit, Titus 3:5 whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior; Titus 3:6 that being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life. Titus 3:7 This saying is faithful, and concerning these things I desire that you insist confidently, so that those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable to men; Titus 3:8

title: Titus 3:9–15
context: After the trustworthy saying Paul fences the church: shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law; after a first and second warning, have nothing more to do with a person who stirs up division. Travel plans, help for Zenas and Apollos, a charge that our people learn to maintain good works, and a closing greeting and grace.
text: Titus 3:9–15 Titus After the trustworthy saying Paul fences the church: shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law; after a first and second warning, have nothing more to do with a person who stirs up division. Travel plans, help for Zenas and Apollos, a charge that our people learn to maintain good works, and a closing greeting and grace. but shun foolish questionings, genealogies, strife, and disputes about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain. Titus 3:9 Avoid a factious man after a first and second warning, Titus 3:10 knowing that such a one is perverted and sinful, being self-condemned. Titus 3:11 When I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, be diligent to come to me to Nicopolis, for I have determined to winter there. Titus 3:12 Send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey speedily, that nothing may be lacking for them. Titus 3:13 Let our people also learn to maintain good works to meet necessary needs, that they may not be unfruitful. Titus 3:14 All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in faith. Grace be with you all. Amen. Titus 3:15

title: Election
context: Before the foundation of the world, God chose a people in Christ to be holy and blameless—both camps read that choosing as grace, and they part over whether it is conditional on foreseen faith.
text: Election Before the foundation of the world, God chose a people in Christ to be holy and blameless—both camps read that choosing as grace, and they part over whether it is conditional on foreseen faith. Election is the church’s word for God’s choosing. Scripture praises the Father who “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” and names “God’s elect.” Arminian and Reformed readers agree the praise belongs to God, not to human merit. They disagree about the ground of the choice: God’s foreknowledge of a grace-enabled response, or God’s unconditional good pleasure that itself creates faith. Arminian readings typically make foreseen, grace-enabled faith (or entry into the elect body in Christ) the difference between the chosen and the rest; Reformed readings make God’s unconditional choice the difference, with faith as the effectual result.

title: Atonement
context: Christ died as a sacrifice for sin—both camps preach a cross of infinite worth; they part over whether the Father intended that death for every person or for the elect in particular.
text: Atonement Christ died as a sacrifice for sin—both camps preach a cross of infinite worth; they part over whether the Father intended that death for every person or for the elect in particular. Atonement is the work by which the death of Jesus deals with guilt. Scripture calls him the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, a ransom, a propitiation, the one who lays down his life for the sheep. Arminian and Reformed teachers agree the cross is substitutionary in some sense and that no one is saved apart from it. They disagree about the design: a sufficient provision for all, applied to believers, or a particular redemption that infallibly secures a people. Arminians typically teach a universal provision (every person’s sins remissible) applied by resistible, enabling grace through faith; the Reformed typically teach a particular design that infallibly obtains faith and salvation for the elect, while still confessing the infinite worth of the death and a gospel offer.

title: Justification
context: God counts the believer righteous for Christ’s sake—both camps preach pardon and acceptance by grace through faith; they part over how faith relates to election, and whether the justified can fall from that standing.
text: Justification God counts the believer righteous for Christ’s sake—both camps preach pardon and acceptance by grace through faith; they part over how faith relates to election, and whether the justified can fall from that standing. Justification is God’s verdict that a sinner is in the right with him. Genesis 15—Abraham believed the LORD, and he credited it to him as righteousness—and the later apostolic gospel of grace, not works, sit at the center. Arminius and the magisterial Reformers were closer here than popular debate suggests: both spoke of imputation and faith. The live forks are whether justifying faith is itself the effect of unconditional election, and whether the verdict can be lost. Both camps preach justification by grace through faith on the ground of Christ. Arminians typically treat believing as a resistible, grace-enabled condition that must continue; the Reformed typically treat faith as the instrumental effect of God’s prior, effectual mercy, and the verdict as final for those in Christ.

title: Regeneration
context: The Spirit makes the dead alive in Christ—both camps preach a new birth, not mere turning over a new leaf; they part over whether that birth can be resisted, and whether it precedes faith or is given with it.
text: Regeneration The Spirit makes the dead alive in Christ—both camps preach a new birth, not mere turning over a new leaf; they part over whether that birth can be resisted, and whether it precedes faith or is given with it. Regeneration is new birth: God raising a person from spiritual death. Jesus tells Nicodemus he must be born from above; Paul says we were dead in trespasses and God made us alive; Titus names the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit. The shared confession is that fallen people need a work God does in us, not only a message we approve. The fork is the mode: irresistible new creation, or a birth bound up with a grace that can be refused. Both preach a Spirit-wrought new creation. Arminians typically bind new birth to resistible, enabling grace and to faith as a response; the Reformed typically treat regeneration as an effectual, supernatural raising that produces faith rather than waiting on it.

title: Perseverance
context: Those in Christ are called to abide, and God is faithful—both camps take the warnings and the promises seriously; they part over whether a true believer can finally fall away.
text: Perseverance Those in Christ are called to abide, and God is faithful—both camps take the warnings and the promises seriously; they part over whether a true believer can finally fall away. Perseverance names the question: will those who have believed be kept to the end? Jesus speaks of branches in the vine that are cut off, of sheep who will never perish, of disciples who walk away. Paul endures “for the sake of the elect,” quotes a trustworthy saying about dying and living with Christ, and names Demas who loved this present world. Arminian and Reformed readers both refuse cheap grace. They disagree whether the warnings describe the ruin of the truly regenerate, or the means by which God keeps his own. Arminians typically teach that a truly regenerate believer may finally fall by ceasing to believe; the Reformed typically teach that those whom God has accepted and called will be preserved—warnings included as means—so that apostasy proves a faith that was not saving.

title: Holiness
context: God is the Holy One—utterly pure, set apart, and worthy of fear and love—and both camps call his people to be holy as he is holy.
text: Holiness God is the Holy One—utterly pure, set apart, and worthy of fear and love—and both camps call his people to be holy as he is holy. Holiness names God’s moral purity and his being set apart. Seraphim cry “holy”; the Father is perfect; the man of God is told to pursue righteousness and to keep the commandment unstained. Arminian and Reformed teachers do not disagree that God is holy. They disagree about how that holiness meets a sinful world: whether holy love makes a provision for all, and whether holy justice requires a particular satisfaction for a chosen people. The verses still come first. Both confess the Holy One and the call to be holy. Arminians typically unfold holiness as perfect love that sincerely seeks all; the Reformed typically unfold holiness as infinite purity that includes a justice satisfied in a particular, effectual redemption—without denying the call to holiness of life.

title: Love
context: God is love, and he has loved in the sending of the Son—both camps refuse a loveless God; they part over whether that love, in the design of salvation, is for every person or particularly for the elect.
text: Love God is love, and he has loved in the sending of the Son—both camps refuse a loveless God; they part over whether that love, in the design of salvation, is for every person or particularly for the elect. Love is not a soft extra in God. Jesus names the Father’s love for the world, for the disciples, and for those who will believe through their word. The two great commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets. Paul blesses the God who chose us in love and kneels to pray that believers may know love that surpasses knowledge. The shared confession: God loves. The live fork is the scope of saving love—world as all persons, or world as the elect in the world—and whether love can be refused. Arminians typically read God’s saving love as sincere toward every person and resistible in its grace; the Reformed typically confess an invitation to all and a particular, effectual love that actually saves the elect—without meaning that God is unloving toward the world he has made.

title: Justice
context: God is righteous—wrath against sin is grave, and he will by no means clear the guilty—and both camps confess it; they part over how that justice orders mercy, not over whether judgment is a mood.
text: Justice God is righteous—wrath against sin is grave, and he will by no means clear the guilty—and both camps confess it; they part over how that justice orders mercy, not over whether judgment is a mood. Justice is God’s rectitude. Wrath is revealed from heaven against ungodliness; God shows no partiality; he is both just and the one who justifies whoever has faith in Jesus; Abraham asks whether the Judge of all the earth will do what is right; Belshazzar is weighed and found wanting; the Son of Man separates sheep and goats. This page is about God’s justice, not the atonement, though it points there. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a soft God who never judges. The live fork is how justice and mercy meet—terms fixed for all who believe, or a particular satisfaction for a chosen people. The verses still come first. Both confess that God is righteous and that wrath against sin is serious. Arminians typically unfold justice as the published terms of mercy to all who believe; the Reformed typically unfold justice as a rectitude God would owe to none, often satisfied in a particular redemption—without either camp denying the coming judgment.

title: Mercy
context: Mercy is God’s pity toward the miserable—not a second name for his love—and both camps confess it; they part over Romans 9’s “I will have mercy,” whether it names whom he wills or a sincere general mercy with particular application.
text: Mercy Mercy is God’s pity toward the miserable—not a second name for his love—and both camps confess it; they part over Romans 9’s “I will have mercy,” whether it names whom he wills or a sincere general mercy with particular application. Mercy is pity toward the miserable. Paul says God is rich in mercy; he saved us according to his mercy; Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul obtained mercy; Daniel pleads that they bring their petitions not for their own righteousness but for God’s great mercies. The Beatitudes open with the merciful. Mercy is treated here apart from God’s love. Love is God’s affection and self-giving; mercy is that love meeting misery and guilt. Both camps refuse a God without pity. Romans 9 is the fork: mercy on whom he wills, or mercy offered on published terms to all who will receive it. The verses still come first. Both confess mercy as pity toward the miserable, distinct from his love. Arminians typically read Romans 9 as God’s right to fix terms of mercy for all who believe; the Reformed typically read it as free pity that is not given to all indiscriminately, while still sending the Son that whoever believes should not perish.

title: Faithfulness
context: God keeps covenant—if we are faithless, he remains faithful—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that his word cannot fail, though they may differ over whom the promises finally hold.
text: Faithfulness God keeps covenant—if we are faithless, he remains faithful—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that his word cannot fail, though they may differ over whom the promises finally hold. Faithfulness is God’s covenant-keeping. He remains faithful, since he cannot deny himself; Jewish unbelief does not undo God’s faithfulness; Abraham was fully assured that God could do what he had promised; he is faithful and righteous to forgive; he sets his bow in the cloud; he cuts a covenant with Abram; Daniel pleads the covenant and loving kindness. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a God who forgets his word. The verses still come first. Any fork is usually about the scope of the promise, not about whether God is true. Both confess that God keeps covenant and that unbelief does not make him a liar. Arminians underline that he remains faithful and still makes good the promise to those who believe; the Reformed typically stress that his verity does not depend on us and that the covenant retains its power toward those he has given to the Son.

title: Omnipotence
context: God can do all that is consistent with his nature—both camps confess the Almighty, and neither treats power as a magic that lies, un-Gods himself, or authors sin.
text: Omnipotence God can do all that is consistent with his nature—both camps confess the Almighty, and neither treats power as a magic that lies, un-Gods himself, or authors sin. Omnipotence is not a blank check. Scripture’s first word is that God created; the Lord asks Abraham whether anything is too hard; Jesus says that with God all things are possible; Nebuchadnezzar learns that none can stay the Most High’s hand. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a weak God and a magical God who can contradict himself. The live question is not whether God is able, but how that ability relates to creaturely will and the origin of sin. The verses still come first. Both confess that God can do all that is consistent with his nature. Arminians typically refuse to let that power author sin or make saving grace irresistible; the Reformed typically unfold omnipotence as actual, particular government—including who is effectually drawn—without meaning that God does evil.

title: Omniscience
context: God knows all things—himself, the possible, and the actual—and classical Arminians are not open theists; both camps confess exhaustive knowledge and part over how that knowledge relates to the decree.
text: Omniscience God knows all things—himself, the possible, and the actual—and classical Arminians are not open theists; both camps confess exhaustive knowledge and part over how that knowledge relates to the decree. Omniscience is not a guess that improves with time. Jesus knows what is in man; the Father knows what we need before we ask; the Spirit will declare the things that are to come; Paul bows before knowledge too deep to track. Arminius and Wesley, no less than Calvin and Westminster, refuse a God who learns. The live fork is not whether God is ignorant, but whether his knowledge of future free acts is grounded in an unconditional decree, or whether—sometimes with middle knowledge—he knows what creatures would and will do without that knowledge itself causing the act. The verses still come first. Both confess that God knows all things, including future free acts; classical Arminians are not open theists. Arminians typically deny that knowledge itself causes those acts (sometimes via middle knowledge); the Reformed typically deny that God decreed because he foresaw, locating certainty in a counsel independent of the creature.

title: Omnipresence
context: God is wholly present everywhere—not spread thin, not locked in a shrine—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that the Father, the risen Christ, and the Spirit are with the church.
text: Omnipresence God is wholly present everywhere—not spread thin, not locked in a shrine—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that the Father, the risen Christ, and the Spirit are with the church. Omnipresence is God’s immensity meeting the world he made. Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when worship will not be tied to this mountain or that; he promises to be in the midst of two or three and to be with his disciples to the end of the age. Jacob wakes and says the Lord is in this place. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a local God and a pantheist smear of God into the furniture. The verses still come first. Any fork is pastoral more than confessional: how nearness comforts, convicts, and orders worship—not whether God is here. Both confess that God is wholly present everywhere and is not confined to temples. There is no historic Arminian–Reformed split on the attribute itself; any remaining difference belongs to how that near God applies saving grace, not to whether he is here.

title: Immutability
context: God does not change in being or character—both camps confess it, and both read “relented” texts as a change of dealing, not a mutable essence; prayer is not wasted.
text: Immutability God does not change in being or character—both camps confess it, and both read “relented” texts as a change of dealing, not a mutable essence; prayer is not wasted. Immutability is God’s sameness. He remains faithful; he cannot deny himself; the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable; he is light without darkness. Genesis 6’s “it grieved him” is in the same Bible. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a God who grows, learns, or improves, and both refuse a frozen God who cannot answer prayer. They handle relenting language the same way in substance: anthropomorphism and a change of treatment, not a change of essence. The verses still come first. Both confess that God does not change in being or character, and both read relenting texts as a change of dealing rather than a mutable essence. Prayer is not wasted. Any remaining fork is whether an unchanging counsel includes resistible grace, not whether God is still becoming.

title: Eternity
context: God is without beginning or end—the King of the ages—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that the Word was in the beginning, or that immortality belongs to God.
text: Eternity God is without beginning or end—the King of the ages—and both camps confess it; they do not disagree that the Word was in the beginning, or that immortality belongs to God. Eternity is not merely a long time. Paul blesses the King of the ages, immortal and invisible; he speaks of the blessed and only Sovereign who alone has immortality; John opens with the Word who was in the beginning; Genesis opens with God already there when time starts. Nebuchadnezzar learns that God’s dominion is everlasting. Arminian and Reformed teachers both refuse a God who came to be, and both refuse to treat “eternal” as a mood. The verses still come first. Any fork is almost none on the attribute itself. Both confess that God is without beginning or end and that the Word was in the beginning. There is no historic split on the attribute itself; remaining disagreement belongs to how an eternal purpose relates to election, not to whether God is everlasting.

title: Sovereignty
context: God rules; nothing is finally outside his hand—both camps confess a King, and they part over whether that rule includes an unconditional decree of who will believe.
text: Sovereignty God rules; nothing is finally outside his hand—both camps confess a King, and they part over whether that rule includes an unconditional decree of who will believe. Sovereignty is God’s kingly right and actual rule. Scripture blesses the God who does all things after the counsel of his will, the Father who draws, the Lord of the wedding feast, the blessed and only Sovereign. Arminian and Reformed Christians both reject a God who cannot save and a world of pure chance. They disagree whether sovereignty means that God determines the outcome of every human choice in salvation, or that he governs in ways that leave a grace-enabled refusal possible. Both confess that God rules. Arminians typically describe a sovereignty that eternally purposes to save believers and governs without irresistible determination of the will; the Reformed typically describe a sovereignty that ordains whatsoever comes to pass—including who will be effectually drawn—without making God the author of sin.
